en: Preface to the Re-engraved *Fofa Jintang Bian* (The Golden Bulwark of the Buddha-Dharma).
A member of the bhikṣu-saṃgha addressed the Master Fikong, saying: "Is True Suchness (*tathatā*) fundamentally empty? He replied: "It is so. [The monk asked:
"Can empty space (*ākāśa*) be destroyed? He replied: "No. [The monk continued: "The substance of empty space is greater than heaven and earth; the substance of True Suchness is greater than..."
Space: while heaven and earth may come to an end, space is inexhaustible. Space can be made empty, but True Suchness (tathatā) is truly not something that can be emptied;
it is simply that which cannot be emptied. For this reason, it does not abide in emptiness. It is without marks, without names, without formation, and without destruction.

That a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru is no idle speculation; that a pebble crosses the ocean is no rare occurrence. When the vast primordial chaos (hóngmóng) was divided, heaven and earth were formed.

It is destroyed; it is not a phenomenon of arising and ceasing. Why then would one need to guard it with golden walls and moats? For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is fundamentally empty, and existence arises through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Sensory objects and faculties reflect one another, and habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*) alternate as illusions. Thus beings drift and sink, turning further into afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thereupon, a Great Sage appeared in the West, who out of compassion universally delivers them, taking Prajñā as the vessel and Bodhi as [the destination].
Taking liberation as the fruit, with the diamond-like [wisdom] as the ultimate goal, and with the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma as the means of discipline;
taking the most eminent among ordinary beings and the Hīnayāna as the rungs of the ladder—since the Han dynasty until the present, it has spread throughout China.

Countless spiritual friends have proclaimed the Mahāyāna to bring about awakening, leaving nothing behind. The Great Canon fills the rafters in its magnificence, and the teachings of the Image-Period Dharma pervade the four continents.

It is profound. Encompassing all that is sentient and insentient, as well as the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), it universally proclaims the sound of the Dharma for all to take refuge in, pervading worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
What need is there for defensive walls or moats? Alas! How earnest is this Buddha’s concern for humanity, and how deep is his anxiety for the Way!
Formerly, when the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa, he secretly charged him with the prediction [of the future], regarding [the view of] annihilation as...
Regarding the Precepts: transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, there were even those pursued by glowing iron wheels. Having no choice, the robe was passed on;
yet it could not be stopped, nor could it be entrusted to kings or ministers. Is this not precisely what our Confucian scholars mean when they say, "Without evidence, one cannot be believed;
if not believed, the people will not follow"? This is surely the concern at hand. Indeed, the Buddha came from Central India, traversing over ten thousand *li* across the shifting sands.
Having entered Zhendan (China), he sought to encompass the void-like teachings to instruct the people. When people first heard them, they were startled and confused;

yet, wishing for these teachings to circulate widely and reach all, he considered how to provide them with golden walls and moats as protection. In antiquity, defense was found in external barriers; today, defense lies in guarding against false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
If one strays onto external paths and rivals the Buddha, the Dharma will be alienated; if false views are driven out and rival the Buddha...
When the Dharma becomes muddled, it likewise falls away. Degraded and led astray by delusions, those at the top forget their roots;

the superior fall into seeking noble status and lofty fame, while the inferior rely on donors to reap a tenfold return for every one invested. Monastic robes block the roads, yet the *utpala* flower of the Dharma is not seen in the world even once in an age.
It is no wonder that doubts and slanders arise in profusion. As the Dharma drifts further away, the defenses become ever more stringent—like a golden fortress.
This work was composed for that purpose. Its records examine from antiquity down to the Hu and Yuan dynasties;

it has gathered and edited all matters and words of emperors, kings, officials, renowned scholars, and eminent sages over several thousand years that contribute to the teachings of the Maitreya (Cishi).
These have been compiled into volumes. Here, gold is spread to form a city, and moats exist without boiling water; this is where one is bathed by the *amṛta* (nectar) of the ocean of awakening.
It is a transmission. This Śrīśaila City, Gṛdhrakūṭa, is a cool and pure land where dragon-elephants dwell and which serves as the track for the Three Vehicles.
It demonstrates the expedient gate for the sons of elders. Will it not provide some small benefit to the human heart and worldly instruction?
The Venerable Tiantai Xing re-edited and carved this to broaden its dissemination. I commend this.

Preface. This work first reveals the essence of space-like *tathatā* (suchness) to expand its scope, so that people may know all things are already perfected, without remainder or deficiency, and are ultimately firm and solid without requiring the protection of moats or ramparts.
Written by the Buddhist layman Feikong (Non-Empty), Yu Ruwe of Huating, in the early summer of the Gengzi year of the Wanli era.

Preface to the *Compilation of the Golden Fortifications of the Buddha-Dharma*. Daizong Taigong, the abbot of Mount Dongshan in former Yue, compiled the *Compilation of the Golden Fortifications of the Buddha-Dharma* in ten fascicles.
Chan Master Yunzhong Xuan brought it to Bo heng and requested a preface. The preface states: "The Buddha-Dharma has spread throughout China..."
It has been one thousand three hundred and twenty-six years since then. Although it was suppressed and refuted, it has flourished as vigorously as ever.
Initially, Bo-heng did not know why this was so; he privately supposed it was merely because its doctrines were sufficient to move people.
Now, upon examining this compilation, I realize that it is truly due to the successive generations of enlightened and wise sovereigns and—

Now, among the dukes, marquises, high ministers, grandees, and scholars who are virtuous, there are none who do not revere and look toward him, shielding and supporting him as his external protectors.
Though they revere and look toward him with such sincerity, those who would intentionally disparage him cannot overcome the volume of their voices.
There was a tree that had grown so large it seemed to embrace a person; yet when people tried to push it aside, no one could overcome its strength.
Was it merely that they could not overcome it? Because of its towering height, they came to know all the more that it could not be destroyed;
because of its embracing of the tree, they came to know all the more that it could not be pushed aside. Suddenly awakening to this, he said: "Using such power to protect that Dharma—how similar!"
How could one contend with such a person? Few indeed would return without being broken.
Thus, is it not the case that the reason the Buddha-dharma flourishes ever more as time passes is due to the protection of those outside the tradition?

Yet, even among those who have personally received the entrustment, there are those who cannot deeply understand or firmly believe in the Way; they disparage it and depart from ethical principles, acting contrary to Heaven’s mandate.
How could one below not be startled? How could one who overturns the world by speaking of calamity and fortune not be deluded?
Yet, how much more so can one put forth their person to oppose the world and distinguish between them, saying:

"Your destruction, rejection, and overturning are based on outward traces (*traces*), whereas my orientation, planting, and establishing are based on the Way (*Dharma*); the Way is its essence, while traces are its externals."
If that which is coarse has fissures through which it may be struck, does not that which is refined likewise have intervals through which it may be exploited?
Then, although the Buddha’s Dharma is lofty, vast, subtle, and wondrous, how could it ensure that it would not be shattered or fall into decline?
How, then, could its followers remain so relaxed and complacent? Therefore, one must not forget the intent of the entrustment and be diligent in...
External protection is more vital than a state possessing golden walls and moats. Alas!
When the former kings established their cities and moats, they did not rely on them as the sole means of survival, yet even those could not be dispensed with for a single day;

how much more so this external protection upon which the Buddha-Dharma relies for its very existence—could it ever be dispensed with for a single day? This compilation by Dazong [is intended for that purpose].
This composition may be said to demonstrate clear insight. How diligent is the application of his mind!
Nevertheless, while fortified cities are the instruments for establishing a state, whether the power and security of that state truly endure depends entirely upon the person.

If there is one who possesses the spirit to repel aggression, then even without impregnable walls or boiling moats, who would dare to insult them? But if there is no such person with the spirit to repel aggression...
Even if a person possesses walls of gold and moats of boiling water, others will still treat them with contempt; how much more so would this apply to the Buddha-dharma?
Thus, those who are its followers must be courageous and diligent, reaching the Way and clarifying its essential principles throughout the world.
If all the people in the world were unable to disparage it and unable to reject it, how could one not exert oneself?
Otherwise, though external protection may be as secure as a fortress of gold and boiling water, what can it avail against those who enter my chamber and take up my own halberd to strike me down?
I, Bo-heng, not daring to measure my own worth, venture to compose this preface to contribute my humble efforts. The twenty-sixth year of Hongwu.
Preface by the Layman Wuwen, Su Bo heng of Meishan, on the wuchen day of the first month of spring in the year of Gui-chou.
Furthermore, for what purpose was this compilation created? Master Daisong Daizong of Dongshan feared that the fortress of the Great Dharma would fall into ruin...
This work was composed as a defense. It consists of ten fascicles, beginning from the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty and extending to the reign of Emperor Shun of the Yuan dynasty.
From among all those individuals, I have selected those whose words were sufficient to protect the Teaching and appended them beneath their respective names, setting them forth for public view.

I have further titled this compilation *The Golden Bulwark and Moat of the Buddha-Dharma*. Truly, it may be called a citadel for the followers of Śākyamuni in this semblance age, serving as a bulwark for a thousand years.
It is the bulwark of the Dharma-gate. Formerly, the two masters Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu once composed essays to disparage Buddhism;
their arguments extended to tens of millions of words. Yet why was it that the more verbose their discourse became, the more flourishing the Buddha-dharma grew?
This is because the Way of our Buddha is vast and all-encompassing, supreme and without rival; one looks up to it and finds it unattainable, and one praises it—

Yet it is impossible to name [a single person] who could do so; emperors and kings have revered it, great men have honored it, and it has been transmitted for ten thousand generations without being altered.
How can it be that, because of the private preferences of a single individual, one might preserve it out of affection or discard it out of aversion? Liu Zhi said:
"Tui-zhi’s fondness for Confucianism was not yet able to surpass that of Yangzi, let alone the fondness for Confucianism of Ou-zi, which was likewise unable to surpass his."
Master Han, how can these two gentlemen, with their bitter indignation and trivial words, seek to attack the teachings of the Sage?

Why do they inflict such suffering upon themselves? I have previously discussed Li Chunfu, saying that it is Buddhists who have never harmed Confucians, whereas Confucians have often harmed Buddhists; this was an exaggeration on his part. For Buddhism is certainly...
It has never harmed the Confucians; how then could the Confucians have ever harmed the Buddhists?
It was merely because figures such as Liu, Zhang, Zhu, and Lü plundered Buddhist ideas to annotate their own texts in order to deceive the people of their time that such claims were made.
Little did they realize that the teaching of our Buddha is like the treasury of a great house, overflowing with precious jewels and treasures; even if one were to bore a hole through it—
What harm does the act of climbing through a wall or breaking through a window do to my wealth?

The Great Master Mingjiao of the Song dynasty also once composed three volumes of a work titled *Fujiao* (Aiding the Teachings), which reconciled the minor differences between Confucianism and Daoism to return to the great harmony of the Buddhist tradition;
later scholars relied upon it as a model. As for this compilation from Dongshan, although its writing does not surpass his own, that which it...
That the editor has compiled this work is also in accordance with the lingering intent of the Buddhist teachings.

Furthermore, as I observe the arguments of the various gentlemen within this compilation regarding their indignation toward the world and their loathing of depravity, their discourse may indeed be called impartial.

However, as it is said in the *Lotus Sūtra* that Devadatta was my "good spiritual friend," then whether he is reviled or praised, he remains like a golden fortress; what loss or gain could there be therein?
Within my teaching. Thus, those who read this compilation should seek its meaning beyond the literal words.

Written on an auspicious day in the seventh month of autumn in the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era, the year of Xinwei, by the monk Shouren, Abbot of Tianxi Jingsi Temple and Left Director of the Bureau of Buddhist Records (Senglusi Zuojiangjing).
Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Daizong Taigong of Yue. In his youth, he studied the teachings of Shu and Si at the local schools;
as he grew older, he pursued the studies of the Śākya clan. He once served as a disciple of Chan Master Mengtang E at Guoqing Temple in Tai, and became his...

He served as the Director of the Imperial Chancery. His learning was vast and his insight penetrating; his spirit was full while his conduct remained restrained. When he gave expression to his thoughts in writing, it was both majestic and profound, elegant and refined.

He devoted himself solely to propagating the fundamental tenets and establishing the teachings as his primary aim, rather than seeking novelty through the display of erudition or the pursuit of ornate style.
He once left secular life to preach the Dharma at Dongshan Chansi Temple in the prefecture, and those who followed him as disciples increased ever more greatly. Hong...

In the nineteenth year of the Wǔ period, he came to the capital. On occasion, he brought forth his work, the *Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān* (The Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Fortress), and showed it to me, requesting that I compose a preface for it.
I therefore said to Dàizōng: "Your composition of this book is surely intended to clarify the Way (*dào*).
Now, the Way precedes heaven and earth yet does not act as their beginning; it follows heaven and earth yet does not act as their end. To exhaust its..."
Subtle, it is something that even sages and worthies cannot create; profound to its utmost depths, it is something that even ghosts and spirits cannot fathom.
It cannot be manifested through sound or smell, nor can it be distinguished through speech or debate.

If this is so, then for you to practice this—by what means will you do so? Daizong replied: "To speak of the ultimate reach of the Way, there are indeed points as you have described. Yet, the Way has no difference."
There is sameness, yet there cannot but be difference within that sameness. The Way is devoid of love and hatred, yet it cannot but have love and hatred;
thus, there is sameness and difference. One cannot avoid having discourses of suppression and exaltation. There is love and hatred, yet one cannot avoid having the discernment of right and wrong.
Sameness and difference, love and hatred, discourses of suppression and exaltation, and the discernment of right and wrong—all these are indeed but the branches.
Furthermore, how could this fundamentally contradict the Way? By examining its function, one clarifies its essence; by following its current, one reaches its source.
Thus, when composing this book, how could I have desisted? Have you ever known those who are lost and have strayed from the Way?
Without someone to precede them and guide them, one cannot expect to reach that which has not yet been attained.

"Is it not difficult? My undertaking this was intended to examine and discern the successes and failures of the past and present, so as to follow the right path and avoid the wrong. Might this not serve as a precursor for reaching what has not yet been reached?
I replied: "Mount Tai, the Lord of Mountains, truly embodies the mind with which our Buddha, the Sage, established his teachings. My—

It has never been said that [this work] had previously reached such a point. I have examined this compilation in its entirety. It covers the journey from the Western *śītavana* (India) to the Eastern *Zhèndàn* (China), spanning from the Zhou and Qin dynasties down to the Song and Yuan.

Within these periods, there were sagacious sovereigns, worthy ministers, renowned scholars, and eminent public figures who were able to promote and elevate the Buddha-dharma to establish good governance;
some were able to verify divine efficacy to repel external aggression; and others... [or opened...]
Whether occurring before or following [the main text], these so-called arguments of suppression and exaltation, and the distinctions between right and wrong— things that cannot be dispensed with—
all have been compiled and synthesized within this collection. This is intended to enable those who read it to gain insight herefrom,
turning back from the minor deviations of their inclinations to unify them upon the straight path, and to still the clamor of other disputations.
In the end, this ultimate principle is such that it does not require debate to be clarified, nor does it require instruction to be understood.
Is it not for this reason that its name is "Golden and Tang Walls" (a metaphor for an impregnable fortress)? Alas! The devotion of Daisō was truly diligent;
he may indeed be called one who has performed meritorious service for our Buddha’s teaching. It was the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era.
Preface by the Śramaṇa Qingjun, Abbot of Linggu Chan Monastery and Left Jueyi of the Senglu Si, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the Xinwei year.
Title: *Fofa jintang bian* (The Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark).
From the time the True Dharma was entrusted to kings and ministers until the present, more than two thousand years have passed.

Throughout these generations, there have always been emperors, kings, dukes, and high officials who served as external protectors of the Dharma; this can be seen at a glance by examining this compilation on the "Golden Fortifications and Moats" of the Buddha-dharma.
Since those who protect the Dharma are as secure as a city with its golden walls and moat, preventing external aggression from entering, they enable the propagation of the Dharma.
Such individuals must also exert themselves with vigor to bring about a revival, so as to fulfill their resolve to protect the Dharma.
If this is done, how could the teachings not flourish? Nevertheless, the construction of golden walls and moats is intended to prepare against external invaders;

while such external enemies can still be repelled when they strike from without, those who assume the outward form and robes of a bhikṣu while internally destroying the teachings are domestic traitors.
When internal enemies arise within one's own home, even if one possesses golden walls and moats as external fortifications, there will be nothing that can be done about it.

How much more so for those in the age of the Final Dharma (mofa), who for the most part are negligent and remain complacent without feeling shame; consequently, the teachings gradually decline and fade away.
Thus, we know that Master Tai’s writing was not intended to boast to the world, but was likely meant to serve as a warning to us, his fellow disciples. Alas!

"May those who are my disciples not fail to be cautious and reflective? Thus it was noted by the Bhikṣu Chonglek of Chansi Temple, Right Śāsanavardhana of the Sengluosi, during the summer of the Xinhui year of the Hongwu era.
