*Fofa Jintang Bian*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai.
It is said that regarding the virtuous words and noble deeds of the eminent masters who have propagated the Teaching since ancient times, there already exist established records.
These have been fully recorded in such works as the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), the *History of the Sangha* (*Sengshi zhuan*), and the various *Records of the Lamp* (*Denglu*).

Yet, regarding the deeds and words of the kings and ministers who protected the teachings throughout the successive dynasties, although they are scattered throughout other books, there exists no complete compilation for comprehensive study;
this has not failed to cause me profound sighs of lamentation. How much more so, then, in the case of our Great Awakened One?
At the time of the Sage’s passing, were there not words regarding the entrustment of the Buddha-dharma to kings and ministers?

Since then, those who have received this charge to provide external protection have appeared from generation to generation; it is for this reason that the *Bulgyo Geumtang Pyeon* (The Golden Wall of the Buddha-dharma) was composed.
Furthermore, I have heard that on the day of the Sage’s birth, during the second year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty...
In the sixteenth year, Jia-yin. Therefore, the chronology of this compilation begins with King Zhao and ends with Emperor Yuan Shun.

All those who have established their names in the "Green Annals" (Qing Shi) and engaged in religious practice such that they are worthy of being held as pillars of the Dharma-gate are recorded in this work.
It is not merely for the sake of providing a defensive bulwark. Alas! I—

How could I have any desire to do such a thing? I merely wish that those who examine this compilation in the future may understand why the former sages and worthies so highly revered [the Buddha], and that they may thereby give rise to a heart of reverence and faith, avoiding the fault of disparagement.
It is simply intended as one aid in transforming people toward goodness.
King Wu of Zhou. Surname Ji; name Fa. Son of King Wen. Capital was Hao. After King Ping moved the capital eastward to Luo.
Beginning from the Jiwu year of King Wu’s reign and ending with the Yisi year of King Nan’s reign. Thirty-seven sovereigns for a total of eight hundred and sixty-seven years.
King Zhao’s posthumous name was Xia. He was the son of King Kang. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-sixth year, Jia-yin (some say the ninth year, Jia-yin;
others say the twenty-fourth year, Jia-yin—neither is correct), the earth and the palaces shook, ponds and wells overflowed, and the sun appeared with a double halo of five colors.
Auspicious light entered and permeated the Taiwei palace, illuminating the Western Quarter everywhere. The King questioned his ministers, but none could discern the omen.

The Grand Astrologer Suyou divined it using the *Yi* hexagrams and obtained Qian (the Creative) at the fifth line of the fifth place. Suyou said, "This is the sign of the birth of a Sage from the West."

"A thousand years hence, the teachings shall come here. The King commanded that this be engraved upon stone and placed before the Celestial Shrine in the southern suburb" (from the *Zhou Shu Yiji* and the *Baima Si Ji*).
King Mu’s posthumous name was Man. He was the son of King Zhao. In the twenty-third year of his reign, radiant light frequently appeared, shining upon the royal capital.

Fearing that an invasion by barbarian tribes was imminent, he dispatched the Chancellor, Marquis Lü, to lead an army to defend it. It was actually a Western Sage preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.

The radiance of his influence reached far and wide. On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-third year, Renshen (some say the fifty-second year, Renshen, which is incorrect), the earth shook violently;
mad winds broke the trees; rivers and streams surged with billows; ponds and wells boiled over; birds and beasts wailed in grief;
and at noon, twelve white rainbows appeared, piercing through from south to north. The King feared for the state and the altars of soil and grain, and summoned the Grand Astrologer.
Shi Huduo performed a divination for him and said, "It is auspicious; may Your Majesty have no anxiety.
This is the extraordinary manifestation of the parinirvāṇa of a sage from the West" (from the *Zhou shu yiji*, "Record of the Baima Temple").
Confucius:
His taboo name was Qiu; his courtesy name was Zhongni. He was the great-grandson of Kong Fu Jia and the son of Shu Liang He.
He was born in the year Gengxu, the twenty-first year of King Ling of Zhou. When the Grand Chancellor of Shang met Confucius, he said:
"Are you, Master Qiu, a sage? Confucius said, "As for being a sage, how would I dare to claim that? However, I am one who has studied extensively and possesses much knowledge.
The Grand Chancellor asked, "Were the Three Kings sages? Confucius said, "The Three Kings were skilled at employing the wise and the brave;
as for being sages, I do not know. The Grand Chancellor asked, "Were the Five Emperors sages? Confucius said, "The Five Emperors were skilled at employing benevolence."

As for "sageliness," even I, Qiu, do not know it. The Grand Chancellor said, "Were the Three Sovereigns sages? Confucius replied, "The Three Sovereigns were those who excelled at utilizing the conditions of their times;
as for sageliness, I, Qiu, do not know it. The Grand Chancellor was greatly startled and asked, "Then, apart from these, who might be considered a sage?
Confucius, with a change in his expression after a brief pause, said, "I have heard that there is a sage in the West who does not govern."

Yet he was not disordered. He inspired confidence without speaking; he acted spontaneously without transforming others. Vast and expansive, the people were unable to give him a name (from the "Zhongni" chapter of the *Liezi*).
Liezi. His name was Yukou. He was a native of Zheng. During the reign of King Zhending, he lived in seclusion at the Garden of Zheng for forty years. No one recognized him;
even the state lords, high ministers, and great officers regarded him as no different from the common masses. He once composed eight chapters of a book. Therein...

It is said: During the time of King Mu of Zhou, a transformed man (*huàrén*) came from a land at the western extremity (the *Tǒngjì* states that this "transformed man" was Mañjuśrī and Maudgalyāyana).

He entered fire and water; he pierced metal and stone; he reversed mountains and rivers and shifted cities and towns. He traveled through the void without falling and encountered solid objects without obstruction.
His thousand transformations and ten-thousand metamorphoses were inexhaustible. King Mu revered him as a deity and served him as a sovereign. He vacated his own palace quarters to [accommodate him].
He resided there. A transformed man (huàrén) considered the King’s palace and halls to be lowly and dilapidated, unfit for habitation.
King Mu then had them rebuilt, leaving the five treasuries (wǔfǔ) as empty spaces, and the terrace was finally completed; it rose a thousand *zhèn* high, overlooking the summit of Zhōngnán.
It was called the Terrace of the Central Heaven (*Liezi*, "The Chapter on King Mu").
Qin Shi Huang, surnamed Ying and named Zheng, lived during the period when the seven states vied for supremacy and the legitimate succession of the throne had not continued for thirty-four years.
The First Emperor extinguished the six states. In the twenty-sixth year, the Gengchen year, he first assumed the title of Emperor. He made Xianyang his capital.
From the Gengchen year of the First Emperor until the Jiawu year of the Second Emperor, there were two sovereigns for a total of fifteen years.

The First Emperor was the son of King Zhuangxiang. In the thirtieth year, the Jia-shen year, eighteen Śramaṇas from the Western Regions, including Śrīlaṅka (Shìlìfáng), arrived at Xiányáng bringing Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras.
The officials reported this to the Emperor, who, deeming them people of a foreign custom, imprisoned them. Śrīlaṅka—
As Fang and others recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, a brilliant light shone forth and auspicious vapors swirled, filling the prison.
In an instant, a golden deity sixteen feet tall appeared, wielding a mace and manifesting his majesty to shatter the prison and release them.
The Emperor was struck with alarm and remorse; he immediately bestowed lavish gifts upon them before they departed (from the *Baima Si Ji*).
The Western Han Dynasty: Surname Liu, given name Bang, courtesy name Ji. A native of Zhongyang Village in Feng County, Pei. Capital: Chang’an.
From the year Gaozu’s Yiwu (195 BCE) until the year Ruzi Ying’s Dingmao (8 BCE), there were fourteen sovereigns for a total of two hundred and fourteen years.

Emperor Wu—whose taboo name was Che—was the middle son of Emperor Jing. He first established the reign title Jianyuan. In the third year of the Yuanshou era, he opened Kunming Pond and obtained black ash.
The Emperor questioned Dongfang Shuo about it, and Shuo said, "You may ask a foreign monk from the Western Regions."
During the reign of Emperor Ming, the Indian monk Kāśyapa Mātanga arrived. Someone questioned him about this [ash], and Mātanga replied, "This is the ash of the kalpa.
(From the *Hanshu* and the *Beishan lu*).
Emperor Ai’s posthumous name was Xin. He was the son of Prince Gong of Dingtao and the grandson of Emperor Xuan.

In the first year of the Yuanshou era, Jingxian was sent to the kingdom of Da Yuezhi, where he received the oral transmission of the Buddhist scriptures from its king and returned with them. At that time, there were already some who observed the fasts and precepts.
(History of the Wei Dynasty, "Biographies of Buddhists and Daoists"):
Huo Qubing was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guanjun and appointed General of the Flying Cavalry (Biaojijiangjun). In the second year of the Yuanshou era, he led ten thousand cavalry out from Longxi.
He marched westward to strike the Xiongnu, passing Mount Juyan and seizing the golden man used by King Xiutu for the sacrifice to Heaven (as recorded in his biography).

Qibing captured this golden man, which was over ten feet tall; Emperor Wu regarded it as a great deity and enshrined it in the Ganshan Palace, where he burned incense and paid it reverence (Wei Shu, "Buddha and Laozi Monograph").
Liu Xiang, courtesy name Zijiang, also known as Gengsheng, served as Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Guanglu Daifu*) during the reign of Emperor Cheng.

In the second year of the Hongjia era, while cataloging books at the Tianlu Pavilion, he frequently encountered Buddhist scriptures. Liu Xiang composed the *Lie xian zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Transcendents), stating: "I have examined and inspected..."

I searched extensively through the archives and compiled the *Illustrations of Transcendents* (*Lie xian tu*), covering those who attained the Way of the Immortals from the time of the Yellow Emperor down to the present day;
one hundred and forty-nine individuals were identified. Among them, seventy-four are mentioned in Buddhist scriptures (as recorded in Fei Changfang’s *Sanbao ji* and Yi Chu’s *Liu tie*).
The Eastern Han dynasty:
the personal name of Gaozu (Gwangwu) was Xiù, his courtesy name was Wénshū; the capital was Luoyang.
Beginning from the year Yiyou of Gaozu’s reign and ending with Jihai of Emperor Xiàn, there were twelve sovereigns over a period of one hundred and ninety-five years.

Emperor Ming’s posthumous name was Zhuang. He was the fourth son of Emperor Guangwu. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year of Yongping (the Gengshen year), while the Emperor was resting in the Southern Palace, he dreamed of a golden man sixteen feet tall, with the light of the sun encircling his neck and the *svastika* (*wanzi*) inscribed upon his chest, flying through the palace courtyard.

He moved unimpeded through the past and the future. In the morning, he questioned his ministers. Then the Grand Astrologer Fu Yi came forward and said, "I have heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions whose name is Buddha.

That which Your Majesty dreamed must surely be him. Wang Zun, the Court Doctor for the National University, replied, "According to my examination of the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Records of Marvels from the Book of Zhou), on the eighth day of the fourth month of the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao of Zhou, the Jia-yin year..."
One day, [the Emperor] heard that a sage had been born in the West, who was none other than the one in His Majesty’s recent dream.
The Emperor took this to be true and immediately dispatched General of the Far Reaches Cai Yin, Colonel Qin Jing, Doctor Wang Zun, and eighteen others.

He was dispatched as an envoy to the Western Regions to seek the Buddha-dharma. In the sixth year, the *guihai* year, Cai Yin encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna in the kingdom of Yuezhi, a neighbor to India.
They obtained a standing image of the Buddha and sixty thousand words of Sanskrit scriptures, which they transported back to the east on white horses.
In the eighth year, the *yichu* year, Cai Yin and his party arrived at Luoyang; Kāśyapa Mātanga entered [the capital].

He presented the scriptures and images, which greatly pleased the Emperor. Kāśyapa Mātanga was accommodated at the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù sì). Dharmaratna also arrived later, traveling by way of circuitous routes.
In the tenth year, the *dingmǎo* year, an imperial edict was issued to establish Baima Monastery (White Horse Monastery) to the west of the city of Luoyang for their residence.

Because the scriptures had been carried there on white horses, it was consequently named Baima Monastery (this was the beginning of Buddhist monasteries in China). In this same year, An Shigao and Kāśyapa Mātanga translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*. 10.
In the first year of the Wuchen (戊辰) cycle, the Emperor visited Baima Temple. Mokṣala and Dharmaratna approached him and asked, "What building is that to the east of the temple?
The Emperor replied, "Formerly there was a mound here; though it was leveled, it rose up again. At night there was an extraordinary light, so the common people called it the 'Sacred Tomb'.
Mokṣala said, "In the past, King Aśoka enshrined Buddha relics throughout the world, totaling eighty-four thousand locations. Within the borders of Zhendan (China), there are nineteen such sites."
This was one such instance. The Emperor went there with him to pay his respects. Suddenly, a circular halo appeared above the stupa, and within the light were three Buddhas.
The Emperor was greatly delighted and said, "Had I not met these two Great Beings, how could I have known of the lingering blessings of the Great Sage?
He issued an edict to build a stupa over it, two hundred feet high. The following year, the light appeared again, and a golden hand emerged from the top of the stupa. The Emperor—

I was fortunate to behold him, his radiance following my every step. In the twelfth year, an imperial decree was issued to enshrine a statue of Śākyamuni Buddha at both Hyeongjeol-ryeong and Cheongyang-tae for the purpose of making offerings.

On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year, during the formal New Year’s audience, more than seven hundred Daoist practitioners from the Five Peaks and various mountains, including Chu San-sin, submitted a memorial asserting that the Buddhist Dharma is false and deceptive.
Teng and Lan then declared, "The Buddha-dharma cannot be destroyed by water or fire; we pray you, let this be verified.

The Emperor then issued an edict to Song Xiang, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to assemble a great multitude at Baima Monastery on the fifteenth day of the first month. An altar was constructed and the scriptures were set ablaze.

The Daoist masters brought forth all their extraordinary scriptures and secret manuals, which they cast into the flames alongside the scriptures and images held by the śramaṇas. Both the Daoist texts and the Buddhist relics were completely consumed by the fire.
Only the Buddha’s scriptures and images remained solemn and majestic; the faithful were all filled with shame and reverent submission.
The Emperor, from this point forward, redoubled his veneration and honor. From this time on, the Buddha-dharma flourished (from the *Han Fǎběn nèi zhuàn*).

Initially, when the Emperor heard that there was a deity in the Western Regions named Buddha, he dispatched envoys to India to seek its Way. They obtained its scriptures, as well as śramaṇas who returned with them. These scriptures...
Generally, it takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its fundamental principle and prizes compassion and non-killing.
It holds that when a person dies, their spirit does not perish but instead assumes another form; thus, the good and evil deeds performed during life all entail retribution.
Therefore, what is prized is the cultivation of the spirit until one attains Buddhahood. Those who refine this path are called *śramaṇas*. Thus, it was first transmitted to China.
As for the arts, they depict their images; among kings, dukes, and nobles, it was only King Ying of Chu who first took a liking to them (*Hanshu*).
When Teng died, Lan himself translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
Emperor Huan’s posthumous name was Zhi. He was the great-grandson of Emperor Zhang.

In the second year of the Yongxing era, the Emperor cast a golden stupa and an image of Laozi within the palace, covering them with a canopy of a hundred jewels, and personally performed sacrifices to them. Consequently, the common people were transformed by his influence and followed his example.
The Buddha’s teachings flourished even more (according to the *Hanshu* and the *Sanbao ji*, this was the beginning of the practice of casting images of gold and silver).

King Ying of Chu—whose personal name was Ying, the son of Emperor Guangwu and younger brother of Emperor Ming—was the very first to venerate the Buddha; he delighted in performing the fasts and precepts of the *futu*. Forever...

In the ninth year of the Ping era, he once presented yellow silk and white fine cloth to the Chancellor, saying: "I am entrusted with the status of a regional vassal, yet my transgressions have accumulated.
I offer this silk and cloth to atone for my sins. The Chancellor reported this to the Emperor, who issued a decree in reply:

"The Prince of Chu recites the subtle words of Huang-Lao and honors the benevolent temples of the Buddha. What cause for suspicion or doubt is there? Return it to him, so that it may assist [his spiritual cultivation]."
It was a grand feast for lay devotees (*upāsaka*) and śramaṇas. Consequently, kings, dukes, and nobles vied with one another to emulate it (as recorded in the *Hanshu*).
Regarding Mouzi:
he was a descendant of [Mencius] Rong and a Confucian scholar from Cangwu. In the second year of the Xingping era of Emperor Xian, due to the chaos of the world, he did not seek official service.

His official ambitions waned, and his resolve for the Buddhist path became keen. He then composed the *Lihuolun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) in thirty-seven chapters. In the text, there is a question that asks: "Why is he correctly called 'Buddha'?
What does 'Buddha' mean? Mouzi replied: "Buddha means 'Awakened. He is like the Spirits of the Three Augusts and the Sages of the Five Emperors.
The Buddha is the primal ancestor of the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*), the progenitor of the divine and the numinous. This is what the word 'Buddha' signifies."
The Awakened One undergoes transformations in a state of mystical rapture; he divides his body and disperses his form, appearing or disappearing at will.
He can become minute or vast, circular or square; he can appear old or young, hidden or manifest. Treading upon fire, he is not burned; stepping upon blades, he is not wounded.

Dwelling in filth, he remains unstained; encountering calamity, he suffers no misfortune. He reaches his destination without traveling; he shines forth without acting. Therefore, he is called a Buddha. It is asked: [Why is this so?]
Now, the ultimate reality is not adorned with flowers; the ultimate words are not embellished. Pearls and jade are rare and thus precious; tiles and rubble are abundant and thus cheap.
When the Sages composed the foundations of the Seven Classics, they did not exceed thirty thousand words, yet all matters were contained therein.

Today, Buddhist scriptures are counted in tens of thousands of fascicles and their words in hundreds of millions; these are beyond the capacity of a single person to master. I consider them to be cumbersome and...
Mouzi said: "The reason the rivers and seas differ from puddles in the street is their depth and breadth.
The reason the Five Peaks are distinguished from mere mounds is their height and grandeur. If their heights did not surpass those of hills and hillocks, lame sheep could scale their summits;
if their depths did not surpass those of trickling streams, young children could bathe in their abysses. The Qilin does not dwell in walled gardens."
Among these, a fish that swallows boats does not swim in a stream only several *ren* deep. Why? Because the small cannot contain the great.
The Buddhist scriptures speak of events from billions of years past and yet describe the essentials for ten thousand generations to come.

Before the Great Primal (*dàsù*) had arisen and before the Grand Beginning (*tàishǐ*) had been born, their subtlety could not be grasped and their fineness could not be entered. Yet the Buddha completely encompasses and weaves together all that lies beyond such vastness.
He analyzed its profound and subtle inner workings, leaving nothing unrecorded; thus his scriptures number in the tens of thousands and his words count by the hundreds of millions.

The more there is, the more complete it becomes; the more numerous the parts, the more abundant it grows. How could there be anything omitted? Question: The Way of the Buddha is most supreme and most great.
Why did Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius not cultivate it? Their words are not to be found within the Seven Classics.
"Since you already take pleasure in the Odes and Documents and find delight in the Rites and Music, why do you further favor the Buddhist Way?
I privately believe this is not something you should adopt. Mouzi replied: "Books are not necessarily the words of Confucius, nor are medicines necessarily the prescriptions of Bian Que.
That which accords with righteousness is followed; that which heals illness is excellent. A gentleman draws extensively from all that is good to support his person. As Zigong said: 'The Master...'"
How could there be a fixed teacher? Yao served Yin Shou; Shun served Wu Cheng; Dan studied under Lü Wang;

and Qiu studied under Lao Dan—yet these are not all recorded together in the Seven Classics. How much more so for the Buddha, whose physical marks and signs, transformations, and spiritual powers are boundless?
How could one abandon them and fail to study them? If there are deficiencies in the matters and meanings of the Five Classics that the Buddha did not record, what is there to be surprised about?
A questioner asked: "The Buddha possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; how is he so vastly different from ordinary men?
This is likely the talk of those with wealthy ears, not a statement of reality. Mouzi replied: "One who has seen little knows much [of their own ignorance]."

It is strange! To see a camel and call it a horse with a swollen back; Yao had eyebrows of eight colors, Shun had double pupils, Gaoyao had a bird-like beak, King Wen had four nipples, Yu had three openings in his ears, the Duke of Zhou had a hunched back, Fuxi had a dragon’s nose, and Confucius had a receding forehead.
Laozi had a sun-like mark on his forehead and deep-set eyes; his nose had two pillars, his hands held ten lines, and his feet stepped upon the "two fives.
Is this not different from other men? Why, then, should one doubt the marks and signs of the Buddha? A question was asked:

"You use the elegant language of the classics and histories, along with flowery rhetoric, to praise the Buddha’s conduct and extol his virtue. That which is lofty surpasses the blue clouds, and that which is broad exceeds the earth."

Qi: "Is it not that you have exceeded your original intent and overstepped the mark? Mouzi said: "Alas! My praise is like adding a speck of dust to Mount Song or Mount Dai, or gathering morning dew and casting it into the vast ocean.
Your slander, however, is like grasping a ladle or cup wishing to diminish the rivers and seas, or taking up a plow and intending to erode Mount Kunlun;
it is like holding up a single fist to obscure the light of the sun, or lifting a clod of earth [to block it]."
"To block the breach of a river, my praise cannot cause Fo-cao to rise; your slander cannot cause him to fall" (from the *Beihongming ji*).

During the Three Kingdoms period, the capital of Wei was Ye; it was later moved to Luoyang. The family name was Cao; his personal name was Pi. He was the son of Cao Cao and a native of Qiao in Pei State. He was posthumously titled Emperor Wen.
Gengzi. From the end of Emperor Yuan’s reign until Jia-shen, there were five sovereigns for a total of forty-five years.
Cao Zhi (styled Zijian) was the younger brother of Emperor Wen and the fourth son of Emperor Wu; he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chen-si. He was profoundly skilled in calligraphy and the arts.
Handan Chun hailed him as a "Heavenly Man. Whenever he read Buddhist scriptures, he would linger over them with deep admiration and praise, regarding them as the ultimate pinnacle of the Supreme Way.

Once, while traveling at Mount Yushan, he heard the resonance of Brahma-heaven sounds in the air—clear, lofty, and plaintive. He subsequently imitated those sounds and transcribed them as *fanbei* (Brahma-chants).
The *Yushan Fan* (Yushan Brahma-chants) used in current liturgical services are the surviving remnants of his compositions. He once also authored...
*Discourse on Distinguishing the Way*. It states that the way of the immortals is false and illusory (*Hongming ji*).
Zhu Shixing was a native of Yingchuan. In the second year of the Ganlu era, he abandoned secular life to become a monk. He once lectured on the *Daode jing* in Luoyang.
There were passages in the sutras whose meaning was not fully understood. Consequently, he traveled to the Kingdom of Khotan and obtained a Sanskrit manuscript.

He intended to dispatch his disciple Farao to return it to Luoyang. However, the Hinayana community in Khotan addressed the King, saying: "The Chinese monk wishes to use Brahmanical texts to confuse and subvert the authentic scriptures.
If Your Majesty does not forbid this, you will surely render the people of Han like the deaf and blind. The King listened to them, and [Fada] Shixing...

Filled with indignation, he said, "This is a Buddhist scripture. He then requested that the scriptures be burned as proof. Lokakṣema vowed, "If the Great Dharma is destined to flow into the land of Han, these scriptures should not be consumed by fire.
Having spoken, he cast the scriptures into the flames; the fire was extinguished, yet the scriptures remained intact, radiating a brilliant light.

The king and his assembly were struck with awe and submission. He subsequently provided the Sanskrit original, which first reached Luoyang in the eighth year of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty (287 CE). (Daoxing)
The scripture is the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Banzhou jing*).
He was of the Liu clan, named Bei, from Yizhou in Shudu. He was a descendant of Jingwang Sheng of Zhongshan. His reign began in the *xinchou* year of the founding of the state.
From the last ruler, Guiwei, to the two rulers, a total of forty-three years.
The capital of Wu was at Wuchang; it was moved to Jiankang. From Taizu, Renyin, until Wuchenghou, Gengzi, a total of four rulers.
The fifty-ninth year.
Emperor Taizu. Surname: Sun; name: Quan; courtesy name: Zhongmou. A descendant of Sun Wu. The second son of Sun Jian and younger brother of Sun Ce. [The state of] Wu.

He was a native of Fuchun County. Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty invested Sun Quan as King of Wu and bestowed upon him the nine emoluments. In the first year of the Huangwu era, he ascended the throne.
In the fourth year of the Chihu era, the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui arrived in Jinling from the kingdom of Kangju. He erected a thatched hut, installed images, and practiced the Way.
When the people of the state first saw him, they were all struck with wonder and amazement. The officials reported this to the authorities, and Sun Quan summoned him to question him. Senghui—
Jin said, "The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has been in parinirvāṇa for a thousand years; yet his sacred relics and śarīras manifest divine responses without limit.
In the past, King Aśoka enshrined them in eighty-four thousand stūpas—this is the legacy of that transformation.

Quan considered this boastful and said, "If you can obtain the śarīras, I shall build a stūpa for them. Should there be no proof of their efficacy, the state shall impose its standard punishment. Thereupon, Hui...
He placed a copper bottle upon a small table and requested a period of seven days; yet there was no sign. He then extended the period to fourteen days, still with no sign.
Zhiquan said, "Go ahead and boil it. Huì silently recited the Buddha’s name, thinking, "How could His True Compassion fail me?
He requested another extension of seven days. At the fifth watch, he heard a tinkling sound from within the bottle. Upon looking, he found it to be śarīra. At dawn, he presented them.

Sun Quan gathered with his high officials to observe it, sighing and saying, "This is an auspicious omen rarely seen in the world. Zhu Fa-hui said, "The spiritual power of this śarīra is such that nothing can destroy it.
Sun Quan ordered a strongman to strike it with a hammer; it was not damaged, and its radiance remained as before.

Sun Quan built a stūpa for it at Fotuo-li and constructed a monastery, enshrining Fa-hui there. He bestowed upon it the name Jianchu (today’s Tianxi Temple). This was the beginning of monasteries and stūpas in the region south of the Yangtze River.
[From the *Hongming ji*].

The Marquis of Wucheng, whose name was Hao and courtesy name Yuanzong, was the grandson of Sun Quan and the son of Sun He. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Yuanxing. Hao did not...
He showed reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma, yet he demolished monasteries and shrines. His ministers remonstrated, saying, "The power of the Buddha is not like that of other deities.
Kang Senghui has moved the divine spirits, and Your Majesty established this monastery. If you now treat it with contempt and destroy it, I fear it will bring calamity upon future generations.

Sun Hao did not believe them. He then dispatched Zhang Yu to the monastery to interrogate Senghui. Senghui’s responses were sharp and immediate; when Zhang Yu returned, he sighed, "Senghui’s talent and eloquence are beyond my capacity."
[The Emperor] measured [the situation]. He humbly prayed that the Celestial Eye would personally inspect it. Huì arrived, having been welcomed by Hào in a horse-drawn carriage.

Hào asked, "The Buddha spoke of the retribution for good and evil; may I hear about this? Huì replied, "When a sagacious ruler governs the world through filial piety, vermilion phoenixes soar and the elderly behold them.
When one nurtures the myriad things with benevolence and compassion, sweet springs gush forth and auspicious grain grows. Since goodness already exists..."
"Examine it: evil is treated in the same way. Therefore, if one commits evil in secret, the ghosts will find and punish them; if one commits evil in public, humans will find and punish them.
The *I Ching* proclaims that accumulated goodness brings remaining blessings; the *Odes* praise seeking fortune without backsliding.

These are indeed the maxims of the Confucian classics and the clear instructions of Buddhism. Huo said, "If that is so, then since the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are already clear, what further use is there for Buddhism?"
Hui said: "The teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius merely indicate their outward traces; the Buddhist teachings explain their essential points in detail. Sun Hao had no way to respond.

(From the *Hongming ji*) On another day, while on guard duty, he found a golden image while tending his garden. Hao ordered it to be placed in a filthy spot as a joke. Suddenly, he contracted a swelling disease.
A divination stated that he had offended a great deity. Hao prayed at various shrines without success. A palace attendant asked: "Why not request [the aid of]..."

Fú said to the Buddha, "Hào realized that it was because of his arrogance toward the image that he had come to this state. He then welcomed the image, bathed it with perfumed water, and made offerings to it.
He further invited Senghui to preach the Dharma and repent for his transgressions. Senghui expounded for him the profound essentials of the teaching and conferred upon him the five precepts.
Thereupon, his illness was cured, and he took Senghui as his teacher, reverently adorning the temple and its pagodas. (From *Fayuan zhulin*)
Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming, was a native of the Yuezhi people. He was a lay Buddhist (upāsaka). At the end of Emperor Xian’s reign, he fled his homeland and returned to Wu.

Sun Quan summoned him for an audience and held his talent in high regard, appointing him as a *boshi* (Court Scholar), but Qian firmly declined and would not accept. Qian had extensively read the classics and scriptures and was proficient in the Six Classics.
According to the *Guoyu*, Zhi Qian was tall and thin with dark skin; his eyes were white with yellow pupils. People of the time said: "Zhi Lang’s eyes are yellow;
though his physical frame is small, he is a treasury of wisdom. Qian received his training from Zhi Liang (style name Jiming), who in turn had studied under Zhi Chen.
The world acclaimed them, saying: "In the whole world, no one possesses such broad knowledge as these three Zhis. Qian translated eighty scriptures.
Section Eight (from the *Hongming ji* and *Shijiao lu*).
Kan Ze, courtesy name Derun, was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji. He was fond of learning and lived in poverty, supporting himself by working as a hired scribe. Regarding his...
Once he had finished writing, he was able to recite it from memory. Thereupon, he read widely through various texts. When Yu Fan saw him, he praised him, saying:
"Kǎn Shēng is a peerless talent, a successor in the lineage of Zhōngshū and Zǐyún. Sūn Quán summoned him for service, appointing him as Assistant Director of the Western Office (Xīcáo Yuàn).

He was subsequently appointed as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifǔ) and served as Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng), being enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng. (From the *Wù Zhì*) He once donated his residence to establish the Dèrùn Temple.

(Qian once asked: "Confucius composed the classics and instructions to educate future generations. Laozi and Zhuangzi cultivated themselves for their own enjoyment, roaming freely in mountain forests and turning their hearts toward tranquility.
Why, then, would they practice Buddhism? Ze replied: "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi were fashioned according to Heaven and applied in accordance with its principles;
they did not dare to contravene Heaven. As for the establishment of the Buddha's teaching, all the heavens receive and uphold it; they do not dare to contravene it.")
The Buddha. From this it can be seen that [the two] are superior and inferior (from the *Hongming ji* and Zong Bing’s “Discourse on Clarifying Buddhism”).
*Fofa jintang bian*, Volume One. Re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
*Fofa jintang bian*, Volume Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai during the Western Jin dynasty.
The capital was Luoyang. It began in the year Yiyou of Emperor Wu and ended in the year Bingzi of Emperor Min. There were four sovereigns for a total of fifty-two years.
Emperor Wu’s personal name was Yan; his surname was Sima, and his courtesy name was Anshi. He was the eldest son of Emperor Zhao of the Wen dynasty and a native of Wen in Henei.
The Emperor greatly honored Buddhist affairs and extensively constructed monasteries (*fangzhi*).
Emperor Hui’s posthumous name was Zhong, his courtesy name was Zhengdu; he was the second son of Emperor Wu. In the first year of the Yuankang era, the Emperor constructed [a monastery] in Luoyang.
Xingsheng Temple. One hundred monks were regularly provided for there (according to local gazetteers).
Xun Xu, courtesy name Gongzeng, served as Director of the Imperial Secretariat during the reign of Emperor Wu. He obtained the bamboo slips from the tomb at Jiji Commandery and compiled them.

He considered this to be the central scripture and had it cataloged in the Imperial Library. In the second year of the Taishi era, he commissioned twelve golden statues of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas at Luoyang;
they emitted a great radiance, and the people of the capital flocked together to gaze upon and worship them (as recorded in his biography and the Tongji).
Yang Hu, courtesy name Shuzi, was the grandson of Yang Xu. He was successively promoted to the rank of Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shangshu Puye).

When he was five years old, his wet nurse was asked to retrieve a gold ring from beneath a mulberry tree in the garden of the Li family next door. The Li family was startled and said, "This is the ring of our deceased son."
He realized that this was none other than the previous incarnation of Li Shi’s son, Hu. During the reign of Emperor Wu, Hu served as the Governor-General (Dudu) of Jingzhou.
He daily provided offerings to the temple on Mount Wudang. When asked the reason for this, Hu replied: "In my previous life, I committed many transgressions;

it was only by virtue of building this temple that I obtained deliverance from them. Therefore, my feelings of devotion and support are particularly focused upon this place. (From his *Benzhuan* and the *Tongji*).

Liu Sahe was a native of Lishi in Bingzhou. His family business was hunting with arrows. In the third year of the Taikang era, he died of illness and entered the underworld, where he saw a foreign monk who directed him to go to the Aśoka Stūpa in Kuaiji to perform repentance. Upon reviving, he left the household life and was named Hui.
Fada traveled to Kuaiji, searching everywhere without success. One night, he happened to hear the sound of bells coming from beneath the earth.

He then prayed earnestly for three days, whereupon a precious stupa suddenly surged forth from the ground. It was one chi and four cun in height and seven cun in width, complete with all the Buddha images.

Upon seeing the stupa, Da practiced with diligent devotion in ritual worship and repentance, for which many auspicious responses occurred (this marks the beginning of the Aśoka stupas; from the *Stupa Records*).
Zhu Yingying was a man of Wu who had long venerated the True Dharma; at the mouth of the Hudu Reach on the Wusong River, he saw two stone images floating upon the river.
Upon its arrival, there was an inscription on the back which read: "Anciently, these were the two Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa of Vaiśālī. Subsequently, they were welcomed to Tongxuan Temple.
Eight years later, fishermen found two green stone bowls on the riverbank and brought them home, using them to store pungent foods. Suddenly, images of the Buddhas appeared within the bowls.
Those who recognized them declared that these were the bowls for the two previous images. They were then sent to Tongxuan Temple; they are currently in Suzhou.
Kaigen-ji (Hōon). During the Eastern Jin dynasty, the capital was established at Jiankang.
Beginning from the dingchou year of Emperor Yuan and ending with the gengshen year of Emperor Gong, there were eleven sovereigns over a period of one hundred and four [years].
The Year.
Emperor Yuan, whose posthumous name was Rui and courtesy name Jingwen, was the great-grandson of Emperor Xuan and the son of Prince Gong of Langya. The first year of Taixing—

In the [second] year, an imperial edict summoned the śramaṇa Zhu Qian to lecture on the sūtras within the palace. The Emperor revered his virtue and ordered him to ascend the hall wearing wooden clogs.
In the second year, the Emperor established the Waguan and Longxing monasteries, gathering a thousand monks from Danyang and Jianye (according to the *Liutie* and *Tongji*).

Emperor Ming, whose posthumous name was Shao and courtesy name Daoji, was the eldest son of Emperor Yuan. In the first year of the Yuanning era, he personally handled the pigments and colors to depict an image of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Within the Great Interior, at the Laxian Hall, he established the two monasteries of Huangxing and Daochang, and assembled monks specializing in the study of doctrine.
One hundred members of the assembly engaged in discourse on the Buddha-way (Tongji).

Emperor Cheng, whose posthumous name was Yan and courtesy name Shigen, was the eldest son of Emperor Ming. In the fifth year of the Xianhe era, he issued an edict for the assembly at Baoshan in Kuaiji.

Dharma Master Yi entered the inner palace to transmit the five precepts. He established Jianzhongxing and Luye Monasteries to house one thousand monks who engaged in the study of translated scriptures and doctrinal exegesis (the *Liutie*).
Initially, Jiyou practiced the dhūta austerities on Shizigang; after his death, he was buried there.
The Emperor erected a pagoda at the site of the tomb. Later, śramaṇas from the region west of the Pass built a monastery upon the site of the tomb.
Xie Hun supported [the proposal] and named it Gaozuo Temple.

Emperor Jianwen’s personal name was Yu, with the style name Daofang; he was the youngest son of Emperor Yuan. In the first year of the Xian’an era, the Emperor visited Waguan Temple to listen [to the Dharma].

Zhu Fata lectured on the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. In the second year [of his reign], an imperial decree was issued to construct a stupa at Changgan Temple; it was magnificent and exceptionally grand.

On the day the construction was completed, light illuminated the eaves and halls. Whenever the Emperor read Buddhist scriptures, he believed that by refining the spirit through such practice, the state of a sage could be attained. (Recorded by Shi Jian)

Emperor Xiaowu’s taboo name was Yao, his courtesy name was Changming. He was the third son of Emperor Jianwen. In the first year of the Ningkang era, the Emperor heard of the fame of Dharma Master Dao’an and issued an edict, stating:
"The Dharma Master, by means of his virtue and the Way, illuminates the realms of humans and devas, causing the Great Dharma to circulate."
The common people rely upon [the state]; it is fitting that they receive the emoluments of princes and dukes daily. The relevant authorities shall provide these supplies at the proper times.

In the second year, Dharma Master Zhu Qian passed away. The Emperor issued an edict stating: "The Dharma Master’s realization of the principles was profound and far-reaching; his character and discernment were pure and lofty. He renounced the glory of the position of Chancellor."
He inherited the practice of donning the black robes and relied upon the proclamation of the Way to save the masses of living beings. That he has suddenly passed away is a source of deep grief;
ten thousand coins may be granted to assist in the construction of his burial mound and stupa.

In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era, the Emperor established a vihāra within the inner palace to honor the Buddha, summoning monks of renowned virtue to reside there and preach the Way. He founded Huangtai Temple and subsequently donated his former residence for its use.

In the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy), regarding the founding of the temple, he wrote a letter to Master Lang of Taishan, saying: "I have heard that your enlightened virtue has shone brightly for some time, its fame soaring over the Eastern Peak.

All living beings have received your moistening grace, and you have skillfully assisted in upholding the times. Now that the ancient capital has fallen and the Central Kingdom is in turmoil, the common people are suffering like bitter herbs;
my heart is filled with lamentation and grief. I wish to join you, O Master, in nourishing all living beings. As a supreme person, you penetrate the subtle mysteries—I trust you intend to do so."
Please understand my intention. I have now dispatched an envoy to deliver one five-colored pearl image, fifty bolts of Mingguang brocade, five sets of ivory mats, and five golden bowls.
Upon arrival, I hope you will graciously accept them. (From the *Hongming ji*)

Wang Dao, courtesy name Maohong, was a native of Langya. He was appointed as Minister of Works (Sikong) and Director of the Secretariat (Lu Shangshu Shi), holding the rank of Grand Preceptor (Taibao) and was enfeoffed as a Duke of a Commandery.
At that time, the Indian Śrīmitra (translated here as Jiyou) traveled to Jiankang and resided at Jianchu Monastery, where he was skilled in preaching the Dharma and performing incantations.

He was skilled in Buddhist chanting (*brahmaghoṣa*). When Wang Dao saw him, he remarked, "He is one of our own kind. Yu Liang, Zhou Yi, Xie Kun, and Huan Yi all visited his door to form friendships with him.

At that time, he was called the Dharma Master of the High Seat (the present-day Gaozuo Temple is located there). Once, while Ji You was discussing matters with Wang Dao, he was loosening his belt and sitting in a relaxed, expansive manner.
Just then, Bian Hu arrived; Ji You immediately assumed a solemn and dignified countenance. Someone asked him the reason for this, and he replied, "This is King [Bian Hu]."
"Lord Fengjian (Wang Xun) gauges people; Commandant Bian (Bian He) fathoms things by their patterns. I shall simply respond to them with these qualities.
(From the *History of the Jin* and the *Biographies of Monks*). —Xie An.

An (Ān) was his courtesy name; he was a native of Yangxia in Chenjun. He lived in seclusion on Mount Dongshan in Yue. At the age of forty, he emerged from retirement to serve as the General of the West’s Assistant Secretary.
During the Taiyuan era, he served as Director of the Imperial Secretariat and was appointed Grand Preceptor (*Taibao*). His posthumous title was Wenjing.

While residing on Mount Dongshan, he engaged in excursions through the mountains and rivers with Zhi Dun and Xu Xun. On one occasion, an imperial decree summoned Zhi Dun into the inner palace to lecture on the sutras. He [An] frequently...
Huìzōng’s collected writings were disparaged by those who adhered strictly to the literal text. Hóng'ān heard of this and sighed, saying, "This is like Jiǔfāng Yīn’s appraisal of horses:
he disregards the color—black or yellow—and seeks instead their spiritual excellence. In the second year of the Tàihé era, Zhìdùn declined an imperial summons and returned to the mountains.
By imperial decree, Wózōu Monastery was established for him to reside in. At that time, Hóng'ān was governing Wŭxīng; he sent a letter to Zhìdùn, which read in brief: "I am thinking of you..."
As the days accumulated and the hours were counted, my longing grew even more intense. Knowing that you intended to return to Shan to manage your own affairs, I was moved to deep sorrow.

Human life is but a temporary lodging; in this brief moment, the refined pursuits and matters of worldly success have almost entirely vanished. All day long I am filled with grief, waiting for you alone.
May you come once more so that we may dispel our longings through conversation; then a single day will be as a thousand years. (From his *Beizhuan* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Wang Xizhi, whose courtesy name was Yishao, was the younger son of [Wang] Dao. He began his official career as a Librarian of the Imperial Secretariat and later served as General of the Right Army.
As the Interior Historian of Kuaiji, he established Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu in the sixth year of the Xiankang era and invited Dharmatrāta from India to reside there.
While in Kuaiji, Wang Xizhi had heard of Zhi Dun’s reputation but did not yet believe in him; later, Dun returned to Shan County.
Wang Xizhi went to visit Zhi Dun to observe his character and vigor. He said to him, "May I hear your discourse on 'carefree wandering' (xiao yao)? Dun composed several thousand words for him;

Xizhi then unfastened his robes and loosened his belt, lingering there until he could not bear to leave. He subsequently requested that Dun reside at Lingjia Temple, intending to remain in close proximity to him.
Shortly thereafter, Dun withdrew once more to the Shanyang Mountains (*Records of the Jin Dynasty* and *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Zhou Ji, courtesy name Xuānpèi, was a native of Yángxiàn in Yìxīng. He was the son of Zhùchù, General Who Subdues the West during the Western Jin dynasty. His family had served the Buddha for generations.
While Ji served as the Governor of Wǔxīng, his household servants were fishing when they suddenly saw golden light overflowing the river and reflecting [upon it].
The current flowed upstream. He cast a net and caught a golden image about three feet high; however, when he tried to lift and move it, it would not budge.
He informed Xi (Xishi) of this. Xi’s daughter served the Buddha with particular devotion, so Xi sent his daughter by boat to go and welcome the image back home to serve and worship it.
A woman dreamed that her left knee pained; when she examined the statue’s knee in the morning, it was indeed perforated and missing a piece.
She subsequently repaired it with a golden hairpin (*Dazang Gantong Lu*).
Tao Kan, courtesy name Shixing, during the Xianhe era served as the Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of eight provinces, including Jiaozhou, Guangzhou, Jingzhou, and Jiangzhou.

He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Changsha, posthumously granted the title of Left司马 (Sima), and conferred the posthumous title of Duke Huan. During the days when Kan was stationed in Nanhai, a fisherman saw him every evening.
A light appeared on the seashore. He reported this to Fan Kan, who dispatched people to search for it. They saw a golden image arriving by riding upon the waves beside their boat.
Upon examining its inscription, they found it was an image of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva created by King Aśoka. Initially, Kan had not placed deep faith in the law of cause and effect;
however, upon obtaining this image, he honored it all the more. He sent the image to Hanxi Temple. The temple had previously...
The statue was unharmed by the fire. Later, when Hui-k’an was stationed at Wu-chang, he sent men to welcome the statue to his headquarters, but the boat sank and the statue was lost.

When Dharma Master Hui-yüan established a monastery on Mount Lu, he prayed for it with a sincere heart; thereupon, the statue arrived of its own accord, gliding smoothly across the water (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Gao Kui was the Governor of Danyang during the Xianhe era. Whenever he saw light appearing within the waters of Zhanghou Bridge, he dispatched an official to search for it.
There, they recovered a golden image of Western Regions style, both its halo and pedestal being incomplete. Kui transported the image to Chang’an.
At the Qian Temple, light emanated from within at midnight, and those who came to observe and prostrate were numerous.

More than a year later, Zhang Xi, a man from Linhai, obtained a gold-and-copper lotus pedestal in the sea and placed it beneath the feet of the image; it fit perfectly. That night, light reached up to the heavens.
After some time, five monks from the Western Regions arrived, shaking their mendicant staffs, and went to see Huikai, saying: "In the past, we obtained [this image] made by King Aśoka."
The image once traveled to Ye, where it was hidden by the riverbank during the chaos; its whereabouts were subsequently lost.
Recently, it appeared in a dream, saying, "It has been obtained by Gao Kui. Desiring to pay homage to it, Kui led him to Changgan Temple.
When five monks saw the image, they prostrated themselves, sobbing and weeping as the image emitted light. Later, at Hepu, the pearl diver Dong Zongzhi found a circular halo.

The matter was reported to Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty, who issued an imperial decree to place [the image] upon the pedestal of the Śākyamuni Buddha statue. Thereupon, the halo and pedestal were finally completed (from the *Gantong lu*).
Xi Chao, whose courtesy name was Jingxing and also Jia-bin, was a native of Shanyang. He served as a secretary in the administration of Huan Wen. Xi Chao questioned Xie An:
[Someone] asked, "How does Zhi Dun’s discourse compare to that of Xi Kang? Dao’an replied, "Xi Kang exhausted his powers of reasoning, yet he only attained half [of the truth].
Chao composed the *Wujie wen* (Treatise on the Five Precepts), which states in brief: "By not killing, one attains longevity; by not stealing, one enjoys constant tranquility;

by not committing sexual misconduct, one remains pure; by not practicing deception, one is always respected and trusted by others; and by not becoming intoxicated, the divine principle is clearly understood. Having practiced these five...
Regarding the precepts: one further cultivates the fasts and abstinences for months and years. As for the three monthly fasts, they are the first, fifth, and ninth months.
As for the six monthly fast days, they are the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of each month.

During all such fasts, one must not taste fish or meat, nor consort with a wife or concubines. One should eat before midday; once midday has passed, one must not partake of any delicious, sweet, or fragrant flavors.
Once, he washed his mind and contemplated the Way, taking refuge in the Triple Gem (*Hongming ji*).

Wang Qiao (some say Qi Zhi-Qiao), a native of Langyao, composed a poem on the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) which says: "The wondrous function is present here; traversing existence, one surveys non-existence."
The spirit arises from the obscure and subtle; consciousness illuminates the coarse. As the subtle accumulates, it draws itself forth; yet its causal efficacy is fundamentally empty.

To dissolve those three contemplations and forget this last trace—thus it is said: "Alas, throughout my life, I have been deficient in wisdom and insight from an early age. Entrusting myself to a person of profound depth, I hope to rely on their hidden power.
I contemplate turning even a hair’s breadth of merit toward that which is deep and unfathomable. How sublime is this thought! I direct my mind toward the Western Realm" (*Lushan ji*).

Xi Zuochi (習鑿齒), courtesy name Yanwei (彥威), was a native of Xiangyang. From his youth, he possessed great ambition and spirit; he was widely learned and possessed extensive knowledge, gaining renown for his literary compositions.

He was successively promoted to the post of Beijia (別駕). At that time, there was the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an (釋道安), who was renowned for his brilliant eloquence and superior talent; he had traveled north to Jingzhou.
When Liu Xi met with Dao’an, Dao’an said, “The sky-pervading Shi Dao’an. Liu Xi replied, “The four seas’ Xi Zaochi.
People of the time considered this an excellent exchange. Later, due to a foot ailment, he was confined to his local neighborhood.
When Xiangyang fell to Fu Jian, Jian, who had long heard of his reputation, had both him and Dao’an carried in litters to his court. Because of his lameness, Jian [treated him with...]
The *Zhenshu* states: "In the past, when the Jin dynasty pacified Wu, the benefit lay with the two Lus; now, having broken Han-nan, we have obtained barely one and a half men of talent" (*Jin shi*).
In a letter to Dao’an, Xi [Zhi] wrote briefly: "I have learned that you, O Arhat, tread the path of rectitude, your inner clarity being perfectly integrated.

Your compassionate instruction shines universally, providing shelter to both monastics and laity alike. Those who take emptiness as their principle realize the truth of impermanence; those who remain in existence..."

He attained mastery over the provisional manifestations of external bodies. When his disciples heard that it took no more than a morning for rain to fall across the six directions, they realized it was the clouds that overspread the heavens;

that the profound source was extended to moisten the eight extremities, they realized it was the flow of the four great elements. All things relied upon its bounty, and both the high and the low were graced by its moisture.
Since the Great Teaching flowed eastward some four hundred years ago, there has been no sage, wise man, or gentleman who has not turned toward it in devotion.
Thesis: The flourishing of the Way’s teachings has never been more magnificent than it is today. May the old and the young alike, both monastics and laypeople, harbor this same aspiration.

If the auspicious clouds should drift eastward and the mani-jewel turn its radiance back, and if you were to once again ascend the throne of the seven treasures and briefly gaze upon the lamp of wisdom, raining down sweet dew upon the lush grasses and planting sandalwood by the riverbanks, then the teaching of the Tathāgata would once more be honored in our own day.
His profound waves and lingering echoes thoroughly washed and purified the world for a generation (*Hongming ji*).
Xu Xun, courtesy name Xuandu, was a native of Gaoyang and a gentleman of the Jin dynasty. He purified his mind through the study of Buddhism; among the high officials of the Jiangzuo region, he was—

He admired him deeply. Emperor Jianwen held his character in high esteem and would invariably visit him every month on a moonlit night. Their pure discourse on subtle principles was continuous and inexhaustible; the Emperor would lean forward in his seat to listen.
He engaged Zhi Dun in a lecture on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, with Daoxun serving as the *dujiang* (the respondent).

Whenever Daoxun posed a question, the assembly believed that Zhi Dun could not provide an answer; whenever Zhi Dun explained a point, the assembly believed that Daoxun had nothing further with which to challenge him. Daoxun once...
The new residence at Yongxing in Kuaiji was established as Chonghua Temple. A four-story pagoda was constructed (details appear cross-referenced in the biography of Xiao Cha).

He Chong—also known as He Zhun—whose courtesy name was Cidao, was a native of Qian in Lujiang. During the reign of Emperor Cheng, he served as Minister of the Interior (Shangshu Ling) and was posthumously honored with the title of Grand Commandant (Sikong). Emperor Cheng...
[The Emperor] was still young. Yu Bing, acting as regent on behalf of his maternal uncle, proposed that śramaṇas should perform full prostrations before the sovereign.
Daocheng and others argued: "Emperor Wu established the new dynasty through its great brilliance, and Emperor Ming perceived the profound with sagely wisdom.

Was it not during these times that śramaṇas found it difficult to bend their knees? Rather, they did not alter the laws for cultivating goodness precisely so as to harmonize the wills of all under heaven."

The memorial submitted by [He] Chong was subsequently shelved. Chong’s nature was fond of the Buddhist scriptures; he venerated and repaired Buddhist temples and provided for the śramaṇas, spending vast sums without stinting (according to the *Ben-chuan tongji*).
He Zhun, whose courtesy name was Youdao, was noble-minded and had few desires. Although both the provincial and central governments repeatedly summoned him, he did not accept.

While his elder brother Chong held the weighty position of a high minister, his power eclipsed that of his time, Zhun wore his sash loosely at his humble gatehouse and remained detached from worldly affairs.
As well as human affairs, he did nothing but recite Buddhist sutras (from the *Book of Jin*).

Wang Xun (also known as Wang Min), courtesy name Yuānlín, was the grandson of [Wang] Dǎo and the eldest son of [Wang] Qiá. He served as the Chief Clerk (*zhǔbù*) to Huán Wēn. During the Tàiyuán era, he became a *sàn*... [official].
Qi Changshi’s younger brother was Mi, whose courtesy name was Jiyen. From his youth, he possessed talent and artistic skill; his reputation surpassed that of his elder brother, Xun.

At that time, there was a foreign śramaṇa named Deva, who had a profound mastery of the principles of the Dharma and lectured on the *Abhidharma* Sūtra for the brothers Xun and Mi. Mi was still quite young.

Before the lecture had even reached its midpoint, he declared that he already understood it. He then proceeded to lecture on it himself before the śramaṇa Fagang and others. Fagang sighed and said, "The great principles are all correct;
it is only that the minor details are not yet refined. Xu and Min donated their private estates to establish Huqiu Temple (as recorded in the Jin History and the temple chronicles).
Wang Tanzhi, courtesy name Wendu, was the son of Wang Shu. A native of Taiyuan, he served as High Counselor (Zhongshu Ling).

He was on very close terms with the śramaṇa Zhu Fadu, and they frequently discussed the mysteries of the afterlife and the retribution of deeds. [Fadu] said that if he were to die first, he would report on these matters. Later...
After a year had passed, the Master suddenly appeared and said, "I, this poor monk, am already dead. Neither sin nor merit is ever in vain;
one must simply diligently cultivate the Way and its virtue in order to elevate and deliver the spiritual intelligence. Having spoken these words, he vanished. Zhi-tan subsequently died as well.
Zhi-tan once donated his garden to establish Anle Temple (as recorded in his biography and the *Sou Shen Ji*).

Sun Chuo, courtesy name Xingong, was the son of Sun Zan. He roamed and lived freely with Xu Xun and Zhi Dun amidst the mountains and waters of Kuaiji. During the reign of Emperor Ai, he served as Director of the Bureau of Historiography (*zhuzuo lang*).

He composed the "Discourse on Illustrating the Way" (*Yudao lun*), of which a brief excerpt states: "There may be those who harbor doubts regarding the Ultimate Way; to illustrate it for them, he said:"

Now, the six realms of existence are vast and remote, and the myriad species are numerous and abundant. Through a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, all are blended together without discernible beginning. Therefore, those with the consciousness of the myriad things each expect to see only what they encounter. Creatures of scale and shell do not understand the affairs of the highlands; the tribes of fur and wing do not recognize the currents of the drifting waves. Those who find their own fulfillment within a narrow well then marvel at the capacity of one who roams the vast ocean. Thus it is said: [The text continues with the famous lines: "Even the great fish, the Kun, would have been startled had he but known the limits of the well.
