Those who soar to a height of several *ren* may doubt their power to reach the heavens;

yet those who remain bound within the confines of worldly teachings and examine only the traces of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius will claim that supreme virtue culminates with Yao and Shun, and that subtle words are exhausted in Laozi and the *I Ching*.
How could they ever behold the wondrous interests beyond this world or the profound illumination within the realm? Now, as for the Buddha, he is one who embodies the Way (*dào*). The Way...
He is the one who guides all things. Responding to stimuli and flowing with conditions, he acts without striving yet there is nothing he does not do.

Because he acts without striving, he is empty, tranquil, and spontaneous; because there is nothing he does not do, his spiritual transformation pervades the myriad things. Someone may object: "The Duke of Zhou and Confucius taught according to the needs of their times.
If the Buddha intends to abruptly abolish killing, by what means will he punish the violent and stop the wicked? The answer is: Not so. The Duke of Zhou...

Confucius is none other than the Buddha, and the Buddha is none other than the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. Thus, when manifesting as an Emperor, he is an Emperor; when manifesting as a King, he is a King.

"Buddha" means "Awakened," just as Mencius described the Sage as the "first awakened. Their essential intent is one and the same. The teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius remedy the corruptions of the age, while the Buddhist teachings clarify the fundamental source;

together they form the beginning and the end, and their ultimate aim does not differ. An objection is raised: "The Duke of Zhou and Confucius take filial piety as their primary principle, yet the śramaṇas..."
The Way [of the monastics] involves abandoning kin for the distant, shaving off beard and hair, ceasing filial care during life, and ending the offering of ancestral sacrifices at death;

yet they claim to propagate the Way, cultivate benevolence, and extensively save all living beings. The answer is: Therefore, the value of filial piety lies in its ability to establish one’s person and practice the Way so as to bring eternal glory to one’s parents.
If one merely crawls to offer tangerines or daily presents the three sacrificial animals, yet cannot cause all things [to flourish], [then such acts are insufficient].

To exalt oneself is not the way to nourish one's parents. Formerly, when the Buddha was a crown prince, he abandoned his kingdom to study the Way. He used tree branches as a canopy and spread grass as a mat;

internally, he contemplated *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) through its six stages: first, counting; second, following; third, stopping; fourth, observing; fifth, returning; and sixth, purification.
His wandering wills reached three or four [realms], and his comings and goings traversed the twelve gates. His spirit was like cold ashes and his form like withered wood.

Sitting upright for six years, he perfected the Way and was titled Buddha. Possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, he walked beyond the three realms and exercised his transformations at will within the infinite borders.
Heaven became clear and earth moist; all things flourished. Even the wriggling insects and the withered plants...
Relying on this, one transforms sorrow into honor and returns to illuminate one’s own country by widely disseminating the sound of the Dharma.
When even the father-king attains awakening and ascends to the site of enlightenment, what filial piety could surpass such honoring of one’s parents?

Among the Buddha’s twelve divisions of scripture, four divisions are dedicated specifically to exhorting filial piety; their earnest intent may be called ultimate. Yet worldly people do not examine their source, and thus...
To utter blind words and false doctrines while immediately launching attacks and challenges is like doubting the brilliance of the three luminaries with the sight of a firefly’s glow,

or marveling at the capacity of the deep ocean with a drop from a crack in the sunbeam. To take such deception as eloquence and such recklessness as clarity can truly be called treating great men with intimacy and showing contempt for the mandate of Heaven (*Hongming ji*).
Dai Kui (also known as Dai Yong), courtesy name Andao, was a native of Qiao Commandery. Desiring to create a sixteen-foot image of Amitāyus Buddha, he found the ancient style to be crude and simple;
thus, he secretly gathered various theories and devoted three years of concentrated thought before the carving was finally completed. He then welcomed the statue to Lingbao Temple in Shanyin.
At the temple, Xi Chao saw him and paid his respects. Grasping incense in his hand, it suddenly burst forth into smoke that rose high above the horizon to the limits of the clouds.
The assembly all marveled at this divine response. Dao Kui’s son was Yong, styled Zhongruo; his talent and skill were equal to those of his father.

Once, Jiang Yi requested that Yong create an image of Avalokiteśvara, but after many years it remained unfinished. One night he dreamed of a deity who said, "Jiang Yi has no [karmic connection] to Avalokiteśvara..."

The name "Yuan" (緣) was changed to "Maitreya" (彌勒). Zhiyong immediately rode off to report this, yet the letter from the barbarian [envoy] had already arrived; both experienced a dream on that very evening.
When the name was changed to Maitreya, it fell perfectly into place as soon as it touched his hand. The image is now at Longhua Temple in Kuaiji (*Tongji*).

Yuan Hong, courtesy name Yanbo, possessed extraordinary talent. He once composed the *Han Ji* (Annals of Han), in which he wrote: "In the land of India in the Western Regions, there exists the Way of the Buddha.

'Buddha' means awakening; it refers to one who brings awakening to all living beings. Its teaching takes the cultivation of goodness and compassion as its primary principle. It focuses exclusively on...

They strive for purity; those who are refined in this regard are called śramaṇas. In the Han language, this means "stilled mind. It refers to stilling the will, abandoning desire, and returning to non-action (wu-wei).
Furthermore, they hold that when a person dies, their spiritual essence (jīnglíng) is not extinguished, but rather continues to receive a new form.
Whatever good or evil one performs during life all has its retribution. Therefore, what is valued is the practice of goodness and the cultivation of the Way to refine the spirit, until—
He is the Buddha. The Buddha’s body is sixteen feet tall and possesses a golden-hued mark. A halo of sunlight encircles his neck. His transformations penetrate everywhere;
thus, he can manifest through all things to bring great salvation to all living beings. Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, moved by a dream, dispatched envoys to India to inquire about the Way.
They returned with his image and several thousand scrolls of scriptures, which take emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as their fundamental principle and encompass all things.
From the subtle to the coarse, there is nothing he does not encompass. He is skilled at crafting words of vast breadth and supreme greatness.
That which he seeks lies within the unity of all things; that which he clarifies lies beyond the reach of sight and hearing. People of the secular world may consider this to be empty and exaggerated;

yet, it ultimately returns to the profound and the subtle, so deep and far-reaching as to be difficult to fathom. Therefore, when princes, dukes, and high ministers contemplate death, life, and the retribution of karma—
At that moment, everyone was startled and lost in self-reflection (from the "Annals of Sacrifices at the Capital" in the *Book of Han*).
Liu Chengzhi—whose courtesy name was Zhongsī—was a native of Pengcheng. He served as the magistrate of both Changxing and Chaisang counties before subsequently entering Mount Lu.
He followed Dharma Master Huiyuan in practicing the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). The Master said, "Your official rank is lofty; why do you not serve?
Chengzhi replied, "When ruler and subject are in mutual suspicion, what can I do? For fifteen years he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recollection of the Buddha.
In the eighth month of the sixth year of the Yixi era, he beheld Amitābha emitting light and touching his head. He immediately burned incense before the image and made this vow: "I..."
"By means of the Bequeathed Teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that there is the Western Pure Land.
I pray that this incense first be offered to the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, and next used as an offering to the Guiding Teacher Amitābha; may he grant me his compassionate inclusion.

Thirdly, it is offered to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, for it is by upholding this sūtra that one attains birth [in that land]. Having spoken thus, he lay upon his bed facing west and passed away. (From the *Cheng*)

He possessed hidden virtues. Although Xie An and Liu Yiqing recommended him with great earnestness, he declined their offer with firm resolve. Consequently, they honored him by bestowing upon him the title "Yimin" (The Recluse) (as recorded in his biography).

Zhou Xuzhi, whose courtesy name was Daozu, was a native of Yanmen. At the age of twelve, he studied under Fan Ning and mastered the Five Classics and the Five纬 (Wěi), which together were known as the Ten Classics;
he was thus praised as a contemporary of Yan Hui. Later, he entered Mount Lu to serve the śramaṇa Huiyuan, where he lived in simple robes.
He maintained a vegetarian diet for the rest of his life and remained unmarried. Together with Liu Yimin and Tao Qian, he was known as one of the "Three Recluses of Xunyang" (Nanshi).
Lei Cizong, whose courtesy name was Zhonglun, was a native of Yuzhang. He entered the Lotus Society on Mount Lu and established a residence beside Donglin Temple. Furthermore...
When Master Huiyuan passed away, he wrote to his sons and nephews, saying: "I have devoted myself to my practice at Mount Lu and served the Venerable Shi for thirty years.
Now that my profound teacher has passed and my virtuous friends have perished, I am still not yet in my old age;
it is still possible to rouse my will to become a bridge for the crossing toward the Western Paradise. From this day forward, do not let me hear of domestic affairs. (Nanshi)

Zhang Ye (also written as Zhuan Ye), courtesy name Laimin, resided in Chaisang, Xunyang. He shared a marriage alliance with Yuanming (Tao Qian). Zhang’s learning encompassed both Chinese and Buddhist traditions;

though summoned repeatedly, he did not accept these appointments. He entered Mount Lu to rely upon Master Huiyuan and, together with Liu Tai, cultivated the practice of Pure Land Buddhism (according to his biography).
Quan, whose courtesy name was Xiushuo, was a descendant of the Ye clan. He possessed lofty and detached sentiments and was deeply devoted to the study of the ancient classics.

When summoned to serve as an Attendant-at-the-Horse (Sanqi Changshi), he did not rise to accept the post. Yu Yue, noting his poverty, appointed him as Magistrate of Xunyang. Quan laughed and said, "The ancients considered a mere knee’s width of space sufficient for comfort.
If one were to bend their will to pursue official emolument, what would there be to call honorable? Thereupon, he entered Mount Lu to rely upon Master Huiyuan for study.
He exhausted the study of the Buddhist scriptures and attained profound realization (as recorded in his biography).
Zong Bing, courtesy name Shaowen, was a native of Nanyang. When Liu Yu served as the Governor of Jingzhou, he summoned Bing to serve as a Chief Clerk. Bing replied: "I..."
"I have lived among the hills and drunk from the valleys for thirty years. How could I bend my waist before the gates of a king to serve as an official?

He then entered Mount Lu to build a dwelling, where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. He once composed the *Mingfo lun* (Treatise on Clarifying the Buddha), as recorded in his biography.
Meng Yi was a native of Pingchang. He served the Buddha with profound sincerity. Xie Lingyun said to Yi, "In being reborn in heaven, you must precede me;
in attaining Buddhahood, you will surely follow behind me. During the Yixi era, Yi served as the Governor of Kuaiji. Initially, Tan-yi...
The Dharma Master traveled east to Kuaiji and entered Qinwang Mountain, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra for twenty years.
One day, a woman dressed in colorful garments appeared before him, carrying a bamboo basket containing a white pig and two large garlic bulbs. She said to the Master:
"I, a humble woman, entered the mountains to gather ferns. The sun has already set, and with wolves and jackals blocking the path, I have no means of returning home.
I venture to ask for one night’s lodging. The Master declined her most firmly; the woman wailed incessantly. He then provided her with a straw mat to stay upon.

At midnight, she cried out in pain, saying her belly hurt, and asked the Master to massage her. He wrapped his tin staff in cloth and pressed it against her from a distance. The following day, the woman...
His colorful robes transformed into auspicious clouds; a pig was transformed into a white elephant, and garlic blossomed into twin lotuses.
Ascending into the clouds, he said to the Master, "I am the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. Knowing that you would soon return to my assembly, I came specifically to test you.
I observed that your mind is like the moon reflected in water, incapable of being defiled. Thereupon, heavenly flowers rained down and the earth shook everywhere.
The villagers who heard of or witnessed this could not help but praise it in admiration.

On that day, while Fayi was rising at dawn to attend to his affairs, he suddenly saw auspicious clouds from the south casting a brilliant light across the courtyard, accompanied by the faint yet distinct sounds of strings, flutes, metal bells, and stone chimes. Upon inquiry, he learned that Pu-xian had manifested his passing.

Consequently, his mastery of the Way was reported to the court. An imperial edict was issued to establish Fahua Temple (the present-day Tianyi Temple). After the Master passed away, his lacquered true body was enshrined within the mountain (according to the *Tongji*).
Tao Qian, whose courtesy name was Yuanming, was a native of Chaisang in Xunyang. He was the great-grandson of the Grand Marshal Tao Kan.

Having served as Magistrate of Pengze for eighty-odd days, he resigned his seal of office and departed the county, composing the "Return to My Native Place" (Guiqulai Ci). This occurred when the Song dynasty received the abdication of the throne.

He resided at Chaisang and frequently traveled to Mount Lu, where he had a disciple and two sons carry him along. At that time, Master Huiyuan and various worthies had formed a religious society (shè);
they sent a letter inviting Yuanming. Yuanming said, "If you permit me to drink, then I shall go.

Having received this permission, he went; however, he suddenly knit his brows and departed. He once composed the *Soushen lu* (Records of Searching for the Divine), which contains many accounts of the miraculous efficacy of the Buddha.
(From his biography).
Luo Han, courtesy name Junzhang, was a native of Xiangzhou. Once, he dreamed during the day that a multicolored bird entered his mouth; from then on, his literary imagination flourished daily.

He served as the Attendant Secretary (*biéjià*) to Huan Wen and was subsequently summoned to serve as a Court Gentleman (*shàngshū láng*). Upon retiring from official service, he composed the "Treatise on Rebirth" (*Gēngshēng lùn*), which states in brief:

"All things have their limits, yet Heaven and Earth are infinite. If all things do not undergo rebirth, then Heaven and Earth would have an end. Since Heaven and Earth have no end, rebirth may be known [to exist].
Furthermore, the spiritual essence and its material form meet in profound harmony, joining together like a tally and its seal. Yet the world universally grieves over this union."

One must inevitably part, yet no one consoles themselves for this inevitable separation; one must inevitably reunite, yet everyone knows that gathering inevitably leads to dispersal, while no one recognizes that dispersal inevitably leads to reunion.
Now, those who debate merely know that the "I" of the past is not the "I" of the present, yet they fail to realize that the "I" of the present is precisely the "I" of the past.
"That which enables the profound observer to equate life and death is also expressed as 'life and death are like waking and sleeping.
How true these words are! (Hongming ji). Gu Kaizhi.
Kai’s courtesy name was Changkang; his childhood name was Houtou. He was skilled at painting. Huan Wen recruited him as a staff member (paramilitary aide) to the Grand Marshal.
At that time, the śramaṇa Huili was constructing Waguan Monastery, and the contributions from court dignitaries did not exceed one hundred thousand coins.

Changkang, who had long been poor, promised one million coins; everyone laughed at him. One day, while painting an image of Vimalakīrti on the wall of the hall, he was about to apply the final touch...
Muzhi said: "Those who see [the light] on the first day shall be charged with a donation of one hundred thousand; those who see it on the second day, fifty thousand;
and on the third day, they shall be charged according to precedent. When the doors were opened, the radiance illuminated the temple, and donors filled the space.
Indeed, one million coins were obtained (from the *Jinling zhi*).
Fan Ning, courtesy name Wuzi, was successively promoted to the post of Secretariat Director (Zhongshu Shilang). He was subsequently appointed as the Governor of Yuzhang.

He once invited Dharma Master Huichi to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. Monks gathered from all directions like clouds. Wang Xun wrote a letter to Ning, saying:
"Between Master Yuan and Master Chi, who is superior? Ning replied in a letter, "They are truly a worthy elder brother and a worthy younger brother.
Xu responded again in a letter, saying, "To even have a brother such as yours is already not easy; how much more so for a younger brother to be likewise worthy? (From the *Biography of Hui-chi*).
Xie Shang, courtesy name Renzu, was the son of Xie Kun. He served the Jin dynasty as General Who Guards the West. Once, Shang dreamed that his father told him:
"A vapor is approaching from the southwest; anyone who encounters it will surely die. You should cultivate merit by building a pagoda and constructing a monastery."
"You may perform an exorcism to ward it off. If you have not yet had the leisure to build a stupa or temple, you may carve the shape of a stupa on the head of your staff.
When you see the qi approach, you can direct it [away] with it. Seng Shang woke up and subsequently carved a small stupa to attach to the head of his staff, keeping it constantly by his side.
Later, indeed, a strange vapor descended from the heavens; at first like a chariot wheel, it gradually grew larger and rushed directly toward Shang’s residence. Shang...
He pointed his staff at them, and their vital energy immediately dissipated. The entire family was saved, but for several li around where the energy had passed, not a single soul remained.
Later, in the fourth year of the Yonghe era, Shang Sui donated his residence to establish a monastery named Zhuangyan Temple (according to the *Jiankang lu*).
He Wujì was a native of Dōnghǎi. During the Yìxī era, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Císhǐ) of Jiāngzhōu. While fighting against Lú Xún, he died clutching his official staff.

He held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem and constructed Zhǐyuán Monastery. Because Emperor Wénxiàn had returned from the west and the imperial fortune was restored in triumph, he exhorted the Emperor...
He promoted the Śākya school and cultivated meritorious deeds (as recorded in the *Bianzheng lun*).
Huan Yi,
courtesy name Shuxia and childhood name Yewang, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yongxiu County during the Taiyuan era for his achievements at the Huai and Fei rivers.
At that time, Dharma Master Huiyuan came from Xiangyang to Mount Lu and took up residence at Xilin Monastery with Huiying.
Desiring to build a monastery on the eastern side of the mountain, he was engaged in the preliminary preparations when a mountain deity descended in spirit, vowing to provide assistance.

For two nights, wind and thunder arose, and clouds and rain made the night dark and obscure. When he went to inspect the site the following morning, there were fine timbers and extraordinary materials standing in rows and piled in abundance.
At that time, Yi was the Regional Inspector of the Nine Rivers. Astonished by his divine and extraordinary nature, he memorialized the throne to establish a monastery there, naming it Donglin;
its main hall was named Shenyun (according to the *Record of Donglin Monastery*).

During the Six Dynasties period of usurpers and pretenders, among the sixteen kingdoms, Liu Yuan of the Han dynasty occupied Pingyang. Under his successor Liu Yao, the state was named Zhao. There were three rulers for twenty-six years.
Later, Li Te of Shu occupied Chengdu; there were five rulers for forty-five years.
[Then came] Former Liang.
Zhang Gui occupied Liangzhou; there were eight rulers for seventy-four years.
Later Zhao occupied Xiangguo; there were six rulers for thirty-four years.
Shi Le, courtesy name Shilong, was originally of Xiongnu descent. Liu Yuan appointed him as General Who Assists Han;

Liu Yao designated him as Grand Marshal, conferred upon him the nine emoluments, and advanced his rank to Duke of Zhao. He established the state name Hou Zhao. In the fourth year of the Yongjia era, Heaven...
Zhu Fotudeng came to Luoyang. He was profoundly adept in esoteric arts; he regularly practiced breath cultivation for self-nourishment and could go without food for many days.

He was skilled in reciting divine mantras and was able to command ghosts and spirits. During a period of rebellion and turmoil in Luoyang, Shi Le was stationed at Gepo, where he was intent solely on slaughter.
Fotudeng wished to go there to convert him. Guo Helü, a general under Shi Le, had long been a devotee of the Buddha-dharma, so Fotudeng went to see him.
He received the five precepts in brief and honored him with the etiquette due to a disciple. When Shi Le was engaged in battle, Fo Tucheng predicted both victory and defeat in advance.
Because Shi Le perceived that Tucheng possessed extraordinary powers, he summoned him for an audience and asked, "In what way is the Buddha-dharma so efficacious?
Tucheng took a bowl and filled it with water, over which he recited incantations. In a short while, a blue lotus appeared within the bowl, its radiance dazzling to the eye. Shi Le...
Because of this, Shi Le revered him. When he went out to battle Liu Yao, he consulted Fo Tucheng. Tucheng said, "The sound of the pagoda bell says: *Xiū zhī tì lì gāng, pú gǔ qú tú dāng*.
This means that if the army goes out, they will capture Liu Yao. Shi Le went out to battle and indeed captured Yao alive.
He served Tucheng with even greater reverence. Shi Le’s beloved son, Bin, died suddenly; lamenting, he said, "I have heard that when King Goufan of Guo..."

The son had died, yet Bian Que was able to restore him to life. "Can you now demonstrate such a feat? [the king asked]. Daorong took a willow branch, moistened it with water, and sprinkled it [over the boy].
He then took Bin’s hand and said, "You may rise. Bin subsequently revived (from the *Book of Jin*).
Shi Hu (Shi Hu;

courtesy name Jilong) was the nephew of Shi Le. He moved the capital to Ye and served Fotudeng with exceptional reverence. He clothed him in brocade and silk and transported him in an ornately carved carriage.
During court assemblies, when he was summoned for an audience, the Crown Prince and the high officials would support him as he ascended the hall. [He appointed] the Minister of Works Li...
The King inquired after his health morning and evening and visited him once every five days. Wherever Sengcheng was located, no one dared to spit, sneeze, or relieve themselves toward that direction.

The people of the country were transformed by this example; they vied with one another to build monasteries, and those who shaved their heads to leave the household life mostly devoted themselves to the Buddha.

Fo Tucheng knew that the Shi clan was about to perish, so he had already undergone transformation [passed away] beforehand. Shi Hu had excavated a pit and prepared a tomb for him. As Tucheng was about to die, he said to Hu:
"The state has set its heart upon the Buddha-dharma and shall surely receive blessings; however, your administration is violent and cruel, and in the end there will be no fortune or protection."
He then sat peacefully and passed away (according to the *Book of Jin*).
Former Yan was ruled by Murong Hu from Dajicheng in Liaodong; there were five sovereigns for thirty-nine years.
Later Yan occupied Zhongshan. Four rulers; twenty-six years.慕容垂 (Tú Mǎo Chuí).

Chui, the fifth son of [Emperor] Rang, wrote a letter to the Venerable Master Lang of Taishan, stating in brief: "Your spirit is clarified within the sacred lineage, and your compassionate protection covers the hundred nations.

Among all living beings, who is not moistened by your grace? I, the Emperor, have inherited the mandate and established the imperial succession; the great army has been successfully mobilized to suppress and sweep away violence and chaos.

You, O Sage, possess spiritual penetration and manifest transformation according to the needs of the occasion. We pray that you may bring about the submission of the four seas without shedding a drop of blood. Now...
A messenger was dispatched to deliver one hundred rolls of official silk, three *kāṣāya* robes, and fifty *jin* of cotton. I pray that you will offer prayers for our welfare.
(From the *Hongming ji*).
Southern Yan.
He occupied Guanggu for thirteen years as one of two rulers.
Murong De, the younger son of [Murong] Huang, wrote a letter to the Monk Lang of Taishan, stating in brief: "Our house has encountered manifold hardships and calamities."

[Your arrival] has occurred repeatedly. I, the Emperor, being devoid of virtue, was born amidst chaotic armies; yet through the great kindness of the Monk [Bodhiruci], the gods and spirits have protected me.
I now dispatch an envoy to deliver one hundred rolls of silk, along with the provision of the stipend of the Prince of Dongqi and the fief of the two counties of Gaoshan and Ren for his support.
Words cannot fully express my intent; this reflects the heart of the Emperor. (From the *Hongming ji*)
In the north, Murong Sheng and Feng Ba of Beiyin occupied Longcheng; these two rulers reigned for twenty-eight years. [During this time], the Former Qin...
He occupied Pingyang for seven rulers over a period of forty-five years.
Fu Jian (personal name Yonggu), the son of Fu Rong and grandson of Fu Hong, attacked and captured Xiangyang, seizing Dao’an and Xi Zuochi.

He was welcomed to Chang’an. Yao Xian went out to the Eastern Garden and ordered Dao’an to share his carriage. The Palace Secretary Quan Yi remonstrated, saying, “Dao’an has altered his physical appearance;
he should not occupy the same vehicle. Yao Xian replied, “Master An is honored for his Way and virtue,” and he then had Quan Yi assist Dao’an in ascending the palanquin.

At that time, an ancient bronze cauldron was discovered in Lantian; there were no one in the court who could decipher the seal script inscribed upon its belly. They questioned Dao’an about it. Dao’an—
It was said: "He was cast during the reign of Duke Xiang of Lu. He strictly commanded the scholars of the three national colleges that whenever they had doubts, they should all consult him.
A saying among the people went: 'In study, if one does not take An as a teacher, there is no principle that can prevent difficulty. An’s appearance was plain and his complexion dark;
he delighted in discussion. Thus the proverb went: 'The lacquer-clad man startles his neighbors. On his left arm, there was a square inch of flesh, protruding like a seal."

Known in the world as Bodhisattva Yinsou (Seal-in-Hand), Jian sent a letter to Master Taishan Lang. It read in brief: "The Great Sage has responded to the era; his numinous skill transcends all bounds.
He provides shelter for the ten directions, and his transformation permeates the infinite. He nurtures all living beings like mountains and seas, and fosters the myriad things like heaven and earth.
I have now dispatched an envoy with a carriage to invite you, and I am sending several jin of purple-gold. [Signed by] Nu.
He had three sons who were capable of performing the duties of sweeping and cleaning; he hoped that [the Emperor] would graciously accept them.
When Yao Jian heard that Kumārajīva was residing in the kingdom of Kucha, he dispatched Lü Guang and others to lead an army westward to invade Kucha.

He told Guang, "If you capture Kumārajīva, send him back immediately by courier. After Guang defeated Kucha, he captured Kumārajīva and returned to Liangzhou. There, he heard that Yao Jian had been killed by Yao Chang.
[He was] harmed. [The *Jin shu* and the *Hongming ji* record that] Kumārajīva was detained in Liang.
Later, Yao Chang of the Later Qin occupied Chang'an. There were three rulers in total for thirty-four years. Yao Chang was the twenty-fourth son of Yao Yizhong.
He was the son of Yao Xing.

Xing, whose courtesy name was Zilüe, was the eldest son of Yao Chang. From his youth, he revered the Three Jewels and applied himself with keen resolve to their study and recitation. As for Lü Guang’s father—

When Fu Jian was defeated, Yao Xing attacked Lü Long, who surrendered. Xing then welcomed Kumārajīva back to the Qin state. Kumārajīva had always been fond of the Mahāyāna and was intent on its propagation.
He sighed, saying, "If I were to take up the pen to compose a Mahāyāna Abhidharma, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra.
However, those with deep understanding are now few; with whom could I discuss this? He composed only two fascicles of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Real-Phase Treatise) for Yao Xing.

He revered [Kumārajīva] as if he were a deity. Once, while preaching the sutras at Caotang Temple, Yao Xing and over a thousand court officials and virtuous śramaṇas listened with solemn countenances.
Yao Xing, like the Xiyao Garden, invited various śramaṇas to hear Kumārajīva expound the Buddhist scriptures.

Consequently, from the high ministers downward, all venerated the Buddha-dharma; the prefectures and commanderies were transformed by this, and those who served the Buddha numbered ten... [of the population].
In his residence, there were nine [cells] (Beishi). Kumārajīva’s disciple Dàolì was diligent and austere in observing the Vinaya; Emperor Wénxù held him in high esteem.

Since Kumārajīva entered Guānzhōng, the number of monks and nuns had reached ten thousand, and [Dàolì] was appointed as the *Sengzhèng* (Director of the Sangha). The Emperor issued an edict stating: "The Great Dharma has flowed eastward, and it is flourishing more than ever today."

The number of monks and nuns sleeping [in the monasteries] is great; it is appropriate to establish a governing framework. The Dharma Master Qieshi has long possessed scholarly erudition and was later renowned for his virtue;

he may serve as the Sangha Administrator (Sengzheng). He shall be provided with a sedan chair and attendants, and his rank shall be equivalent to that of a Palace Attendant (Shizhong). Furthermore, Sengqian and Chanhui shall be appointed as the Chant Leaders (Yuezong).

He appointed Fachi and Hui-bin as Monastic Registrars (*senglù*), with their respective ranks differing according to seniority. Kumārajīva then examined the old translations and found them to be largely erroneous;

he corrected them all. He subsequently translated the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā* (Renwang), the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Dapin), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and other sūtras.

Daorong composed the *Tong sanshi lun* (Treatise on the Three Periods of Time) to demonstrate the principle of cause and effect; kings and dukes held him in high esteem and praised him (*Sengshi* and *Gaoseng zhuan*).
In the Western Qin, Qifu Guoren occupied Longyou; there were four rulers for twenty-seven years.
Nanliang Tufan Wugu occupied Guangwu. Three rulers; eighteen years.
Later Liang.
Lü Guang occupied Guzang for four rulers over eighteen years.
Northern Liang was occupied by Duan Ye at Zhangye for three rulers over forty-three years.
Jūqú Méngxùn was of Xiongnu descent. After he killed Duàn Yè and established himself as ruler, he moved his capital to Gūzàng. There, the Kuchean śramaṇa Dharmakṣema arrived;
Méngxùn detained him and had him translate the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, the Karuṇapuṇḍarīka-sūtra, the Raśmiprabhāsa-sūtra, and other scriptures. At first, Méngxùn...
About one hundred li south of Liangzhou, he established five Buddha images, some carved from stone and others molded from clay, manifesting in a thousand variations and ten thousand transformations.
He also fashioned a stone image for his mother, which was exceedingly efficacious.

When Sūn, following the death of his son, conceived the intention to destroy the monastery and expel the monks, the image shed tears like a spring; Sūn prostrated himself in repentance, redoubling his devotion and piety.
(*Gantong lu*). At that time, Tuoba Gui was the King of Zhongshan. Having heard the prophecy (*chan*), he desired to pay his respects and dispatched an envoy to invite him.

Daoxun would not permit it. Tuoba Gui sent the Duke of Gaoping, Li Shun, a second time to confer upon Daoxun the title of King of Liang and bestow the nine emoluments (*jiu xi*), instructing him, saying:
"Dharmakṣema’s virtue and wisdom are vast and great; I long to see him. You may send him by express courier. Daoxun replied: "Your servant..."
"I have served the imperial court without failing in my duties. My previous memorial requested that you remain, and now I have come again to pursue you.
You are my teacher; I would rather die than go against your will. Sui said, "The court admires your loyalty and righteousness, which is why they have bestowed such exceptional honors upon you.
Now, because of a single practitioner, you would ruin a great achievement. I cannot bear to let you vent your indignation over a momentary fit of anger."
It should be said that he lost the Emperor’s intent of showing him courtly favor; I earnestly advise Your Majesty not to accept [the request].
Xuēn ultimately did not dispatch him, and Càn returned to the West and passed away (Tongji).
Li Gao of Xiliang occupied Dunhuang. There were three rulers for twenty-two years. This was the Xia dynasty.
He Lian Bobo occupied Shuofang. [His reign lasted] for three rulers over twenty-five years.

*Fofa Jintang Bian*, Volume Three.

The capital was Jianye. Beginning with Emperor Wu’s gengshen year and ending with Emperor Shun’s wuyou year, there were eight sovereigns over a total of fifty-nine years.
[Emperor] Wu...
The Emperor’s name was Yu; his surname was Liu; his courtesy name was Deyu. He was a native of Suili Village in Pengcheng County.

During the Emperor’s humble years, while traveling to Zhulin Temple in Jingkou, he lay alone before the lecture hall. There appeared a dragon insignia of five colors. When the monks saw it, they informed the Emperor.
The Emperor said with joy, "The Master speaks no falsehoods. When the Emperor was still the Duke of Song, he converted his former residence at Jingkou into Puzhao Monastery.

In the first year of the Yongchu era, a vegetarian feast was held in the inner palace, and the śramaṇa Daozhao delivered a discourse stating that a hundred years pass swiftly and suffering and joy are but a fleeting moment.
The Emperor approved of this and separately bestowed thirty thousand coins as alms. The Emperor also once personally transcribed the Vinaya scriptures.
Reciting the Sanskrit texts orally, he constructed four temples, including Linggen and Fawang. He also established Dongshan Temple (as recorded in the *Diji*, *Tongji*, and *Jigulüe*).

Emperor Wen, whose personal name was Yilong, was the third son of the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu). In the fifth year of the Yuanjia era, the Emperor established Chanling Temple and regularly provided sustenance for a thousand monks.
In the eighth year, the Emperor asked Guṇavarman: "I wish to observe the fasts and precepts and refrain from killing, yet I am constrained by [the demands of] governance."
Wu said, "I have not attained my aspirations. Guṇavarman replied, "The cultivation of a sovereign and that of a commoner differ.
A commoner is of humble station and inferior reputation; his words lack authority. If he does not overcome himself, how can he achieve anything? A sovereign takes the four seas as his home."

When the myriad people are treated as one's own children, every virtuous word uttered brings joy to both officials and commoners; when a single benevolent policy is disseminated, humans and spirits are brought into harmony.
Consequently, wind and rain arrive at their proper seasons and the hundred grains flourish. To observe such fasting is indeed a great virtue.
How could it be considered a vast salvation merely by abstaining from half a day’s meal or sparing the life of a single bird? The Emperor sighed and said, "The common folk are deluded."

"Those who distance themselves from ultimate principles (li) and those who stagnate in proximate teachings—according to what you, Master, have said, one may indeed discuss the boundary between heaven and humanity" (*Hongming ji*).
In the ninth year, Zhu Daosheng returned to the capital and resided at Qingyuan Temple. The Emperor deeply praised and sighed over him.

Consequently, when the Emperor visited Dazhuangyan Temple to convene a great assembly, he personally sat on the ground together with the fourfold assembly. At the time of the midday meal, as the assembly did not eat after noon, the Emperor...
The Emperor said, "It is only midday. Daosheng replied, "The bright sun adorns the heavens; how could it not be midday? He raised his bowl and ate immediately.
The Emperor was pleased (*Song shi*). When Guṇabhadra (translated as "Gongde Xian") from India arrived at Jinling, the Emperor dispatched an envoy to welcome him at the outskirts of the capital.

He was appointed to reside at Jetavana Monastery. Emperor Xiaowu repeatedly invited him into the palace to receive offerings; He Shangzhi and various princes and dukes all served him as their teacher (according to his biography).
Emperor Xiaowu...

The Emperor’s posthumous name was Jun, his courtesy name was Xiulong, and he was the son of Emperor Wen. On the anniversary of Emperor Wen’s death in the first year of the Xiaojian era, the Emperor held the Eightfold Precepts (Bāguānzhāi) at Zhongxing Temple.
After the midday meal concluded, his attendants, including Yuan Min and Sun [et al.], further presented him with fish and meat.

The Emperor was enraged and demoted both of them from their official posts. In the second year [of his reign], an imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Daoyou as the Dharma Master of the Xin'an Garrison Temple;
he was highly esteemed by the expectations of the age. In the second year of the Daming era, the Emperor summoned the Dharma Master Tanzong to perform a rite of repentance for his transgressions.

The Emperor then said, "What crime have I committed that troubles you with this repentance? Tanzong replied, "Shun said, 'If I err, you shall assist me,' and Yu said, 'If the myriad regions have faults...'"
"The fault lies with me alone. Your Majesty treads the Way with humble reflection; how could you alone be an exception? The Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the seventh year, the śramaṇa Huiyi intended to immolate himself at Mount Zhongshan. Upon arriving at Yunlong Gate, he took leave of the Emperor. The Emperor went out the gate to meet him.

Huiyi entrusted his Buddhist teachings to him as a final charge. On the day of the self-immolation, both monastics and laypeople filled the mountain, and the Emperor also visited the site in person. Huiyi personally...
He held a candle to set it ablaze while reciting the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter from the Lotus Sūtra. When the fire reached his eyes, his voice ceased.

That night, the Emperor dreamed that Fayin arrived carrying a monk’s staff and again entrusted him with the Buddha-Dharma. The following day, the Emperor established a religious assembly and ordained monks;
he built Bhaiṣajyarāja Temple at the site where Fayin had burned his body (from the *Sengzhuan*).
Emperor Ming’s posthumous name was Yi; his courtesy name was Xiu. He was the eleventh son of Emperor Jingwen.

In the third year of the Taishi era, an imperial edict established Xinghuang Monastery at Jianyang Gate, and the śramaṇa Daomeng was charged with its leadership. The Emperor said: "It is man who can propagate the Way. The Way...
Relying on others to propagate [the Dharma], he has now found the Dharma Master. Not only does he benefit the common people through the Way, but he also brings glory to the world’s reputation.

Consequently, an imperial decree was issued for Sengmeng to lecture on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun). High officials assembled in full, and the Emperor personally attended to listen. The edict stated:

"Dharma Master Meng propagates the Way with great efficacy and is a guest-friend of the Emperor. He shall be granted thirty thousand coins, as well as attendants and a carriage. Furthermore, an edict was issued for Sengjin.

He served as the Sangzheng (Sangha Rectifier) for the realm. An ensemble of musical instruments was bestowed upon him, along with a monthly stipend of thirty thousand coins, a carriage, and laborers (the *shijian*).
In the fourth year, when the Emperor completed the construction of Xianggong Temple, he opened a grand lecture hall and decreed that Fayuan should serve as the Dharma Master.

The Emperor attended the lecture assembly in person, and the high officials gathered in the seats; those who witnessed it considered it an honor. (From the *Monk Biographies*). The Emperor once asked Master Zhi about Niu Mountain.
"What sacred deity resides on this mountain? Zhi replied, "Mañjuśrī leads ten thousand bodhisattvas; he dwells at Mount Wutai during the summer and at Mount Niushou during the winter.
Furthermore, a pratyekabuddha entered meditative absorption here. For these reasons, the temple is called 'Buddha Cave' (as recorded in the *Pratyekabuddha Stūpa Record*).

The Emperor commissioned a sixteen-foot golden image, regularly consumed vegetarian food every morning, and daily recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*. He was moved by grace to obtain śarīra relics, which he then enshrined."
*Hongpu Temple* (from the *Lidai Fabao Ji*).
In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, Emperor Wen said to the Attendant-in-Ordinary He Shangzhi: "Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun have often remarked that..."

The Six Classics were originally intended to benefit the world through worldly customs. If one seeks the essential truth of the spirit and nature, one must take Buddhist principles as the guiding compass.
Recently, I have seen Yan Yanzhi’s *Treatise on Refuting the Nature of Attainment* and Zong Bing’s *Refutation of the Black-and-White Treatise*;

both clarify the ultimate principle and inspire the human mind. If the entire land were to be thoroughly imbued with this transformation, I would achieve Great Peace while sitting at ease. — Shangzhi.

He said: "Since the crossing of the Yangtze River, those such as Wang Dao, Zhou Yi, Yu Liang, Xie An, Dai Kui, Xu Xun, Wang Meng, Xi Chao, Xie Shang, Wang Tanzhi, and my own ancestors and brothers (the He Chong brothers)—there was none among them who did not receive the teachings and take refuge [in the Dharma].
In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent; in a town of a thousand houses, if a hundred people..."

If one cultivates the ten wholesome deeds, the hundred people will be harmonious and friendly. If a person can practice even one good deed, they eliminate one evil; if one evil is eliminated, one form of punishment ceases.
When one punishment ceases within the family, ten thousand punishments cease within the state. This is what is meant by the "clear intent" of achieving Great Peace while sitting still.
Thus, when Tancheng arrived in Zhao, the two Shi rulers diminished their violence; the Spirit Tower emitted light, and Fu Jian [ceased his tyranny].

"Deprivation and cruelty [are countered by] the divine way assisting in transformation; this is manifest and clearly observable. As for the labor of building temples and monuments, although it may seem like a massive expenditure, the repayment of blessings and the honoring of gratitude must not be abruptly severed.
Yang Xuanbao stepped forward and said, "This discussion concerns the boundary between Heaven and man;

how could it be appropriate for a subject such as I to intervene? I venture to say that the powerful armies of Qin and Chu, and the annexations of Sun Wu—these have nothing to be gained from [such pursuits]."
This was so. Shangzhi said: "If one honors the reclusive and hidden, then warriors will cease their toil. If one prizes benevolence and virtue, then the martial spirit will dissipate.
If one takes Sun Wu as one's ideal and aims for conquest through military action, then one will find no value in the Way of Yao and Shun—not to mention the teachings of the Buddha.
The Emperor was delighted and said: "The Śramaṇa community having you is like the school of Confucius having Ji Lu."
"Evil words do not enter his ears" (*Song shi*).
Wang Xuemu, courtesy name Yande, was a native of Qi in Taiyuan. When he raised troops to campaign against the Wei, Xuemu was appointed as General Who Pacifies the North.
General [Xuanmo] received the appointment of General Who Assists the State and was placed under the command of Xiao Bin.

When Xuanmo violated military discipline, Bin intended to execute him. Shen Qingzhi earnestly remonstrated, saying: "Folide (Emperor Taowu of Wei)’s prestige shakes the world; how could Xuanmo possibly withstand him?

Furthermore, to kill a battle-hardened general would only weaken our own forces. Thereupon, the execution was halted. Previously, when Xuanmo was about to be put to death, he dreamed that someone told him to recite—

Reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra one thousand times can bring liberation from [calamity]. Furthermore, he orally transmitted the sūtra as follows: "Avalokiteśvara. Namo Buddha. One has a causal connection with the Buddha;
one has a karmic affinity with the Buddha. The Buddha-dharma is characterized by mutual affinity: permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Recite the name of Avalokiteśvara in the morning."
In the evening, he would contemplate Avalokiteśvara; every thought arose from his mind, and every thought never departed from it. Once awakened, he recited [the name] without ceasing.
Suddenly, the execution was halted. Later, he rose to the rank of Kaifu (Grand Marshal) and passed away at the age of eighty-two (*Nanshi* and *Bingtongji*).

Fan Tai (also known as Fan Yue), courtesy name Bolen, was a native of Shunyang. He had extensively read the classics and histories and was fond of composing literary works. In his later years, he served the Buddha with great devotion;
to the west of his residence, he constructed the Jetavana Vihāra. His son, Yue, courtesy name Weizong, compiled the *Book of the Later Han*. Its western...

The *Yùlùn* (Treatise on the Regions) states briefly: "The divine transformations of the Buddha-dharma originated from India, yet among the geographical records of the Western Han, there was no mention of it.
Zhang Qian merely noted that the land is hot and humid and that people fight riding elephants; Ban Chao only recorded that they venerate the *Fútú* (Buddha) and refrain from killing.
As for the merit of the profound texts and sublime Dharma in guiding and transforming [sentient beings], nothing has been transmitted or described therein. Thus have I heard.

This is what was said later. That land is situated in the center of the Middle Kingdom; its jade-like harmony and vital energy are such that spirits and sages descend and gather there, while the virtuous and noble are born therein.
As for its divine traces and wonders, they transcend the realm of human reason; as for its manifest responses and verifications, these events surpass the boundaries of the mundane world.
Yet, why is it that no one has heard of them being transcendent? Is it because the Way was closed during past eras, and the destiny for its revelation has only opened in this final age?
(Han Shu). Zhou Yong (Yong), courtesy name Yanlun, was a native of Runan.

He was the tenth-generation descendant of Zhou Yi, the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness under the Jin dynasty. Emperor Ming had a considerable fondness for the profound principles of metaphysics (*xuanli*).

Because Sengyong possessed eloquence and righteousness, he was introduced into the inner palace and stayed there in close attendance. When the Emperor committed cruel and poisonous deeds, Sengyong did not dare to remonstrate openly;

instead, he would recite from the scriptures accounts of karmic causes and effects regarding sin and merit. The Emperor also ceased his actions slightly because of this. Sengyong’s voice and rhetoric were elegant and refined, and he excelled in Buddhist principles.
He composed the *Sanzong lun* (Treatise on the Three Natures), explaining the meanings of *śūnyatā* (emptiness) and *prajñapti* (provisionality). [The Crown Prince...]
[The Emperor] asked, "As for your diligence, how does it compare to that of Yin? Yong replied, "The three miserable realms and the eight difficulties are things from which neither of us can escape;
yet each of us has his own burdens. The Crown Prince asked, "What are these burdens? Yong said, "A wife who is too attentive and meat that is too rare.
Yong once established Mount Ci Temple on Mount Zhong and invited Huiyue to reside there; this is the present-day Caotang Temple (Nan shi). Yong once sent a letter to...
Yin said briefly: "Among the great transformations, none surpasses birth and death; among the things most precious to life, none exceeds one's nature and destiny (*xingming*).
Since nature and destiny are of such vital importance to that [other being], the flavors [of its flesh] may be deemed light by me.

Although you, O Elder, do not personally tread upon the species of blood-flavored creatures, how could you fail to procure geese and carp from the butcher’s shop? And yet, though the *zouyu* (the mythical 'unicorn') may be hungry, it does not [eat meat] of its own accord."
He did not eat the "grass of death," and from this his lineage was cut off; [he] removed the scent of blood (from the *Hongming ji*).
Xie Lingyun:
the son of General of the West An Xi, Xie Gui, and the great-grandson of Xie Yi. Lingyun was fond of learning from his youth and read widely.
Among the many scholars of his time, his literary excellence ranked first in the region south of the Yangtze River alongside Yan Yanzhi. He inherited the title of Duke of Kangle.
Appointed as Governor of Yongjia, he returned to Shining (the present-day East Mountain Temple in Shangyu) where the graves of his grandfather and father were located.
During his stay at Shining, he composed various poems concerning his country estate there. Lingyun was haughty and disdainful toward others; upon reaching Mount Lu, he encountered...
Huiyuan was profoundly moved and submitted his heart in reverence. He immediately constructed a terrace at the monastery to translate the thirty-six fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

He excavated a pond and planted lotuses; Huiyuan and the various worthies together cultivated the practice of purity (*śubha-karma*). Xie Lingyun sought to join the society, but Huiyuan declined him on the grounds that his mind was still too distracted.
He once composed a hymn in praise of the Buddha, saying: "This Great Awakened One is spiritual by virtue of the mind; when defilements are exhausted..."
Wisdom illuminates; teaching reaches the ultimate clarity of insight. The threefold penetration reveals that there is no self, as one extends aid to all sentient beings.

Principle obstructs the activities of the mind, and the Way transcends form and sound. The Bodhisattva praised them, saying: "If a person looks up to this school, they give rise to their fundamental nature and cast away discursive thoughts. By means of meditative concentration, they nourish wisdom, and thus accord with harmonious principle.

Beginning with the four immeasurables and culminating in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), their pursuit of the ultimate is perfected. All external things are discarded; this is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha."
The Śrāvakas joined in praise, saying: "Their aversion to suffering is great, yet their resolve to benefit others is small; like that illusory city, they provisionally obtain the treasure.
By inducing them with Nirvana, you rescue them from birth and old age. What originated as the three chariots has now been transformed into the Single Path.

In a eulogy for the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, he addressed his younger cousin Hui-lian, saying: "The Dharma-treasury grew up in the royal palace; cherishing the Way, he departed from the capital city. His vow..."
Forty-eight. "The vast vows rescue all living beings; how wondrous is the Pure Land! Those who come are all pure and eminent.

In these declining years, where shall I find rest? I must surely set out at dawn, following the transformation of nature. Furthermore, there are eight verses from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* praising through metaphors:
foam, bubbles, a mirage, a plantain tree, an illusion, a dream, a reflection, an echo, floating clouds, and lightning. (Quotation complete)
*Hongming ji*. Yan Yanzhi, courtesy name Yannian, was preeminent in literary composition during his time and was renowned as an equal to Xie Lingyun. Emperor Wen once summoned him...

He was not seen [in public]. Emperor Xiaowu conferred upon him the rank of Jinguang Luofu Dafu. At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Huilin, who wore monastic robes while remaining in the secular order to disparage the Dharma;

he authored the *Baihei lun* (Treatise on the White and the Black). He Chengtian, the Governor of Hengyang, was intimately acquainted with Lin and enthusiastically engaged in debate with him, authoring the *Daxing lun* (Treatise on the Attainment of Nature). Confined to a single perspective, he reviled and slandered the Buddhist teachings. Yanzhi refuted...
The *Tàxìnglùn* (Discourse on Attaining Nature), Sengzhao’s *Báihēilùn* (Discourse on White and Black), and Daosheng’s *Míngfó* (Elucidating the Buddha) are all profound and expansive;
they are particularly renowned for their principles and serve to inspire and encourage people’s minds (*Hongming ji*).
Yuan Can and He Zhenzhi. Yuan Can’s courtesy name was Jingqian.

He served as the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat and held the rank of Minister of Education (Situ). The reclusive scholar Gu Huan, although adhering to both teachings, favored Daoism in his personal inclination.
Yuan Can composed a treatise to refute him, asserting that while the teachings of Confucius and Laozi take the governance of the mundane world as their foundation, the Śākya [Buddhist] school...

Taking transcendence as its primary tenet, its departure is already distinct, and its destination is likewise different. Furthermore, the Way of the Immortals (xian dao) prizes the transformation of the physical form, whereas Nirvana (niepan) prioritizes the cultivation of the spirit.
Those who transform their forms may reach the profound mysteries with white hair, yet they remain unable to escape death;
those who cultivate their spirits diminish worldly delusions day by day until they abide in serene permanence. The Way of Nirvana is the realm where there is no death. Cultivating...

If the spirits are such as this, what is meant by their being "the same"? At that time, the Attendant He Zhenzhi, upon seeing the *Quanyixialun* (Treatise on Exhorting Barbarians and Chinese), was deeply unsettled by it.
He sent a letter to Tanyou, stating in brief: "I know, therefore, that India is the central land within the great trichiliocosm;

thus, its spiritual resonance reaches the Supreme Sage. Since the Sage’s response lies there, his influence extends here. The clouds of the Dharma teachings move forth, and the rain of the Law is bestowed upon China."
The Way is one; form is two. The Way is the true; form is the mundane. To extinguish the mundane and return to the true necessarily requires departing from that mundanity.

Thus, while Confucius preserved his physical form to maintain ancestral sacrifices and fostered affection toward his six kin, Laozi took the cultivation of life and nourishment of nature as primary, regarding external things as secondary.
This [Laozi’s approach] may be called "exhaustively good," yet it cannot be called "exhaustively beautiful. How could it be compared to the Way?
The *Bodhi* [Era] was established by the Holy Muni.
It began in the Jiwei year of Emperor Gao (479) and ended in the Renwu year of Emperor He (502). There were seven rulers over a period of twenty-three years. The capital was Jiankang in the Qi state.

The Emperor Gao was named Daocheng; his courtesy name was Shaobo. His surname was Xiao, and he was a native of Lanling. He was the twenty-fourth-generation descendant of the Han Prime Minister Xiao He.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Jianyuan era, the Emperor visited Zhuangyan Temple to listen to Dharma Master Xingyuan lecture on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
The high officials and ministers assembled in full. Because the imperial throne was somewhat distant, they could not hear the sound of the Dharma.

Zhang Xu, the Director of the Secretariat, requested that the lecture seat be moved closer to the Emperor’s seat. Huiyuan did not comply. The Emperor then moved his own seat closer to listen to the Dharma. The Emperor once transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*. On the eighth day of the fourth month, he regularly cast golden images; on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he established the "Bowl Offering" (*bōshén*) at the entire monastery to provide meals for the monks.
He founded Zheshan and Zhengguan Monasteries (according to local gazetteers and the *Hongming ji*).
Emperor Wu—his taboo name was Yi, his courtesy name Xuanyuan—was the eldest son of Emperor Gao. In the first month of the second year of the Yongming era, Xingyuan of Dinglin Monastery passed away.
The Emperor sent a letter to his disciple Faxian, saying: "I have learned that Xingyuan has met his end; my disciples have already been informed by me during the night."
"You possess profound knowledge. It would be best for you to depart from here at once. I look forward to meeting the Dharma Master so that we may discuss your auspicious dream.

In the seventh year, the Emperor, believing that the Great Being Baozhi was deluding the masses, had him arrested and sent to the prison in Jiankang. Prisoners saw the Great Being wandering through the markets and streets;
yet upon inspection, he was still found within the prison. He then said to the officials, "Outside the gate, there are two carriages with food served in golden bowls. You..."
"You may accept it. Subsequently, Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling sent offerings. Lü Wenhuan, the Magistrate of Jiankang, reported this to the Emperor. The Emperor expressed regret and apologized.
He welcomed [Sengzhong] into the imperial palace and lodged him in Huilin Garden. That year, Sengzhong passed away. Sengzhong had once been seen by the Emperor in the Qianzhi Hall;
he addressed the Emperor simply as "the poor monk" (*pindao*). The Emperor asked the Chancellor Wang Jian about this, and Wang replied: "In antiquity..."
"What title do śramaṇas use? he asked. He replied, "Since the Jin and Song dynasties, most have used 'poor man of the Way' (píndào). However, you should allow me to take a seat.

The Emperor said, "To bow or prostrate would be excessive; there is no objection to using one's name. The Emperor greatly honored the teachings of the Dharma and established the two monasteries of Zhaoxian and Youxuan (according to the *Shijian fangzhi*).

Emperor Ming’s posthumous title was [Wenxuan], his name being Luán (Luan), and his courtesy name Jǐngqī (Jingqi). He was the son of Prince Dao of Shì'ānzhēn (Shi'an Zhenwang). He changed the reign era to Jiànwǔ (Jianwu).

The Emperor frequently observed the six periods of fasting and cultivated the ten wholesome deeds; he recited scriptures such as the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, established Guīyī Temple (Guiyi Si), and commissioned the construction of the Thousand Buddhas.
*Jinxiang* (Local Gazetteer). Xiao Ziliang, styled Ziliang, was enfeoffed as Prince of Jingling.
Together with Crown Prince Wenhui, he was both deeply devoted to Buddhist principles; moreover, Ziliang frequently summoned [monks].

He invited renowned monks to lecture on the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). The flourishing of the honored Dharma was unprecedented in the region south of the Yangtze River. At times, he personally served food and water to the assembly of monks.
Ziliang once dreamed that the Heavenly King Tathāgata of the Universal Radiance World in the East preached the *Dharmaparyāya of Pure Abiding and Pure Conduct*.
Consequently, he composed the twenty fascicles of the *Jingzhuzi* (The Son of Pure Abiding). "Pure Abiding" is the Chinese translation of the Sanskrit term *brahma-vihāra*.

"Sā" means to purify one's body, speech, and mind, abiding in accordance with the precepts. A "pure practitioner" is so called because when all karmas are purified, they transform and act within the world (as recorded in the *Hongming ji*).
Liu Ji’s mother, Lady Ming, fell ill. Ji recited the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva several tens of thousands of times.
One night he dreamed of a monk who said, "The lady's lifespan has come to an end. Because of your sincere devotion and steadfast resolve, I shall extend it for you. Sixty days later...
He passed away. When the mourning shed was erected at his grave, he wailed with such intense grief that two white cranes were often seen flying side by side beside it (*Nanshi*).

Liu Xiao (also written as Xu Xiao), courtesy name Shiguang, was a native of Pingyuan. He lived in seclusion to pursue his aspirations, serving his mother and elder brother with filial piety and fraternal devotion. Whenever his mother fell ill...

Liu Xiao dreamed that he was administering medicine; the following day, he felt some relief. His younger brother Liu Xu (style name Yandu) often wore a turban made of grain husks and was clad in a patched robe (*nà-yī*).

He frequently roamed through mountains and marshes, lingering there until he forgot to return home. Xu was skilled in profound discourse (*xuán-yán*) and was particularly adept in the Buddhist scriptures (*shè-diǎn*).

Together with his elder brother Xiao, he attended lectures at various temples on Mount Song and subsequently built a hermitage by the eastern stream of Songyi Temple, intending to spend the rest of his life there.
*Zhi* (from the *Nanshi*).
Liu Qiu, courtesy name Lingyu, was a native of Nanyang. During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he served as the Magistrate of Dangyang. Later, he moved his residence to Jiangling.

He did not serve in office and subsequently abstained from grain. He subsisted on *yu* rhizomes, hemp, and grass, wearing cloth sandals. He maintained a long-term fast and performed liturgical recitations during the six periods of the day without fail.
Setting aside all literary arts, he devoted himself exclusively to the profound study of Buddhist principles. He composed commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

At the beginning of the Jianyuan and Jianwu eras, he declined all summons and appointments. In the winter of the second year of Jianwu, he moved his residence to Jiangzhou. Shortly thereafter, white clouds hovered around him.
As he was pacing about the eaves and corridors, a rare fragrance entered the room; upon hearing the sound of a *qing* bell, he passed away (from the *Nan shi*).
Ming Sengshao, whose courtesy name was Xiulie, was a native of Pingyuan. He styled himself the "Gentleman of Pingyuan. His ancestors were from the lineage of Wu Taibo.
Yi was the son of Baili Xi. Mengming took his father’s name as his surname; Sengshao was a descendant of him.
Sengshao heard of the long-standing virtue of the śramaṇa Sengyuan and went to visit him. At that time, Sengyuan resided at Dinglin Temple.
Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty wished to go to the temple to see him. Sengyuan asked Sengshao, "If the Son of Heaven comes, how will you, Layman, respond to him?"
Shao said, "A man of the mountains and marshes ought indeed to carve out a cave-dwelling to escape the world. If my refusal is not accepted, I shall follow the precedent of Master Dai.
During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, I once visited Mount She and resolved to spend the rest of my life there. An old villager then cautioned him, saying:

The mountains were infested with fierce tigers and venomous snakes; for this reason, they had long been abandoned by travelers. Sengshao said, "Among poisons, none surpasses the three poisons [of greed, hatred, and delusion].

If one possesses loyalty and integrity, one can tread upon fire and water; what power then can a fierce beast exert? He then constructed a thatched hut and lived there for some twenty years, having no dealings with the world of men.
Once, while lecturing on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* with the Dhyāna Master Fadu, he suddenly [awoke] in the middle of the night.

He saw golden light illuminating the room; within the light were the forms of terraces and pavilions. In the seventh year of the Yongming era, he consequently donated his residence to establish a temple.
Furthermore, he dreamed that a rock possessed the radiant splendor of the Tathāgata, and he conceived the desire to carve an image. Shortly thereafter, he passed away.
Sengshao’s second son, Zhongzhang, who served as the Magistrate of Linyi, then collaborated with Master Du to carve three images of Amitābha Buddha.
One *zhang* and one foot five inches, including two bodhisattvas (*Xiqiasi ji*; *Nanshi*).
Wang Jin (style name Jianqi), a native of Langye, was a man of learning who served as the Clerk of Records (*lu shi can jun*) during the Qi dynasty. He founded Toudu Monastery.
The inscription reads briefly as follows: "Now we have heard that those who draw water from a pond that rises and falls cannot fathom its depth;
those who look up at the azure color of the heavens cannot know its distance. How much more so for that which lies beyond sight and hearing—existing yet as if non-existent."
The manifestations of mental activity are neither born nor extinguished. For this reason, Vimalakīrti remained silent in the kingdom of Magadha to open the ford for ceasing speech;
he sealed his lips in the city of Vaiśālī to provide passage upon the road of attaining the meaning.

Yet, when the scope of the *Yi* hexagrams reaches its limit within this realm, that which is beyond all designation takes form on the other shore. As for "the other shore," if one leads it toward existence...

Having distanced oneself from the four currents of existence and pushed them toward the Unconditioned, one then humbly propagates the Six Perfections; these cannot be known through the stages of learning, nor can they be reached by the conceptual mind.
This is even more so regarding the aggregates of Nirvāṇa, let alone the Dharmakāya, which is perfectly manifest and established in profound accordance with the cosmic norm.
A single sound accords with all things as the *gong* and *shang* notes operate in secret. Thus, the Tathāgata appeared for the benefit of the world, taking birth in the royal house;

relying on the carriage of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), he rescued those swept away by the rushing river of time. He opened the gate of the eightfold noble path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*) to provide great shelter for an age of mutual ruin.

He practiced the gift of non-abandonment, proclaimed unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*), manifested a brilliance that does not shine [in vain], and exercised the skillful means (*upāya*) of forgetting artifice. At that time...
The meaning is profound and far-reaching; the task of enlightened activity is complete. Yet, he brushed away his robes beneath the twin *śāla* trees and cast off his sandals upon the golden sands;

he was not bound by coming or going, returning instead to the silence of non-substantiality and non-action, and to the spirit that is neither disturbed nor exhausted. How great is this unceasing majesty!
Once the True Dharma had vanished and the teachings of the Elephant Vehicle had declined, Mātr̥ceṭa offered his subtle praise and Nāgārjuna sought through the void. Together—

He shook the sagging ropes of discipline and restored all that was severed; he spread the Dharma-cloud over the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), bringing morning coolness to the burning house, and he shone the sun of wisdom upon the broad thoroughfares, turning the deep gloom of night into dawn.

Thus, he was able to provide a master of strategy from within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, while the ninety-six heterodox schools found no firm defense against him. Subsequently, as the teachings were extended eastward, the practice of the doctrine shifted south.

The two *Zhuang* kings of Zhou and Lu personally manifested the illumination of the night vision; the two *Ming* emperors of Han and Jin both inscribed their names upon the adornments of the vermilion and green.
Thereafter, surviving texts appeared at intervals and monasteries stood in rows facing one another. Daosheng and Kumārajīva followed in each other's tracks west of the mountains;
Lin Yuan followed closely behind in Jiangzuo. As for Toudou Monastery, it was established by the śramaṇa Huizong (*Wenxuan*; previously composed by [the author]).
*Sengshi* (Ten fascicles).
Kong Zhigui, courtesy name Dezhang, was a native of Kuaiji. From his youth, he enjoyed a fine reputation; when Governor Wang Sengqian saw him, he held him in high esteem.

He was appointed as Chief Clerk (zhubù). Together with Jiang Yan, he took charge of literary composition and rose to the rank of Left Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs (shàngshū zuǒchéng).

He once submitted a memorial in response to Xiao Ziliang, which stated in brief: "The people have long since received your benevolence in guiding and uplifting them, and have deeply benefited from your great compassion and expansive instructions.

As for the Great Awakened One’s luminous teachings and the true source of Prajñā—the very principles that the people have revered throughout their lives—they have never been contravened; we continue to look up to and receive them."

I have relied upon Your Excellency’s instruction and drawn from Your Excellency’s influence. Guided by the Right Vehicle and led by the Universal Precepts, the six obstructions of the people have been suddenly dispelled and the five passions are now being diligently cultivated. They have turned their hearts to prostrate themselves and uphold the teachings;

unexpectedly, in a single day, they attained sudden and great enlightenment. That which guides this awakening originates entirely from Your Excellency. I am overcome with the utmost joy. (From the *Hongming ji*)
*Fófǎjīntāngbiān*, Scroll Three. Re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎjīntāngbiān*, Scroll Four.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai during the Liang Dynasty.
The capital was established at Jiankang. Beginning with Emperor Wu’s *wénwǔ* year (*rénwǔ*) and ending with Emperor Jing’s *dìngchōu* year, there were four sovereigns for a total of fifty-six years.
[The first was] Emperor Wu.
The Emperor’s taboo name was Yan, his courtesy name Shuda. He was a native of Zhongli in Nanlanling, surnamed Xiao.

Upon ascending the throne, the Emperor resolved to share the same vow as all living beings toward Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and to together realize Universal Knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Governing with hands folded in ease, he extensively propagated the teachings of the scriptures (as recorded in the *Sanbao ji*).

In the first year of the Tianjian era, Baozhi arrived at the capital; the Emperor held him in great honor and affection. He issued an edict stating: "His traces reside within the mundane world, yet his spirit roams the profound mysteries."
[He was] serene. Neither water nor fire could burn or submerge him; neither snakes nor tigers could harm or frighten him. In terms of Buddhist principles, he surpassed the level of the Śrāvakas;
in terms of his reclusion, he was a transcendent superior even to the highest hidden immortals. How can one constrain him with worldly laws and ordinary sentiments?
From now on, let him propagate the teachings as he pleases; do not prohibit him. (From the *Benzhuan*). In the second year, [the monk] Yunguang of Fayun Temple...

When the Dharma Master preached the sutra, heavenly flowers of precious jewels rained down. The Emperor, believing this was a sign that he had attained sainthood (*arhatship*), burned a memorial at night in the Hanguang Palace to invite Baozhi and Yunguang to a vegetarian feast.
On the following day, Baozhi arrived alone. The Emperor marveled at this (according to the *Monastic History*).

On the eighth day of the fourth month of the third year, the Emperor led over twenty thousand monastics and laypeople to ascend the Chongyun Palace; there he renounced the Daoist path to embrace Buddhism and personally composed [a text].
Prayer Text. In the ninth year, the Emperor established Guangzhai Monastery at his former residence and cast a great Buddha image of gilded copper.
In the tenth year, he constructed Daji Jing Monastery on Mount Zhong and provided for a thousand monks with lectures held during the four seasons.

In that same year, Hao Qian and others traveled to India to invite a sandalwood image; its king had a replica carved and entrusted it to Qian. That year, they returned, and the Emperor welcomed them to the capital.

At the Imperial Mausoleum, he established a *zhāi* ceremony to ordain monks, issued a general amnesty, and prohibited killing. From that time on, the Emperor ate vegetarian food and renounced sensual desires (*Tongjian*).
In the thirteenth year, when Baozhi was about to pass away, he went to the inner palace to bid farewell to the Emperor. The Emperor was greatly alarmed and asked, "How long will my life last?
Baozhi did not answer, but instead pointed to his head and then to his neck. When Baozhi entered nirvana, the Emperor built a stupa for him at Zhongshan Temple.
It is said that on the eighth day of the fourth month in the eighteenth year [of the Liang dynasty], the Emperor invited Dharma Master Huie about to the Dengjue Hall;
setting aside his imperial robes, he donned the monastic *kāṣāya* and received the Bodhisattva precepts. In the seventh month of the Gengzi year of the Putong era, Bodhidharma arrived at Guangzhou.

The Regional Inspector submitted a memorial reporting this, and the Emperor dispatched an envoy to welcome him. In the eleventh month, he reached Jinling, where he did not respond to the Imperial summons.
Hei subsequently crossed the Yangtze River and entered Wei. In the first year of the Datong era, he completed the construction of Tongtai Temple.

On the third day, the Emperor visited the temple and performed the ritual of "offering his body. In the first year of the Zhongdatong era, he again visited Tongtai Temple and established a fourfold *amogha* (unrestricted) assembly, practicing the "Great Renunciation of Purity," and expounded upon the title of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly (*Tongjian Sengshi*). In the fourth year of the Dading era, he renovated the Long... [text continues].

He established the Ganshi Monastery and provided offerings of the food of unimpeded Dharma-joy for seven years. In the seventh year, the Emperor visited Hualin Garden to lecture on the *Golden Letter Prajñā-triśikṣā Sūtra* (as recorded in the *Jigulüe*).
The Emperor occupied the throne for forty-nine years; he honored the Buddha and followed the Dharma, abstaining from alcohol and prohibiting the consumption of meat.
Although he lived in a dark chamber, he always wore his robes and cap; even in the heat of summer, he never bared his shoulders.

He visited five temples, including Guangzhai and Tongtai, where he regularly provided for a thousand monks. He composed various prefaces and treatises whose subtle principles were worthy of contemplation.
Possessing pure karma, he passed away at the age of eighty-six (Shi Jian).
Emperor Jianwen’s personal name was Gang; his courtesy name was Shizuan, though some say it was Liutong. He was the third son of Emperor Wu.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Dabao era, he issued an imperial decree ordaining men into the monastic order and personally composed a prayer text, which stated in brief: "I, your disciple Xiao Gang, by means of..."

This merit of establishing a fast to deliver sentient beings universally delivers those of the six realms and four modes of birth from craving and desire, forever uproots ignorance, and leads them to cultivate Prajñā as true children of the Buddha (*Hongming ji*).
The Emperor entrusted his heart to the wondrous Dharma and extensively surveyed the profound scriptures.
He compiled the *Zhuanfaji* (Record of the Collection of Dharma) in two hundred fascicles and the *Fobao lianbi* (Linked Jades of the Dharma Treasure) in over four hundred pieces.
He also founded Zijing and Baoen Monasteries (*Bianzheng lu*).
Emperor Yuan’s posthumous name was Yi; his courtesy name was Shicheng. He was the seventh son of Emperor Wu.

While he was the Prince of Xiangdong, he donated his palace to establish Tiangong Monastery and invited Fachong to reside there, where he devoted himself to the veneration of Buddhist affairs. He ascended the throne at Jiangling and changed the era name to Chengsheng.
He once composed a book titled *Jinlouzi*.

Xiao Tong, styled Deshi and with the childhood name Weimo, was the eldest son of Emperor Wu. After his death, he was posthumously honored with the title Zhaoming. At the age of five, he could recite the entire canon from memory.

He was well-versed in the Five Classics and possessed a natural disposition for Buddhism. Within the Eastern Palace, he established the Huiyi Hall (Hall of Wisdom and Meaning) and invited the renowned monks of the realm to reside there, designating it as a place for the assembly of the Dharma. He perused almost the entirety of the Buddhist sūtras and śāstras.
