He compiled liturgical manuals for religious rites and established doctrines such as the Three Truths (*trisatya*). For twenty years since leaving the palace, he had not maintained musical entertainment, devoting himself solely to—
He took the Dharma as his joy. He fell ill and passed away; the whole world wept for him as if they had lost a close relative (*Liang Shu*).
Prince Shaoling, whose name was Lun, was a son of Emperor Wu. He submitted a memorial stating: "Lun has heard that the majestic marks of the Tathāgata are so sublime as to transcend all existence..."
O Summit! Your subtle and wondrous form shines boundlessly and vast. You manifest for all beings by means of the golden wheel; you respond to the common folk by relying upon the silver grain.
You whet the sharp blade of Prajñā and gather the wondrous fruit of Nirvāṇa. You float across the bitter sea of birth and death, delivering beings to the other shore of eternal bliss.
Thus, you can lower the clouds of compassion and let fall the rain of sweet nectar. At the seven locations and eight...
The principle of his conversion and instruction is inexhaustible; the methods for benefiting beings through the Four Truths and the four periods of teaching are endless.

He causes those lost in the dense forest of false views to gaze upon the gateway of the Dharma without weariness, and those who are deaf, blind, and parched with craving to yearn for its profound depths and turn back from their delusions.

The Bodhi tree first sprouted in Kapilavastu, and the sound of his virtuous teachings flourished in the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang. Relying on these three types of supernormal knowledge, he illuminates the deluded.
Regarding the loss of the path: by relying on these seven factors of enlightenment, one may extricate oneself from the suffering of the long night.

It is fortunate that we have encountered the Emperor, a Bodhisattva who responds to Heaven and governs all things, who sits upon his throne to preside over the people. He bestows unhindered eloquence to welcome the common folk and, through the power of his original vows, gathers in and protects sentient beings.

Thus, he is able to administer medicine according to the individual's condition, manifesting expedient means to reveal the causal roots, exalting the purport of the One Vehicle and expanding the Ten Stages.

This is the foundation [of our practice]. Thus, the myriad realms turn toward it and all receive the gift of correct consciousness; spirits of both the hidden and manifest realms alike receive guidance and salvation.
Humanity gives rise to the vow of Equal Enlightenment, and all things arouse the mind of Bodhi.

In the past, when I had not yet fathomed the source of principle, I followed external paths—like one who, desiring sweet fruit, instead plants bitter seeds. Now that I have awakened from my delusions, I roughly understand the direction of my return and receive [the teachings].
The Bodhisattva’s Great Precepts restrain both body and mind. One abandons the heterodox winds of Laozi and enters the true teachings of the Dharma-stream.

I humbly pray that Your Majesty’s divine compassion will graciously grant your permission. [From the *Hongming ji*] He once abdicated his palace to establish a temple (the present-day Tiefo Temple in Wuchang).
Prince Jian'an's name was Wei;
he was the eighth son of Emperor Wu. During the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Senghu who saw a light between the cliffs at Shicheng Mountain in Shan County.
He then carved it into the form of a Maitreya Buddha image; however, he had only just completed the face of the Buddha when [the work was interrupted].
The project to protect the deceased was continued by the śramaṇa Sengshu at the end of the Qi dynasty, yet it too remained unfinished.

When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty led his army eastward, he found that funds were insufficient for the expenses; consequently, Prince Jian'an took the bronze Buddha from Xiangyang and melted it down to make coinage.

Later, when the Prince governed Jiangzhou, he was suddenly stricken with a malignant disease. In the sixth year of the Tianjian era, Lu Xian of Wujun, the Magistrate of Shifeng, dreamed of three monks.
People said to Hui-xian, "Prince Jian'an has been afflicted by illness that has not yet healed; if you can restore the stone statue in Shan County, he will surely recover.
For some years, Hui-xian had gradually forgotten this. Suddenly, he encountered a monk who asked him, "Do you still remember the matter concerning Prince Jian'an?
The monk vanished instantly. Hui-xian was greatly enlightened and informed the Prince of this. The Prince immediately summoned Sengyou of Dinglin Temple to administer the Vinaya.

The Master provided him with gold, instructing him to oversee the construction of the image. In the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era, the work was completed: the pedestal was fifty feet high and the Buddha’s body was one hundred feet tall.
After the image was finished, the King’s illness was immediately cured. Initially, the Jin-dynasty śramaṇa Tan Guang had gone to a stone chamber on Mount Shan to sit in meditation.
A tiger and a python came before him; Tan Guang conferred the precepts upon them, and they departed. There was also a mountain deity there.
He arrived in full regalia, and Guang preached the Dharma for him. Thereupon, Guang established a monastery called Yin’guo;
his fellow student Yulan further founded a temple beside it called Xuanhua; and Hu also built a monastic complex called Shicheng.
These three monasteries stood like the legs of a tripod (from Liu Xie’s *Stele of the Stone Image* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Lu Chui served as the Director of the Bureau of Personnel in the Ministry of Personnel. Together with his elder brother Lu Liao and his younger brother Lu Zu, they all possessed great reputations and were known as the "Three Lus.
At the beginning of the Tianjian era, he joined Liu Xiaochao and others in the "Longmen Excursion. He once composed the epitaph for the stupa of Dharma Master Zhizhi.
Briefly stated: The Dharma Master himself said his surname was Zhu and his name was Baozhi. He mingled his tracks with the common crowd and used obscure speech;

he had no fixed dwelling place, and his clothing, food, and drink were irregular and inconsistent. During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he moved in and out of Mount Zhong and traveled between the capital and its suburbs, yet his extraordinary nature was not yet known.
At the transition between the Song and Qi dynasties, he gradually manifested miraculous traces: with disheveled hair and bare feet, he carried a staff and held a mirror.
Sometimes he would demand wine and food, and at other times he would not eat for several days; he frequently exposed matters concerning longevity and peril.
Consequently, his fame spread far and near, and people vied with one another to provide sacrificial offerings. Crowds of local officials and commoners gathered wherever he stayed.

Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, deeming him a deceiver and a show-off, had him arrested and sent to the Jiankang prison, where he was held under strict guard and confinement; yet on the following morning, he was still seen wandering through the marketplace.
The news spread through the marketplace and everyone was astonished, passing it on to one another. The county authorities immediately searched for him, yet he remained within the census register.

That night, he again spoke to the jailer, saying, "Two carriages of food will arrive outside the gate; you may take them. Shortly thereafter, Crown Prince Wenhui and King Wenxuan provided the offerings.
When this matter was reported to Emperor Wu, the Emperor felt deep remorse and submission. He welcomed [the Master] into the inner gardens and treated him with great generosity.
He enjoyed the highest honors. On the sixth day of the twelfth month of the Bingyin year during the Zhongda era, he passed away at midnight in the Buddha Hall of Huālín Yuán.

The inscription reads: When he was about to transform [beings] in the City of Vaiśālī, the Golden Grain (Kanakamuni) descended as a spirit. When he was about to visit the lands beyond the borders, the Jade Maiden (Yaśodharā) entrusted her life to him.

He humbled his body to extend the teachings; he manifested his utility while concealing his name. How magnificent was this Great Being! His provisional traces appeared in the imperial capital. As for his lineage... [text fragment ends]
In detail: dwelling in the towns and villages, he is rarely seen. He is like a geyser erupting from the earth, or like an apparition appearing in the void.

I lament these sights and take pity on this whirlwind of worldly phenomena. To guide others across the boat-bridge of liberation, he employs skillful means (*upāya*). His words do not establish fixed rules; his conduct does not conform to ordinary norms.

At times he distinguishes himself from the multitude; at other times he manifests as one of them. Whether sitting or standing, he may vanish or remain. He may analyze the physical body or separate the spirit. Through earnest cultivation and transformation, he leaves no trace and no mark.

The Ford. His form was active while his mind was tranquil; outwardly wild, yet inwardly discerning. He observed the past to gauge the future; he perceived the subtle to know the manifest. A step taken and the walls stood firm; a word spoken and the winds were bowed.

Those who merely recognized his spiritual wonders could not fathom his depth. When his karma was exhausted, it was difficult to find a successor; when his causes were exhausted, no one came to his aid.
The cloud of wisdom ceased by day; the lamp of compassion grew dim at night. Before the golden coffin had decayed, the entire cave remained intact. Alas for the darkness!
Silence. He returned to this profound gateway.
Fu Xi, courtesy name Xuānfēng, was a native of Yìwū. He was born on the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jiǎnwǔ era of Emperor Míng of the Qi dynasty.
He married into the family of Fu Xuanci and took the surname Liu. He had two sons named Pujian and Pucheng.
A Śramaṇa from the Western Regions, Śaṃthūta, instructed Huixi to observe his reflection in water; thereupon, he saw a halo and a jeweled canopy. Huixi smiled and attained awakening.
He subsequently built a hermitage among twin *śimśapā* trees on Mount Song in Yiwu, where he styled himself the "Great Sage of Future Rebirth at the Twin Trees."
The official ordered his disciples to present the letter at the palace gate, addressing Emperor Wu as the Sovereign of the Nation and the Bodhisattva Who Saves the World.

The Emperor’s reply was issued, stating: "Great Being, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, you may come as you please. The Emperor had previously ordered the gates locked in order to observe his intentions.

The Great Being drew a wooden mallet from his sleeve; with a single strike, all the gates opened. He beheld the Emperor in the Hall of Kind Words (*Śubhavāda*). The usher announced him, but he did not bow;
he ascended directly to the imperial couch and conversed face-to-face. After the meal was concluded, he departed for Mount Zhong and sat beneath the pines of Dinglin Monastery.
The Great Being returned to the East to build monasteries and transcribe scriptures; he visited the capital three times, yet it was impossible to ordain monks or laypeople there.

Counting [the days], one day the Great Being (Mahāsattva) appeared before the Emperor wearing a patched robe (*kaṣāya*), a crown upon his head, and sandals on his feet. The Emperor asked, "Is this a monk?
The Great Being pointed to his crown. "Is this the Way (*mārga*)? He pointed to his sandals. "Is this a layman? He pointed to his patched robe.
While the Great Being was practicing the Way in the mountains, he constantly saw the Seven Buddhas before him and Vimalakīrti behind him; only Śākyamuni...
Jia frequently conversed with the Great Being (Mahāsattva). Seven days after the Great Being entered parinirvāṇa, Chen Zhongqi, the Magistrate of the county, came to pay his respects.

During the transmission of the incense, he still turned over the various incense-offering trays as if they were palms; the entire assembly was struck with wonder. An imperial decree was issued for Xu Ling to compose a stele inscription for the mountain monastery.
The Great Being once composed the *Xinwang Ming* (Inscription on the Mind-King), which circulated in the world (as recorded in his biography).

Liu Xie, courtesy name Yanhe, was a native of Dongyan. He served as a Tongshi She-ren (Courtier for Ceremonial Affairs). Prince Zhaoming held him in high esteem; indeed, regarding all temple and pagoda inscriptions...
The steles were all composed by him. In this year, he requested to leave the household life and was granted the name Huìdì.
He authored the *Wénxīn diáolóng* in fifty chapters, which discusses the literary styles of antiquity and the present (according to the *Nánshǐ*).
He was named Dian Yin, styled Zixi.
He was the son of Yan and the grandson of Shangzhi. Dian had bright eyes and elegant eyebrows; his appearance was dignified and refined. He did not take pride in his family lineage.
He subsisted on vegetarian food and did not drink wine. At the end of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he was summoned to serve as the *xian* (attendant) to the Crown Prince.

Ma Qi was repeatedly summoned by the early Qi dynasty to serve as Secretariat Director, but he did not accept either appointment. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty had a long-standing friendship with Dian;

when the Emperor summoned him to be Palace Attendant, Dian likewise did not rise to the call. He shared an unbreakable bond of friendship with Xie Lun of Chenjun, Zhang Rong of Wuguo, and Kong Dezhang of Kuaiji.
The Dian family had followed the Buddhist faith for generations. His younger brother, Yin, styled Zijì, served under the Qi dynasty as the Governor of Jian'an.

Later, Qian was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shangshu Ling). He entered Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong to listen to lectures on the Buddhist scriptures, mastering them all thoroughly.

Zhi Yin, however, because Mount Kuaiji abounded in spiritual wonders, went there to travel. He resided at Yunmen Temple on Mount Ruoye. His two elder brothers, Qiu and Dian, both followed him in reclusion;
the world called Dian "Mount Dain" (the Great Mountain) and Yin "Mount Xiaoshan" (the Small Mountain), while Qiu was known as "Mount Dongshan" (the Eastern Mountain). It is said:
He Shi was one of the "Three Highs" (of Wu). Hei Yin subsequently moved back to Wu and went to the Western Temple at Huqiu to lecture on the sutras and treatises.
He constantly prohibited the killing of living beings; once, when a hunter was pursuing a deer, the deer ran directly toward Yin and lay down, refusing to move.

Furthermore, extraordinary birds resembling cranes gathered at the lecture hall and became tame and familiar. He Dian and He Yin both established great principles and clarified the Buddha-dharma (*Nanshi*).
Shen Yue, courtesy name Xiwen, was a native of Wukang in Wu Commandery. He did not drink wine and had few desires from his youth. His living quarters were simple and frugal;

he built a residence on a suburban hill, for which he once composed the "Fu on Suburban Dwelling" (Jiaojufu) to record these matters. He served in office as high as the Vice President of the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Puye), and his posthumous title was [Xing].
Yin once composed a text of repentance, which states in brief: "I, the disciple Shen Yue, prostrate myself and address the Buddhas and the assembly of holy ones.
From this present life back to the beginningless past, my accumulated karmic offenses are so vast and varied that they truly cannot be calculated by words or imagery."
My consciousness was dim regarding past conditions, leaving me unable to testify to them. From the time I first reached childhood, I possessed a mind of craving and desire;

I did not recognize compassion, nor could I distinguish between sin and its retribution. Furthermore, looking back upon my youth, when my blood and breath were at their peak, I was entangled by the accumulation of habitual tendencies.

My anger shifted toward those who were merely straightforward, and with a harsh countenance and severe voice, I caused turmoil from morning until evening, never resting even as dusk fell. As soon as a preceding thought had passed away, a subsequent thought would arise again.
Ah! Like ripples on a foot-long wave, they ceaselessly arise; like the passing of a mere inch of shadow, moments fly by. Remorse and regret crowd my heart, leaving me ignorant of where to place it.
Now, before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and in the presence of the great assembly of the present Sangha, I vow to discipline myself and pursue self-reproach.

Furthermore, I have composed one scroll titled *The Treatise on Midday Meals*, which states: first, [the pursuit of] power, profit, and illustrious fame; second, [the allure of] seductive beauty and frivolity.
First is meat; second is wine; and third is that which is sweet, savory, rich, and greasy—all of which cause the mind and spirit to become clouded and deluded, making it impossible to attain the Way.

Therefore, the Sages prohibited these three matters. There are texts such as the "Vow Text for the Assembly of a Thousand Monks," the "Treatise on Compassion," the "Vow Text for Paying Homage to the Buddha," and the "Text on Casting Off the Body" (found in the *Hongming ji*).
Tao Hongjing, styled Tongming, was a native of Moling. His mother, Lady Huo, dreamed that two heavenly beings arrived at her home holding incense burners in their hands;
shortly thereafter, she became pregnant and gave birth to Hongjing. At the end of the Song dynasty, he served as a tutor to the princes. During the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty...
In the middle of the day, he removed his court robes and hung them at the Shenwu Gate. He submitted a memorial to decline his emoluments and retired to the Huayang Cave on Mount Juyong.
There he was titled the "True Man of Huayang. Having long-standing ties with Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, there was no major state matter upon which the Emperor did not consult him;
thus, he was popularly known as the "Minister within the Mountains. At the age of eighty-five, he passed away without illness. His posthumous title was Zhengbai (Pure and Upright).
Tao Sheng once erected a Bodhi White Stūpa on Mount Sanmao. Furthermore, he dreamed that the Buddha conferred upon him the prophecy of his name as the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama.
He then proceeded to the Aśoka Stūpa in Zan County, where he took a vow to receive the five great precepts. At the time of his death, he did not wish to bathe;

instead, he used a large *kāṣāya* robe to cover the top of his bedding so that it reached over his hands and feet. His disciples followed this practice. Senghongjing composed a record stating: [text follows].
The *Zhen'gao* states: "The Perfected Man Qingxu Pei had thirty-four disciples; eighteen of them studied the Buddhist Way.
The Perfected Man Ziyang Zhou had fifteen disciples; four of them understood the Buddha-dharma.
On Mount Tongbai, Wang Zijiao had twenty-five disciples; eight of them studied and practiced the Buddha-dharma" (*Liangshu*, "Biographies of the Three Wu").
Ruan Xiaoxu was a native of Chenliu.
At the age of thirteen, he mastered the Five Classics; at sixteen, he encountered a family tragedy. After completing the mourning period, he entered Mount Zhong to attend lectures.
He once used a deer forest as a *vihāra* (monastery), surrounding it with groves and ponds to sever all social ties; thus, few in the world [knew him].

He was able to meet him. He was on intimate terms with Pei Ziyě alone. After [Pei] passed away, his disciples conferred upon him the posthumous title of Wenzhen Chushi (Scholar of Literary Integrity).

He once modeled his work after Liu Xin’s *Qilüe* (Seven Categories) and subsequently composed the *Qilu* (Seven Records), which cataloged internal and external books and documents. The sixth of these is titled the *Fofa Lu* (Records of the Buddha-Dharma) (*Nanshi*).

Yu Xian (style name Yanbao) was a native of Xinye. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted, and he was well-versed in the classics and histories. By nature, he delighted in forests and springs;

he maintained a vegetarian diet and wore simple cloth garments, never engaging in worldly business. When Emperor Wu raised his army, an imperial decree appointed him as the Secretariat Director of the Pingxi Commandery. During the Putong era, an imperial decree [summoned him].
He was appointed as a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate, but he declined both positions. In his later years, he followed the teachings of Śākyamuni;

he established a *dōjō* within his residence and performed ritual recitations during the six periods of the day. Suddenly, after midnight, he saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan (Yuàngōng).

He addressed Sēn as "Master Shangxíng" and, having bestowed incense upon him, departed. Four years later, Master Yuan came again and said, "You must not remain here for long. Having finished speaking, [he vanished].
He passed away. The entire household heard a voice in the air proclaiming, "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.
Emperor Wu revered him and bestowed upon him the title Master of Chaste Integrity (Nanshi).

Dào Gài (courtesy name Mòguàn) was the great-grandson of Dào Yànzhi. He served as Minister of Personnel (*Liùbù Shàngshū*). In his private residence, he maintained a vegetarian diet, slept on a grass mat in an empty room, and had no female attendants.
Morning and evening, he followed monks in ritual chanting. Emperor Wu provided him with three sets of pure vegetarian meals each month.
All the stipends he received were dedicated to the two temples on Mount Jiang. When he passed away, his countenance remained as if alive; he died with two fingers bent.
(From the Liang History).
— Jiang Yan.

Yan, courtesy name Wéntōng, was appointed as a Palace Attendant during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty. During the Tiānjiàn era, he was promoted to Jinzǐguānglù Dàfū and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lǐlíng.
He composed the *Wúwéi Lùn* (Treatise on Non-Action), which states in brief: "A young gentleman of many generations visited the gate of Master Wúwéi and asked:
'Master, your wisdom and virtue are brilliantly integrated; your Way and righteousness are pure and far-reaching. There is no learning you have not investigated, and no... "

These matters have not been fully understood. Take, for instance, the scriptures of Śākyamuni’s Tripiṭaka, the books on the Way and its Power by Master Li (Laozi), the writings on the Six Arts by Confucius, and the arts that encompass all the various schools of thought;
these are truly the models and standards for ten thousand ages and the paragons of excellence for their respective times.
"Your Excellency has nobly retired from the world, concealing your traces to cultivate virtue and refusing office; this is indeed what those in official robes find contemptible.
The Master smiled and replied to him, saying: "I have heard that great beings descend into the world to extensively plant the roots of compassion, shattering the cage of birth and death."
He ascends to the other shore of Nirvana. He expounds the Three Vehicles to entice sentient beings; he discards all marks to return to the Real.

To those with wisdom, his coming and going are not perceived; to those with hearts, his beginning and end remain unknown. Thus he causes them to attain a state of profound stillness and eternal abiding.

Forever severing divergent paths, there is no change and no transition; one forever casts off a hundred anxieties and nourishes the spirit in tranquility, making the settling of the will one’s vocation.
Desiring that the words "Heaven will grant blessings" be unfailingly realized, one may unfold or roll up as one pleases, advancing or retreating according to nature.
To live in seclusion without regret, dwelling in obscurity with eternal integrity—what is there to be honored? What is there to be disparaged? You have attained this; I...
"What loss has he suffered? The young master felt abashed and withdrew with hesitant steps (*Hongming ji*).

He Jingshu—He Jingshu was a native of Donghai. During the Liang dynasty, he served as the Magistrate of Changcheng. He was upright and incorruptible, refusing all gifts and offerings. When the summer festival arrived...
Suddenly, he posted a notice at his gate accepting donations. Within a few days, he obtained one thousand *hu* of rice, all of which he used to substitute for the taxes and corvée labor of the poor.
He once obtained sandalwood to fashion a Buddha image, but it lacked a halo (*prabhāmaṇḍala*). Consequently, he dreamed of a śramaṇa coming with a monk’s staff and saying:
"In whose house can a paulownia shield be sought? The next day he purchased one. He asked, "How did you know this? Jingshu told him of his dream.
The He family was both surprised and delighted, and they gave it to him (*Nanshi* and *Gantong lu*).
The Later Liang had its capital at Jiangling. There were three rulers for thirty-three years. [The last was] Emperor Xuan.
The Emperor’s posthumous name was Chai. He was the third son of Crown Prince Zhāomíng. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Dàdìng.

He summoned the monk Qiān to serve as the Great Sangzhèng (Chief Administrator) of Jingzhou. When the Emperor was first enfeoffed as the Prince of Yuéyáng, he had governed Yuezhou, where he renovated both the brick and wooden stupas.
Previously, the śramaṇa Tányàn had constructed these stupas together with Xǔ Xún; however, before they were completed, Xún passed away. This continued until...
Fayuan was one hundred and twenty years old when he announced to his disciples, "Xu Xuandu is coming. When Xunzha arrived at the commandery, he went directly to the temple to visit the stupa.
Fayuan came out and called to him, saying, "Xu Xuandu, why have you come so late? The stupa from days of yore remains as it was before.
Fayuan then applied the power of samādhi to him, and Xunzha immediately realized that his previous life had been that of Xu Xuandu.
He then expanded the original buildings to pray for the blessings of his mother, Lady Baolin; thus it was named Baolin Temple (according to the temple records and the monastic supervisor).
Emperor Ming’s posthumous name was Kui. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Tianbao.
In Jingzhou, he constructed the four temples of Tianhuang, Zhiqu, Daming, and Baoguang, as well as the Siwang Temple (Bianzheng Lu).
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Four, Revised by the Tiantai Monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Five,
Compiled by the Shamen Xintai of Kuaiji.
The Tiantai śramaṇa Zhenqing read [this record] while in Jiankang, the capital of the Chen dynasty.
It began in the Dingchou year of Emperor Wu and ended in the Jiyou year of Emperor Houzhu. There were five sovereigns in total, spanning thirty-three years.
The year [was such-and-such].
Emperor Wu—whose taboo name was Baxian and whose courtesy name was Xingguo—was surnamed Chen. He was a native of Changxing in Wuxing. His origins were extremely humble; he himself claimed that...

He was a descendant of Shi, the Han-era Grand Administrator of Taichou. In the first year of the Yongding era, an imperial edict was issued to welcome the Buddha’s tooth relic from the residence of Lady Du, where a fourfold *amogha* (unobstructed) assembly was convened.
In the second year, he established the Dong’an, Xinghuang, and Tiangong monasteries in Yangzhou.
In the fifth month, the Emperor visited Dazhuangyan Temple to practice the rite of "casting away the body. On the following day, a memorial was submitted requesting his return to the palace.

He convened assemblies to provide offerings for the monks, distributed alms, and practiced the release of living beings. Of the more than seven hundred temples in Jinling that had been almost entirely destroyed by Hou Jing, the Emperor ordered their complete restoration.

He promoted the translation of scriptures and the exposition of the Way, issued an edict to transcribe the Tripitaka, commissioned the casting of gold and copper Buddha images, and ordained several individuals as both *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*.
(Bianzheng Lu). Emperor Wen’s posthumous name was Qiàn;
his courtesy name was Zihuá. He was the elder brother of Emperor Wu and the eldest son of King Zhāoliè. In the first year of the Tiānjiā era, he issued an imperial decree to the śramaṇas...

Men Baoqiong served as the Great Sang-tong (Patriarch) of the capital. In the fourth year [of the reign], he convened a Great Unobstructed Assembly at the Dajidian Hall to perform the ritual of the "Sacrifice of the Body.
He renovated old temples, transcribed Buddhist scriptures, and ordained monks on a scale twice that of the previous dynasty (as recorded in the *Liutie*).

He once composed the *Fahua Chanwen* (Text for the Lotus Repentance), which states in brief: "I humbly observe that through various causes and conditions, the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future have each already preached, or shall preach..."
Each of these skillful means is nothing other than true speech; all are the wondrous Dharma. In principle, there is no duality of extremes; in their destination, they must all converge.
It is only that the stages and ranks are divided into shallow and deep, and awakening varies in its speed. The rain of Dharma is of a single flavor, yet those who receive it differ;

the thunder of Dharma is a single sound, yet those who hear it are distinct. For this reason, the Small Vehicle and the Sudden Teaching each bear their respective names, such as "Śrāvaka" (Voice-hearer).

The Bodhisattva, following from this, took different paths. For instance, at the Deer Park, he first taught the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) of the sheep-cart, which concerns the nirvāṇa of extinction through ashes and the liberation of segmented existence.
Through the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Buddhas, he conformed to the faculties and capacities of the multitudes; this is called the "half-syllable" (*ardha-akṣara*).

It had not yet been called the "Three Points. Furthermore, when the three were unified into one to return to the root and revert to the source, the Mahāyāna sūtra was preached as the *Anantārtha* (Infinite Meanings).
The illusory city was extinguished midway, and the precious chariots were mounted at the crossroads. The bright pearl within the robe, which had been hidden, now appeared;
the precious jewel from the topknot was finally obtained. A jeweled stūpa emerged from the void, and Bodhisattvas surged forth.
The Great Earth manifests rare and wondrous events, and the subtle and sublime Dharma is realized—most supreme and most honored, difficult to encounter and difficult to meet.
As a disciple who, while still an ordinary person on the causal ground, has taken up the burden [of the teaching], I desire to follow the precedents of antiquity to rescue the common people.

Therefore, relying on the mind through the seven factors of enlightenment and binding my mindfulness to the four right efforts, I abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle to manifest the teaching of non-duality and study the way of the Tathāgata.

Proceeding thus, they open the gate of non-duality, drawing forth the masses of deluded beings and guiding those in confusion. Now, at this place, we respectfully establish the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Repentance for [number] monks.

We pray that the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna shall emerge from the earth and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra shall arrive through the air upon his elephant, both entering the ritual arena to bear witness to our merit.
May we collectively uphold the nature and characteristics of reality and together reach the state of non-arising.

(*Hongming ji*). Emperor Xuan’s taboo name was Xu, his courtesy name was Shaoshi. He was the second son of Emperor Zhaolie. In the first year of the Dajian era, he established the Taihuang [Monastery] in Yangzhou.

He further constructed a seven-storied pagoda at the temple. In this year, the Daoist master Ouyang Zhengze and others of the Jiuxian Guan on Mount Nanyue submitted a false memorial accusing Master Si of Mount Nanyue, claiming that he had accepted bribes from the Qi dynasty, gouged out the heart of the mountain, and was subsequently inciting demonic spirits.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy to pursue the Master. Seven days later, the Master arrived at the capital; the officials at the gates of all four city gates all saw the Master entering.

Struck with awe and awakened to its divine power, the Emperor welcomed the Master into the palace hall to provide offerings. He did not inquire about anything else, yet because the Daoist had practiced deception, he was sentenced to execution by public display;

the Master pleaded earnestly on his behalf, and thus he was pardoned. In the third year, an imperial edict was issued that all monks within the realm who had not yet completed five summer retreats since receiving the precepts must participate in the Vinaya department.
Large lecture halls for hearing the Vinaya were established at the major monasteries in the capital and provincial cities. [The Emperor] commanded Daoyuan...
He served as the Director of Vinaya Masters. The authorities provided him with clothing and food. During these seven years, he also constructed a seven-storied great stupa.

While the Emperor occupied the throne, he commissioned golden and copper Buddha images, transcribed the Tripitaka, and ordained monks and nuns on a scale that grandly emulated the former dynasty (the period of the Buddhist Supervisors).

The Later Sovereign, whose personal name was Shubao and courtesy name Yuanshou, was the eldest son of Emperor Xuan. In the first year of the Zhide era, he issued an edict appointing the śramaṇa Huikong as the Great Sangzheng of the capital.
In the second year, he issued a decree ordering the Dharma Master Zhiju of Huqiu to attend the Taiji Hall.
He lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. In the third year [of the reign], an imperial decree summoned Dhyāna Master Zhiyi to the capital to reside at Lingyao Monastery.

In the fourth month, he attended the Taicheng Hall to lecture on the titles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. After some time, he moved his residence to Guangzhai Monastery. The Emperor visited to listen to his lecture on the *Renwang-banruo-jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra).

At that time, the court deliberated that since many among the monks and nuns lacked professional training, they wished to require them to undergo scriptural examinations. However, [the Master] did not comply.
The officials who were conducting the searches all ceased their activities. Master Zhiyi admonished them, saying, "Tishya recited ten thousand words daily yet could not avoid falling into ruin;
Paṇḍita remembered but a single verse and thereby realized the four fruits of arhatship. To discuss the Way earnestly, how does it depend on voluminous recitation?

The Emperor was greatly pleased and immediately halted the searches. In the first month of the fourth year, he issued an edict for Master Zhiyi to attend the Chongzheng Hall to serve as Preceptor for the Crown Prince.
He conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon his son. He established a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks (according to the *Original Biography of Zhizhe* and the *Tongji*).
Xu Ling, whose courtesy name was Xiaomu, served as Minister of the Ministry of Personnel. When he was several years old, the śramaṇa Baozhi rubbed the crown of his head and said:
He was a stone qilin from the heavens who once listened to the Venerable Zhiyi lecture on the sutras and consequently made five vows: first, to maintain right mindfulness at the time of death;

second, not to fall into the three miserable realms; third, to take rebirth among human beings; fourth, to leave the household life as a celibate youth; and fifth, never to become a monk of worldly or secular character.
Later, during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he was born into the Zhu family of Jinyun. When he was eighteen years old and about to take a wife, [he renounced his home].
On the road, he encountered a foreign monk who said to him, "Young man, why do you intend to violate your former vow? The monk then showed him his five vows.

Having heard this, the young man no longer returned home; he immediately went to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai to become a disciple of Dharma Master Zhang’an, from whom he inquired about and received the essentials of the mind.
He realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and was given the title Chan Master Zhìwēi (according to the *Monastic Biographies* and the *General Record*).

Chen Bozhi, courtesy name Cezhi, was posthumously titled Prince of Yongyang. He was the eighth son of Emperor Wen. At the beginning of the Zhide era, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector of Dongyang.
He requested Master Zhi to open a lecture series and received the Bodhisattva precepts from him, observing the etiquette of a disciple while listening to his expositions by day.

He practiced seated meditation at night. Yuan was the son of Prince Houzhu. On the fifteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of Zhide, he held a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks at Chongzheng Hall and invited Zhiyi to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon him. The text of his request for the precepts states:
"To revere the Way and honor the teacher has been a tradition since ancient times. I pray that we may form a karmic bond through successive lifetimes, thereby fulfilling our original vows" (Tongji).

Jiang Zong (江總), courtesy name Zongchi (總持), was the grandson of Jiang Qian (蒨). Having lost his father at a young age, he lived with his maternal relatives. Thus, Du Fu’s poem says: "Jiang Zong was raised by his maternal family.

He served as a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (尚書) during the Chen dynasty. He once compiled the "Petition of the Chen Officials for the Emperor’s Confession" (*Chen qunchen qing Wudi chanwen*), which states in brief: "The Emperor..."

The Bodhisattva was sagacious and wise, brilliant and discerning; his breadth and depth equaled that of the sages. His mind was like empty space, and his insight reached the ultimate depths of Prajñā.

He gave rise to great and vast vows to bear the burden of all sentient beings. When the divine way flourished, he received this magnificent mandate. Yet, as the era of the hundred kings drew to a close, the times fell upon hardship.
The Five Peaks were shrouded in dust, and the six armies were in constant motion. His thoughts turned to the toil and suffering of the people, which deeply moved the Imperial heart. Thereafter—

Having deeply realized suffering and emptiness and attained ultimate faith in non-self, he then sat at the site of enlightenment and dwelt in quietude within his meditation chamber. Firmly establishing the roots of goodness, he perfected the practice of *dāna*.

Whether it were stone walls, mountains, and rivers, precious chariots, elephants, and horses, or even his own head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as his wife, children, kingdom, and city—he relinquished them all with solemnity and without exception.
Having made offerings to the Triple Gem, he then desired to shake off his robes for Mount Kōngtóng and stride loftily across the six realms of existence.
He retired to dwell in seclusion among the forest groves, traveling in the company of the Śākya clan. The Purple Microcosm Palace was left vacant, and the Yellow Canopy remained unoccupied;

the supreme spirits were stirred with alarm, and the vast earth was filled with trepidation. We disciples are bound by the delusions of craving and have constructed a web of afflictions through our karma.

Heaven gave birth to the people and established rulers to shepherd them; the common folk, in their weary toil, have no one to look up to but the sovereign. How could it be permitted that the Most Honored One should remain [in seclusion]?
To occupy a position of ten thousand chariots while extending a solitary wandering spirit; to be a sovereign and yet perform the deeds of a commoner.
Furthermore, when the barbarians harass the Central Kingdom and bandits and traitors plot their schemes, the watchtowers of Shuiren are alerted by the sun shining upon the fires of Ganquan;

when there are many mounds of corpses in the four suburbs, the majesty of the warships has not yet been displayed. If the Seven Sages were to lose their way and wander aimlessly upon the banks of the Fen River, [the world would fall into chaos]. Eight...
If the Emperor were to suddenly depart for the shores of the Yáo-chí Pond, upon whom would the world rely, and who among the ministers could offer him service?
We respectfully set aside such-and-so much money and such-and-so many goods, looking upward as an offering to the Triple Gem and the Great Assembly, to redeem the Emperor and all the Princes.

May what has been surrendered be restored entirely to their original positions. We prostrate ourselves with the hope that the Triple Gem of the ten directions and the virtuous monks present before us, by the power of their compassion...
Employing an unimpeded mind, the jade-luan carriage turned its reins. The golden gates opened wide; the hundred officials looked up with bated breath, and the gentry stood side by side.
With humble and sincere sincerity, I venture to make this request even at the cost of death (from the *Hongming ji*).
The Northern Wei dynasty had its capital at Pingcheng. It began with Emperor Taizu’s Bingxu year and ended with Emperor Xiaowu’s Jiayin year, until Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang.
There were thirteen sovereigns for a total of one hundred and forty-nine years.
Emperor Taizu:
His posthumous name was Gui. He belonged to the Tuoba clan. He was the legitimate grandson of Emperor Zhaocheng and the son of [Emperor] Xianming.

In the second year of the Huangshi era, an imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Faguo of Zhao Commandery as the *śramaṇa-tong* (Patriarch of the Clergy). This occurred during the initial pacification of Zhongshan and the various commanderies passed through.
When the state sees śramaṇas, all pay them respect; it prohibits the military from committing any offense against them. In the first year of the Tianxing era, an imperial edict stated:

"The rise of the Buddha-dharma has been far-reaching for a long time. Its merit in providing salvation extends secretly to both the living and the deceased. As for the divine traces and the bequeathed Dharma..."

Faith may thus be relied upon. His Imperial Decree ordered the relevant authorities to construct and adorn images and models within the capital city, and to repair and maintain the monasteries, so that those who possess faith and devotion would have a place of refuge. Thereupon, a five-storied stupa and a Sumeru Hall were erected in the capital.

The meditation halls and lecture halls at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa were all constructed with great magnificence (according to the *Wei Shu*). He wrote a letter to the Venerable Master Lang of Mount Tai, saying:
"Your Reverence’s virtue is equal to the seas and mountains, and your divine wisdom is far-reaching. I hope you will lend your strategic counsel to bring peace to the frontier regions.

I have now dispatched an envoy to deliver twenty rolls of silk, fifty pieces of white woolen cloth (*pāṃśukūla*), and two alms bowls. Upon arrival, I pray that you will accept them. The Emperor was born [with these gifts].

Knowing and placing faith in the Buddha, he constructed a fifteen-story stupa on Mount Yu. He also established two monasteries, Kaithai and Dingguo, and commissioned the transcription of scriptures and the casting of golden images (as recorded in the *Hongming ji* and local gazetteers).
Emperor Mingyuan (personal name: Si) was the eldest son of Taizu Daowu. In the first year of Yongxing, an imperial edict conferred upon Faguo the title of Marquis of Yicheng, Protector of the State.
In the first year of Shenrui, Faguo was further enfeoffed as the Viscount of Zhongxin (the beginning of the practice of monks receiving secular official titles). He constantly...
In the first year of the Taiyuan era, Faguo was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Ancheng. He died at the age of eighty;
the Emperor attended his funeral three times and bestowed upon him the posthumous title of General Laoshou (Venerable Longevity) and the honorific title of Lord Ling of Zhao Hu.
By imperial decree, Buddhist images were established in the capital, and śramaṇas were commissioned to propagate the teachings among the common people (*Beishi*).
Emperor Taizu (personal name: Tàomíng), the son of Emperor Yuán, issued an edict in the first year of the Shìguāng era ordering all temples throughout the empire to change their names to Zhāotí.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, the statues of various temples were carried in procession through the broad streets; the Emperor ascended the gate tower to observe the event from above, scattering flowers [upon them].
He performed rites of propriety. In the second year, on the Emperor’s birthday, a ritual arena for celebrating longevity was established at a Buddhist monastery.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, the śramaṇa Xuangao of Liang was exceptionally skilled in meditative contemplation;

the Emperor dispatched an envoy to welcome him to Pingcheng, where he treated him with great reverence and commanded Crown Prince Huang to serve him as his teacher. However, the Emperor became deluded by the words of Cui Hao and Kou Qianzhi and subsequently proceeded to destroy the Teachings.
[From the *Beishi*]. In the first year of the Zhengping era, the śramaṇa Tanshi had previously gone into hiding after the Emperor suppressed the Dharma.

Upon learning that the Dharma was about to flourish again, he traveled to the capital with his staff. When the officials informed the Emperor, the Emperor ordered him to be executed, but he was not harmed.

Enraged, the Emperor drew the dagger from his girdle and struck him himself, yet he was still not harmed. He was then thrown into a cage of tigers; all the tigers crouched in fear. Startled, the Emperor then invited him [to court].
Tanshi ascended the hall, prostrated twice, and apologized for his transgressions; he was granted permission to resume his instruction (Beishan lu).
Wencheng, whose personal name was Jun, was the eldest son of Jingmu Huang and the grandson of Taowu. In the first year of the Xing’an era, the ministers collectively petitioned him.
To restore the teachings of Śākyamuni, he issued an edict stating: "Now, those who act as emperors and kings must reverently serve the enlightened spirits and manifest the divine way.
If one can bestow kindness upon the common people and provide benefit to all classes of beings, their meritorious legacy shall be recorded and celebrated, even if they lived in antiquity."

How much more so for Śākyamuni Tathāgata, whose merit rescues the great trichiliocosm and whose grace flows through the realms of dust. Those who investigate the cycle of birth and death praise his profound insight;
those who examine the meanings of the texts value his wondrous gateways. He assists the prohibitions and laws of royal governance and augments the virtuous nature of benevolence and wisdom.
He repels the multitude of heterodoxies and expounds the True Dharma; therefore, from previous generations down to the present, there has been none who does not revere him. This is likewise my...

The state has always held [the Sangha] in high esteem. During the reign of Emperor Taizu (Wu), whose virtuous influence spread far and wide, śramaṇas and Daoist practitioners were as numerous as groves.
Yet, within the monasteries, there were those belonging to wicked factions. The previous dynasty investigated and punished those found guilty;
however, the authorities misunderstood the intent and prohibited everything outright. Emperor Jingmu often lamented this, and I, having inherited the great legacy, am likewise resolved to address it.
He promoted the Holy Path by ordering that each prefecture and county throughout the realm establish one Buddhist monastery (*stūpa*).

He permitted those who wished to become *śramaṇas* to do so, and mandated the restoration of all monasteries, pagodas, scriptures, and images. Initially, five *śramaṇas* from Kaśmīra arrived at the capital;

encountering the suppression of the Buddha-dharma, they had maintained the Way under the guise of practicing medicine. On the day they were to be ordained, the Emperor personally shaved the hair of these five men.

He treated the Master as his teacher and appointed him as a śramaṇa. In the first year of the Tonghe era, an imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa-tong Tan Yao as the Metropolitan Superintendent of the Śāo-xuan Monastery, honoring him with the rites due to a teacher.
The Emperor restored the Buddhist teachings and extensively ordained monks and nuns (*Weishu* and *Sengshi*).

Xianwen, whose personal name was Hongwen, was the eldest son. In the first year of the Tian’an era, he issued an imperial decree appointing Sengjin as the Sangzheng (Chief Administrator of Monks) for all under heaven.
In the first year of the Huangxing era, he constructed the Yongning Temple and a seven-story pagoda at the Northern Terrace in Chang’an; the pagoda stood thirty *zhang* high.
Furthermore, he commissioned a great Buddha statue at Tiangong Temple, forty-three *chi* in height, using one hundred thousand *jin* of copper and six hundred *jin* of gold (*Tongjian*).
The Emperor was deeply devoted to Buddhist studies; he frequently invited court officials and *śramaṇas* to discuss profound principles together.

Possessing a mind that longed for renunciation from the world, in the sixth month of the first year of the Yanxing era, he issued an edict to abdicate the throne to the Crown Prince and moved his residence to Chongsheng Temple.

He resided in the Guanggong Palace and was titled Shanghuang (Retired Sovereign). He established Luyuan Monastery in the Northern Garden and dwelt there with Chan monks, studying and discussing the profound and lofty [teachings] with Yao Gao and Yuan Yun.
Yao Gao composed the "Luyuan Fu" (The Rhapsody on the Deer Garden) [as recorded in the *Beishi* and the *Shijian*].
Emperor Xiaowen, whose personal name was Hong, was the eldest son of Emperor Xianwen. He changed the family name to Yuan.

In the second year of the Yanxing era, by imperial decree, the Tripitaka Master from the Western Heaven, Jikaya (translated as "Faithful in Matters"), translated five sections of the *Za bao jing* (Sūtra of Miscellaneous Jewels). Liu Xiaobiao served as the scribe for the transcription, presented to the Sovereign.
An edict was issued stating: "From now on, in sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral altars, do not use living animals as offerings; offer only wine and dried meat.

In the first year of Chengming, the Emperor established Jianming Monastery. In the fourth year of Taihe, an imperial decree appointed the monk Xian as the Metropolitan Superintendent of Śramaṇas (Sha-men du-tong).

In the sixteenth year, an edict was issued permitting one hundred persons from each large prefecture to [assemble] on the eighth day of the fourth month and the fifteenth day of the seventh month every year.
Regarding the monks: fifty from the central provinces and twenty from the lower provinces were established by imperial decree as the permanent standard (the *shijiān*).

In the seventeenth year, an edict was issued for the Dharma Master Yide to be permitted to enter the palace three times a month, so that I might partake in and receive the flavor of the Way, thereby glorifying the court.
Furthermore, on several occasions he visited Wangyuan Temple to discuss the Buddha-dharma with the śramaṇas. In the nineteenth year, [the Emperor] visited Xuzhou.
At the White Stupa Temple (Baitasi), he ordered Dharma Master Daodeng to lecture on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Addressing his attendants, he said, "I have examined this treatise;

it can explain away people's deep-seated attachments and lead them to enter the state of quiescence. He issued an edict expressing his grief and sorrow, bestowing silk and providing a vegetarian feast for the monks (*Beishi*).

In the twenty-first year, an edict was issued for the eighth day of the fourth month to welcome the Buddha statues from the various temples of the Luoyang capital into the Changhe Palace, where flowers were scattered over them.

He paid reverence [to the scriptures] as a constant practice throughout the year. During his twenty-nine years on the throne, he never set a book from his hand; in his leisure moments, he would lecture upon them himself.
All the ladies of the six palaces observed the six fasts (*ṣaḍupavāsa*), and he ordained numerous monks and constructed many temples (as recorded in the *Shijiàn*).

Xuānwǔ (宣武), whose personal name was Kè (恪), was the second son of Emperor Xiàowén. In the first year of the Yǒngpíng era, an imperial decree was issued for Le Nà Mó Tí (勒那摩提)— which means "Ratnamati" (寶意, "Jewel-Mind")—
to translate the *Ratnakūṭa-śāstra* at the Tàijí Hall, while Bódhìliúzhī (菩提流支)— which means "Bodhiruci" (覺希, "Awakening-Rare")— was to do so at the Zǐjí Hall.

He translated the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which the Emperor personally received by dictation. In the second year, at the Shiqian Hall, the Emperor lectured on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* for the assembly of monks and court officials.
At that time, the Wei court exclusively venerated the teachings of Śākyamuni and neglected the secular classics.
The Secretariat Director Pei Yanjun submitted a memorial, stating that although Emperor Guangwu of the Han and Emperor Wu of the Wei were amidst the chaos of war, they never ceased [their studies].

Letter: When the late Emperor returned to the capital from leading his armies, he did not set down his scrolls even for a moment. This was surely because he understood that learning brings manifold benefit and thus never ceased his studies.
May Your Majesty likewise ascend the Dharma-seat to personally expound upon the Great Awakening; then all who behold and listen will have the dust of their obstructions cleared away.

I humbly pray that you will peruse both the scriptures and the books, preserving both the teachings of Confucius and Śākyamuni. Only then will both the internal and external realms be fully encompassed, and both the ultimate and conventional truths be thoroughly elucidated. (From the *Tongjian*). At that time...

More than three thousand people from the Western Regions arrived in Luoyang, outside the Middle Kingdom. The Emperor separately established over one thousand rooms at Yongming Temple to accommodate them;
those far and near followed this example, and there were none who did not serve the Buddha (Beishi).

Emperor Xiaoming, whose personal name was Xu, was the second son of Emperor Xuanwu. In the first year of the Shenguī era, an imperial edict was issued for all prefectures to establish five-storied *stūpas*.
In that same year, Empress Dowager Hu commanded Song Yun and the śramaṇa Huisheng and others to travel to India in the West to seek Buddhist scriptures.
In the fourth year [of the Taihe era], Song Yun and others returned from their mission to the Western Regions, having obtained one hundred and seventy sections of Buddhist scriptures.
In the first year of the Zhengguang era, the Emperor donned the ceremonial cap of manhood and commanded śramaṇas and Daoist priests to lecture on the Way within the imperial palace.

The Emperor asked, "Did the Buddha and Laozi exist at the same time? The Daoist priest Jiang Bin replied, "The *Kaitian jing* states that Laozi was born in the third year of King Ding’s reign; his age..."
85. Entering the West to Convert the Barbarians (Hu). [The text] takes the Buddha as his attendant. The śramaṇa Tanmujuei said:
"Our Buddha was born in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao and entered parinirvāṇa in the fifty-third year of King Mu.

From the year of his passing until the third year of King Ding, a total of three hundred and forty-five years elapsed before Laozi was born. Yet [the text] claims that Laozi converted the barbarians by means of the Buddha."
"To serve as an attendant would surely be a grave error. Bin said, "When the Buddha was born during the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, what written records exist?

Daozhi replied, "The *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou) and the *Han Fa Ben Nei Zhuan* (Inner Biography of the Origin of the Dharma in the Han) both contain explicit accounts. The Emperor then ordered his ministers to examine and determine the authenticity of these texts.
The Grand Marshal Xiao Zong and others presented a memorial of indictment, stating that the crime of circulating the spurious *Kaitian* scripture was intended to delude the masses.
By imperial decree, Tanbin was banished to Mawei (Beishi). In the gengzi year of the Zhengguang era, Bodhidharma entered Wei from Liang and resided at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
He sat facing a wall. When the Emperor heard of the Master’s extraordinary deeds, he issued three edicts inviting him to court, but the Master did not come.

The Emperor then bestowed upon him a *mona* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, a golden bowl, a silver water flask, and silken fabrics; the Master would not accept them. Only after three such returns did he finally accept them (*Zhengzong ji*).
Xiaowu (Emperor Xiaowu). His taboo name was Xiū, and his courtesy name was Xiaozé. He was the third son of Prince Huái of Guangping Wumù.
In the first year of the Yongxī era, he established Zhǐqǐ Temple, where he provided offerings for the monks and lectured on the Dharma (as recorded by the Śramaṇa Jiàn).
Gao Yun, courtesy name Bogeong, was appointed Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat when Emperor Xiaowen ascended the throne. The Emperor once visited his residence;

there were only a few thatched huts, with coarse blankets for bedding and woolen robes for clothing, and nothing in the kitchen but salt and vegetables. The Emperor remarked, "In antiquity, there have been those as pure and poor as this."
This was so. He was granted five hundred bolts of silk and one thousand *hu* of grain. At the age of ninety-eight, he once composed the "Ruru Garden Rhapsody" (*Lüyuan Fu*), which states in brief:

"When our Sovereign succeeded to the succession, Heaven bestowed upon him transcendent brilliance and wisdom. He looked back to the Ruru Garden of old and gave rise to the sublime meaning of the Three Turnings of the Wheel.
Having revitalized the profound tradition that had long been obscured, it has found its resting place after a void of a thousand years. Thereupon, he commanded—

Master craftsmen were selected to carve this image on the Western Ridge. With focused sincerity and upright thought, they looked up to model themselves after the divine countenance, so that the true likeness might be rendered with some semblance, its golden radiance shining forth brilliantly.
They constructed a hall upon the sacred cliff, soaring a hundred fathoms high and perfectly straight.

Flying beams were stretched across floating pillars, and lotus blossoms were arrayed upon the ornate coffered ceiling. It was as if facing the Jetavana Grove in person; who could say it was not a true site of enlightenment?

The path leading here is remote; one must sigh at the establishment of such divine achievement, which stands preeminent, surpassing all antiquity. This is truly due to the harmonious assistance of the spirits and deities, whereby it preserves integrity and maintains auspiciousness.
A celestial grotto was excavated for meditative dwelling, and a double flight of stairs was opened to facilitate access.

As for those who investigate the Way, their conduct is upright and simple; admiring his virtue and cherishing his reputation, they take up their staffs to come and tread this ground, maintaining the state of an Arhat.

He observed the weighty prohibitions and tasted the profound scriptures of the Tripiṭaka. Sometimes he walked back and forth through the forest; sometimes he sat in silent stillness with upright composure.

Thus, all manner of virtues converged upon him, and the five obstacles were simultaneously dispelled. Though the Way seemed about to vanish, it became ever more manifest; though his reputation was about to be tarnished, it grew even more illustrious.
He aspired to ascend like the clouds of the *jingyun* (the celestial realm) and envied the lofty transcendence of Māndhātṛ, seeking to leave the dust of the world behind.

Thus he transcended the mundane world and entered the profound depths of the Mysterious Gate. He established the Prince of the Dharma (the Crown Prince) in his rightful station and received the supreme title of "Most High" (*Taishang*).

Abiding in non-existence while governing existence, and maintaining stillness to quell restlessness, he caused the ten thousand nations to follow his transformative influence and led all living beings as their guide.
Facing south in accordance with the rites of sovereignty, he remained in a state of non-action (*wuwei*), forever resting his mind upon the Void and the Sublime. Furthermore, he once composed...
The biography was composed by Dharma Master Tanshi (in the *Hongming ji*).
Yang Xuanzhi—Xuanzhi once served as the Governor of Qicheng. When Bodhidharma arrived in Wei and stayed at the Qiansheng Temple on Mount Yumen, Xuanzhi...
A question was asked: "Your disciple has turned his heart toward the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom remains clouded and dull, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle.
I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will reveal the essential tenets. The Master spoke in verse: "One does not give rise to aversion upon seeing evil..."
He does not observe what is virtuous and strive to practice it; he does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly; nor does he cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment.
He has mastered the Great Way beyond measure and penetrated the Buddha-mind with transcendent liberation. He does not share the same path as ordinary beings or sages;
he is loftily named a Patriarch. Xuanzhi, his grief and joy mingling, said: "I pray that you will dwell long in this world to transform and guide all beings."
There was [Daoxuan] (Chuanteng), who once composed the *Luoyang qielan ji* in five fascicles. Its preface states briefly:

"The accounts of the Three Summaries and Five Classics, and the doctrines of the Nine Schools and the Hundred Masters, all take human society as their principle while their meanings encompass that which transcends the heavens.

Yet, regarding the source of the One Vehicle and Two Truths, and the purport of the Six Supernatural Powers and Threefold Penetration, these are detailed at full length in the Western Regions, but no records exist here in the Eastern Land. From [this point...]

At the zenith of the day, he experienced a dream: the full moon emitted its radiance, adorning the gate of the sun with the likeness of white brows and eyebrows, while the chamber of night was depicted with the form of deep-blue hair.

When the Imperial Wei dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven and took possession of Mount Song and the Luo River, faith became increasingly widespread and the teachings of the Dharma flourished beyond measure.

Princes, nobles, and high officials cast aside their elephants and horses as if discarding worn-out sandals; commoners and wealthy families relinquished their wealth and property as if they were mere traces left behind. Thus it was that—

The monasteries stand side by side like the teeth of a comb, and precious stupas are arrayed in dense rows. They vie with one another to capture the forms of celestial beings and compete to emulate the shadows cast by mountain peaks.
The golden spires rival the Cloud Terrace in height, and the lecture halls match the opulence of the Apang Palace.

How could it be that these structures are merely clothed in fine silks and embroideries, or their foundations draped in crimson and purple? When the many calamities of the Yongxi era arrived, thorns grew into forests, and both inside and outside the capital city...
More than a thousand temples have become desolate and distant, rarely heard of; fearing that future generations might lack a record of them, I have thus composed this account.
However, as the number of temples is vast, it is impossible to transcribe them all in detail. What is recorded here consists only of the great monasteries (*mahāvihāra*);
among those that are smaller, I have also included records of their auspicious and extraordinary occurrences. In total, there are five chapters (The Record of the Triple Gem).
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Five, re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Six,
compiled by the Shamen Xin Tai of Kuaiji.
The Tiantai śramaṇa Zhenqing read [the records]:
During the Eastern Wei, the capital was Luoyang; it was later moved to Ye. The Emperor’s name was Shanjian; his posthumous title was Xiaojing. He reigned for one period, sixteen years.

The Western Wei dynasty had its capital at Chang’an. Beginning with Emperor Wen in the year Yimao and ending with Emperor Gong in the year Bingzi, there were three sovereigns for a total of twenty-one years.
Emperor Wen’s personal name was Baoru. He was the grandson of Emperor Xiaowen and the son of Prince Jingzhao Yu.

In the first year of the Datong era, he issued an edict appointing the śramaṇa Daozhen as the Grand Overseer of Śramaṇas (Śramaṇa Dàtǒng). In that same year, he constructed Prajñā Monastery. The Emperor constantly exercised compassion in his conduct. He always...

He practiced faith and equanimity; he recited the Lotus Sūtra with his mouth and maintained the pure precepts with his body. He constructed a pavilion for the seven factors of enlightenment as a chamber for the four dhyānas (from the Bianzheng lun).
Northern Qi.
The capital was Ye. Beginning with Emperor Wenxuan in the Gengwu year and ending with the Young Sovereign in the Dingyou year, there were six rulers for a total of twenty-eight years.
[The reign of] Wenxuan...
The Emperor’s taboo name was Yang, his courtesy name was Zijin, and he belonged to the Gao clan. He was the second son of Gao Huan and the younger uterine brother of Wenxiang.

In the first year of the Tianbao era, an imperial edict summoned the eminent monk Fachang to the inner palace to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and he was appointed State Preceptor (the institution of the State Preceptor began with this).

In the second year, an edict summoned Sengchou to the inner palace, where the Emperor reverently received the teachings of dhyāna from him; consequently, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from Chou, who remained within the palace for four years.
After more than ten days, an imperial edict was issued to construct Yunmen Monastery in the city of Ye to house him.
Furthermore, an edict was promulgated to establish the Ten Heads of the Office of Monastic Affairs (Zhaoxuan), appointing the śramaṇa Fashang as the Great Head (Dadong).

Over fifty clerical staff positions were established, and the monastics and nuns under his jurisdiction numbered more than four million, all of whom received his moral instruction. The Emperor constructed an altar and performed the prescribed rites, honoring him as National Teacher. [He] spread his hair...
He had the Emperor ascend the throne by stepping upon it. The Empress, consorts, and high ministers all received the Bodhisattva precepts.
In the sixth year, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an edict to abandon Daoism; the Daoist Lu Xiujing, unable to contain his indignation, fled to the Wei state.

When Emperor Wenxuan received the abdication of Eastern Wei, he especially venerated Buddhism; Lu Xiujing resented this and requested to compete with the sons of Śākya in a contest of dharma. Lu Xiujing...
He cast spells so that the robes and alms bowls of the śramaṇas all flew up, and the beams and pillars of the palace all shook.
Jing then boasted, saying, "If the śramaṇa displays one [miracle], I shall display two. He now manifested a slight artifice, and the śramaṇa was humiliated and withdrew.
The Emperor looked back and said to the Grand Preceptor (Dàtǒng) Fǎshàng, "Is there truly no one in the Buddha-dharma? Fǎshàng ordered Tánxiǎn, a monk of the lowest rank, to defeat him. Xiǎn, using—
Chan Master Chou placed his robe and alms bowl on the ground, commanding them with a mantra not to move; he then placed the robe and bowl upon a beam, yet they remained motionless.
Jing and the others looked at one another, their faces turning pale with fear. Xian stood on one leg and said, "I have manifested one; you may manifest two. Jing had no reply.
The ministers all clapped their hands in joy. The Emperor issued an edict, saying: "The Dharma-gate is non-dual; this is the True Doctrine."
In one regard, seeking the true path takes stillness and tranquility as its foundation. For those who practice the Way of the *Jiǔ* (Sacrificial Libationer), the flavor is that of fermented grain;
where, then, is purity and emptiness? Dried meat is what they find sweet, while compassion is forever absent. Above, this differs from benevolent temples; below, it deviates from sacrificial rites.

It should be strictly prohibited and no longer honored or served. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*). In the seventh year, because the Sanskrit scriptures in the inner treasury had not yet been translated, the Emperor commanded three...
Nalanda Yasas was enshrined at T'ien-p'ing Temple for the translation [of scriptures]. The Emperor personally prostrated before the Sanskrit texts and said to his ministers:
"This great foundation of the Triple Gem deserves our singular veneration. In the tenth year, the Emperor visited Kan-lu Temple in Liao-yang;
there he dwelt in meditation and engaged in profound contemplation, issuing an edict that nothing but matters of great military or state importance should be reported to him (from the *T'ung-chi*).

Emperor Wucheng, whose personal name was Zhan, was the ninth son of [Emperor] Huán. He changed the reign title to Taíning. He converted the San-tái Palace into the Dàxīngshèng Monastery. The imperial edict stated in brief:

"I have succeeded to the precious mandate and shall perpetuate this as a blessing for my house. Looking up with reverence to the will of my predecessors, I remain deeply respectful toward the Mysterious Gate (Buddhism)."

The Three Terrace Palace (Sān tái gōng) was converted into Dàxīngshèng Monastery. In the second year of the Héqīng era, by imperial decree, Dharma Master Huìzàng lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in the Tàijí Hall.
That same year, the Emperor constructed an altar within the palace and formally invited Master Shàng to bestow the precepts.
He spread his hair upon the ground and commanded Master Shàng to step over it before ascending the seat. Furthermore, he founded Bào dé Monastery and decreed that the Master should preside over it.
The Emperor held the Buddha-vehicle in profound reverence. He initiated the construction of a precious stupa, donating his own rare and imperial robes as alms.

He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for months, holding numerous assemblies. He established monasteries on tiered terraces and in separate pavilions, filling them with jade, pearls, and gems as ritual offerings (from the *Hongming ji*, supervised by Shi).
The later sovereign was named Emperor Wei (personal name: Wei), styled Ren-gang. He was the eldest son of Emperor Wencheng. He changed the era name to Tian-tong.

In the first year of Long-hua, he issued an edict to repair the pagoda at the Baima Monastery in Ye-du, which had been built by the monk Fotudeng. Three śarīras were obtained and enshrined within a precious vase.
King Yong of Guangwu set out a crystal bowl and performed a ritual of circumambulation and prayer; suddenly, the śarīra floated upon the surface of the water (from the *Tongji*).

Yan Zhitui—Zhitui served as a Gentleman of the Palace Gate during the Wuping era and rose to the rank of Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices. His entire family observed a vegetarian diet. Deeply...
He believed in Buddhism. His *Yan Jiaxun* (Family Instructions of the Yan Clan) circulates in the world; its "Chapter on Taking Refuge in the Heart" states:

"The pursuit of immortals involves the expenditure of gold and jade, which is largely a vain waste. Even if one were to attain immortality, one would ultimately still face death and could not transcend the world;
therefore, I do not encourage you all to study it. As for the Buddhist doctrine of the three periods of existence, it is both credible and verifiable. My family has long been devoted to it."
Be careful not to treat this lightly; the subtle principles therein are fully contained within the sutras and treatises, so I shall not elaborate upon them here.
I fear, however, that you may still lack firm resolve, and thus I have merely offered these brief and earnest exhortations. Regarding the instruction on abstaining from killing, it says:
"The gentleman of the Confucian school cannot bear to witness life being taken, nor can he bear to see death; hearing their cries, he cannot bear to eat their flesh. Gao Chai and Zeng...
I, Xi, do not yet know whether those within the Inner Teaching are all able to refrain from killing; this is surely because you, O Benevolent One, naturally apply your mind to it.
Among the myriad classes of living beings, there is none that does not cherish its life. You must certainly strive to practice the abstention from killing. To examine its origin:

the four elements and five aggregates analyze the existence of form, while the six vessels and three vehicles transport and carry all sentient beings. The ten thousand practices are all empty, and the thousand gates lead one into goodness.

How could his eloquence and wisdom be merely the breadth of the Seven Classics or the hundred schools of thought? It is clear that it surpasses what was reached by Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi.
The inner and outer teachings are fundamentally one body; they differ in their gradual and sudden approaches and vary in depth, yet they are not distinct in essence.
The initial gate of the Inner Canon establishes five prohibitions, which correspond to the Five Constants of the outer books. As for benevolence, [the practitioner] does not...

The prohibition against killing is for the sake of righteousness; the prohibition against theft is for the sake of propriety; the prohibition against lewdness is for the sake of ritual; the prohibition against wine is for the sake of wisdom;

the prohibition against falsehood is for the sake of faithfulness. To turn toward the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius while turning one’s back on the tradition of Śākyamuni—how deluded this is! (Yan Shijia Jiaxun)

Du Bi (style name Fuxuan) was a native of Quyang in Zhongshan. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted; as his family was poor and lacked books, he attended the local prefectural school to pursue his studies.

He excelled in calligraphy and composition, earning the high esteem of his contemporaries. At the beginning of the Xiaochang era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty, he was appointed to the National University.

The Doctor [Zhi] Bian was appointed as the Magistrate of Qucheng in Guangzhou. His administration was characterized by purity and tranquility. Upon entering the Northern Qi, he served as an envoy to Western Wei for Gao Huan (Shenwu).
When the Wei Emperor saw him in the Jiulong Hall, he said, "Your Reverence is a man of refined learning; I have a question to ask you.

Regarding the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-nature mentioned in the scriptures, are they the same or different? Bian replied, "They are but a single principle. The Emperor asked again: "As for those who explain..."

[The Emperor] said, "Everyone falsely says that the *dharmatā* is broad and the Buddha-nature is narrow; how can this be? Bi replied, "In being broad, it becomes broad; in being narrow, it becomes narrow.
If one discusses the essence of its nature (*xingti*), it is neither narrow nor broad. The Emperor said, "Since you say it becomes broad and becomes narrow, how can it be neither narrow nor broad?
Bi replied, "If one says it is broad, then it cannot be narrow; if it were fixedly narrow, it likewise could not [be broad]."

He is able to be expansive; because he is neither expansive nor narrow, he can be both expansive and narrow. Although that which is accomplished differs, the means by which it is accomplished remain ever one.
The Emperor praised this as excellent (Beishi, Biography).
Lu Faho resided in seclusion on Baili Island in Jiangling. His clothing, food, and dwelling were in every respect identical to those of a śramaṇa observing the precepts.
When Hou Jing dispatched his general Ren Yue to attack the Prince of Xiangdong at Jiangling, Faho went to visit the Prince.
He requested to lead an expedition. He summoned approximately eight hundred disciples from among the various Mian tribes to Jiangjin.
Prince Xiangdong dispatched Hu Sengyou, who led over a thousand men to join him. Fahu used divine power to command the spirits of a shrine to dispatch hidden troops, who defeated the enemy.
Furthermore, he once went to a large tree north of the city of Xiangyang; he marked a square area of two chi and ordered his disciples to dig there, where they found a tortoise.
It was one and a half chi in length. He struck it with a staff and said, "You wish to emerge but cannot; you have already lived for several hundred years.
Had you not encountered me, would you ever have seen the light of heaven? He then conferred upon the tortoise the Three Refuges precepts, whereupon the tortoise entered the grass.
Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty (who was the Prince of Xiangdong) appointed Fahu as the Regional Inspector of Yingzhou and Duke of Jiangcheng County. He once assembled a great fleet of warships.
He intended to raid Xiangyang and enter the Wuguan Pass. Emperor Yuan feared he would cause rebellion and sent someone to stop him.
Fahu said, "Fahu is one who seeks the Buddha; I do not even hope for the seat of Śakra or Brahmā, so how could I plot for the throne?"
"However, I have a karmic connection with the Buddha of Empty Hand (Karasu-butsu) from my time as a subject.
Seeing that the King must have retribution approaching, I have come to his rescue. Fahe first built Shouwang Temple on Bailizhou;

once the Buddha hall was framed, he further trimmed the beams and pillars, saying, "In about forty years, the Buddha-dharma shall suffer from lightning and hail. This temple is secluded and remote..."

This was to avoid calamity. When the Wei army conquered Jingzhou, the palace buildings were completely burned down; the regional commander intended to dismantle the Buddhist hall of Prince Shou, but desisted because he found its timber too short.
