Later, when Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou suppressed the Buddha-dharma, this temple was situated within the territory of Chen and thus escaped the disaster.
In the spring of the sixth year of Tianbao, Prince Yue of Qingjiang led an army to the banks of the Yangtze River, and Fahuang surrendered the entire province.
During the Northern Qi dynasty, Emperor Wenxuan appointed Fǎhé as Grand Marshal (Dàdūdu) of the military affairs of ten provinces and Duke of Tàiwēi.
When he went to the palace gate to announce his presence, he did not state his official rank or title, but simply called himself "The Recluse of Mount Jīng.
Emperor Wenxuan bestowed upon Fǎhé one million coins, ten thousand bolts of silk, a prime residence, one hundred *qǐng* of farmland, and two hundred male and female slaves. Fǎhé...
He emancipated all the slaves and servants he had acquired, saying, "Each may go according to their own conditions. He distributed his money and silks in alms until they were exhausted at once.
He used the house granted to him to establish a Buddhist temple, while he himself lived beside it no differently than an ordinary person.

One day, without illness, he informed his disciples that the time for his death had arrived; he then burned incense, performed prostrations, and passed away while seated upon a rope bed. Emperor Wenxuan opened the coffin.
Upon inspecting it, they found nothing but an empty coffin (Beishi).

Wei Shou, whose courtesy name was Boqi, was a native of Julu. During the Heqing era, he was appointed as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. He compiled the "Buddhist and Daoist Annals" (Folaozhi) for the Weishu.

In brief: among all classes of living beings, the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*) throughout the three periods of time is never extinguished. Whatever good or evil one performs will inevitably entail retribution.

By gradually accumulating superior karma, one refines away coarseness and vulgarity; passing through countless forms, one purifies and tempers the spirit until reaching the state of non-arising and attaining the Way of the Buddha.
At the beginning of this cultivation of the mind, one relies upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—this is called the Three Refuges. If...
There are the "Three Fears" of the noble person (*jūnin*). Furthermore, there are the "Five Precepts": abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants.

Their general meaning is identical to benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity. It further explains rebirth within the six realms, the practice of the six *pāramitās*, and the profound and esoteric significance of the Buddha’s true and manifested bodies—neither arising nor ceasing—as well as the proliferation of the teachings through reliquaries, stupas, and temples.
(Buddhism and Laozi). During the Later Zhou dynasty, the capital was Chang’an.
It began in the *dingchou* year of Emperor Min and ended in the *jingsi* year of Emperor Jing, spanning five rulers and twenty-four years.
Yuwen Tai, courtesy name Heituo, was a native of Wuchuan in Dai Commandery.
He served as Grand Master (Dashi) to the Western Wei and once provided offerings for a hundred Dharma masters who investigated the sutras and śāstras and lectured on the Mahāyāna.
He commissioned the śramaṇa Tanxian to compile the *Essentials of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtras* (*Neidian lu*). Tai composed the *Zhuoyuan*, *Zhiqu*, and...
The Mahāyāna temples of Zhongxing, Tianbao, Shoushan, Fanyun, Dafutián, and others in Zhongding, Weiguo, were established;
one thousand monks were ordained (according to the Bianzheng lu). Emperor Tai posthumously conferred the title of Emperor Wen upon him.
Emperor Min’s personal name was Jue, and his courtesy name was Dhāraṇī. He was the third son of Emperor Wen and succeeded to the abdication of the Western Wei.

In the first year of his reign, he issued an edict appointing Master Sengshi as the Tripiṭaka Master of the Zhou State. By imperial decree, the śarīra relics were enshrined at Changnian Monastery in Puzhou. [The śarīra...]
Light emerged from the vase, whereupon a stupa was erected to commemorate this auspicious marvel.

While the Emperor was hunting at Mount Tan, he pointed toward the mountain from afar and asked his ministers, "Do you see anything? Only Lu Guang, the Secretary for Records, replied, "I see a śramaṇa.
The Emperor said, "It is he indeed," and immediately withdrew his troops and returned. He then ordered Guang to construct a stupa at the spot where he had seen him; [he] dug...
The foundation measured one *zhang*. He obtained a *śikya* staff and an earthen alms bowl (*piṭaka*) (from the *Tongji*).
Emperor Ming’s personal name was Yù; his childhood name was Tongwan-tú. He was the eldest son of Emperor Wen. He changed the era name to Wuchéng. The Emperor issued an edict to construct a monastery.

Briefly stated: Filial piety moves the divine; gazing upon Heaven, one’s debt is boundless. There was none who did not spread gold to construct *ārāmas* (monasteries) and flow silver to create precious halls.
Only then do we know that the Deer Park is within reach and the Peacock Grove is not far off.

It was ordered that the Grand Preceptor, Duke of Jin, supervise the construction of both the Dazhigu and Zhengqi Temples (*Hongming ji*). For the late Emperor, [the Emperor] wove a statue of Vairocana.
The statues of the Buddha and two Bodhisattvas each stand twenty-six feet high; there are twelve sandalwood images, as well as vajras, lions, and so forth (*Bianzheng lu*).
Emperor Wu; his posthumous name was Yong, and his courtesy name was Nīratu. He was the fourth son of Emperor Wen. In the third year of the Baoding era, an imperial edict stated:

"The year is Zhaoyang (the first of the three yangs, the spring month). The Dragon has gathered at Tianjing (as for 'the Dragon having gathered,' the Azure Dragon of the East serves as the head of the year; Tianjing refers to the year being in the year of the Monkey). It shall now be ordered that the relevant authorities...
He commissioned the production of the entire Tripitaka, beginning with the teachings on arising and ceasing and concluding with the discourse on *nirvāṇa*.

In the first year of the Jiande era, an imperial edict summoned Dhyāna Master Sengwei to the capital; the Emperor personally received his precepts and instructions. By imperial decree, the empresses, consorts, dukes, and ministers all received the ten wholesome precepts.
He was ordered to reside at Tianbao Temple in the capital. The Emperor, a devotee of the Buddha, constructed temples, erected pagodas, ordained monks, and transcribed [the scriptures].
There were over one thousand scriptures. Later, [the Emperor] was deluded by the Daoist Zhang Bin and consequently issued an edict to suppress the Teaching (*fangzhi*).
Emperor Xuan, whose personal name was Bin and courtesy name Qianbo, was the eldest son of Emperor Wu. In the first year of Dacheng, previously, the śramaṇa Daolin...
He presented himself for an audience based on his scholarly achievements. He engaged in debate with Emperor Wu for twenty days, exchanging views seventy times, yet the Emperor could not best him.

Consequently, he granted permission for the restoration of the teaching. However, as Emperor Wu passed away, it was only upon the persistent requests of the monastic community that this was finally realized.

The Emperor granted his permission. He then issued an edict stating: "The late Emperor was deluded by heterodox arguments and deemed the teachings of Śākyamuni and the Way (Daoism) to be of no benefit;

therefore, he abolished them so they were not practiced. However, as these great teachings are of profound significance, how could they be fit for dismissal? Thus, the two teachings shall be restored. (From the *Tongji*).
Emperor Jing’s posthumous name was Yan; he later changed his name to Chan. He was the eldest son of Emperor Xuan.

In the first year of the Daxiang era, an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm to restore the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism and to re-establish Buddhist images. The Chancellor, Yang Jian, together with the monks Zhizang and Linggan of Zhigou Monastery...
They shaved their heads once again. Two hundred and twenty monks were ordained (according to the *Tongji*).

The Sui capital was Chang’an. Beginning from the first year of the Xinchou cycle under Emperor Gaozu and ending with the fourth year of the Dingchou cycle under Emperor Gong, there were three sovereigns and thirty-seven years.
Year. The Emperor Gaozu’s name was Jian.
His surname was Yang. He was a native of Huayin in Hongnong and the fourteenth-generation descendant of Yang Zhen, the Grand Commandant of the Han dynasty. Initially, there was...
The divine nun was named Zhixian; she came from Hedong. She said to the Empress Dowager, "This child is most extraordinary;

he must not be raised among the laity. The nun personally nurtured him. When he had grown up, she told the Emperor, "The teaching of the Buddha is about to perish, and all spirits and deities are turning toward the West.
You shall later attain great nobility. The Buddha-dharma will temporarily decline, but it shall be revived thanks to you. This occurred during the Zhou dynasty.

Emperor Wu had abolished the teachings, and the Bhikṣuṇī hid herself within the imperial household; she passed away before long. When [Yang Jian] became the Son of Heaven, he greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma (Sui Shu).
In the third month of the first year of the Kaiguang era, an edict was issued to establish one Buddhist monastery at each of the Five Sacred Mountains (Sanbao Ji).
In the second year, the śramaṇa Tanyan had an audience with the Emperor and exhorted him to restore the Buddha-dharma. Thereupon, an edict was promulgated stating: "The Zhou..."
Temples abolished during the early period were all restored and renovated. Those within the jurisdiction were permitted to leave secular life as they wished;

furthermore, they were ordered to contribute money based on their household population to establish scriptures and images. Consequently, Buddhist scriptures became more numerous among the common people than the Six Arts (the classical Confucian texts).

In the third year [of the reign], an edict was issued to establish *gālanas* (monasteries) at locations of strategic topographical advantage in the capital. It was decreed that wherever there were monks practicing, a temple could be established.
(*Bianzheng lu*). In the fourth year, the Emperor issued an edict to Vinaya Master Lingzang, saying: "I, your disciple, am a secular Son of Heaven; you, Vinaya Master, are a monastic Son of Heaven.
Should there be those who wish to leave secular life, let it be up to you, Master, to ordain them. Consequently, the number of ordained monks reached tens of thousands.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said: "The Vinaya Master transforms people toward goodness; I, your disciple, restrain people from evil. Our intentions are one and the same."

[From his] Biography. In the fifth year, an imperial edict stated: "The Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to the kings of nations. I am the Honored One among men and have received the Buddha’s entrustment.
From this day forward, every month, I shall regularly invite fourteen monks to the Daxingshan Monastery to recite all the sūtras.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the thirteenth year, the Great Sui Emperor, the Buddhist disciple Yang...
I, Jianjing, pay homage to the Triple Gem of the ten directions. During the Zhou dynasty, the regular order was disturbed; the sacred traces were insulted and destroyed;

stupas and monasteries were demolished and abandoned; and scriptures and images were lost. Consequently, the ignorant had no means to guide those in confusion, and the wise had no way to seek out the holy spirits.

By virtue of my past karmic connections with the Triple Gem, I have now attained this auspicious destiny. As the parent of the people, I am intent upon rescuing the common folk. As for those abandoned images...

He ordered that all the lost scriptures be carved and compiled. He repented for such grave offenses as the destruction of images and the mutilation of scriptures by the Zhou dynasty, as well as the maltreatment of monks and the demolition of monasteries (from the *Kaishuang Ji*).
In the sixth month of the first year of the Renshou era, when the Emperor was still a commoner, he encountered a foreign monk who gave him a packet of śarīra relics, saying:
"In the future, you, Dānapati, shall become a compassionate father to all under heaven. These are the remains of the Great Awakened One..."
The Emperor offered worship to it himself. When he ascended the throne, he once held the śarīra in the palm of his hand with the Dharma Master Tanyuan to count them;
the number was sometimes less and sometimes more, remaining uncertain. Tanyuan said, "The Dharma-body of all Buddhas transcends numerical measure; it cannot be fathomed by the world.
The Emperor then first placed it in a casket made of the seven precious gems. Upon reaching this point, he suddenly remembered that incident, and so [he took] Qishan...
Stūpas containing śarīra relics were erected in thirty provinces, including Yong, Tai, Hua, Song, and Heng. The imperial edict stated:

"I look up with reverence to the Perfectly Awakened One, who possesses great kindness and great compassion, rescuing and protecting all sentient beings and serving as a bridge for the multitudes. Having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, I shall cause the holy teachings to flourish once again."
I intend to cultivate meritorious deeds together with all within the four seas, so that we may forever establish good causes and ascend together to the wondrous fruit.

To this end, I shall dispatch thirty śramaṇas who are well-versed in the characteristics of the Dharma and capable of proclaiming the Way, each accompanied by two attendants and one civil official, along with one hundred and twenty catties of frankincense.
These shall be sent to thirty provinces to distribute the śarīra relics and erect stūpas, with the following deadline:

On the fifteenth day of the tenth month at noon, [the relics] were enshrined together in the stūpas. Subsequently, memorial petitions from fifty-three prefectures—including Qin, Shan, Heng, and Hang—reported auspicious omens.

In the first month of the second year, an imperial edict was again issued to construct stūpas in fifty-three prefectures, including Qin, Shan, Heng, and Hang, with the date set for the eighth day of the fourth month at noon for the simultaneous enshrinement, following the same ritual procedures as before. Each case recorded miraculous responses (as recorded by Wang Shao in the *Hongming ji*). The Emperor...

He reigned for twenty-four years. He constructed temples and built stupas, transcribed the Tripitaka, fashioned Buddha images of gold, silver, and sandalwood, ordained monks, and established assemblies beyond measure (Shijiao lu).

Emperor Yang’s posthumous name was Guang. He was the second son of the High Ancestor (Emperor Wen). In the first year of the Kaihuang era, he served as the Prince of Jin, presiding over the region of Yangzhou.
At that time, Master Zhiyi of Tiantai was staying at Mount Lu. In the eleventh year, the Prince invited the Master to his seat of government and hosted a thousand [monks].
Senghui conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the King and said to him, "Since Your Majesty has respectfully adhered to the sacred prohibitions, you should be named Zongchi (Universal Retention).
The King replied, "Since the Great Master transmits the lamp of the Buddha-dharma, he should be titled Zhizhe (The Wise One). After some time, the Master returned to Mount Lu.
In the fifteenth year, the Master passed away at Shicheng on Mount Tiantai. The King ascended the throne in the year of Yichou.
The era name was changed to Daye. Temples were constructed, images were cast, assemblies were established, and several monks were ordained (according to the *Chizhe zhuan*).

Xue Daoheng, whose courtesy name was Xuanye, was a native of Fenyin in Hedong. When the High Ancestor assumed the mandate through abdication, he was appointed as an Attendant of the Chancellery. During the reign of Emperor Yang...
When the Emperor succeeded to the throne, he was appointed as the Prefect of Panzhou. In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, Tanyan passed away.
Emperor Wen suspended court proceedings and issued an edict for the princes and officials below them to go and attend to Daoheng. He composed a memorial inscription, which read in brief:

"The Sage Emperor has initiated his auspicious reign, and the teachings of the Image Age have flourished once more. You stand preeminent among those in black robes, rising as the foremost leader. Out of deference to the gravity of the imperial throne, you have manifested the ritual of teacher and disciple."

By means of this, the Three Jewels are widely protected; by relying on this, the Two Truths are proclaimed. It serves as a virtue for inducing people toward goodness and a method for assisting the state in practicing benevolence.
It is sufficient to follow in the footsteps of Kumārajīva and Sengzheng, and to surpass Dao’an and Huiyuan.

How could one have thought that the Pillar of the Dharma would suddenly lean and the Compassionate Boat would so abruptly capsize? This is not merely a cause for sorrow among the fourfold assembly, but is surely a source of bitter grief for the Sovereign himself. (From the *Bianzheng Lu*)
Li Shiqian, courtesy name Shiye, was a native of Zhaojun. He lost his father while still a young child and became renowned for his filial piety toward his mother.
His paternal uncle, Li Zang, often praised him, saying, "This boy is our family’s Yanzi. At the age of twelve, he served under the Wei Prince of Guangping, Zan.

He served as a Counselor to the Beikai Commandery. After the Sui dynasty established its rule over the world, he resolved never to hold office again. He never drank wine or ate meat, and his speech was never characterized by words of violence or harm.
He was skilled at discussing the profound principles of the Way (*xuanli*). Once, there was a guest in the assembly who did not believe in the Buddhist doctrine of karmic retribution.
Yu Shiqian exhorted him, saying: "The accumulation of goodness results in blessings; the accumulation of evil results in calamity. [He further cited the example of] the noble families awaiting...

Feng: Sweeping the graves and gazing for the funeral procession—is this not indeed a response to good or ill fortune? The Buddhist scriptures say: "Transmigrating through the five realms of existence, there is no end.
This is precisely what Jia Yi meant when he said that the myriad transformations have never had a limit; it refers to the phenomenon of suddenly becoming a human being.
Before Buddhism had yet spread to the East, the worthy ones already knew this to be so. As for Gao Yao becoming... [text ends]
Neng (nu-lái; a three-legged turtle) became a *tíjué* [cuckoo]; Bãojūn became a dragon; Niú'āi became a tiger;
a gentleman became a crane; a commoner became a monkey; Péngshēng became a pig; Rúyì became a dog; Huángmǔ became a [yuán/??]; Xuānwǔ became a turtle;
Dèng'ài became an ox; Xúbó became a fish; the attendant at the gate became a crow; a scholar became a snake; Yáng Yù... before him.
"Li Shen was the son of the Li clan. Is this not what is meant by the Buddhist teaching that one undergoes transformation and receives a different form after death?

The guest said, "Xing Zicai once remarked, 'How could the pine and cypress, in their subsequent rebirths, transform into the common *chū* and *lì* trees? I consider this to be true. Sishuan Qian said, "This is a discourse based on a lack of understanding.
Transformation is entirely created by the mind. How could wood possess a mind? The guest asked again about the three [types of transformation].
Regarding the relative superiority of the teachings, Liu Shiqian said: "Buddhism is the sun; Daoism is the moon; Confucianism is the five planets.
The guest was unable to refute this and desisted (from the *Sui shu*).

Fei Changfang was a native of Chengdu. He had previously been a śramaṇa, but returned to lay life during the Buddhist purge under Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou. With the rise of the Sui dynasty, he entered the translation bureau.

In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, he served as a *fanjing xueshi* (scholar for translating scriptures) and submitted the fifteen-fascicle *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Record of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era).
(*Hongming ji*). Wang Tong, whose courtesy name was Zhongyan, was a native of Longmen in Luoyang. In the thirteenth year of the Daye era, he fell ill and heard that Emperor Yang had been...
Harm came upon him. Weeping, he arose and said, "The people have long been weary of turmoil; perhaps this will inaugurate the era of Yao and Shun.
That I do not participate in it is my fate. Tong died at home. His disciples posthumously conferred upon him the title Wénzhōngzǐ (Master of Literary Profundity).

His disciples, including Xuē Shōu, compiled his sayings and titled them *Zhōngxuē* (Discourses of the Middle). In its chapter on the Duke of Zhou, it says: "When the Odes and the Books flourished, Qin..."
The world perished; it was not the fault of Zhongni (Confucius). The profound mystery flourished and the Jin dynasty fell into chaos;
it was not the fault of Laozi and Zhuangzi. Ritual fasts were practiced and the Liang state perished; it was not the fault of Śākyamuni. Someone asked about the Buddha.
Wénzhōngzi said, "He was a sage. "What is his teaching like? He replied, "It is the teaching of the West. In the Middle Kingdom, it would lead to stagnation. Wénzhōngzi...
The Master read the *Dangyi* and said, "In this, the two teachings are thus one. Someone asked about the way of longevity and the path of the divine immortals (*shenxian*).
Wenchengzi replied, "If benevolence and righteousness are not cultivated, and filial piety and fraternal respect are not established, what purpose is there in seeking longevity?
(Wenchengzi). Wenchengzi’s younger brother was named Ji; he composed a book titled *Dongaozi*.

Xin Yanzhi, Yanzhi by name, was a native of Didu. He had extensively studied the classics and histories and shared the same aspirations for learning as Niu Hong. Later, he entered Guanzhong and settled in Jingzhao.

Emperor Wen of the Northern Zhou saw him and held him in high esteem, appointing him as Secretariat Director. When Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty received the abdication of the throne, [he continued his service].
With the exception of Tai-chang Shao-ying, he served as the Prefect of Lu-zhou. He constructed a fifteen-story *stūpa*.
A local man named Zhang Yuan died suddenly and then revived, saying that his spirit had traveled to heaven. There he saw a hall of extreme magnificence and beauty.
A celestial being said, "The Prefect Xin has performed great meritorious deeds; this hall was built to await him" (*Sui shu*).

Yang Susu, whose courtesy name was Chudao, was a preeminent figure of his time for his extraordinary strategies and sublime literary works. He served in successive offices, reaching the rank of Shangzhuguo and being enfeoffed as Duke of Yue.
Holding the Buddha-dharma in high esteem, he constructed Guangming Temple; he also built Si-jue Temple on Mount Hua. Ssu once...
While walking and practicing meditation, he saw a painted image on a wall and asked a Daoist, "What is this illustration?
The Daoist replied, "It is the 'Illustration of Laozi Transforming the Hu and Becoming a Buddha. Sengsu said, "I have heard that when Laozi transformed the Hu, the Hu people would not accept him.
Only when Laozi manifested himself as a Buddha did the Hu people finally accept him. Thus, it is Buddhism that can transform the Hu, not the Dao; why then do you speak thus?"
Did Laozi convert the Hu? Why would Laozi need to convert the Hu into Buddhists rather than converting them into followers of the Dao?
The Daoist practitioners were unable to respond (Tongji).
The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark, Volume Six. Re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
The Compilation of the Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark, Volume Seven.
Compiled by the Shamen Xintai of Kuaiji.
The Tiantai śramaṇa Zhenqing read [this history] while residing in Chang’an,
the capital of the Tang dynasty. It begins with the Wuyin year of Gaozu and ends with the Bingyin year of Emperor Ai, spanning twenty-one sovereigns and two hundred years.

In the eighty-ninth year [of the Zhou dynasty], there was the High Ancestor, whose personal name was Yuan and whose courtesy name was Shude. He was surnamed Li and was a native of Chengji in Longxi. His grandfather was Hu, who was posthumously honored with the title Emperor Jing.
His father was Bǐng, posthumously titled Rén Gōng. He gave birth to the High Ancestor (Gāozǔ) in Cháng'ān.
In the first year of Wǔdé, the Emperor established a *dōucháng* at the southern thoroughfare of Zhūjuémén and convened an *wúzhē dàhuì*.

Furthermore, he commanded sixty-nine monks and sixty-nine Daoists each to perform ritual practices (*xíngdào*) for seven days in the Tàijí Diàn and to provide vegetarian meals for one thousand monks. In the third year, he constructed Língxuān, Huìchāng, and Shèngyè monasteries.
Regarding the Five Temples of Compassion and Realization: [Fajing] once donated his former residence in Jinyang to establish Xingsheng Temple.
He also constructed Yixing Temple in Bingzhou and fashioned three sandalwood statues for Emperor Taizu Yuanhuang to dedicate for the benefit of the deceased.

In the fourth year, Fu Yi, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy, submitted a memorial advocating the destruction of the Buddhist teachings. Dharma Master Falin responded to the imperial decree to debate the matter. Yi’s proposal was as follows:
Consequently, [the *Bianzheng lun* and the *Jiù Tángshǐ*] were set aside. Emperor Taizong’s taboo name was Shimin.
He was the second son of Gaozu. On the first day of the first month of the first year of the Zhenguan era, an edict was issued regarding the virtuous monks in the capital...

Each monastery shall perform the ritual observances for seven days within its own precincts. All necessary provisions for the vegetarian offerings and other requirements shall be supplied by the relevant authorities.

In the second year, an imperial edict was issued, which stated in brief: "The divine way establishes its teachings with compassion as the foremost principle. Its profound transformation permeates all things, providing the foundation for the nurturing of life.
I, the Emperor, reverently uphold the Great Treasure and cherish the common people; my heart of pity extends to all things. It is for this reason that I seek [the truth] far and wide."
The profound bounty and hidden assistance of the luminous spirits are such that we hope the nine merits shall be duly ordered and the five blessings shall accordingly respond.

It is fitting that the hundreds of millions under heaven look upward and pray for added protection. You may have the monks and Daoists of the temples and monasteries throughout the capital and all provinces recite scriptures and perform rites for seven days and seven nights.
(From the *Bianzheng lu*). In the third month of this year, an imperial edict was issued stating: "Since the founding of the righteous [dynasty] by the Sui..."

His resolve was set upon rescuing those drowning in distress. In his vigorous campaigns to subjugate the East, he leveled and annihilated every place he directed his forces toward. The number of those wounded and slain is beyond reckoning;

those personally executed by his hand approached one thousand. Yet, reflecting that the holy teaching of the Tathāgata deeply prizes benevolence and compassion, and that among the precepts the prohibition against killing is paramount, he commanded the relevant authorities to establish vegetarian feasts and perform ritual services at all the monasteries within the capital.

For seven days and seven nights, he performed prostrations and repentance with utmost sincerity, hoping that the hardships of the three miserable realms might be resolved and the sufferings of ten thousand kalpas brought to great salvation through this means.
He extinguished the mind of resentment and obstruction and set out upon the path to Bodhi (*Old History of the Tang*).

On the intercalary twelfth month of the third year, an imperial edict stated: "The Sui dynasty lost the Way, and the nine provinces were in turmoil. I personally led the supreme army and brought about this [peace]."

I clearly understand the severity of punishment. I fear most deeply that those beneath the Nine Springs may still sink into cauldrons and boiling water, and that those within the Eight Difficulties may forever be entangled in the conflict of ice and fire.

Therefore, to establish fields of merit to save their wandering spirits, one may construct monasteries and shrines at every site where military engagements occurred since the commencement of the righteous cause, for the sake of those righteous men and prisoners who lost their lives on the battlefields. One should invite eminent companions and look toward the Dharma.
The drum’s reverberating transformation turned the blazing fires into blue lotuses; the pure Brahma-sound, upon being heard, changed the ocean of suffering into nectar.

The officials measured and determined the locations and established monasteries accordingly, submitting a detailed report of these matters to express the Emperor’s compassionate intent (from the *Jiu Tang Shu*).
In that same year, Dharma Master Xuanzang presented a memorial at the palace gate to travel to the Western Regions to retrieve scriptures not yet received.
The Emperor did not grant permission; he fled in secret. In the fifth year, the Emperor established Qingshan Palace as Cide Temple and erected Yaotai Temple at Zhaoling.
In the seventh year, an edict was issued prohibiting the catching of fish in dams and enclosures, along with a ban on slaughter, and three thousand monks and nuns were ordained (*Bianzheng Lu*).
In the eleventh month of the ninth year, the Imperial Decree stated: "The Three Vehicles share a common path; their purpose is to deliver and save [sentient beings]..."
First, the Eightfold Noble Path takes refuge in and prioritizes compassion. It flows as an ocean of wisdom to nourish all living beings;

it clears away the forest of afflictions to serve as a bridge for all things. In its spontaneity, it embodies the Way; in its principle, it accords with supreme benevolence. Its wondrous fruits and superior causes correspond to the accumulation of goodness.
I, the Emperor, reverently emulate the Golden Wheel and humbly receive the precious mandate. Regarding the teachings of ultimate virtue, there is nothing far-reaching that I do not contemplate.

The regulations of the Great Sage leave no hidden corner unexamined; he desired that people might be freed from the entanglements of worldly existence and that families might attain benevolence and longevity.

Lately, however, due to wars and turmoil, the ranks of the monastic community have diminished. The flowered terraces and jeweled stupas stand with their doors unattended, and the blue-lotus-hued heads of the monks are weathered by wind and rain.
Reflecting upon this decay and ruin, I am truly filled with sorrow. Therefore, in all the provinces throughout the empire where there are temples, it is fitting—
The ordination of monks and nuns was limited to a maximum of three thousand per year. In the fifth month of the fourteenth year, Dharma Master Du Shun passed away.

He had initially been held in high esteem by Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, who provided him with a monthly stipend; by this time, the Emperor’s reverence for him had increased further, and he frequently invited him into the palace to serve him as he would a Buddha.
In the fifth month of the fifteenth year, the Emperor visited Hongfu Monastery and summoned the śramaṇa Daoyi.
The five men were granted seats and told that the founding of the temple was specifically for the posthumous honor of Empress Dowager Mu. As he spoke, his tears fell.

He personally composed the memorial text, and once the ritual of dedicating the merit was concluded, he said to Wei Yi, "Recently, because Laozi is the progenitor of my imperial lineage, I have placed Daoism first;
you gentlemen must surely feel some resentment. Wei Yi replied, "Your Majesty honors your ancestors and has established this formal precedent; we, Yi and the others, [are honored]."

"I am grateful for your grace; how could I dare harbor any resentment? The Emperor said, "The relative magnitude of the Buddhist and Daoist paths, and the respective status of Śākyamuni and Laozi, I have long known.
How could I consider one superior simply because it happened to be at the head of the procession? Therefore, I placed Laozi first in order to distinguish the sequence of kinship and distance."
It is not that I have failed to be attentive toward the Buddha. Since the founding of my kingdom, I have never established Daoist temples or monasteries;
rather, Buddhist temples have been built at every site of former battlefields. Even my ancestral residence in Taiyuan has been dedicated to the service of the Buddha.

Such is the disposition of my heart, which you ministers have likely not yet understood. If I do not express my intentions, others will remain ignorant of them. Thus, in the seventeenth year, an edict was issued on the fourth...

When Master Zuxin was summoned to the imperial court, messengers went and returned four times. Zuxin remained firm, lying down and refusing to rise. The Emperor bestowed upon him precious silks to fulfill his resolve (as recorded in the *Shijiàn*).

In the eighteenth year, an imperial edict stated: "Since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he has entrusted the protection and maintenance of the Buddha-dharma to kings and great ministers during this degenerate age.
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* (*Yìjiào jīng*) is that which was spoken by the Buddha at the time of his nirvāṇa; it contains his final exhortations and instructions."

The disciple’s [memorial] is most detailed and essential. The people of this degenerate age, both monastics and laypeople, do not know to revere and uphold it. I harbor eternal devotion to the holy teachings and intend to propagate and expound them.
It is fitting that the relevant authorities produce many copies of the scripture and distribute one volume each to the officials of the capital and the provincial governors.

If they observe that the conduct of monks or nuns does not accord with the scripture, they should exhort them through both public and private means to ensure they follow it in practice. (Old History of the Tang, 10)
In the first month of the ninth year, Xuanzang returned to Chang’an. Fang Xuanling, the Grand Guardian of the Capital, submitted a memorial to inform the Emperor.
In the second month, Xuanzang had an audience with the Emperor at the Yiluan Hall. The Emperor said, “Why did you not report your departure?

Xuanzang replied, “When I departed, I submitted my petition three times but received no permission; thus, I traveled privately. The Emperor said, “Since you were able to risk your life to seek the Dharma for the benefit and welfare of all living beings, [I am deeply moved].”

"I greatly commend this," the Emperor said. Xuanzang thereupon submitted that he had obtained six hundred and fifty-seven sections of Sanskrit sūtras and śāstras from the Western Regions and requested permission to translate them at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song.
The Emperor replied, "I have recently established Hongfu Monastery for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu; you may perform the translations there.
He then issued an edict appointing Fang Xuanling to oversee the project, with all necessary provisions and resources provided entirely from the imperial treasury.
In the twenty-second year [of the Zhenguan era], in the sixth month, the Emperor visited the Yuhua Palace in Fangzhou and summoned Xuanzang.

The Emperor asked, "What sutras have you translated recently? Xuanzang replied, "I have recently translated the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Upon examining it, the Emperor said to his attendants, "The Buddhist teachings are vast and extensive;
they are like gazing at the heavens or looking out over the ocean—there is no limit to their height and depth. As for the classics of the Nine Schools..."
It is like a small inlet eventually merging into the vast ocean. The worldly claim that the Three Teachings reach the same goal is but empty talk.

Consequently, he commanded the relevant authorities to transcribe the newly translated sūtras and śāstras and distribute them to the Governors-General of the ten circuits. He composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripiṭaka" to serve as their preface.
He bestowed upon Xuanzang one hundred pieces of gold, a polished monastic robe, and a precious sword. On one occasion, he asked Xuanzang about the benefits of the Dharma-gate.

"What should take precedence? [He] replied, "The propagation of the Dharma requires people; the ordination of monks is paramount. The Emperor was pleased (*Jiù Tángshǐ Jīgǔlüè*). The *Preface to the Holy Teachings* (*Shèngjiào xù*) states in brief:
"Now I have heard that the Two Polarities possess form, manifesting their encompassing and supporting functions to contain all living beings; the Four Seasons have no visible shape," and so forth.
They conceal themselves within cold and heat to transform all things. Thus, by observing Heaven and examining the Earth, even the common and ignorant can recognize their beginnings;

yet, in clarifying the Yin and penetrating the Yang, even the wise and sagacious rarely exhaust their numerical patterns. Therefore, we know that when forms are manifest, they can be verified and even the foolish are not deluded;

but when the form is hidden and cannot be seen, even the intelligent remain silent about it. How much more so for the Way of the Buddha, which honors the profound void, rides upon the obscure, and governs the silent, extensively saving the myriad species!
It governs the ten directions: in its vastness, it pervades the universe; in its subtlety, it encompasses even a hair’s breadth. The wondrous Way is profound and mysterious;
though one follows it, its limits remain unknown. The flow of the Dharma is serene and still; though one draws from it, its source cannot be fathomed.
Thus, the rise of this Great Teaching was rooted in the Western Land; it crossed over to the Han court through a radiant dream and illuminated the Eastern Realm with its flowing compassion.

Thereupon, his collected teachings spread far and wide, rescuing all sentient beings from the three miserable realms; his bequeathed instructions were proclaimed to distant lands, guiding the multitudes of living beings toward the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Among them was the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who in his youth possessed an upright and quick intelligence, early on awakening to the three emptinesses (*trishūnyatā*); as he grew, his spirit and character came into profound accord with the truth.
Having first embraced the four kinds of patience and directed his mind toward the Pure Land, he traveled to the Western Regions for seventeen years.

He sought out and requested the authentic teachings, totaling six hundred and fifty-seven sections, which he then translated and disseminated throughout the Central Kingdom (China). Thus, the sacred teachings that had been deficient were restored to their entirety, and the sentient beings who had been burdened by sin were returned to the state of merit.
Now, it is hoped that this scripture will circulate and be bestowed, enduring as long as the sun and moon; may these blessings spread far and wide, [never ceasing].
Heaven and Earth are eternally vast.

Emperor Gaozong’s taboo name was Zhi, his courtesy name was Weishan. He was the ninth son of Emperor Taizong. In the first year of the Yonghui era, an imperial edict was issued to Huigui of Tiangong Monastery.
The Chan Master was appointed as one of the Four Great Masters (Sida Shi) with the rank of Chao-san Dafu.
In the fifth year [of the Zhenguan era], by special imperial decree, the śrāmaṇera Kuiji (the younger cousin of Weizhi Jingde; he is the founder of Ci'en Monastery) was ordained as a bhikṣu.

In the fifth month of the first year of the Xianqing era, an edict was issued stating that for monks and nuns who violate the laws of the state, they shall be governed according to the monastic code (vinaya) and shall not be subject to the same legal penalties as the common people. In the sixth month of the third year, the Emperor...

When the construction of Ximing Monastery was completed, embroidered images and long banners were brought forth and enshrined within it. The Emperor said: "The two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism both converge upon the same goodness.
The Buddhist school dwells in the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*); the Daoist gate finds virtue in non-virtue (*avadya*).

You masters have studied the Way through antiquity and the present; your respective schools of practice concern emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*). It would be fitting for you to discuss these principles together to mutually enlighten one another. [The Emperor then summoned] the śramaṇas Huili and Daoshi...

The scholar Zhang Huixuan and seven others discussed the principles of doctrine together in the Baifu Hall; the Emperor was pleased. Li was appointed as the *duweina* (monastic administrator) of Ximing Monastery (*shijian*).
In the tenth month of the fourth year, by imperial decree, Yuhua Palace was established as a monastery to honor the late Emperor; the Master of Dharma Xuanzang was summoned to reside there.
On the second day of the second month of the first year of the Linde era, the Master of Dharma Xuanzang passed away, and the Emperor wept for him.
He mourned deeply and suspended court for five days. Looking at his attendants, he said, "The national treasure is lost forever; this can truly be called heart-rending.

By imperial decree, following the precedent of the Tathāgata, he was enshrined in a golden inner coffin and a silver outer coffin, and a stupa was erected on the eastern plain of the Shan River. In the tenth month of the second year of the Qianfeng era, Vinaya Master Daoxuan passed away.
An edict was issued expressing sorrow and lamentation, and it was commanded that his portrait be depicted and his image sculpted in all monasteries throughout the empire.

[As for his being a model (according to the *Jiu Tang Shu* and the two masters’ stupa inscriptions): When the Emperor was in the Eastern Palace, he composed the "Record of the Manifestation of the Sage" (*Shusheng Ji*).

It states briefly: "Now, to propagate the orthodox teaching, there is none but one of wisdom who can broaden its texts; to honor and expound the subtle words, there is none but a worthy one who can determine their purport.
Indeed, the holy teaching of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the profound essence of all dharmas and the guiding track of all scriptures. [It comprehensively encompasses...]
Vast and far-reaching, its profound purport is remote and deep; it exhausts the subtle refinements of emptiness and existence and embodies the essential pivot of arising and ceasing.

Its diction is luxuriant and its Way expansive, such that those who seek it cannot fathom its source. Its phrasing is manifest yet its meaning is obscure, such that those who practice it cannot measure its limits.
Thus we know that where the Sage’s compassion extends, no goodness fails to arrive and no evil fails to be severed.

He has opened the mainstays of the Dharma-net and propagated the orthodox teaching of the Six Perfections; he has rescued the multitudes from their mire and suffering, and unlocked the secret door of the Tripiṭaka.

We humbly reflect that Your Majesty, the Emperor, governs with effortless ease, while those from the eight remote regions bow their heads in court and the myriad nations pay homage. The stone chambers have returned their precious scrolls.

The patterns upon the leaves [of the scriptures] and the verses of the myriad expositions from the Golden Casket have caused the waters of Lake Anavatapta to flow through the eight rivers of the divine realm, and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to join the verdant ridges of Mount Song and Mount Hua.

How could one have foreseen that on nights of profound darkness, the light of the wisdom-standard would be kindled, and on mornings in the burning house, the moisture of the Dharma-rain would descend? Thus, the hundred rivers, though their currents differ, converge in one place.

Within the ocean [of teachings], the myriad distinct meanings are all synthesized into the ultimate reality. The Dharma Master Xuanzang traveled afar across the Ganges River and repeatedly ascended the Snowy Mountains;

he spent seventeen years traveling back and forth seeking the Way. On the sixth day of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, by imperial decree at Hongfu Monastery, he translated six hundred and fifty-seven works. The Emperor composed a preface for these various scriptures, whose principles encompass...

The sounds of metal and stone possess the brilliance of wind and clouds; my writing seeks to embrace their moistening grace. In governing, I have always considered myself like light dust adding to a mountain or a falling dewdrop supplementing a stream.
I have briefly set forth these broad outlines to compose this record.
Empress Wu’s posthumous name was Zhao. She was a native of Wen-shui in Bing-zhou and the consort of Gaozong.

In the third year of the Chuixiong era, the Indian śramaṇa Śīlabhadra (translated as Rìzhào, "Sunlight") translated the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* and other scriptures in Chang’an. The Empress composed a preface for them. This was in the first year of the Caru era.
An imperial edict was issued for the śramaṇa Fǎlǎng and eight others—nine persons in total—to retranslate the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*.
They were all enfeoffed as Counts (xiànggōng) and granted purple *kāṣāyas* and silver tortoise-shaped pouches (the granting of purple robes began with this).

At the beginning of the first year of the Zhèngshèng era, the Empress, because the Chinese translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* had not yet been fully assembled, dispatched an envoy to the kingdom of Khotan to welcome Śikṣānanda. Upon his arrival, he reached the Eastern Capital, Dàbiàn.
At the Empty Temple, [the text] was retranslated by Bodhiruci into eighty fascicles. Later, he composed a preface.

In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, an envoy was dispatched to bestow upon the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, a crystal alms bowl, a worn dharma robe, white woolen cloth, incense, and tea.

An imperial edict was issued to the governor of Shaozhou to provide relief and security for the mountain monasteries. In the second year of the Shengli era (the *Jigu lüe* states this was the first year of Chang’an), an edict was issued for Dharma Master Fazang to lecture on the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Foshouji Monastery.
When he reached the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," both the lecture hall and the ground shook violently.
That same day, he was summoned to the Changsheng Hall to expound its profound meaning; the Empress was left in a state of utter bewilderment.
The matter remained undecided. Zang pointed to the golden lion at the corner of the palace hall as a metaphor; the Empress suddenly attained enlightenment.
She enfeoffed the Master as the Bodhisattva Precept Master Xianshou and compiled his teachings into the *Jinshizi Zhang* (The Treatise on the Golden Lion).
Scholars respectfully refer to this tradition as the Xianshou Teaching (*Gaoseng zhuan* and *Jiu Tang shi*).

Emperor Zhongzong’s taboo name was Xian. He was the seventh son of Emperor Gaozong. His mother was Empress Wu Zetian. In the first year of the Shenlong era, an imperial edict was issued summoning the Sixth Patriarch to the capital.
The text of the decree stated: "I have been providing the two masters, An and Xiu, with offerings within the palace. The two masters said:"
The Chan Master Neng of the South has secretly received the robe and dharma of Great Master Ren; he should be summoned to inquire about the Dharma.

We now dispatch the Inner Attendant Xue Jian with an imperial edict to welcome him. We pray that the Master will look upon us with compassion and hasten to the Capital. The Master declined the invitation by letter, citing illness.

Jian returned to the capital to present his report. Furthermore, an envoy was dispatched to bestow upon him a *kāṣāya*, a water jar, and an alms bowl, in order to convey the Emperor’s profound admiration for him (*Chuan deng lu*).
By imperial decree, the Tripitaka Master Yijing was commissioned to translate the *Mayūra-vyamsa-sūtra* and other scriptures within the Inner Sanctuary (Neidaochang).

The Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (*Shengjiao xu*) to serve as the preface to these scriptures. In the second year, the construction of Shengshan Monastery was completed; the Duke of Shayong, Huifan, was ordered to preside over its consecration.

The Silver Light Grand Master of Splendid Virtue (Yinqing Guanglu Dafu), serving as the Abbot of the Monastery; the Śramaṇa Wansui, promoted to the Court Dispersing Grand Master (Chaosan Dafu) and enfeoffed as a Count (Xian Gong), serving as the General Superintendent of Affairs (Du Weina);
and the Śramaṇa Guangqing, serving as the Acting Director of the Palace Attendants (Jianjiao Dianzhong Jian) and appointed as the Commissioner for Meritorious Works (Gongde Shi).

In the eighth month, an imperial edict was issued to test the scriptural exegesis of novice monks throughout the empire; those who demonstrated thorough mastery without impediment were granted ordination. (This marks the beginning of the practice of testing candidates for ordination through scriptural examinations, according to the *History of Tang*.)

In the second year of the Jinglong era, an imperial edict was issued for Cui Siliang, the Magistrate of Gaoyang, to go to Sizhou to welcome the Great Master Śāṅgha to the capital, where he resided at Jianfu Monastery.
Both the Emperor and his hundred officials addressed him as their "disciple. Emperor Ruizong asked Chan Master Wanhui, "Who is Śāṅgha?
He replied, "He is an emanation of Avalokiteśvara" (*Tongji*).

Emperor睿宗 (Rui-zong), whose personal name was Dan, was the eighth son of Gaozong. In the first year of the Jingyun era, he issued a general amnesty for the empire and bestowed titles and ranks upon the various officials.

Thousands of monks and Daoists were universally ordained (*Tang Shi*). On the third day of the third month of the second year, Śākyamitra (Sengqie) entered parinirvāṇa; by imperial decree, [the funeral rites] were conducted at...

When the clay statues at Jianfu Monastery were enshrined and a pagoda was built, a foul stench suddenly filled the city. By imperial decree, they were permitted to return to Sishui, whereupon a wondrous fragrance immediately wafted forth.

They were subsequently escorted back in their entirety to Puguangwang Monastery, where a pagoda was erected (as recorded in his biography). In the tenth month, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Wanhui to the palace, where he was lodged in the Jixian Academy.
In the twelfth month, he suddenly requested water from the River Wei in Weixiang; though those on both sides of the river could not comply, [he eventually obtained it].
He obtained [the site]. Daoxuan replied, "The ground in front of the cave hall may be used. After drinking water, Daoxuan passed away in a state of profound stillness.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister (Situ) and Duke of Guo. By imperial decree, his portrait was painted in the Jixian Academy (as recorded in his biography).

The Emperor further commissioned Bodhiruci, together with Fazang, Chenwai, and others, at the Ganlu Pavilion in Beiyuan to translate the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*. The Chancellor Zhang Yue and the Right...
Cheng Lu Zangyong, Dr. He Zhizhang, Secretariat Drafter Lu Xiangxian, Minister of Revenue Guo Yuanzhen, and Palace Attendant Wei Zhigu served as literary supervisors and guardians.
In the first year of the Xuantian era (712 CE), Bodhiruci and others presented the newly translated *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* in one hundred and twenty fascicles.
[The Emperor] composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (*Shèngjiào xù*; *Tǒngjì*).

The Emperor of the Xuanzong era, whose personal name was Longji, was the third son of Emperor Ruizong. In the first year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued to construct a Maitreya Buddha Hall at An Guo Temple using timber from the imperial quarters.
In the second year, the Emperor questioned the Dharma Master Shenguang, the Superintendent of Monks for the Left Ward, regarding the Buddha.
"What benevolence and virtue does he possess toward sentient beings that causes one to abandon sovereign and kin, forsake wife and children, and serve him as a teacher?

Shen Guang replied, "The Buddha’s benevolence toward sentient beings exceeds that of heaven and earth; his brilliance surpasses that of the sun and moon; his virtue outweighs that of parents; and his righteousness exceeds that of sovereign and minister.
The Emperor said, "Heaven, earth, the sun, and the moon possess the merit of creation and transformation; parents and sovereign-minister possess the merit of generation and completion."
De asked, "Why do you say that the Buddha surpasses all these? Shen Guang replied, "Heaven can only cover, but cannot support;
Earth can only support, but cannot cover. The sun illuminates the day but not the night; the moon is bright at night but dim during the day."
A father can only give birth but cannot nourish; a mother can only nourish but cannot give birth. When a ruler possesses the Way, his ministers are loyal;
when a ruler lacks the Way, his ministers are sycophantic. By extension, their virtue is thus incomplete. Yet the Buddha’s virtue toward sentient beings is not like this:
in terms of its canopy, it universally covers the four modes of birth; in terms of its support, it sustains all six realms of existence; in terms of its illumination, it...

It illuminates the ten directions. In terms of clarity, it radiates brilliance throughout the three realms of existence; in terms of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it rescues beings from the sea of suffering;

in terms of compassion (*karuṇā*), it delivers those in both the dark and light worlds; in terms of sanctity, it is the king among all sages; in terms of spiritual power, it possesses mastery over the six supernormal faculties (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Thus, it universally saves the living and the dead, and leads away both the noble and the humble. I pray that Your Majesty will take heed and look upon it with reverence. The Emperor was delighted and said:
The Buddha’s grace is such as this; were it not for a teacher, it could not be proclaimed. "I, the Emperor, shall revere and honor [the Dharma] in every lifetime" (Tang History).

In the third year [of his reign], he issued an edict summoning Master Xingyuan to an audience. He questioned him regarding the principles for securing the state and pacifying the people, as well as the essential points of the supramundane Dharma.

He also once asked how the destiny of the dynasty would fare. Xingyuan replied, "The imperial carriage shall undertake a journey of ten thousand *li*, yet the altars of soil and grain will ultimately be blessed. Subsequently, with gold...
He combined them and presented them [to the Emperor]. One day, the Emperor opened and inspected them; it was merely a small amount of *angui* (Asparagus racemosus).
During the rebellion of An Lushan, the Emperor fled to Shu and reached Wanli Bridge. Not long after, he indeed returned. He then realized the significance of the prophecy.

When Emperor Zhaozong was first enfeoffed as the Prince of Ji, the state of Tang reached its end with him; thus it is said, "ultimately auspicious" (*zhong ji*). (From the *Biography of Yixing*). In the fourth year, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi...
Upon arriving at the capital, he was quartered at Ximing Monastery. Later, due to a drought, the Emperor sent Gao Lishi to summon Daoxue to pray for rain.
Daoxue said, "The current drought is but what it ought to be. If you insist on forcing the dragons to appear, the rain that follows will surely be violent.
The Emperor pressed him, saying, "People suffer from the heat; even wind and thunder would be enough to bring relief. Daoxue then filled a bowl with water and stirred it with a small knife.

He recited a mantra in the Sanskrit language. In a moment, there appeared an object like a dragon, as large as a finger, which raised its head above the surface of the water and then submerged beneath the base of the bowl.
After a short while, white vapor rose from the bowl, ascending straight up for several feet. Alarmed, he said to the *lixi* (strongman): "Depart at once! The rain is coming.
Shortly thereafter, a great wind arose with thunder and lightning, and torrential rain poured down as if from a tilted vessel; trees were uprooted by it. The [monastery]...
In the eighth year, the Emperor ascended the Huanao Pavilion and summoned the Dharma Master Daoyin and the Daoist Yin Qian to engage in debate for over forty rounds.

Yin Qian was defeated in argument; by imperial decree, his treatises were compiled and included in the canon, titled the *Kaishan Fudao Lunheng* (Biographies of Eminent Monks and the History of Tang).
In the nineteenth year, he produced the Imperial Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra, which was distributed throughout the empire (*Catalogue of Scriptures*, entry 26).
In the [Kaiyuan] era, an imperial edict was issued for each prefecture and commandery throughout the realm to establish a major monastery, with the name of the reigning year used as its title;

these were all designated as Kaiyuan Monasteries (*Tang Shi*). In the fifth year of the Tianbao era, an edict ordered the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to enter the palace and establish an altar to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the Emperor.

During a summer drought, he was again commanded to pray for rain, which fell in great torrents. He was granted a purple *kāṣāya* robe and two hundred rolls of silk. In that same year, an imperial decree was issued for the ordination of monks throughout the realm.
Both monks and nuns were required to obtain certificates from the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu).

In the twelfth year [of the Kaiyuan era], when the Western Tibetans invaded Anxi, Amoghavajra was summoned to the palace to recite the secret mantras for the protection of the state under Emperor Renzong. The Emperor personally held the incense burner.
A deity appeared wearing armor, and the Emperor asked, "What deity is this? Amoghavajra replied, "He is the eldest son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North. Amoghavajra then recited...

He dispatched them with esoteric incantations. On the twentieth day of the fourth month, a report was submitted from Xiliang stating that on the eleventh day of the second month, some thirty *li* to the northeast of the city, amidst clouds and mist, there appeared divine soldiers of great stature;
a radiance shone from the gate tower to the north of the city, and the sound of drums and horns in the sky shook heaven and earth.
The Western Turks were struck with fear, rolled up their banners, and fled. Upon reading the report, the Emperor issued an imperial decree accordingly.
Statues of the Heavenly Kings were installed on the watchtowers of all the city gates (according to Amoghavajra’s tradition).

Emperor Suzong, whose personal name was Heng, was the third son of Emperor Xuanzong. He ascended the throne at Lingwu and changed the era name to Zhide. At that time, there was widespread turmoil due to banditry and rebellion.

The [rebellion] was at its height. Some advised the Emperor that he should rely on the protection of the Buddha; accordingly, he issued an edict for one hundred *śramaṇas* to enter the palace to perform rites, chanting and reciting sutras morning and evening.
In the second year of the Zhide era, an edict was issued ordering Yuán Jiǎo to establish a Bhaisajyaguru-rāja ritual site at Kāiyuán Monastery in Fèngxiáng.
Suddenly, forty-nine sprouts grew from within the dharma assembly, appearing as *li* trees. Yuán Jiǎo and the others submitted a memorial of congratulations. The Imperial Response stated:
The auspicious peaches flourished in abundance—a portent of the nation’s prosperity. Growing within the precincts of the monastery, they also shared in the splendor of the Bodhi tree.
Moved by this extraordinary omen, I celebrated together with the Master. In the first year of the Qiannian era, the Emperor established an inner chapel within the palace.

He engaged in lecturing, reciting, and chanting hymns. He subsequently issued an edict for each of the Five Sacred Peaks to establish a monastery, selecting śramaṇas of eminent conduct to preside over them.

In the second year, he issued a decree that each province throughout the empire should establish a *fangsheng chi* (pond for releasing living beings), and commanded Yan Zhenqing, the Regional Inspector of Shengzhou, to compose an inscription for it.
In the first year of the Shangyuan era, he dispatched an imperial messenger to Shaoguo’s Caoxi to escort the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch into the palace.
He paid his respects. In the second year, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Huizhong of Nanyang to the capital. The edict stated:
"I have heard that the Supreme Vehicle of the Tamer has long been at peace within our central lands. The Great Hero’s entrustment truly rests upon my person.

Since such a favorable opportunity now exists, do not consider it a hardship. To come to the capital with staff in hand is not far; having purified your mind for so long, hasten to fulfill my wishes. The Master then proceeded to the capital.
He was installed at Qianfu Temple and treated with the etiquette due to a teacher. The Emperor asked the Master, "What Dharma did you obtain at Caoxi?
Zhong said, "Does Your Majesty see that single cloud in the sky? The Emperor replied, "I see it. Zhong said, "Nail it down! Hang it up!

One day, having purified himself through ritual bathing, the Emperor presented ten questions to the Master; the Master’s answers were to the Emperor's satisfaction. Thereupon, the Emperor became deeply focused.
Xuanli of the Mind (Chuan deng lu of the Old Tang History). Emperor Daizong’s personal name was Yu.
He was the eldest son of Emperor Suzong. In the eleventh month of the first year of the Guangde era, the Tibetan army captured the capital. The Emperor—
While [the Emperor] was at Mount Wutai in Xingyin, Mañjuśrī appeared and bestowed secret teachings upon the Emperor.
When Guo Ziyi recaptured the capital and the imperial carriage returned to Chang’an, an edict was issued to construct a Mañjuśrī Hall on Mount Wutai, using copper tiles and coating them with gold.
In the second year, an edict was issued for three hundred monks of the Inner Quarters’ Dharma Hall to lecture and recite the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In the first year of Yongtai...

In the [Xth] year, an imperial edict was issued to all officials that they must not beat or humiliate monks or nuns. In the fifth month, the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch were sent back to Caoxi.
In the ninth month, a cast gold and copper Buddha image was completed; the Emperor led the hundred officials in paying their respects to it.

In the seventh month of the first year of the Dali era, the Alabana (Ullambana) Assembly was held within the palace, where thrones were set for the seven sacred emperors beginning with Gaozu and Taizong.

He offered prayers for their posthumous merit as an annual custom. In the third year, an imperial edict ordered Amoghavajra to establish a ritual altar at Daxingshan Temple, where he was commanded to confer the *abhiṣeka* upon high-ranking officials and generals;

he was subsequently titled "Great Master of Vast Wisdom" (*Daguangzhi Sanzang*). Furthermore, an edict summoned Chan Master Fagin of Mount Jing to the imperial presence, where he was treated with the etiquette due to a teacher.
When the Master requested to return to his mountain retreat, he was granted the honorary title "National One" (*Guoyi*). In the fourth year...
A ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) was established at the Daming Palace, where he was moved by the manifestation of Buddha-light. The Chancellor Pei Mian presented a memorial of congratulation.

In the fifth year, Amoghavajra was promoted to the rank of *Kaifu Yitongsan* and enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui. In the ninth year, the Emperor dreamed that a Pratyekabuddha from Mount Niushou in Jiankang came to visit him;
he then issued an edict for Gu Shen, the Director of the Household of the Crown Prince, to construct a seven-story pagoda on that mountain.
In that year, a Daoist named Shi Hua gained favor through his magical arts. He consequently requested permission to set up a blade-ladder to compete with the śramaṇas in their methods.

An imperial decree was issued for the two monastic districts to select monks to respond to the challenge. The śramaṇa Chonghui submitted a memorial requesting to defeat him. The Emperor led the hundred officials to witness the spectacle.
Hua walked upon the blades and ascended; he beckoned Chonghui to climb. Chonghui stepped onto them and ascended; they went back and forth without injury. Then—

He ordered firewood to be piled like a blazing conflagration in the courtyard. Huiju entered and called out for the flowers; the flowers were so ashamed they broke into a sweat and did not dare look him directly in the eye.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon Hui the title of State-Protecting Tripitaka Master (as recorded in the *Jiugushi*, *Jigelü*, and *Lunheng*).

Emperor Dezong’s personal name was Shi. He was the eldest son of Emperor Daizong. In the first year of the Jianzhong era, the śramaṇa Yuanzhao presented his newly composed *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shu*).

By imperial decree, he was granted purple robes, appointed as an Inner Attendant (*neikongfu*), and promoted to the rank of Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (*jianjiao honglu qing*), with an estate of three hundred households.

(General Record). In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, an imperial edict was issued for the Vinaya Master Daocheng to enter the palace and bestow the Three Refuges precepts upon the consorts, ladies-in-waiting, and eunuchs;

he was subsequently granted the title of Great Circle (Dayuan) Vinaya Master. In the fourth year, an edict was issued to welcome the finger-bone relic of the Buddha from Famen Temple in Fengxiang into the inner palace for veneration, after which it was transmitted to various temples for public worship. On the fourth month of the fifteenth year, the Emperor’s birthday, an imperial decree was issued...
The Director of Ceremonies prepared the ceremonial carriage to escort Professor Chan Master Chengguan into the inner palace hall to propagate the fundamental tenets of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

As Chengguan ascended the seat, he declared: "How magnificent is the True Realm! It is the source from which all phenomena arise; it encompasses both emptiness and existence while remaining free from characteristics, and it enters into words and images yet leaves no trace.
Its wondrous existence is not existent, and its true emptiness is not empty. Our Buddha attained this and wondrously realized true awakening."
He has cleared away the habitual tendencies of defilement and dwells in profound stillness within the realm of myriad transformations; he engages in activity within the midst of the single void.

He merges his body with the *kṣetras* so that they contain one another, and his radiance flows forth to illuminate the far reaches. Our Emperor has attained this [and so forth]. The Emperor turned to his ministers and said:
"The words of my teacher are elegant and concise; his phrasing is classical and rich. He is able to cool me with the sublime Dharma."
The Emperor then conferred upon him the title of National Teacher Qingliang (according to the *Biography of Qingliang*). Emperor Shunzong’s posthumous name was Song;
he was the eldest son of Emperor Dezong. While still in the position of Crown Prince, he asked Chan Master Fuguaru Man about the Buddha.
"From which direction did he come? Toward which direction did he go when extinguished? Since it is said that he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? Manmǎn replied:

"The Buddha came from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and went toward the unconditioned when extinguished. His Dharma-body is equal to empty space; he eternally abides in the state of no-mind. He asked again:
"The Buddha was born in a royal palace and was extinguished at the Twin Trees. He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, yet you also say—"

"It cannot be described," [the Master] said. Man replied, "The Buddha-body is fundamentally unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*); it is through deluded sentiments that false discrimination arises. The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it has never undergone birth or cessation...
(and so forth). The Emperor was greatly pleased. In the first year of the Yongzhen era, he once questioned National Teacher Qingliang regarding the mind-dharma of the ultimate Way.
The Master answered, "The ultimate Way is rooted in the mind; the mind-dharma is rooted in non-abiding. The mind...
"The essence of spirit is aware and never obscured; its nature and characteristics are quiescent... (and so forth). He once asked Master Śrī:
"How can the sentient beings of this great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood? Śrī replied: "The Buddha-nature is like the moon in water;
it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped. The Emperor understood his meaning (*Chuan deng lu*).

Emperor Xianzong, whose personal name was Chun, was the eldest son of Emperor Shunzong. In the tenth month of the first year of the Yuanhe era, he issued an edict for all monks of virtuous conduct throughout the realm to proceed to the capital to propagate the Dharma.
In the second month of the second year, he decreed that the śramaṇa Duafu should record the affairs of the Left Street (monastic administration), along with Ling Sui.
Record of Monastic Affairs of the Right Street. An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Dayi of Mount Ouhu in Xinzhou to enter the Linqide Hall.

A vegetarian feast was prepared and various eminent monks were invited to discourse on the Way. The Emperor attended to listen to the deliberations. A Dharma Master asked, "What is meant by the Four Noble Truths? Dayi replied, "The Sovereign is the One Truth;
where then are the other three? He was further asked, "What is Zen? Dayi pointed toward the empty space.
The Dharma Master had no reply. The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master lectures on the infinite sutras and śāstras, yet even this single point he cannot manage.

The Emperor asked Daoyi, "What is Buddha-nature? Daoyi replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked. The Emperor understood in silence. From this, he came to hold the Chan school in even higher esteem.
In the fifth month of the fourth year, an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities to separately cast a golden seal for him, adding the title "Qing" (Pure).
The State Preceptor Liang was titled the State Preceptor for the Monastic Administration (Shijian), presiding over the affairs of the Imperial Gate.

In the eighth year, he bestowed the posthumous title "Daji" upon Mazu of Jiangxi, and his stupa was named "Dazhuangyan. In the ninth year, by imperial decree, he bestowed the posthumous title "Dazhi" upon Baizhang Huaihai.

The stupa was named "Great Jewel Victorious Wheel. In the tenth year, Ma Zong, the Regional Inspector of Lingnan, submitted a memorial to the Emperor stating that the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi had not yet been granted a posthumous title.
By imperial decree, he was bestowed the title of Chan Master Dajian, and his stupa was named "Numinous Illumination.
In the fourteenth year, the Emperor dispatched the Palace Attendant Du Yingqi to welcome the Śākyamuni relic from within the True Body Stupa at Huguo Temple in Fayun Monastery, Fengxiang.
A finger bone of Kāśyapa Buddha was brought inside. The Emperor personally went to Anfumen Gate to welcome and prostrate before it.

He kept it within the palace for three days to offer worship, during which time five-colored lights appeared. The various officials offered their congratulations. It was escorted through all the monasteries in succession, with its majestic ritual processions, music, banners, and pennants being exceptionally grand and magnificent.
Han Yu, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, submitted a memorial offering vehement remonstrance. The Emperor was greatly incensed and demoted him to Chaozhou.
The Provincial Inspector (according to the Old Histories and the *Lamp of the Dharma Transmission*).
Emperor Muzong, whose posthumous name was Heng, was the third son of Emperor Xianzong. In the third month of the first year of the Changqing era, Liu [Xun], the Regional Commander of Lulong...
He collectively petitioned for the twenty-odd prefectures of You and Yan to return to the court and requested ordination as monks.
An imperial edict was issued granting them monastic robes, and he was titled the Great Enlightenment Master (Dàjué Dàshī). His residence was designated as Bào'ēn Temple (Old History).

In the second year, the Left Street Monastic Registrar Língfù was dispatched with an imperial edict to summon the Chan Master Wúyè of Fénzhōu to the capital. Upon arriving and having delivered the edict, Língfù bowed his head and said:
"I pray that you, Master, will arise and attend to me. The Master smiled and said, "What virtue do I possess to trouble the Sovereign so often?

You may go on ahead; I shall follow immediately. Thereupon, he bathed, sat upright, and passed away. Xu Fǔ returned and reported these matters to the Emperor, who sighed in admiration and bestowed upon him the posthumous title of National Teacher Dàdá (Great Attainment) [as recorded in the *Chúndēng Lù*].
He once composed a eulogy for Vinaya Master Xuán of Nánshān, which begins: "In every age there arises an enlightened person, acting as a..."
Envoys arrived; dragons and ghosts submitted, while devas and humans served him. His fame spread across the Five Indies, and his reputation shook ten thousand li.
As the golden sun sank in the west, the Buddha-sun rose in the east. Bowing my head in refuge, I take as my master the Patriarch of Vinaya.

Jingzong’s imperial name was Zhan. He was the eldest son of Emperor Muzong. In the first year of the Baoli era, an imperial decree was issued to establish Fangdeng ordination platforms at two monasteries:
An Guo Temple in the Left Street and Xingfu Temple in the Right Street. Liu Gui, a General of the Central Guard, was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Left and Right Streets.

The Virtuous Envoy selected those who practiced the precepts as Great Virtues (Mahāśramaṇas) and ordered them to test the youth’s mastery of the scriptures before he was granted ordination (*Tongji*).

Emperor Wenzong, whose personal name was Āng, was the second son of Emperor Muzong. On the birthday of the tenth month of the first year of the Tahe era, an imperial edict was issued by Bai [Jingxi], the Director of the Secretariat Library.

In the fifth year [of the Yonghui era], Bai Juyi, the State Preceptor Yilin of Anguo Temple, and the Daoist Yang Hongyuan of Shangqing Palace held a discussion on the Three Teachings at Linqide Hall (from the *Yuelu Tianwen Ji*). At that time, the Emperor was fond of eating clams.
One day, an image of a Bodhisattva appeared within a clam. An imperial decree was issued for Chan Master Weizheng of Taishan to inquire about it. Weizheng said: "Things have no..."
"This is merely a response to your emptiness; it is simply to broaden Your Majesty’s faith. He quoted the Sūtra:

"If there are those who should be saved by this body, he immediately manifests this body and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said, "The Great Being has already manifested himself, yet I have not heard him preach the Dharma.
Zhenzheng replied, "Does Your Majesty regard this as permanent or impermanent? Do you believe it or not? The Emperor said, "It is a rare and marvelous thing."

"How could one not believe it? Cheng said, "I have finished preaching the Dharma. The Emperor was greatly pleased and immediately issued an edict that all monasteries throughout the empire must establish images of the Holy Avalokiteśvara (Shijian).
In the third month of the third year of the Kaicheng era, Chengguan passed away. Because the Emperor revered him as a patriarch and a sage, he specifically suspended court for three days.
High-ranking officials wore white mourning garments, and his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.
Emperor Xuanzong, whose personal name was Chen, was the thirteenth son of Emperor Xianzong. He was enfeoffed as Prince Guang. Emperor Wuzong resented him and confined him in the rear garden.
The eunuch Qiu Shiliang secretly ordered him to shave his head and become a monk; he then traveled throughout the world and visited An of Yanguan.
The Chan Master An said to the Emperor, "The time has come; do not linger like a mud-dwelling serpent. He then entrusted him with the Buddha-Dharma.

Upon the death of Emperor Wuzong, Yang Gong, the Commander-in-Chief of the Left Shenche Army, exhorted the Prime Minister and the various officials to welcome and install him. He ascended the throne and changed the era name.
In the intercalary third month of the Dazhong era, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "During the final years of the Huichang reign, monasteries were consolidated and abolished.

Although it is said that the teachings of foreign lands provide a source for the principles of governance, the people of the Middle Kingdom have long practiced these ways. The reforms were excessive, and the resulting circumstances were contrary to proper principle.
Regarding the sacred sites of the Spirit Mountain and the monasteries abolished in the fifth year of Huichang, all those who were formerly established there..."

The monks were permitted to continue their restoration and maintenance of their residences (*Tang Shi*). In the second year, an imperial decree was issued to establish monasteries and ordination platforms for the *Samantabhadra* (Fǎděng) precepts in the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang, as well as in Jingzhou, Yangzhou, Bianzhou, and Yizhou, so that those among the monks and nuns who had been ordained more than once might receive the precepts again.
Five monasteries were established on Mount Wutai, with fifty monks ordained at each. In the third year, an imperial decree appointed the śramaṇa Língyàn as the Left [Grand Master].
In the fourth year, by imperial decree, the temple where Master An of Yanguan, Hangzhou, resided was granted the name Qifeng Temple.
