In the first month of the fifth year, an edict summoned Chan Master Hongbian to the inner palace. The Emperor asked, "Why is there a distinction between the Northern and Southern schools of the Chan tradition?
The Master replied, "The Chan gate originally has no North or South. It was only when Master Hongren had two disciples—"

One, Huineng, was able to reside in Lingnan; the other, Shenxiu, propagated the teachings in the north. Although their attainment of the Dharma was one and the same, there were differences between sudden and gradual regarding their guidance and the awakening of others.
Hence it is said: "Sudden in the South, Gradual in the North. The Emperor asked: "What are the names of precept, concentration, and wisdom?"

The Master said: "To guard against what is improper and to cease from evil is called *śīla* (precept). For the six sense faculties to encounter objects without the mind following after conditions is called *samādhi* (concentration).

For both mind and objects to be empty, such that one’s illumination and discernment are free from delusion, is called *prajñā* (wisdom). What is meant by 'expedient means' (*upāya*)? The Master said: "To conceal reality and cover over appearances is the gateway of skillful expediency.
"What is the Buddha-mind? The Master said: "'Buddha' refers to awakening; 'mind' is another name for the Buddha. There was... [text ends]
When asked how one should practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, the Master said: "Those of middling or inferior faculties cannot achieve sudden enlightenment.

Therefore, the Buddha opened the gate of contemplation, instructing them to recite the Buddha's name so as to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. On this day, Hongbian presented his memorial to the Emperor.
At the seventh watch after sunset, the Emperor was pleased and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Yuanzhi (Old History; Five Lamps).

Emperor Yizong’s personal name was Cui. He was the eldest son of Emperor Xuanzong. In the fourth month of the third year of the Xiantong era, an imperial edict was issued for the two monastic districts and four temples to each establish ordination platforms (*jietan*) to ordain monks.
Huanyong of Daci Mountain in Hangzhou passed away; Emperor Xizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Xingkong.

The pagoda is named "Samādhi and Prajñā. He further composed a eulogy for it: Treading upon the reality, his mind awakened to the boundless. Nanquan and Zhaozhou engaged in spirited debate and response.
Lacking cold spring water while dwelling there, a tiger ran forth to provide it for him. Only his virtue is fragrant; the breeze is clear and the sun is bright.
On the third day of the twelfth month of the sixth year, Deshan Xuanjian passed away while seated; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Jiexing.

On the tenth day of the fourth month of the eighth year, Linji Yixuan sat upright, recited a verse, and passed away; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huizhao, and his stupa was named Chengling.
On the [third] day of the third month of the tenth year, Dongshan Liangjie entered nirvana; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Wuben.
The Master’s stupa was named Huijue. In the eleventh year, Emperor [Xuanzong] bestowed upon Vinaya Master Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain the honorary title Chengzhao.
In the fifth month of the twelfth year, the Emperor visited An Guo Temple and granted Zhi Xuan a precious throne made of *candana* and aloeswood, over twenty feet in height.

In the third month of the fourteenth year, he commissioned a jeweled canopy for the pagoda, along with colorful banners and flowered parasols; by imperial decree, those from both monastic districts were sent to Fengxiang.

Xiang went out to welcome the Buddha’s relics. On the eighth day of the fourth month, they arrived at the capital. The Emperor took his place at the Anfu Gate to receive them with prostrations and enter the palace to pay his respects.
When some of the ministers came forward to remonstrate, saying that when Emperor Xuanzong had welcomed the Buddha’s relics he soon passed away, the Emperor replied, "I have obtained them while alive;
I have no regrets even if I die. The Emperor frequently established lecture halls within the inner palace, personally chanting the essential meanings of the scriptures with his own hands.
The Sanskrit text was transcribed for use in chanting (as recorded in the *Jiǔshǐ*, *Jīgǔlüè*, and the *Hùpǎosì Jì*). Emperor Xīzōng’s personal name was Xuān;
he was the fifth son of Emperor Yìzōng. In the first year of the Guǎngmíng era, fleeing the invasion by Huang Cháo, he took refuge in Chengdū.
An imperial edict summoned Dharma Master Zhixuan to the imperial residence for discussion; he was granted the title National Teacher Wudao and remained at court for a long time.

He eventually took leave to return to Jiulong (Biographies of Eminent Monks). Furthermore, the posthumous title Great Master Wuxiang was bestowed upon Yongjia Xuanjue, and his stupa was named Jingguang.

Emperor Zhaozong, whose personal name was Ye, was the seventh son of Emperor Yizong. On his birthday in the first year of Longji, an imperial decree was issued for monks and Daoists from both monastic districts to enter the inner palace to engage in scriptural discourse.
In the third year of Qianning, an imperial decree was issued to rebuild the thatched hall at the site where Dharma Master Kumārajīva had translated the scriptures.
Tangsi Temple. In the fourth year [of the reign], an imperial edict conferred the posthumous title "Great Master Zhenjì" upon Zhaozhou Congshen (Tongji).
*Fófǎ Jīntāng Biān*, Scroll Seven. Re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing, *Fófǎ Jīntāng Biān*, Scroll Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai;
[recorded by] Xiao Yu.

Yu, whose courtesy name was Shiwen, was the son of Emperor Ming of the Later Liang and served as Chancellor to the Gaozu. The Grand Astrologer Fu Yi submitted a memorial seven times requesting the abolition of Buddhism;
the Gaozu presented this document to his ministers for deliberation. The high officials all said, "Buddhism has flourished since successive dynasties;
it promotes goodness, restrains evil, and provides invisible assistance to the state. There is no reason to abolish it. Yu replied, "The Buddha is a sage..."
However, Yi opposed this. [The Emperor] declared that those who disparage the Sage have no law by which to be governed and should be punished for their crime.

Taizong said to him: "The Way of the Buddha is subtle and profound; its sacred traces are worthy of reverence. Furthermore, its manifestations of karmic retribution are manifest and clear. Why is it that you alone do not realize its principles?"
Yi’s responses offended the Emperor’s will, and Taizong detested him; from that time on, Yi was never spoken of again for the rest of his life.
Yu built Jinliang Temple in Lantian and invited Chan Master Faxi to reside there (as recorded in the *Jiu Shu* and the *Gaoseng Zhuan*).
Pei Ji, courtesy name Xuanzhen, was a native of Sangquan in Puzhou. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as the Vice Director of the Jinyang Palace.

When the High Ancestor ascended the throne, he said to Ji, "It is you who have enabled me to reach this position. He was subsequently appointed as the Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs. The High...
One day, the Founder asked his ministers, "Fu Yi constantly claims that Buddhism is useless. What do you think?

Jiji replied, "When Your Majesty first raised the righteous army, your will was set upon the Triple Gem. When you spoke of ascending the throne as the Son of Heaven, you vowed to open the Gate of Mystery."

Now that the six directions have returned to benevolence and we possess the wealth of the four seas, if one wishes to adopt the words of Yi, would this not detract from past virtue and manifest present faults? (Jiu Tang Shu)

Li Shizheng served as the Ritual Master (Dianyi) for the Qin Prince’s household. In the ninth year of the Wude era of Gaozu, he composed the *Neide lun* (Treatise on Internal Virtue) to criticize [the views of] Zhuan Yi.
Its preface states in brief: "As for the One of Ten Powers who acts as a charioteer, he steers the Dharma-boat across the sea of suffering. Through the three vehicles..."
Drawing [beings] upward, it levels the path through the burning house. In the breadth of its exhortation to cultivate goodness and advance virtue, it surpasses what is found in the Six Classics;

in the depth of its prohibition of evil and prevention of calamity, no school among the Nine Streams can compare to it. Furthermore, the Buddha merely promotes goodness and does not encourage evil among his subjects;

the precepts are fundamentally for the prevention of wrongdoing—how could they harm the governance of family or state? If every person observes goodness and every household honors the precepts, [the world will be transformed].
How could punishments be so widespread? How could calamities and chaos arise without cause? (And so forth). I have respectfully composed three treatises.

In the "Discerning Delusions" chapter, I clarify the commonalities and obscurations between the heterodox and the orthodox. In the "Understanding Fate" chapter, I distinguish between the interplay of misfortune and fortune.
The "Chapter on Emptiness and Existence" refutes the dogmatic views of nihilism and eternalism. The "Chapter on Dispelling Delusions" states briefly:
A certain intelligent scholar said to a loyal and upright gentleman, "Śākyamuni was born in India; his teachings largely emerged from the Western Regions.

His fame and status cannot rival those of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, nor do his merits and virtues find mention in the *Canon* or the *Annals*. He is truly revered by distant barbarians, but not by those within the Middle Kingdom."

The teachers and scholars of the Xia dynasty said: "The loyal and upright gentleman has observed that Youyu originated from the Western Rong, yet he assisted Duke Mu of Qin in establishing the foundations of hegemony;
and Li Dayi was born among the Northern Rong, yet he served Emperor Wu of Han to eliminate dangers and calamities.

Why must one necessarily adopt those who share the same customs while rejecting those from different regions? As for extending one's own empathy to all things, how does this compare to the vastness of the Buddha’s compassion?"
By observing the branches, one knows the root; how could this be as distant from the Buddha’s teaching? In exhorting the good and punishing evil, how could it be as expansive as the Buddha’s?
In clarifying emptiness and analyzing existence, how could it be as profound as the Buddha’s?
Viewed from this perspective, its Way is marvelous; the virtue of the Sage cannot surpass it. How can one be born in a foreign land and yet disparage that Way? (And so forth.)
Regarding his *Tongming* (Extending Life), there are two chapters on "Emptiness" and "Existence" which are not recorded here (*Hongming ji*).
Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui. Xuanling’s courtesy name was Qiaoian.
When Taizong ascended the throne, because Xuanling possessed the talent to decide victory or defeat and stabilize the state, [he was appointed].

Gong was promoted to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. He held the position of Chancellor for fifteen years, was enfeoffed as the Duke of Wei, and was posthumously honored with the title Wenzhao.

During the time when the śramaṇas Xuemu and Xuanzang were translating sūtras and śāstras, an imperial edict charged Xuanling with supervising these affairs. Ruohui, whose courtesy name was Keming, [was also appointed].

When Emperor Taizong ascended the throne, he was promoted to Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs (*you puye*). Together with Fang Xuanling, he managed the affairs of state. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lai.

He revered the Way of Dharma Master Yuankuan and constantly inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. At the end of his life, he summoned Yuankuan, wishing for him to be his teacher in every successive lifetime (from the *Sengshi*).
Changsun Wuji, whose courtesy name was Fuji, assisted Emperor Taizong in pacifying the world, his merit ranking first among all. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qi.
In the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong distributed newly translated scriptures by Xuanzang to the Governors-General of the ten circuits. [The text continues: "To display..."
It was circulated and disseminated. Wu Ji and Chu Suiliang, the Director of the Secretariat, memorialized: "The Buddhist teachings are profound and mysterious; neither gods nor men can fathom them.

Your Majesty’s supreme Way is brilliantly manifest as you have established the Triple Gem. You dispatched Master [Xuanzang] to traverse perilous paths to seek scriptures, which he has now returned to translate.
These are like the initial preaching of Āmrapālī, appearing as if the golden mouth of the Buddha has newly opened; all this is due to Your Majesty’s sagely virtue."

This is what has been brought forth by our karmic retribution. We, your humble and ignorant subjects, have had the fortune to witness and hear this; the waves of the sea of suffering now have a vessel upon which to rely.
How much more so, since Your Majesty’s vast and far-reaching compassion causes it to be spread throughout the Nine Provinces, so that all the teeming masses may partake of the wondrous Dharma.
For us, this is a joyous encounter after billions of kalpas; we cannot contain our profound gratitude and good fortune. (Old History of the Tang)
Chu Liang (Liang), courtesy name Ximing, was a native of Hangzhou. He was one of the Eighteen Scholars. In a letter to Vinaya Master Xian, he wrote briefly:
"I, your disciple, have been fortunate in my life and early on entered the karmic conditions for the Dharma. Recently, at Mount Hua, I established a monastic residence. This...

This mountain harbors rare mysteries and commands the misty clouds; it is a place where the worthy and the sages alike find their ultimate refuge. Although its structures have long existed, the practice of meditation and recitation remains sparse.

Furthermore, to uphold the Three Jewels, one must rely on the strength of the "elephants and dragons" (the great disciples), and to serve as the vanguard for the fourfold assembly, one requires the flock of "swans and ducks" (the virtuous).

You Dharma Masters possess a profound mastery of the scriptures and your reputations are renowned throughout both the mundane and the supramundane. We look up to you with hope that you will deign to comply with our humble request.

I pray that you will deign to descend from your traces and appear before us; then the distant legacy of Shi Yuan’s meditative abode may be emulated, and the pure dust of Wang Xun’s vihāra shall not remain obscure—this is my earnest wish (from the *Hongming ji*).
Yu Shinan (虞世南), courtesy name Boshī, was a native of Yuyao in Yuezhou. During the Daye era, he held successive offices culminating in that of Librarian of the Imperial Library (Shumu Lang).

During the reign of Emperor Taizong, he served as a Scholar of the Hall of Broad Literature (Hongwen Guan Xueshi). Later, he retired from office with the rank of Silver Light Grand Master of Splendid Honor (Yinqing Guanglu Daifu). His portrait was depicted [among the court officials].
The Lingyan Pavilion. He was posthumously titled Wenyi. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, Yan Shouwen submitted a memorial stating:
"When I, your disciple, suddenly encountered a grave illness in my youth, on the day my condition improved through the application of my mind, I offered a vegetarian feast for a thousand people.
Now, I respectfully provide vegetarian food for a thousand monks at this ritual site. By the power of this vow, I hope that in life after life I shall always be free from sickness and affliction. (7)
"Throughout the long course of the world, those of the six realms—whether enemies or kin—are all the same as they are today; this is my vow" (from the *Fàtiè*). The *Dìwáng lüèlùn* states:

The Prince said, "Liu Wu of the Liang dynasty eliminated the cruel and the violent to successfully establish his imperial enterprise. Ruling from the southern face for over fifty years, he truly possessed the Way of both civil and martial governance.
As for his devotion to the Buddhist scriptures and his emulation of the conduct of the śramaṇas, he did so as a sovereign of ten thousand chariots."
If one cultivates even the small virtues of a common man until they are free from defilement, how could it be that the Way is not effective when the peril of ruin has already arrived?

Why would the blessings of humility fail to take effect? Master Shi (whose personal name was Shinan) said: "The Buddhist teaching is the bridge for transcending the world and the track for leaving behind the dust of the mundane.
It operates within the square inch of the mind and transcends the realm of existence and non-existence. Once the burdens of worldly dust are exhausted—"
Once攀緣 (pān-yuán; clinging/mental objects) has ceased, one subsequently enters the gate of liberation.

As for the methods for transforming the secular world, there are giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. How are these any different from benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity?
It is simply because that which is cultivated constitutes the cause, and its retribution constitutes the fruit. When people cultivate these six practices, they all...
For the most part they are incomplete; if there is even one deficiency, the fruit likewise perishes accordingly. Thus, Zongming was ugly in appearance but wise in mind;
Zhao Yi excelled in talent but was humble regarding his status; Luo Bao was wealthy but lacked righteousness; while Yuan Xian was poor yet possessed the Way.
Their differences were as vastly divergent as this. Prosperity and ruin, gain and loss—all must necessarily depend upon this. Below...

Ordinary men and commoners, seeing that Bi Gan’s heart was cut out, concluded that loyalty and integrity cannot be practiced; hearing that King Yan lost his state, they concluded that benevolence and righteousness are not worth emulating.
If this were so, then the bandit Zhi could sleep soundly with his head on his pillow at Dongling, and Zhuang Qiao could hang up his carriage in Western Shu;
would it not be truly noble for them to have met their ends in peace? The Prince said: "As for man..."
"Is the path cultivated by a ruler different from that of the common people? The Master replied: "A sovereign dwells in a position of supreme dignity and holds the gate of life and death.
His power is like a swift wind or cloud, and his strength can crush mountains and peaks; his majesty and virtue are vast, and his influence is rapid.
In cultivating the Way, he ought to take universal salvation as his concern and benevolence and forbearance as his essence. If there is even a single being who loses their proper place..."
If one takes what has been cast into the moat and extends this single principle to all things under heaven, one will grasp the true essence of the Way.

If, however, one’s benevolence does not reach even the reeds by the marsh and one’s transformation does not moisten those beyond the seas, then even a meager, solitary act of goodness is of no account.
(From the *Lüe lun diwang*, composed by Shi Nanshan. Later, after Nanshan had passed away, Taizong saw him in a dream and consequently issued an edict, saying:

Li Shinan’s virtuous conduct was pure and complete, and his aspirations were set upon loyal service and beneficial counsel. That he has suddenly passed away in accordance with the natural transformation of things leaves me deeply grieved.
Yesterday, I suddenly beheld this man in a dream at night; moreover, he offered forth candid words as if we were old acquaintances from our former lives.

You may immediately prepare a vegetarian feast for five hundred monks and commission one statue of the Buddha at his home, to provide merit for his afterlife and to express my intention to honor our shared past.
(Old History of the Tang). When Emperor Taizong defeated Xue Ju at Bingzhou, he established Zhaoren Temple.
Xu Zhongyan composed the inscription for its stele, with contributions from Chu Suiliang, Li Baiyao, Yan Shigu, Xu Jingzong, Zhu Zishē, and Cen Wénben.
Sui Liang, whose courtesy name was Dengshan, was the son of Sui Liang. During the Zhenguan era, he was successively promoted to the post of起居郎 (Record Keeper).
He was subsequently appointed as 諫議大夫 (Censor-in-Attendance) concurrently with the duties of Record Keeper. When Emperor Taizong defeated Song Jingang at Jinzhou, he established Ciyun Temple.

The Emperor then commissioned Liu Suiliang to compose the inscription for the stele. Li Baiyao, whose courtesy name was Zhonggui, was a native of Dingzhou. In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he served as a Secretariat Drafter (*zhongshu sheren*).
He presented the "Treatise on Feudalism" (*jianfen lun*), and the Great Ancestor adopted his advice, appointing him as the Right Attendant-in-Ordinary (*you shuzi*) to the Crown Prince.

When Taizong defeated Liu Wuzhou at Fenzhou, he established Hongji Temple and commissioned Baiyao to compose its inscription. Furthermore, he once composed the [Great... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)
The preface to the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states briefly: "The studies of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna all take this treatise as their foundation;
if one does not master it, one cannot yet propagate the Dharma" (as recorded in the *Benzhuan* and the *Dadianlu*). Yan Shigu, whose courtesy name was Zhouxian, was a native of Langye.

Emperor Taizong once lamented that the Five Classics had fallen into corruption; Yan Shigu examined, determined, and rectified them. The Emperor subsequently distributed the standardized texts throughout the realm.

Shortly thereafter, he was appointed as the Vice Director of the Secretariat. When Taizong defeated Dou Jiande at Zhengzhou, he established Cishi Temple and commissioned Shi Gu to compose its inscription.
Xu Jingzong was a man of unknown origin; when Taizong defeated Huo Laosheng at Lüzhou, he established Puji Temple and commissioned Jingzong to compose its inscription.
Zhu Zishē was a native of Suzhou; during the Zhenguan era, he served in succession...
He was appointed as a Scholar of the Hongwen Hall. When Emperor Taizong defeated Wang Shichong at Luozhou, he established Zhaojue Temple and commissioned his son, Li Sha, to compose its inscription.

Cen Wenben, whose courtesy name was Jingren, was a native of Dengzhou. In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he was appointed Secretary郎 (Lang) and subsequently promoted to Chief Secretary (Zhongshuling).
When Emperor Taizong defeated Liu Heitan at Mingzhou (present-day Guangping Prefecture), he established Zhaofu Temple.
Wenben was commissioned to compose the inscription for the stele. In his youth, Wenben had frequently recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Once, while traveling by boat on the Wu River, the vessel capsized and everyone aboard perished; Wenben was submerged in the water, at which point someone said to him, "If you simply recite the Buddha's name, you will certainly not die.

He was then swept up by the waves and emerged onto the shore, escaping with his life. Later, when he hosted a vegetarian feast at his home, a monk departed late and said: [...the rest of the passage...]
He said, "The world is currently in turmoil; may you, sir, fortunately not be caught in the calamity. Eventually, you will encounter a period of great peace and attain wealth and honor.
Having finished speaking, he vanished. When Wenben later went to his place of retreat, he again found two śarīras in his bowl (as recorded in the *Jiu Tang Shu* and the *Tong Ji*).
Liu Qiu Yin served as the Prefect of Taizhou during the Zhenguan era. As he was about to take up his post, he suddenly suffered from a headache caused by wind; medical treatments failed to cure it.
Fenggan happened to visit his home while traveling and claimed he was skilled at treating this ailment. Yin ordered him to treat it. The Master—
He sprinkled water on him, and he was immediately healed. Daoyin asked the master where he had come from; the master replied, "I have come from Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.

Daoyin asked again, "What worthy men are there at Mount Tiantai? The master said, "If you see them, you do not recognize them; if you recognize them, you do not see them. If you wish to see them, you must not grasp at appearances.
Hanshan Manjusri has hidden his traces at Guoqing, and Shide Samantabhadra appears like a poor man. Daoyin then proceeded to the prefecture.
He immediately went to Guoqing Temple and asked for the courtyard where Fenggan resided. The monk Daoqiao led him to an empty room where many tiger tracks were visible;
he said that the Chan Master was there, spending his days solely pounding rice to provide for the community, while at night he would sing songs for his own amusement.

He also inquired about Hanshan and Shide, and Daoqiao led him to the front of the hearth, where he saw the two men laughing heartily as they sat by the fire. Zhenyin stepped forward and prostrated himself before them. The two—
A passerby shouted, "Fenggan is so talkative! He does not even recognize Amitābha; why do you bow to him?
The two men immediately took each other's hands and laughed, then headed toward the Cold Rock (Han-yen) without returning to the monastery.

Daoying then ordered Daoqiao to record three hundred songs and poems from the walls, bamboo, and stones of village houses and estates, compiling them into a single volume. Daoying composed a preface for it.
And he also praised the practice of the world (Preface to the Poetry of Han and Shi). Sun Simiao was a native of Jingzhao.
In the first year of the Shangyuan era, Emperor Gaozong summoned him for an audience and appointed him as an Advisor to the Throne (Jianyi Dafu), but he firmly declined the honor.

The Emperor asked which Buddhist scripture was the greatest. Daomiao replied, "None is greater than the *Avataṃsaka*. The Emperor said, "Recently, Master Xuanzang translated the *Prajñāpāramitā* in six hundred fascicles;
why is that not considered great? Daomiao replied, "The Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka* is the gateway to all things;
from within a single gate, one may produce thousands of great volumes of scripture. The *Prajñāpāramitā*, however, is but a single gate within the *Avataṃsaka*."
[The Emperor] listened. Thereupon, the Emperor first began to uphold the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. In this year, Si-miao requested to return to the mountains;

he entered Zhongnan Mountain to live in seclusion, dedicating his will to the Buddhist scriptures and transcribing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by hand. Lu Zhao-lin praised Si-miao, saying: "In his lofty discourse on the 'Correct and One' (*Zhengyi*), he was the Zhuangzi of old;
in his profound entry into the 'Non-dual' (*Buer*), he was the Vimalakīrti of today. (From the *Huayan jing ganying zhuan* and the original [text]).
[End of] Tradition. Sīmāo resided on Mount Zhongnan and was on friendly terms with Vinaya Master Xuán. At that time, there was a great drought.

A monk from the Western Regions established an altar at Kūṇḍing Lake to pray for rain; after seven days, the water level had receded by several feet. An old man came to the Master at night seeking his help.
He claimed to be a dragon deity within the pond. The Master said, "You may go and seek out Mr. Sun. The old man went to his residence.
Sun Simiao said, "I have heard that there are thirty divine prescriptions in the Dragon Palace of Kunming. If you can transmit them, I shall save you.
The old man replied, "These prescriptions are not permitted by the Supreme Lord to be transmitted indiscriminately. Now that the situation is desperate," he suddenly presented the prescriptions.

When [the water] reached [its limit], Si-miao said, "Return; you need have no further concern. From that time on, the pond swelled and overflowed. Si-miao composed the *Qianjin fang* (Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold) in thirty fascicles;
he placed one prescription at the end of each fascicle so that the world could not distinguish between them (*Youyang zazu*).
Du Xingyi was a native of Jingzhao. He served as the Director of the Dianke Bureau of the Honglu Si.
When the Śramaṇa Buddhapāli (translated here as Juehu) of Kaśmīra arrived at Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, he encountered an old man who asked him: "What [is your purpose]?"
He came and said, "I wish to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The Elder asked, "Have you ever brought the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī* with you? He replied, "No.
The Elder said, "The sentient beings of this land commit many transgressions. You should go back and retrieve that dhāraṇī to circulate it in this land for great benefit.
I shall show you where Mañjuśrī resides. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished. Thereupon, Póli...

He returned to his native country to retrieve the mantra. In the first year of the Tiānlù era, he arrived in Cháng'ān. Emperor Gāozōng ordered Xíngxíng Yǐ and the Tripiṭaka Master Rìzhào to co-translate the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī Sūtra*.

They encountered instances where imperial names were used and avoided them all; they changed "World-Honored One" (*Śāstṛ*) to "Holy Honored One" (*Śrī-guru*) and "to cure and treat" to "to rescue and eliminate.
Gāozōng said, "How could the words of the Buddha’s scriptures be subject to the avoidance of imperial names? He then issued an edict ordering the corrections.
In the first year of the Hongdao era, Pali again took the Sanskrit manuscript and translated it together with the monk Shunzheng of Ximing Monastery;
this version is largely the same as that translated by Xingyi, though with minor differences (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, entry on Shi Jian).

Fang Rong, courtesy name Guanrong, was a native of Qinghe. He served as the Chief Minister (Pingzhangshi) of the Chancellery and Secretariat. In the first year of the Shenglong era, he was demoted to Gaoyou;
upon reaching Guangzhou, he encountered the śramaṇa from Central India, Prajñāmitra, who was translating the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* at Zhizhi Temple.
At the temple, Rong served as the scribe. Guan, whose courtesy name was Cili, was the son of Rong; he served as the magistrate of Tonglu County.
While traveling with the Daoist Xing Hepu, they passed through Xiakou Village and entered an abandoned temple, where they sat beneath an ancient pine tree.

They sent someone to dig into the ground and discovered letters from Lou Shide addressed to Master Yong, which were stored inside a jar. Xing said to Guan, "Do you recall this? Guan was struck with a sudden realization.

However, he realized that his former life was that of Chan Master Yong (according to the *History of the Tang*). Chan Master Shenhui commissioned an artist to depict the lineage from Bodhidharma to the Sixth Patriarch;
Yuan Guan then composed the "Preface to the Diagram of the Six Leaves" (*Tonglun*).

Zhang Yue, courtesy name Daoji (also styled Shuo zhi), was a native of Luoyang. During Empress Wu’s examination of men of talent and integrity (*xianliang fangzheng*), Zhang Yue ranked first in his responses to the imperial questions.

He was subsequently promoted to Left Assistant in the Palace Library (*zuobuque*). During the Kaiyuan era, he served as Chief Secretary of the Chancellery (*zhongshuling*) and was enfeoffed as Duke of Yan. His posthumous title was Wen ("Literary").
Zhen was eloquent, refined, and vigorous in his speech. He was particularly skilled in the Buddhist scriptures and composed a preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, which states in brief:

"The myriad practices arise from the mind; the mind is the master of man. The Three Vehicles converge in the One; the One is the source of the Dharma. To know that the mind is unobtainable is true attainment;
to see the One and have nothing that is not penetrated is perfect penetration. He also composed the *Fadiyuan Fa* (Dharma of the Dharma-Ground Court).
The Hall Praise says: This Buddha has the characteristic of space; this Dharma is the subtle and wondrous light. Concentration and wisdom are never separate; this Sangha is the harmonious assembly.
Persons are empty and dharmas are also empty; even these two emptinesses are further empty. Dwelling the mind in the treasure of the three emptinesses—this is called the place of the Three Refuges.
If seeing does not stain, and knowing does not grasp at consciousness, this is called true seeing; it is also called...
Liberation is knowledge. The Buddha contemplates that all phenomena are free from arising and ceasing; they are thus.

He spoke [this verse], entrusting ten *jin* of incense to Wu Pingyi to deliver to Caoqi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. The poem says: "The Great Master has abandoned the world and departed, Yet he leaves behind his Dharma-body.
I pray you send this unimpeded incense, To reach the South Sea at will. (From the *Benzhuan* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*)
Song Jing (styled Jing) was a native of Nanhe in Xingzhou. He was upright and possessed great integrity. Devoted to learning, he was skilled in literary composition.

He passed the jinshi examination and, during the Kaiyuan era, was appointed as Chancellor on the same day as Zhang Yue. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Guangping and posthumously honored with the title Wenzheng. He served as the Governor of Guangzhou.
On the day of the seasonal festival, he entered Caoqi to pay homage at the stupa of the Sixth Patriarch and made a vow, saying: "I, your disciple, vow to protect the Great Dharma throughout my life;
I pray for a single auspicious sign to manifest this sincerity. As soon as he finished speaking, a subtle fragrance permeated the air and sweet rain poured down.
Wonhyo rejoiced and departed after composing a poem (as recorded in his biography and the *Tonglun*).

Li Hua, courtesy name Xiashu, was a native of Zhaozhou. During the Tianbao era, he was appointed as an Inspector of the Censorate. He once studied *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) under Chan Master Jingshan Daoruan of Jingxi.
Jingxi composed for him a single essay on the "General Meaning of *Śamatha-Vipaśyanā*," which encompassed the essence of the extensive treatises. At that time...
The fellow students were Cui Gong, Attendant-at-the-Horse-Rider (Sanqi Changshi), and Tian Dun, Grand Master for Remonstrance (Jianyi Daifu).
When Master Yuanse, the teacher of Mount Jing at Heilin Monastery in Runzhou, passed away, Huaru composed the inscription for his stele, which stated in brief:
"The Master spent sixty-one summers within the stage of Bodhi; his life from birth to death spanned eighty-five years. Can those who attend the mourning rites even begin to fathom this?"

There were even those who traveled across the river to present offerings and wailed while gazing toward the temple; for ten *li* around, flowers fell like rain and fragrant clouds arose from the four quarters of the sky.
Banners, canopies, and jeweled nets shone so brightly that they eclipsed the sun and moon. They enshrined his entire remains and erected a stupa on the western side of Mount Huanghe.
The Magistrate of Boyi in Yuanzhou observed the rites of mourning for the Master; thus, Qi Han, Zhang Jun, Liang Sheng, Xu Jiao, and others all received the Bodhisattva Precepts.
Disciple: Among those who follow the Way, none have a reputation more eminent than this man. I, your disciple, once heard the Way from him at Mount Jing;
he was to me as Yue Zhengzichun was to the Master (as recorded in the *Jiu Tang Shu* and his epitaph). Guan, whose courtesy name was Yuanbin, was a descendant of Hua Cong.

He passed the "Grand Eloquence" (*Hongci*) examination and was subsequently appointed as a Proofreader (*Jiaoshu Lang*). Upon his death, Han Yu composed an epitaph for his tomb. When Guan composed his writings, he did not rely on external sources...
Following in the footsteps of his predecessors, he was at that time said to be the equal of Han Yu.

While observing the mourning period for his father, he drew blood to transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and distributed it among others to provide merit for his father’s repose in the afterlife. A wondrous fragrance emanated from his residence, lingering intensely for many days;
the scent reached even his neighbors (according to his biography and the *Zhu lin*).
Li Tongxuan, whose style name was Tongxuan, was a native of Taiyuan and a scion of the imperial clan. During the reign of Empress Wu, he lived in seclusion and did not serve in office.
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, because the commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* were overly prolix, he took the newly translated scriptures to Gaoseng Temple in Meng County, Taiyuan.

I, this slave, spent more than three years composing the treatise, consuming only ten jujubes and a single *bǎiyè* (cypress-leaf) cake each day; thus, the world called me the "Mahāsattva of Jujubes and Cypress Leaves.

Later, I moved to the ancient Buddha Hall of the Mǎ family, where I remained for ten years. Carrying my scriptures and books, I departed, and after traveling twenty li, I encountered a tiger blocking the road.
The elder stroked it and said, "I am about to compose a treatise on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; can you clear the way for me?"
As for his place of residence, he simply carried his scripture-bag upon his back and followed [the master] to the front of an earthen cave at the foot of Shenfu Mountain, where he settled.
The Elder then composed his treatise within the cave; every evening, light emitted from his mouth to serve as a lamp.
There were two women who daily drew water for the Elder, prepared incense, and provided paper and ink. At every mealtime, they would...
He prepared pure offerings and placed them before the Elder; when the meal was finished, he removed the vessels and departed. In this manner, he did so for five years.
When the Elder had completed his treatise, [the monk] vanished without a trace. In the twenty-eighth year, the Elder passed away peacefully on Mount Shenfu.

He authored the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka) in forty fascicles, as well as the *Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts), which synthesizes the profound meaning of the ten gates and elucidates the conditions of dependent origination to dispel delusion.

The *Ten Clarifications* (*Shiming*), the *Ten Mysteries*, the *Six Aspects*, the *Verses in Praise of the Ocean of Meanings of the Hundred Gates*, and other such works were all transmitted to the world (as recorded in his biography).

Yan Zhenqing, whose courtesy name was Qingchen, was the fifth-generation great-grandnephew of Yan Shigu. He was widely learned and skilled in literary composition. During the Kaiyuan era, he was recommended for office...
He passed the jinshi examination and served successively as Right Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs, being enfeoffed as the Duke of Lu Commandery.

Li Trueqing once received the precepts and sought the Way from Huiming of Huzhou, and later sought the Way from Yanjun of Jiangxi. He also composed the "Stele for the World’s Ponds for Releasing Living Creatures."
The summary states: In the third month of the second year of the Qianduan era, Emperor Shizong commanded Shi Yucong and Zhang Tingyu to propagate a gracious edict.

Beginning at Xingdao in Yangzhou and extending to Jiangning in Shengzhou, eighty-one *fangsheng chi* (pools for releasing living beings) were established within a five-li radius along the rivers and surrounding the city walls, both above and below, to proclaim imperial brilliance and expand compassion.
It is love. The *I Ching* says: "His sincerity reaches even the piglets and fish. The *Book of Documents* says: "Even unto the birds, beasts, fish, and turtles, all were transformed.

Who other than Your Majesty could be one of ancient wisdom and sagacity, divinely martial yet refraining from killing? In the past, King Tang of Yin was so perfected in benevolence that he spared one side of his hunting net.
Emperor Wu of Han bestowed such grace that he received the reward of the pearl-bearing oyster. Though the flowing water rescued the parched land—
The invocation of the name of the Victorious Jewel (Ratnashrī) may have been limited to that particular occasion; yet it still bestows blessings upon later generations.
How much more so today, when all that moves and all that is planted—whether dwelling in water or on dry land—take the entire world as their pond and receive its blessings throughout the realm!
Riding upon the power of the empowerment of the *dhāraṇī*, one exhausts the ocean of afflictions and the fords of birth and death.
Measuring this against antiquity, how could it ever have been its equal? (From the *Tang Shu*).
Qi Han, courtesy name Xixin, was a native of Yifeng in Dingzhou. He passed the imperial examinations at the beginning of the Shengli era of Empress Wu’s reign.

He served as the Judicial Administrator of Puzhou and later became the Circuit Intendant of Henan during the late Kaiyuan era. He once sought instruction from Master Su of Helin, regarding whom he held him in the esteem of a younger brother.

Zi Li again submitted a memorial, stating: "The Ultimate Way is worthy of veneration; it should be followed with devotion and reverence. Yet, to subject them to whipping and flogging brings disgrace upon their physical appearance and demeanor.
If monks and Daoists commit offenses, I hope they may be dealt with strictly according to the codes and regulations for monks and Daoists.
The local prefectures and counties must not arbitrarily inflict punishments. The Emperor’s decree was granted (from the *Jiu Tang Shu*).

Wang Wei, styled Jingwei and with the courtesy name Mojie, was a native of Taiyuan. During the Kaiyuan era, he passed the jinshi examination and was successively promoted to the rank of Right Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs.

Both he and his younger brother Wang Jing were deeply committed to the Buddhist faith; they wore plain clothing, subsisted on simple vegetarian food, and, after the death of their wife, remained celibate. They lived in solitude for thirty years.
He possessed a villa in Wangchuan where he frequently went to wander and compose poetry. Upon the death of his mother, he requested that the Wangchuan residence be converted into a Buddhist temple.
Jing (style name Xiagqing) was fond of learning from his youth; together with his elder brother Wei, he achieved renown and attained high honors in the imperial examinations.
During the rebellion of An Lushan, he was appointed as Deputy Governor of Taiyuan to assist Li Guangbi, and later was ennobled as Palace Attendant. Jing was a devotee of Buddhism.
This was especially so; he abstained from meat and blood. Emperor Daizong once asked him whether the Buddhist teachings on karmic retribution truly exist.
Li Jin replied: "The longevity and prosperity of our state's mandate cannot be achieved without the planting of meritorious karma in past lives.

Once the reward of merit is fixed, even if there are occasional minor calamities, they will ultimately cause no harm. This is why, although the poison of An Lushan and Shi Siming flowed and their influence flared up..."
Yet both suffered the calamity of losing their sons. Poguo Huaien raised troops in rebellion against the court but died on his way out of the city;

the Uyghurs and Tibetans launched massive invasions deep into the territory but withdrew without a fight. None of these events were within the reach of human power. How can one say there is no karmic retribution?
Because of this, the Emperor believed him deeply (from the *History of Tang* and his own biography).

Yuan Deshou (courtesy name Zizhi) was a native of Henei. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with filial piety. Having passed the jinshi examination, he carried his mother on his back as he entered the capital.
Having passed the imperial examination, he served as the Magistrate of Lushan. After his mother passed away, he lived in a hut beside her grave and transcribed Buddhist sutras using his own blood.

When he finished writing the last character, he was moved by a fragrant scent that lingered for an entire day before fading. He was posthumously honored with the title Master Wenxing; the world held his conduct in such high esteem that they did not address him by name.
He was called Yuan Lushan. When Yuan Jie lamented for him, he said: "The Master lived for sixty years;
he never knew the charms of women, never possessed ten mu of land, never wore clothing made of finished silk or cloth, and never ate food prepared with the five flavors.
My grief for him is intended as a warning to those who are dissolute, greedy, sycophantic, or addicted to fine silks and rich meats" (Jiu Tang Shu).
Du Hongjian, along with Zhang Yi, Qiao Lin, Chen Shaoyou, Du Huangshang, and Gao Ying, were all former retainers in the staff of Guo Ziyi.
Later, they all served as Grand Ministers (*xiang*). When Hongjian was first appointed to govern Ba and Shu, he arrived at Yizhou and dispatched an envoy to Baiya.
He invited Chan Master Wuzhu into the city to inquire about the Dharma. His disciple asked, "I have heard Master Jin speak of the three-phrase Dharma-gate:
'no-recollection,' 'no-thought,' and 'do not delude. I do not know whether these are one or three. Wuzhu replied, "'No-recollection' is named precept (śīla);

'no-thought' is named concentration (samādhi); 'do not delude' is named wisdom (prajñā). However, when the single mind does not arise, it fully possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither one nor three."

Third: At that time, the sound of a crow was heard. The Master asked the Teacher, "Did you hear it? The Teacher replied, "Whether there is hearing or no hearing does not concern the nature of hearing.
When there is sound, it is the auditory object (*śabdaviṣaya*) that arises of itself; when there is no sound, it is the auditory object that ceases of itself.
Yet this nature of hearing does not arise following the sound, nor does it cease following the sound. To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape the flow of the auditory object."
It transforms. This applies even to form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, which are likewise so. The Duke and his subordinates were filled with joy and praised it as excellent.
The Duke asked again, "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing one's nature'? The Master said, "All people drift along with their thoughts;

this is because they do not recognize the true mind and do not see their original nature. As for the true mind: when thoughts arise, it does not follow them in arising; when thoughts cease, it does not depend on them."

He was serene, neither distracted nor disordered; he lived in ordinary ease and mastery. Everything he encountered was as it should be, for there was nothing that did not manifest his true nature (*dharmatā*).

From this point on, Hongjian settled his mind in the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*). In his later years, he entered the相位 (the position of Chancellor). He resigned due to illness, and at the time of his death, he bathed and ordered his court robes to be worn over his *saṃghāṭī* robe.
Having shaved his beard and hair, he took leave of the assembly and passed away. His body was cremated according to the rites of a *śramaṇa*. (From the *Chuan deng lu*)
He once composed an inscription for Vajrabodhi to commemorate his virtues.

Yuan Zai, whose courtesy name was Gongfu, was a native of Fengxiang. He was devoted to learning and skilled in literary composition. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, an imperial edict was issued to recruit those who were proficient in the *Zhuangzi*.

Liu Cai was a scholar among the four sons of the elder Liu Liewen. He entered the imperial academy with high distinction and held successive offices, eventually serving as a Grand Coordinator (Tongpingzhangshi) and being promoted to Vice Director of the Chancellery (Zhongshu Shilang).
Emperor Daizong took pleasure in ancestral sacrifices but did not yet hold the Buddhist dharma in high regard; he would often ask leisurely about its origins.
Liu Cai and Wang Jin extensively expounded upon the retribution of karmic merit, and the Emperor’s inclination turned toward them. Consequently, Buddhist rites were performed within the inner palace.
The Buddha. When barbarians invade, it is necessary to assemble all the śramaṇas to recite the *Ratnarājasūtra* for the Protection of the State as a means of averting calamity (*Jiu Tang Shu*).

Liangfu Dufen: at the beginning of the Wude era, he served as Secretariat Director; in the second year of the Longshuo era of Emperor Gaozong, an edict was issued requiring Buddhists and Daoists to perform prostrations.

The Sovereign and His Parents commanded the ministers to deliberate upon this matter. At that time, De-fen served as the Grand Director of the Imperial Academy (Sichengguan). He submitted this deliberation:

"I humbly consider that the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism possess a profound and vast spirit of compassion and reverence. As the state has followed these traditions for generations, they have consequently come to be honored and esteemed.

Since their methods have long been established, it is necessary to accord with their principles. However, I earnestly maintain that the practice of prostration is likely not consistent with reason. Why is this? Because shaving the hair is distinct from wearing the ceremonial cap and sash."

As for these rituals: holding an almsbowl is surely not the etiquette of sacrificial vessels and meat offerings. To extend grace, one prays for concentration and wisdom; there is no need for prostrations and kneeling before one’s venerable parents.

To repay their kindness, one hopes for *tathatā* (Suchness); why must one bend the knee before a compassionate sovereign? Once one has departed for the mountains and forests, it is not that one lacks the status of a guest at the imperial court.

While the distinctions between the court and the wilds are indeed different, it is only logical that one should hold such matters in high esteem. Now, if you demand that I conform to the teachings of name and form (*mingjiao*), [there is...]
This would be to do injustice to its essential meaning. Your subjects are ignorant and dull-witted; we request that it be appropriate to follow the practice of not prostrating.

At that time, among the public discussion, those who requested that one should prostrate numbered over three hundred, while those who requested that one should not prostrate numbered over five hundred. On the eighth day of the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued, stating:

"I have deliberated upon the various opinions and deeply investigated their profound implications. However, the spirit of the [sages of] Mount Ji and the River Ying held their principles in high esteem. Looking back to former ages, it is indeed..."
There is indeed such a person. Henceforth, it is not appropriate to prostrate or kneel (as recorded in the *Hongming ji*).
Wang Bobo, courtesy name Zian, was a native of Longmen in Jiazhou. At six years of age, he was skilled in literary composition. At the beginning of the Linde era, Liu Xiangdao...

While traveling through Guannei, Bo submitted a memorial to state his own case. His virtuous path was manifested at court, where he ranked highest in the imperial examination on policy. Before reaching the age of twenty, he was appointed as a Chao-san-lang.
He frequently presented eulogies at the palace gate; upon hearing of his reputation, the Prince of Pei summoned him to serve as a compiler in his administration.
When his father, Fu Zhi, was demoted to the post of Governor of Jiaozhi, he ordered Bo to go there to visit him. While crossing the sea, Bo drowned and died.
His elder brothers Fu Min and Fu Ju, along with Bo, Lin Yi, and Jian, were collectively known as the "Three Pearl Trees" (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*).

He once composed the *Record of the Śākyamuni Portrait*, the *Stele of the Vimalakīrti Portrait*, and the *Record of the Enlightenment of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*. Regarding the *Record of Enlightenment*, it says: "Observe now, O Śākyamuni..."

Regarding his descent to manifest in this world: the body of the pure dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing; yet, through the power of great compassionate vows, he manifested birth.
Reaching the Tuṣita Heaven, he was the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra; descending upon the kingdom of Kapilavastu, he was named Sarvārthasiddha.
The Son of the Golden Sphere chose his family, and King Śuddhodana became his father. Mounting the jade elephant as the sun rose, he manifested [his arrival].
Manifesting within the womb of Mahāmāyā, he became a King of the Golden Wheel.
He was first born beneath the Aśoka tree, his eighty minor marks of excellence as radiant as fragrant flowers, and his thirty-two major marks of a Great Being as brilliant as the full moon.
He took seven steps in each of the four directions and was bathed by the waters of the nine seas. He manifested like the Udumbara flower.
The Lion’s Roar: It is said that the stage of the womb has already been exhausted and he has early realized the eternal body;
yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he returns. Now, he manifests his traces here, returning to the swaddling clothes to appear like an infant for the purpose of divination.
He was filled with sorrowful regret before the seer Asita; he was startled up in the temple of Maheśvara; and whether as a youth or...

He studied the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) for the purpose of military instruction; the arrow towers and arrow wells still remain. He practiced wrestling; the elephant tracks and elephant pits are still there.

Having experienced sensual pleasures for ten years, he manifested a tour of observation at the four gates. Delighting in the body of a *śramaṇa*, he felt revulsion toward old age, sickness, and death.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Kṣāntivādin alerted him by revealing the ugly countenances of the courtesans. [The gods of] the Śuddhāvāsa...
The Lady held up the vessel; Channa leaped forth to prepare the carriage. They crossed the city of Kapilavastu on the eighth night and dwelt upon the Snowy Peaks for six years.
Men expressed their sorrowful longing for their lord; the horse licked away falling tears like a string of pearls.

He brandished his precious sword and cut off his dark-blue locks, which were enshrined in a stupa rising from the celestial palace. Taking his imperial robes to exchange for a deerskin garment, his form became like that of a mountain deer. He struck [the door]...
This is what the forest seers have attained: they realize that worldly concentration is not ultimate truth. By eating barley and hemp, they subdue suffering and transcend pleasure.

Furthermore, when a jade zither plays a melody, the music is completed through the central tuning. So too, the Buddha’s fruit is the perfection of the cause; he demonstrates the provisional middle way as the path toward that fruition.
Thereby, in choosing his dwelling, he passed by the dragon’s cave; in bathing his body, he entered the Nairañjanā River;
for his food, he accepted the milk-rice of Nanda; and for his seat, he accepted the auspicious *kuśa* grass.
With his final and most excellent body, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to perfect the profound cause of liberation, and ascended the precious diamond throne.
One hundred and forty merits are not shared with the two vehicles; eighty-four thousand dharma-gates transcend the ten stages.
Thus, the demonic armies were intimidated by the power of compassion and returned in sorrow and fear to their beautiful women; the poison was defeated by the mind of meditative concentration.
The coarse and inferior were transformed into the sublime; thereupon, the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā leaped for joy and bore witness, while the Devaputra of the Void proclaimed it far and wide.
Like a lotus emerging from the water, its brilliance shone boundlessly; like the cassia moon suspended in the sky, it illuminated all.
His radiance was transparently penetrating. After seven days had passed, he accepted the parched grain and honey from Trapusa.

Awakening them with a few brief words, he bestowed upon the merchants the precepts through a single sound. He granted them the blessings of humans and devas. Having already attained Buddhahood, he surveyed the conditions for conversion;
he felt compassion for the two sages who had not encountered his thunderous voice, yet rejoiced that the five companions were capable of following his Dharma-transformation. Thus, by...
The sensory faculties of worldly beings are dull and inferior, while the sagely wisdom is profound and deep. If one follows the Dharma, the Dharma does not accord with the faculties;
if one follows the faculties, the faculties do not reach the Dharma. Thus, there is none who is not long submerged in the river of craving, blinded by the delusions of pleasure.
Since it would not have been beneficial for them to hear [the teaching], he provisionally spoke of entering extinction. Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, drove forth his three...
The Lord of the Sahā World [Śākyamuni] was surrounded by the eighteen Brahmās of the Trayodaśa Heaven;
they bowed their heads in salutation and paid their respects with single-minded devotion, entreating him to turn the Wheel of Dharma and exhorting him to teach according to what is appropriate.

The Tathāgata then reflected upon the universal rule of the Sugatas and followed the noble counsel of the Buddhas of antiquity, responding to the humble desires of sentient beings. At that moment, the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared and together offered words of praise.

This is the terminology. First is the division of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna). Together they first opened up the realm of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). From this, he departed from the Bodhi tree and proceeded to the Deer Park.

For three months he disciplined his faculties; five men attained deliverance. Kauṇḍinya realized the Compassionate Honored One’s primary teaching, thereby first attaining understanding and receiving a name.
Śāriputra met Aśvajit to receive his transmission; having seen him on the road, he attained the Truths. Kaśyapa followed in his footsteps.
He served as his master and led his disciples to return together to the same path. Kāśyapa gathered his traces to subdue the mind; leading his great assembly, he turned his seat [toward the Buddha].

There was none who did not find joy as the great rain of nectar poured down, universally responding to all without exception. Whether in the celestial realm or the human realm, in the Śiṃśapā grove or the Śītavana forest—everywhere it reached.
Whether at Lake Rājagṛha or Vulture Peak, whether in the Ocean Palace or the Mango Grove, whether by the Monkey River or in the Dragon’s Fire Cave;
whether dwelling in Vārāṇasī or residing in Magadha, whether relying on the Sthira Forest or staying by the Music Tree.
Sometimes on the peak of Laṅkā by the seashore, or at the cliff of Potalaka on a mountain; sometimes in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, or in the Golden Land of Śrāvastī;
sometimes appearing in emptiness according to thought; sometimes submerging from a mountain to emerge from a palace; sometimes preaching the Dharma by means of the six directions;
sometimes manifesting a transformation body of three feet in height; sometimes covering with the palm and transforming the fingers; or sometimes with flowing light...
The Buddha appears: sometimes a single body universally manifests as many bodies; sometimes this world becomes luminous within other worlds;

sometimes he transforms the impure so that the pure covers the defiled; or, following worldly convention, he uses the conventional itself to reveal the truth—like an echo responding from an empty valley.
It is like a great bell awaiting a strike. Within this interval, he expounded upon the four existences (*catasraḥ bhavāḥ*) of the *Āgamas*,

the eight voidnesses (*aṣṭau śūnyatāḥ*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Śrī-mālā-siṃhanāda*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Buddhapiṭaka*, the *Kṣitigarbha*, the *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Vajracchedikā*,
the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* of the ten thousand practices, the *Anantārtha* of the One Vehicle, the *Mahākaruṇā-puṇḍarīka*, the *Dharma-dhvaja-dhāraṇī*, and the *Vimala*.
It is called the *Sūtra* (Discourse); it is the auspicious response (*prātihārya*) of Sudatta; it distinguishes between the *Vṛttaka* (Past Deeds) and the *Jātaka* (Birth Stories);
it differentiates between the *Geya* (Verses) and the *Ge-yā* (Repetitive Verses). There are the three animals—the elephant, horse, and rabbit—crossing the river;

and the three vehicles—the sheep, deer, and ox—leaving the house. Some call it "existence," "emptiness," or "abiding in the middle"; some call it "non-existence," "turning," "illumination," or "maintaining"; and some call it "sudden" or "gradual."
It is so. Some call it half, others call it full. It is a teaching that is constantly taught without being spoken; it is a hearing that is constantly heard without being heard.

It can be relied upon through its sustaining power, and it is never forgotten through its transformative empowerment. There is nothing small that is not great; there is nothing boundless that is not central.
The three vehicles enter together into the single Buddha-vehicle; the three natures return together to the single Dharma-nature. Truly, this may be called the Father.
A mother to the young and a guide through both peril and ease, he suspended the sun and moon within the dark night and spread a vessel across the illusory sea.
Acting as clouds and rain, he caused withered hearts to flourish once more; serving as a savior and a refuge, he pointed the way to the realm of longevity for those at their journey’s end.
When his work was completed and his merit achieved, he did not dwell therein, intending to return to the root and revert to the source, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
He entered *nirvāṇa*. By the power of his pointing finger, he traveled from the ground to the Kimśuka River; light flowed from the gate of his face, startling dust-filled lands.
Mountains shook and the earth quaked, as all together raised cries of agony. Creatures of different species changed their appearances, and all alike manifested blood like *śephālikā* flowers.
He accepted the final offering of Cunda and received the secret words of Vaiyāghrapadya. He proclaimed the four virtues to reveal the three *ī* vowels, and pointed toward the myriad existences...

He returned to the state of ultimate oneness. Having fully answered the forty-two questions of Muchalinda Kāśyapa (No. 81), and having delivered Subhadra (No. 82), his transformative mission was nearing its end.
He shattered the erroneous calculations of the ten sages, enabling them to attain awakening as soon as they heard the morning teaching.

He established the noble precedent of the four stupas, which will long nourish future generations. Thus he sought to clarify that all conditioned phenomena possess cessation, and to manifest the signless through non-existence.
He was born; he ascended to the Vajra-body and traversed the realm of empty space. Even the sun and moon would fall like meteors—how could the glow of a firefly endure for long?
He exhorted those with permanent bodies to be free from negligence. Thereupon, he returned to the Jade Throne and lay his head at the Crane Forest (Heli).

He traveled extensively through the gates of samādhi, intending to restore the nature of the Single Truth. He entered the stages of *niyata* and *ardha-niyata*, and finally transcended both the half and the whole.

Transcending [the world], he relied upon the samādhi of the four dhyānas and entered the profound, perfect stillness of parinirvāṇa. At that time, humans and devas wailed and collapsed; birds and beasts cried out in grief;
whirlwinds and storm clouds arose, mountains roared, and waves surged backward. Following the ancient rites of a Cakravartin King, they were about to prepare the funeral ceremony;
they ordered the Mallas to lift the coffin, yet none could move it. Thereupon, the golden coffin rose by itself and circumambulated Kuśinagara.
In the great city of Kuśinagara, the precious torches did not ignite, halting the grand ceremony of cremation.
Yet, there was Ajātaśatru in Rājagṛha, who first conceived a dream-vision of the Compassionate Honored One of the Ten Epithets;

and Mahākāśyapa traveled far down from Vulture Peak to behold and pay homage to the thousand-spoked wheel-marked feet. Finally, with fine *tūla* cotton wool, the holy fire spontaneously ignited, consuming the sandalwood of the royal assembly.
Regarding the new commentary on the *Dānagāthā*: the water from Śakra’s golden vase remains; his power of aspiration still endures and his compassion still perfumes the world.
He shattered his supreme adamantine body to become the remaining relics of the *śarīra*. Thereupon, the eight kingdoms provided solemn guard, and the fourfold army maintained a dignified appearance.
Each held their own golden casket, vying with one another to return and erect precious stūpas. Thus, [the relics such as] the teeth and the hair, the *Kā*...
Yaśas performed worship in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace with either charcoal or ash. King Aśoka established [the relics] within the realm of Jambudvīpa.
Thus, when the golden words of the Way remain throughout kalpas of dust and when the Dharma persists, the Elephant King departs while his offspring follow;

one lamp extinguishes while another continues. There is none who does not welcome the Great Kāśyapa with a thousand-fold assembly like gathering clouds, or who does not hear Ānanda’s thunderous roar three times.
The wheel [of the Dharma]. Śaṇavāsa manifested his meditative concentration in the future; Kukkula filled the room with counting-sticks.
Beginning from the miracle at Vaiśālī and ending with the omen of the flowing milk, the vessels differ while the water remains the same; the lamps vary while the light is ultimately one.
Thus, regarding the wondrous existence within the true emptiness of the Mahāyāna, Mañjuśrī and Maitreya differ in their respective schools; yet as for the Hīnayāna—
The woolly folds were divided and the gold was analyzed; the Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools were its original branches.
Whether the Daśabhūmika was propagated extensively, or a thousand sects flourished, Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna succeeded to its fragrance, while Asaṅga and Vasubandhu spread its beauty.

Some, like Āryadeva, had their eyes opened to become vessels of the Dharma; others, like Dignāga, roared at the stone to fly forth with renown. Some removed the heterodox schools with a hundred verses, or ten...

The Master assisted and supported [the Dharma] through his final verses: some heard the sutras and ascended to Tuṣita at night; some awaited the Buddha and took refuge in a cave within the asuras’ realm;
some vowed their heads upon a sword as a solemn pledge; some offered gold upon an elephant to invite Śākyamuni;

some were rewarded with fiefdoms for their abilities; some erected victory banners after achieving triumph; some were named "Lamp" for their discourse on the principles of Prajñā; and some investigated the *Kuśala*...

To discard it as erroneous is called hail; though their paths diverge and their tracks differ, they ultimately converge at a single source. From the realm of existence to emptiness, all return to the ten thousand virtues.

From the time the rainbow pierced the sky during the Shang and Zhou dynasties, until the Han Emperor dreamed of the golden man, the teaching reached the land of Shenzhou and its sound spread throughout Huaxia.

I, Bo, was born in this degenerate age and have had the fortune to receive these true discourses. Although I have recorded and continued the narrative of the Golden Words, [it remains that... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Adrift and alone, he did not meet with the Jade Response (the Buddha). What we have seen and heard is limited to this; yet the essential purpose is clearly manifest.

Thus, I shall leave the remaining texts aside and refrain from further elaboration. Thereupon, I compose this inscription: Transformation arises from the primal source; success is achieved in response to the Bhadrakalpa.

Myriad practices reveal the True Doctrine; three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* accumulate vast merit. For the sake of the Dharma, he appeared in the world; descending in spirit, he manifested his birth from the side. Between his eyebrows...

He slung the bow of the Heavenly Emperor across his chest; his eyes were like blue lotus petals. The immortal masters shed tears for him; the heavenly deities vied with one another to receive and support him.

His consecration was due to take place in the palace, yet the flying wheel transformed and spread to the borderlands. Noble as the sun and moon of heaven, his lineage inherited this majesty; his countenance was like that of an elephant piercing the cheeks of a lion.

To whom could he transmit his sublime teachings? Alone and heroic, he strummed his lute. He was startled by old age and death during his travels; he leaped over the city walls, abandoning his ministers and concubines. He fell [into the world].
He bartered his precious sword for clothing and encountered a band of hunters; he took refuge among the deer, feigning weakness and timidity.

When the people who ate the deer all knew of him, they were struck with awe as he sat amidst the grass, facing the south. Pure as a lotus rising from the water, his brilliance surpassed a mirror opened from its case.

Like mountains and seas in their loftiness and depth, like clouds and thunder in the swiftness of their expression, his teachings flourished throughout the three seasons, and the roots of the myriad species found natural satisfaction. (4)
I ask but wish to offer a response: A thousand immortals have passed one after another; Maitreya is recorded as the one who succeeds him. His remaining texts were entrusted to Kāśyapa;
though he lay beneath the tree, spring was in vain. The fragrant wood has already consumed his remains, yet his compassionate heart reaches far and wide. His śarīra radiates with brilliant splendor;
born at a later time, I alone am fortunate to have been touched by its lingering waves.
Li Bai’s courtesy name was Taibai. He was a ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Xingsheng. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he arrived in Chang’an and went to visit He Zhizhang.
Upon seeing his writings, Zhizhang sighed and said, "You are a celestial immortal banished to earth. He reported this to Emperor Xuanzong, who summoned him for an audience.
At the Jinxuan Hall, he was granted a meal, during which the Emperor personally prepared the soup for him. An edict was issued appointing Bai as a Hanlin Academician.
Bai composed the "Eulogy on the Transformation Tableau of the Western Pure Land with a Preface," which states:

"I have heard that to the west of the Golden Heaven, where the sun sets, ten trillion *kṣetras* away from the Central Kingdom, lies the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). The Buddha of that land possesses a body of..."
It measures six million billion nayutas of yojanas. The white tuft of hair between his eyebrows curls gracefully to the right, resembling five Mount Sumerus.
His eyes are clear and white like the waters of the four oceans. He sits upright preaching the Dharma, serene and eternally present.

It is like a pond of bright golden sand, with precious trees lining its banks, railings covering it entirely, and jeweled nets spread all around; towers made of carnelian and lapis lazuli stand upon it.
The ornaments of the Hall—the lapis lazuli and agate—glitter with the splendor of the steps and pavements; these are all things realized by the Buddhas, whose words are never false (and so forth).
The eulogy says: Toward the west, where the sun sets, I gaze afar upon the countenance of Great Compassion; his eyes are as pure as the waters of the four oceans.
The body’s radiance is like a mountain of purple gold; through diligent mindfulness, one will surely be reborn there. For this reason, it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

With its nets of pearls, precious jewel-trees, and celestial flowers scattered upon fragrant pavilions—these scenes appear as if painted before my very eyes. I vow to take refuge in that place of enlightenment. By means of this ocean of merit, may I attain that same state.
May the profound grace serve as a bridge across the waters; the sins of eighty billion kalpas shall be swept away like light frost by the wind.

May I behold Amitāyus and long aspire to the radiance of his white tuft of hair. Furthermore, he composed a hymn of praise for Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva: "The fundamental mind is like empty space, pure and without a single thing.
When lust, anger, and ignorance are incinerated and dispersed, one perceives the Buddha through perfect illumination. By painting the sacred image in five colors, one awakens to the truth."

This is not a false transmission. Sweeping away the myriad ailments, there is a refreshing and cool clarity like the heavens. I praise this ocean of merit, which shall be proclaimed forever throughout distant ages.
He further composed a eulogy for Master Zhigong, saying: "The moon in the water is utterly ungraspable; The void of space has no master.
With silken cap and black-clawed feet, he travels alone without peer. His blade is as sharp as a ruler’s edge, fanning away delusion."
[The Emperor] commanded that the sacred countenance [of the Buddha] be depicted in colors. Where does it abide? Where is its locus? (From the *Benji*).

Du Fu, courtesy name Zimei, was a native of Duling. In the second year of the Zhide era of Emperor Suzong, he was appointed as a Shiyi (Imperial Remonstrance Censor). Later, he served as a Minister of Works.

It is said: His body was three hundred and sixty feet tall, and his eyes were twenty feet wide; all other marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*) were fully complete. There were nine stories of pavilions covering [the stupa].
Furthermore, he compiled the *Śuka-avadāna*, of which a brief excerpt states: "The primal essence (*yuanjing*) bestows the five pneumas (*wugqi*) upon the myriad species.

Although they consist of scales, shells, fur, or feathers, there must be those who respond to the pure and refined essence. Some blaze with the brilliance of the fire of separation (*lihu*), while others receive..."
The *qīcāngjīng* (the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*) all correspond to the patterns of human culture (*wénwén*), thereby serving to accord with the administration of the times.

Thus, there were those among the avian species who transformed their nature to practice eloquent speech; they realized the mark of emptiness through non-thought and left behind their true bones even after death.

When someone presented a parrot, Hé Dōng’s Pèi Shì remarked that the name of this bird is recorded in the Sanskrit scriptures (*fànjīng*). Its intelligence was exceptionally similar to that of humans; he constantly associated with it and treated it with reverence.
He began by instructing him in the prohibitions of the six periods of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa*). At noon, he would not eat out of season, nor would he take food until the end of the night.
Sometimes he was taught to recite the Buddha’s name; then [the bird] would lift its head and spread its wings as if listening attentively.

Every dawn and throughout the long nights, it would emit a harmonious and elegant sound, chanting "Amitābha Buddha" with each voice following the next. One day, it appeared haggard and exhausted. The one who had been training and nurturing it struck the *ghaṇṭā* (bell).
He then said, "I am about to depart from here to return to the West. With each strike of the *qing* stone he uttered one invocation of the Buddha's name;

after ten strikes, the ten recitations were completed. He folded his wings, set down his feet, and passed away suddenly. According to the Buddhist scriptures, when the ten recitations are completed, one attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land.
Furthermore, it is said that those who have attained the wisdom of the Buddha leave behind *śarīra* relics upon death. He then ordered the body to be cremated, and *śarīra* relics were obtained.

Yu, style name Tui-zhi, was a native of Nanyang in Dengzhou. His father was Zhongqing. Yu became an orphan at the age of three and was raised by his paternal aunt, Lady Zheng.

He knew how to read books on his own; he could memorize several thousand words every day. In the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, an imperial edict was issued to welcome the finger-bone relic from the pagoda of Famen Temple in Fengxiang to the capital.
It was kept within the Forbidden City for three days, during which time five-colored lights appeared.

The hundred officials offered their congratulations, and [the relics] were sent successively to various monasteries. Princes, dukes, officials, and commoners venerated them and made offerings, fearing they might not arrive first.

At that time, Han Yu served as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Punishments; he submitted a memorial offering extreme remonstrance. The Emperor was greatly incensed and intended to sentence him to death.

Pei Du and Cui Qun said: "Yu’s words are indeed acrimonious and provocative; it is truly appropriate to punish him for this. However, were it not for his innermost devotion to loyalty, how could he have reached such a point?"
