I have long hoped for the opportunity to meet you in person, and thus I have ventured to trouble you with this letter. This past week has been clear and bright, and not excessively hot;
if you could take advantage of your leisure to visit me, it would truly be a great fortune. With humble regards. Another letter states: Yu writes. Huiyun arrived and I was honored by your reply.
I am filled with profound awe and can never cease my sense of wonder. What you have shown is vast, profound, and far-reaching; it cannot be measured in a moment’s thought. A tradition says:
"Writing does not exhaust speech, and speech does not exhaust intention. If this is so, would the intention of the Sage ultimately remain invisible?
Discussing it in this manner, reading it even a hundred times is not equal to facing him in person. Yue said: "The Way is without stagnation."
Practice is free from bondage. If one is not attached to anything, then the seclusion and stillness of mountain forests are no different from a city wall.

Master Dadian’s discourse was most vast and profound, yet he insisted on remaining in the mountains and forests rather than visiting the prefectural seat; he spurred himself toward cultivation by establishing himself in a place of emptiness and freedom from entanglement.
This is not the way of the Universal Path (Tongdao). To weary oneself with coming and going, while finding peace only in what is familiar, is not the Way.
Thus it was. [Mencius] did not speak further. Thereupon, Dadian arrived at the commandery and treated him with even greater reverence. He detained the Master for ten days.
Later, while Mencius was performing a sacrifice to the deity on the sea, he ascended Mount Ling and visited Dadian’s dwelling to inquire about the Way, saying, "What is the Way?
The Master remained silent for a long time. Mencius was at a loss (and so forth). Dadian asked Mencius, "Your countenance is somber; you seem to be dissatisfied. Why is this?"
Ye said, "Yue, when you are employed at court, your enjoyment of emolument is generous.

Yet, were you once to have your loyal words rejected and be exiled and driven far away across the Ling and Hai mountains, where poisonous mists and pestilential vapors break out daily, how could your life be preserved?
How, then, could you find any joy? Dian said, "When you speak straightforwardly at court, are you being loyal to your sovereign while disregarding your own person? Or rather—"

"Does he still disregard his own person and speak so forcefully merely to pursue fame? Furthermore, for what matter was your dismissal? Muzhi replied, 'The Sovereign has welcomed the Buddha’s bone into the inner palace.
I, Muzhi, hold that Buddhism is but the law of the barbarians. During the Three Dynasties, there were no Buddhas, yet their reigns lasted for a long time.
As for the Jin, Song, Liang, and Wei dynasties, which served the Buddha, they either suffered premature death or fell into chaos. He feared the Sovereign..."
The Emperor was deluded by this; therefore, he disregarded his own person and rejected [the Buddha]. Wang Dian said: "If this were so, then your words would be erroneous.
The Buddha is a great vessel who provides shelter for both gods and men; his Way is that which speaks of the subtle workings of all things."
Their words exhaust the principles of nature and destiny; their teaching is to abandon evil and pursue good, to discard the false and return to the true.
They regard all under heaven as a father regards his son. To destroy them is like a son wielding a blade against his own father.
I have heard that those who observe people well look at where the Way resides, rather than comparing the status of those who dwell within it.
As for the land: Jie and Zhou resided there, as did the followers of Zhi and Qiao; all were people of the Central Kingdom. Yet they are not to be emulated because they lacked the Way.
Shun was born in the Eastern Yi lands; King Wen was born in the Western Yi lands; Youyu was born among the Rong; and Ji Zha came from the Man.
How could those two sages and two worthies be called barbarians and thus not emulated? By these five...

During the eras of the Emperors and the Three Kings, there were no Buddhas, yet they lived long lives. Why then were Waibing’s reign limited to two years and Zhongren’s to four—how premature their deaths!
If those who serve the Buddha are short-lived and bring disorder, then Emperor Ming of the Han was a preeminent sovereign of his age, and Emperor Wu of Liang lived to the age of eighty-six;
how could it be that all such people must meet with premature death and chaos? Furthermore, you yourself recite the Buddhist scriptures.
"May I ask about those points where his views differ from those of the former kings? Yu said, "I have no leisure to read their books.

Tian replied, "If you claim that the Buddha does not speak the words of the former kings because you have never read their books, how can you know for certain that he does not discuss the words of the former kings?
When the Buddha speaks with ministers, he must rely on loyalty; when he speaks with sons,"
"It must be based upon filial piety. Yet when it comes to its ultimate expression, it is boundless;
it is formless; it is the most subtle of the subtle. Miu said, "Does the Master’s teaching end here?
Dian replied, "That which I have told you was spoken according to what you were capable of receiving; it is not the ultimate of the ultimate. Miu said, "I am fortunate."

"May I hear him when he arrives? Jiandian replied, "If you truly cultivate your mind, exhaust your nature, fathom the principles of things, and reach the ultimate decree of Heaven, only then may you hear him.
Subsequently, Liu Yu was transferred to Yuanzhou, where he again visited Jiandian’s hermitage and offered two sets of robes.
Mencius said, "I am about to leave you, Master; I would be grateful to hear a single word from you.
Dian replied, "I have heard that one who easily trusts others will surely find their own integrity easily altered; one who easily praises others will surely find their slanders easily unleashed.
You have heard my words and easily trusted them; how do you know that upon hearing other doctrines, you will not again regard me as wrong? (From *Bèijǐ gǔlüè*).

Quán Deryú (權德輿), courtesy name Zàizhī (載之), was a native of Lièyáng in Qīnzhōu. At the beginning of the Yuánhé era, he was appointed as Minister of the Ministry of Rites and concurrently served as a Chief Councilor.
He once composed the "Record of the Seated Meditation of Chan Master Cǎoyī," which states in brief: "On Mount Nányuè in Xìnzhōu, there is a seated meditation [hall]..."
...a place where a Zen Master resided. The Master lived there for thirty years; the people of the prefecture called him "The Grass-Clothed One.
His feet never touched the ground, and his mouth never tasted flavors. Regardless of the season—whether cold or hot—he occupied nothing but a single meditation seat.

Both his physical body and his wisdom were utterly pure. Occasionally, subtle words and gentle speech could be heard. Whether traveling through the distant or near regions of that domain, in accordance with [the needs of] those who encountered him...
From the roots above to those below, it is like rain moistening the myriad things or wind circulating through the air; by merely crossing its threshold, all shall attain entry.

Were one not to operate the profound mechanism within the boundless and exhaust the source and bottom of the true mark (*dharmatā*), then the four seasons would assail from without and a hundred ailments would arise from within.
What the ancients called "leaving behind things and departing from people to stand alone" refers to Chan.
The Master attained this. Alas! The people of the world allow their minds to wander by being moved by external things;

when the mind is shifted by these things, profit and harm arise, and good fortune and misfortune take form. Bound and fettered, they are swept away and do not return. Yet the Perfected Man returns stillness within movement and restores his nature within emotion.
It is from this that the distinctions between longevity and early death, benevolence and baseness, are produced. This is the ultimate truth of the world.
This is merely one account. Regarding the Way of the Chan masters, was it not like weeds and tares? (Tongji).

"I do not ask about Mount Sumeru containing a mustard seed; how is it that a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru?

The Master said, "People say you, Excellency, have read ten thousand scrolls of books—is this true? Bo said, "Yes. The Master said, "From the crown of your head to your heels, you are no larger than a coconut.
Where would you place those ten thousand scrolls? At these words, Bo attained realization (*Tang Shi* and *Chuan Deng Lu*).
Li Mi, whose courtesy name was Changyuan, initially had no wife and abstained from eating meat. Emperor Daizong forcibly issued an imperial decree requiring him to eat meat and take a wife.

During the reign of Emperor Dezong, he was promoted to Minister of the Ministry of Rites and concurrently served as a Chief Councilor (Tongpingchangshi), being enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ye. Hearing that Chan Master Zan resided at Mount Nanyue, he went to visit him.
People called him Lan Can. Li Mi went to visit him; hearing the sound of the sutras being translated, he first felt sorrowful and later joyful. Realizing he was a recluse, he waited for a long time.
Lan Can pushed aside the embers, took out a taro root, and ate it while saying, "Take this as your reward for becoming a Chancellor for ten years.
When Li Mi came to power, he spoke of Lan Can’s noble conduct to the Emperor, who issued an edict to summon him. When the messenger arrived at the stone cave, [Lan Can was no longer there].
When the imperial decree was announced, Zhan sat motionless with cold tears hanging from his chin, paying no heed to it.
When the messenger returned and reported this, Emperor Dezong marveled at and revered him all the more (as recorded in the *Jiu Tang Shu* and the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
Meng Jian, whose courtesy name was Jidao, served as a Minister of State during the Yuanhe era. He had long been fond of Buddhism. Han Yu wrote to him, saying:
"Good and evil accumulate, and calamity and blessing arrive according to their kind. How can one abandon the Way of the Sage and follow that of the barbarians?"
[The teaching continues... The simplified reply states: Your letter says, "Accumulated good and accumulated evil bring calamity and blessing according to their respective kinds.
If this is so, then the Śākya teachings have been distinguished with great precision; they aim entirely for people to accumulate good.

Thus, Kāśyapa [the Buddha] taught the Six Perfections for those of great capacity, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for those of middling capacity, and the Four Noble Truths for those of lesser capacity. Furthermore...
It is said: "Rely on the Dharma, not on the person. Suppose the deeds of Feilian and Eilai were such that they led to the ruin of states and the destruction of their own persons;
how then could even those of the Central Kingdom (Huaxia) be followed? Conversely, the works of Yu of Xia and King Wen have bestowed benefits upon ten thousand generations;
how then could even those of the Rong and Di tribes be rejected? Your Excellency has needlessly brought yourself into disgrace by relying on the doctrines of the barbarians.

The bodies of sages and worthies—how could the Dharma of sages and worthies be subject to insult? Such a thing is utterly unacceptable. It is simply that you, Excellency, have not yet received [this teaching];
had you done so, you would have ceased [your opposition]. This petty act of defilement and disparagement—how can it be called the accumulation of goodness?
As for those books of Yangzi, Mozi, and the Master of Lao (Laozi), what they describe is produced from partial and empty principles; they are not the Middle Way.
It is essential. The teaching of the Śākyas is not otherwise; it clearly elucidates the root sources of accumulated evil and examines the subtle details of divine retribution throughout the world.
It speaks with crystalline clarity of the divergent paths of good and evil, so as to broaden that Way.
How can you, Master Han, treat it with the sentiments of a simple, ignorant old man or woman? Nevertheless, its Dharma is practiced in...
"O World! To cause every person to fear evil and cultivate goodness themselves—does this not greatly assist the protective barriers of the Buddha’s transformative teachings?
(Included in the Collected Works of Han Yu).
By Liang Su.

Sù (courtesy name Jìngzhī) was a native of Āndìng. He served as a *bǔquè* (Supplementer) and chronicler in attendance upon the Crown Prince. Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Court Secretary of the Ministry of Rites (*Lǐbù lángzhōng*).
Having studied the Tiantai teachings under Master Jìngxī, he attained a profound mastery of their essential principles.

Finding that the texts and meanings of the *Zhǐguān* were so vast and extensive that readers would expend excessive time over them, he edited and condensed them into six fascicles, which circulated throughout the world. There exists the *Tiantái chánlín* [Biographies of Tiantai Chan Masters].
Temple Stele; General Principles of Tiantai *Zhi Guan*; Treatise on the Biography of Master Zhizhe (*Tongji*).
Yu Di (style name:
Yunyuan) was appointed as the Regional Commander of the Eastern Circuit of Shanann in the fourteenth year of the Zhenyuan era. Initially, he served in Hu...
On the day of the Prefectural Governor’s audience, he presented the collected poems of the śramaṇa Jiaoran of Zhushan for preservation in the Imperial Calligraphy Hall.
Yi had once asked Master Ziyu: "What is it that 'a black wind blows its boat, causing it to drift and fall into the realm of rākṣasa demons'?"
The Master said, "Yu Di, you hired hand! Why do you ask such a question? At that moment, Yu Di turned pale with fear.
The Master pointed and said, "This very thing is what causes one to drift and fall into the land of the rākṣasa demons. Upon hearing this, Yu Di accepted it with faith (from the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
Li Jifu, Wu Yuanheng, Gao Chongwen, Xue Hua, Zheng Yuke, Lu Changyuan, and Jifu. [Li] Jifu’s courtesy name was Hongxian.

In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he was promoted to Minister of the Central Secretariat (Zhongshu Shilang) and concurrently served as a Chief Coordinator of State Affairs (Tongpingzhangshi). He once requested...

Master Qingliang Guanding composed one fascicle of the *Huayan zhengyao* (The Essential Meaning of the Avatamsaka). Wu Yuanheng, whose courtesy name was Bo Cang, served as Chancellor during the Yuanhe era;
he once requested that Qingliang compose the one-fascicle *Fajie guan xuanjing* (The Mysterious Mirror of the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm).

Gao Chongwen’s ancestors migrated from Bohai to Youzhou, where they lived together for seven generations without separating; during the Kaiyuan era, the state twice honored their residence by decreeing it a "Filial Piety Gate. He held various high offices.

General of the Golden Watch, who had distinguished himself in the capture of Liu Bi, was enfeoffed as Prince of Nanping. He requested from Qingliang one fascicle of the *Jingdeng shuowen* (Mirror Lamp Explanations).

Xue Hua, serving as the Regional Inspector of Huazhou, together with Meng Jian, Qian Hui, Bai Juyi, Du Gao, and others, requested that Qingliang produce ten fascicles of the *Huazangjie tu xinjing shuowen* (Diagram of the Flower Treasury Realm and Mirror Explanations of the Seven Locations and Nine Assemblies).
[Volume]. Zheng Yuying, courtesy name Juye, was a native of Xingyang in Zhengzhou. He passed the jinshi examination and was appointed as a Grand Councilor (Tongpingzhangshi) during the Zhenyuan era.
He requested that Qingliang compose the *Huayan gangyao* (Essentials of the Avatamsaka) in three volumes. Lu Changyuan was a native of Wu.
He served as the Prefect of Ruzhou. He once composed a preface to the *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*), which states in brief:
"The *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* is what the Western regions call the *Pariniṣpanna-sūtra*. 'Great' (*mahā*) is like the expanse of the universe covering all."
"Method" (fang) is like the earth that supports all; "extensive" (guang) encompasses the myriad existences as its meaning. "Buddha" (fo) is the preeminent title among the ten epithets;
"flower" (hua) is the profuse embroidery of one's conduct and practice. "Adorned" (yan) is the completion of dignified reverence. Its merit is vast and its virtue is perfect.
It is the lineage of the Dharma teachings and the source of the sutras and śāstras—just as rivers and streams flow toward the Eastern Sea, and stars and constellations [converge at the pole].
They form a circle around the North Star; its subtlety and profound depth are beyond the reach of words.
Furthermore, he once requested that Qingliang compose one scroll titled *The Perfectly Interfused Contemplation of the Three Sages* (the stele inscription for National Teacher Qingliang).

Zhang Zhongsu served as a Hanlin Academician. In the second month of the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong issued an edict ordering Zhongsu to compose an inscription for the Buddha’s bone relic.
It stated in brief: "At Mount Mingyue in Fayun Monastery, Qiyang, there is a relic created by King Ashoka..."
The stupa enshrined a finger joint of the Buddha. Emperor Taizong specially constructed a temple and added a multi-storied pagoda to it.

Emperor Gaozong moved it to the capital at Luoyang; Empress Wu offered it a precious casket; Emperor Zhongzong recorded it in the national history; Emperor Suzong enshrined it within the inner palace;

and Emperor Dezong paid it homage in the imperial court. According to its original biography, it must be opened once every thirty years; when this occurs, the jade lamps are harmonized and the golden mirror shines bright.
The light shone forth; the ominous vapors vanished; the harvests were abundant (from the *History of the Tang*).
Bái Jūyí, courtesy name Lètiān, was originally from Tàiyuán. Later he moved his residence to Xiàguī. Bái Jūyí was exceptionally quick-witted and intelligent.
He was a man skilled in literary composition. At the age of seventeen, he passed the jinshi examination. During the Yuanhe era, he ranked second in the imperial examination on statecraft.

His official career reached the rank of Minister of Justice (Xingbu Shangshu). While residing in the eastern capital, Bo Juyi dredged a pond, planted trees, and constructed a stone pavilion at Mount Xiangshan;
he styled himself the Layman of Xiangshan and also called himself the Master of Drunken Recitation. He once sought the essentials of the mind from the Chan master Ning.

The Master took these eight words and expanded them into eight verses. The eight words are: awakening (覺), contemplation (觀), concentration (定), wisdom (慧), clarity (明), penetration (通), salvation (濟), and equanimity (捨).

The verse concerning contemplation says: "With the eye within the mind, observe the forms outside the mind. From what do they arise? By what are they lost? Observe and observe again, and you will distinguish the true from the false.
(These eight verses appear in the *Chángqìng jí*). In the fourth year of the Yuánhé era, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Wéikuān to court.
When Emperor Wenzong asked about the essentials of Chan, he commanded Han Yu to question the Master, saying: "Since you are called a Chan Master, why do you preach the Dharma?
The Master replied: "Supreme Bodhi—when it is applied to the body, it is the Vinaya; when it is spoken from the mouth, it is the Dharma; when it is practiced by the mind, it is Chan."

The Vinaya is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is not separate from dhyāna. In the second year of the Changqing era (822), when Yuan Jue was serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, he went to seek the Way from Chan Master Niaoke.
The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Yuan Jue remarked, "Even a three-year-old child can say this.
The Master replied, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man must practice it."

"I cannot. Bai Juyi was convinced by these words; he performed a prostration and departed. Later, when he went to Mount Lu to visit Chan Master Chang of Guizong, he found the Master plastering a wall.
The Master asked, "Are you a scholar of the gentlemanly kind, or a scholar of the commoner kind? Bai Juyi replied, "A scholar of the gentlemanly kind."
The Master struck the mud mortar once. Bai Juyi immediately passed him the mud. The Master took it and used it.
After a long while, he said, "Could this be the quick-witted Minister Bai? Juyi replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "You have only the lot of passing mud.
He once exhorted one hundred and forty-eight people to form an assembly for rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven, to recite the name of Maitreya while walking, and to contemplate him while sitting.
The countenance of Maitreya. May I be born in Tuṣita in a future age. In his later years, he suffered from wind-stroke and paralysis;
he subsequently dedicated his will to the West, praying to be reborn in Sukhāvatī. He painted a single scroll depicting the transformation scene of the Western Paradise and made this vow for it:
"In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, there are no evil realms nor any manifold sufferings. May those like my own body who suffer from illness be reborn together with Amitābha."
At the abode of the Buddha of Longevity (Amitāyus), he sat upon his meditation mat reciting the Buddha’s name one night and suddenly passed away.
Han Yu once received the Eightfold Precepts from Master Ru at Botasi nine times (*Jiu Tang Shu* and *Chuan Deng Lu*).

In the third year of the Taihe era, the stone-carved Sūtras on the walls of Chongxuan Temple in Suzhou were completed; Han Yu composed the inscription for them, which states in brief: "As for opening, showing, awakening, and..."

Entering the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas, he delivers boundless beings through the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and extends the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) infinitely. Nothing is more venerable than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), composing the *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna*, and abiding in inconceivable liberation, nothing is more ultimate than the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
Gathering the four types of birth and the nine classes of beings into nirvana without remainder, yet truly there are none who are delivered—nothing precedes this.
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, for destroying transgressions and accumulating merit to purify all evils, nothing is more urgent than the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.

Regarding the aspiration for rebirth according to one’s vows, nothing is more essential than the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Regarding the contemplation of true reality through right view, nothing surpasses the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*.
Regarding the elucidation of self-nature and the recognition of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), nothing is more profound than the *Dharmatā-guhya Sūtra*.
Among the sūtras that take emptiness as their object and rely upon Buddha-wisdom, none surpasses the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*.
These eight types of sūtras encompass the essential tenets of the twelve divisions and the three vehicles; the secret treasury of the myriad Buddhas is fully contained therein (*Chángqìng jí*).
Pang Yun, whose courtesy name was Daoxuan, was a native of Hengyang. His family had been practitioners of Confucianism for generations, yet he resolved to seek the ultimate truth.
He first visited Chan Master Shitou Xiqian and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Shitou covered his mouth with his hand.
Suddenly, he attained a profound realization. One day, Guishan asked him, "How do you act throughout the day?
Zhiyun replied, "If you ask about the affairs of daily life, there is no place to open one's mouth. He then presented this in verse to Guishan, who approved of it.
Later, he went to consult Mazu Daoyi, asking, "Who is the person who does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Mazu said, "Wait until you can suck the Western Ocean dry with a single gulp..."
The River Monk then spoke to you; Yun immediately grasped the profound essentials. During the Yuanhe era, he traveled north to Xianghan and lived in a small cottage west of the city.
He had a daughter named Lingzhao, who regularly wove bamboo mats and baskets to sell for her daily sustenance.

As he was about to pass away, he told Lingzhao to go out and observe whether it was morning or evening. When she returned at noon to report, the girl suddenly said, "The sun has already reached its zenith, yet there is an eclipse."
When Huìyùn went out the door to look at her, the girl immediately ascended her father’s seat, sat with palms joined, and passed away. Huìyùn smiled and said, "My daughter is sharp and quick-witted.
He then remained there for another seven days. When the provincial governor Yú Dí came to inquire after his illness, Huìyùn said to him, "I only wish that you would empty all that exists;
be careful not to reify what does not exist. Having finished speaking, he rested his head upon Dí’s knee and passed away (*Chuan deng lu*).
Liu Zongyuan, courtesy name Zihou, was a native of Hedong. From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and peerless. His compositions were outstanding, grand, and refined.

He passed the jinshi examination and the Examination for Broad Learning and Eloquence (Bóxué Hóngcí Kē). During the Zhenyuan era, he was appointed as an Inspector of the Censorate. During the Yuanhe era, he served as...
He served as the Prefect of Liuzhou and was later demoted to the position of Sub-prefect of Yongzhou. Thereupon, he withdrew into the mountains and marshes;
his submerged hardships and pent-up emotions were all channeled into his writings. The preface to "The Preface on Sending Master Jun Back to Visit His Parents" states briefly:

"The Way of the Golden Immortal (Buddha) is rooted in filial piety and reverence, and subsequently accumulates manifold virtues before returning to emptiness and non-being. Its teachings are termed Chan, Dharma, and..."

Regarding the Vinaya: this Venerable Master was single-mindedly devoted to the practice of the precepts; his constancy and steadfastness grew ever more firm. Is he not one who serves as a model for later students?

In instructing all living beings, every encounter brings them blessings. Is he not one who accumulates manifold virtues? When visiting the high ancestral hall, he perceives the distant as if it were near.
Was he not one whose fundamental nature was filial piety and reverence? He composed the *Epitaph for Master Banzhou of Mount Nanyue*, which states in brief:

"The Master’s mind was vast and his conduct was subtle; his person was humble, yet his Way was exalted. He held that since wisdom must be brought forth through meditative concentration, one must necessarily rely upon the *Vinaya*.

The Master then constructed a meditation chamber on a lofty ridge, calling it the 'Banzhou Terrace. Alas! There is nothing to be attained through cultivation; therefore, mindfulness is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). It does not...
Because it grasps the Dharma, the Vinaya constitutes the Mahāyāna. The myriad practices are strenuous, yet the single nature is eternally as it is;
the limits of its quiescent functioning cannot be apprehended. The preface to the *Preface Sent to the Venerable Hāochū* states briefly:

"The Confucian Han Tuìzhī criticized me for my fondness for the words of the Buddha and censured me for associating with Buddhists. Furthermore, he said that upon reading the *Preface Sent to Yuánshēng*, I did not refute the Buddhists."
That there are indeed aspects of the Buddha’s teachings that cannot be rejected is evident, as they frequently accord with the *I Ching* and the *Analects*.

If one truly delights in them, they are perfectly consistent with human nature and emotion (*xingqing*); they do not differ from the Way of Confucius. Although Han Yu claimed to love Confucianism, he was unable to surpass Yang Xiong.
Yet Yang Xiong’s writings drew upon the insights of Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei; the Buddha’s teachings, by contrast, do not even reach the level of Zhuangzi and Mozi.
Is it because the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei are strange, eccentric, perilous, and treacherous? One might say it is because they are "barbarian" (yi).

If one truly does not believe in the Way and rejects it on the grounds that it is barbarian, then would one instead take as friends the evil Eral and the robber Zhi, while deprecating Ji Zha and You Yu?
This is certainly not what is meant by "discarding names to seek reality. What I accept accords with the *I Ching* and the *Analects*; even if a sage were to be reborn, [he would agree].
It cannot be refuted. What I, Zui, condemn is merely its outward manifestation. In the *Jingtu yuan ji* (Record of the Pure Land Cloister), it is briefly stated:
"Tens of thousands of li to the west of the Central Plains lies a land called Shendu (India), the site where Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested.
That Buddha said: 'To the west, beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of buddha-lands, there is a world called Sukhāvatī. The Buddha...
He is titled the Tathāgata Amitāyus. In his land, there are no three evil realms or eight difficulties; it is adorned with various jewels.

Its people are free from the ten fetters and nine afflictions, and they take the assembly of sages as their companions. If there are those who can, with a sincere heart and great vow, turn their minds toward this land, provided their power of mindfulness is sufficient, they shall be born in that realm.
There they will forever transcend the triple world and attain the stage of non-retrogression. These are his words.

There is nothing deceptive about this. During the Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Yong* (Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection), which greatly encouraged its practice at that time.
Subsequently, the Great Master Tiantai Zhiyi authored the *Shijingtu Shiyi Lun* (Treatise Explaining the Ten Doubts Concerning the Pure Land) to propagate its teachings;
those who were deluded relied upon it. Indeed, there are many who departed after leaving behind extraordinary traces. [This concludes the section] compiled by the Vinaya Master Daming of Nanyue.

The Stele. It states briefly: "Confucianism is established through ritual (*li*); without benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*), it perishes. Buddhism is maintained through the precepts (*vinaya*);

without meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it is lost. Therefore, one who departs from ritual in the pursuit of benevolence and righteousness cannot be discussed as a Confucian;

one who diverges from the precepts in the pursuit of concentration and wisdom cannot be discussed as a Buddhist. The Draft Stele for the Sixth Patriarch, Master Neng. It states briefly: "Since the beginning of sentient beings..."

Thus, those who delight in strife and plunder lose their fundamental substance. When they become perverse, divergent, and licentious, flowing away without returning to the origin, the teachings of the Buddha appeared later;

they push aside these distractions and lead one back to the source, aligning with what is called "being still from birth. The House of Liang delighted in performing conditioned activities (*saṃskṛta*), which Bodhidharma censured.
As the art of Emptiness became increasingly manifest, it was transmitted six times to the Great Mirror (Huineng). His Way takes non-action (*wuwei*) as its being and takes Emptiness as...

The Cavern is reality. It takes vastness and non-dissipation as its ultimate goal. Its teaching of humanity begins with the inherent goodness of human nature and ends with that same inherent goodness;
it requires no weeding or tilling, for it is fundamentally still (the full text is found in this collection).
Li Ao, courtesy name Xizhi, was the tenth-generation descendant of Li Chong, the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs during the Later Wei dynasty.

He passed the jinshi examination and, at the beginning of the Yuanhe era, served as a Doctor of the National University and an Editor of the History Bureau. He once held the post of Prefect of Langzhou and looked up to and admired [the teachings of] Yao [Fang].
Master Shanyue Yan’s reputation for the Way was such that [Dongshan Liangjie] repeatedly invited him to visit but he did not go. Dongshan then entered the mountain specifically to pay his respects.
Yayaoshan sat upright reading a sutra and paid him no attention at all. Liaowu remarked, "Seeing the person is not as good as hearing of their fame," and brushed past him before leaving.
Yaoshan called out to Ao. Ao turned his head. Yaoshan said, "How can you value the ears and despise the eyes? Ao then prostrated himself, rose, and asked, "What is the Way?
Yaoshan pointed to the sky and then pointed to a pure water jar. Ao said, "I do not understand. Yaoshan said:
"Clouds are in the blue sky; water is in the jar. Hào bowed in thanks and presented this verse: My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane;
Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture. I have come to ask about the Way with no other business: Clouds are in the blue sky; water is in the jar.
One night, as the Master ascended the mountain, the clouds suddenly parted and the moon appeared. He let out a great roar, the sound of which fell upon Liyang.

It was eighty or ninety *li* away. When Lü Ao heard of this, he again sent a verse, saying: "Having chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments, Throughout the year there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.
At times I ascend directly to the peak of a solitary mountain, And beneath the moon, parting the clouds, let out a single cry.

Lü Ao once composed three essays on the "Restoration of Nature" (*Fuxing*). The first states: "When the emotions (*qing*) are clouded, nature (*xing*) is hidden; when one forgets the emotions, nature is restored. Its...

The second means that when there is no thought, there is tranquil illumination. The third means that if one is muddled and does not contemplate, one will ultimately not clarify the Way (from the *Chuan deng lu* and the *Ben ji*).
By Pei Du.

Du, courtesy name Zhongli, was a native of Wenxi in Hedong. He served through four successive dynasties. During the reign of Emperor Wenzong, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as Military Governor of Hedong.
In his second year of office, he was appointed Chief Secretary (Zhongshu Ling) and enfeoffed as Duke of Jin; his posthumous title was Wenzhong.

He once sought instruction in the Way from Chan Master Guoyi Qin along with more than thirty others, performing the rites due to a dharma heir. While serving in Hedong, he petitioned for the restoration of Foguang Temple on Mount Wutai.
A celebratory cloud appeared. Emperor Wen saw Mañjuśrī riding a lion in the air, followed by a multitude of ten thousand attendants.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy to provide offerings for ten thousand bodhisattvas. On that same day, another celebratory cloud appeared (*Xintin ji*).

Yu Chengxuan, whose courtesy name was Chengxuan, passed the imperial examination in the eighth year of the Zhenyuan era. He was in the same cohort as Han Yu and Ouyang Jian; their class was known as the "Dragon and Tiger Roll.
He once composed the inscription for the Jingguang Pagoda in Fuzhou, the preface of which states in brief: "The Inspector General, Lord Liu, the Military Supervisor..."

He caused the fish-lord to speak among themselves, saying: "There is no greater way to repay one's lord than by honoring blessings; there is nothing greater than honoring blessings than by planting roots of goodness;
there is nothing greater than planting roots of goodness than the Buddha-dharma. Is it not in the Buddhist stupa that the very essence of this teaching resides? Now, as for the stupa..."
Above, it reaches the various heavens; below, it stabilizes the three realms. The shadow it provides is like the illumination of the sun and moon, dispelling darkness to bring forth light.
The resonance of its bells is like the playing of metal and stone instruments; hearing the sound gives rise to goodness. Such merit as this shall entirely accrue to the sovereign.
Since his plans are thus well-conceived, those who look upon one another leap for joy. Those who consume the king’s stipends take pleasure in giving alms, bearing the burden of serving the Emperor.
The laborers were delighted and presented their work with skill; the workers did not voice any complaints regarding their toil.
When the task was completed, the Emperor praised them and bestowed upon it the title "Jingyuan Wugou Jingguang Pagoda" (Old History of the Tang).
Liu Yuxi, whose courtesy name was Mengde, was a descendant of Zhongshan. He passed the jinshi examination and attained the degree of "Broad Learning and Magnificent Prose" (Bóxué Hóngcí).

He served as an Inspector (jiànchá) of the Ministry of Rites (Lìbù Langzhōng) until his death. He once composed the second stele inscription for the Sixth Patriarch, Dajian Chánshī, titled "Yuánhé... [The text ends here].
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], the tenth year, an imperial edict posthumously honored the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, Master Neng, bestowing upon him the posthumous title of Dajian.
This was reported by Ma Zong, the Governor of Guangzhou, in a memorial. Consequently, his petition was granted.
Three years later, a monk named Daolin led his disciples from Caoxi and arrived, saying, "I wish to erect a second stele; this is the aspiration of the students. Thus it was. Vei.
In the middle five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna arrived in China with the sūtras;
people first heard their words, like those in deep darkness beholding the dawn. In the latter five hundred years, Bodhidharma arrived in China with the Dharma;
people first transmitted his mind, like those at the break of day beholding the bright sun. From Bodhidharma, there were six transmissions.
Reaching the Great Mirror, it is like a wish-fulfilling pearl threaded upon a string; there is a sequence of before and after, yet no distinction between them.

What the world calls the True Doctrine is what is known as the Sudden Gate. Originally, Bodhidharma came together with the Buddha’s robe; having attained the Way, he transmitted it as the seal of truth.
As for the fact that the Great Mirror (Dajian) set it aside and did not transmit it, was this because he regarded it as a mere trap or snare, or as a discarded dog?

Or was it because everyone considers themselves beyond compare, and thus he deemed it better to set it aside? I cannot know for certain. According to the records, the Great Mirror was born in Xinzhou;
he left home at thirty, passed away at forty-seven, and received his posthumous title one hundred and six years after his death. It began from...

He traveled to the Eastern Mountains of Qi and received a prophecy from the Fifth Master before returning home. Emperor Gaozong dispatched a high-ranking eunuch to summon him twice, but he did not comply with the imperial decree;
instead, he held speech as his highest value. The Emperor revered and followed his words. The inscription reads:

"The birth of the Perfect Man knows no fixed category; he shares the same form as others, yet his wisdom transcends them. From the teeming southern borders, a truly extraordinary being was born. His father..."
Heaven (Qian) and Earth (Kun) alone emulate the primal qi. With a single word of sudden enlightenment, he did not tread the first stage.
Five generations of succession transmitted the precious vessel to him. Seated in meditation at Caoxi, he was styled the Southern School. Disciples came in dense crowds like water flowing eastward.

He administered the wondrous medicine to cure their muteness and deafness. Though the imperial decree could not summon him, he was permitted as a hero of the Dharma. As the sun of the Buddha grew distant, the masses...

Words accumulate in the billions; those attached to emptiness and those clinging to existence each run toward their own domain. I have established the true raft to raise it aloft in the Southern Land.

It is cultivation without cultivation and attainment without attainment, capable of enabling students to return to their natural office. It is like one who is lost in darkness looking up at the North Star;
once attained, it is spontaneous and ultimately cannot be transmitted. To transmit it by word of mouth or entrust it by hand is to be hindered by existence. [It] remains...

Those who obtain [the robe] within the hall receive it as a divine grant. Furthermore, he composed an inscription for the Buddha’s robe, which says: "The Buddha’s words were not practiced, yet his robe was contested.
To favor the near and distance the noble has been the constant sentiment of all ages. When Confucius was born, there was not even a single *li* of land [belonging to him];

after his dream-like final rest, his sandals have endured for a thousand years. In the past, the Liang dynasty was as wild as a mad elephant; Bodhidharma came to save the world to act as its physician."
O King, when words do not heal, one must shift through things; it is like holding a tally or seal while passing through the Fu-guan gate.

The people do not know the officials, yet they look upon their carriages with awe; the common folk do not know the Buddha, yet they prize his robes as precious. As for robes of dyed color, the Way does not reside therein;

it is by following them that one comes to believe in the Way, which is why they are considered treasures. Before the Sixth Patriarch was manifest, his emergence was subtle; once he returned to Lang...

Alas! The worldly folk are ignorant and deluded. Without a vessel of faith, to whom shall sentient beings turn? This was opened as a convenient gateway; it was not intended merely for the transmission of robes.
All things must have an end; how could transmission be without its limit? All material objects must eventually reach their exhaustion; why rely so long upon these robes?

Those who know the end of things beforehand find that their utility is inexhaustible. My Way is imperishable; what need is there for robes? When their utility has already been exhausted, who would not treat them as mere straw?
Gou. Li Deyu, courtesy name Wenrao, was the son of Ji Fu. His ancestors were from Zanhuang. When Emperor Mu took the throne, he was promoted to the Hanlin Academy.
Lin Xueshi served as Minister of Education (Situ) and concurrently as Chief Councilor (Tongpingzhangshi); he died as Administrative Assistant for Revenue (Sihu Canjun) in Yiazhou.

Emperor Yizong posthumously honored him with the title Duke of Wei. During the Baoli era, the Duke established Ganlu Temple using his residence and the Huaihai Academy to provide merit for the deceased Emperor Muzong.
It was named "Ganlu" (Dew) because heavenly dew descended at that time (according to his biography and the Illustrated Gazetteer of Runzhou).
Wan Jingru, Jingru.

A native of Luzhou. Three generations lived together as a single household. Upon the death of his parents, he dwelt in a hut at their tomb and transcribed Buddhist scriptures with blood drawn from his own body.
He severed two fingers of his hand, which immediately grew back. Emperor Xuanzong issued an edict to honor his family (from the "Biographies" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*).
Wu Daozi (Daozi) was a native of Yangzhai. Originally named Daozi, he changed his name to Daoxuan during the Xuanzong reign. He was a master of painting whose brushstrokes possessed a divine power.
Emperor Xuanzong summoned him to serve as a court artist (*gongfeng*). At Jinggong Temple, he painted the *Transformation of the Hells*, which was viewed by all the people of the capital.
Everyone feared sin and cultivated goodness; even the butchers and wine-sellers in the two markets could not sell their goods (*Minghua ji* and *Tongji*).

Du Xunhe, courtesy name Yanzhi, had early achieved renown for his poetry. During the Dazhong era, he passed the imperial examinations and was subsequently promoted to the position of Vice Director of the Department of State Guest.
Lang died at the beginning of the Tianyou era. He styled himself Mountaineer of Jiuhua. A collection of his poems circulated in the world.

One of his poems sent off a monk reads: "The path of profit and fame—both are unreliable; A hundred-year life is like a short-lived flame before the wind. I only fear that as a monk you have not completed your purpose;
If you have completed your purpose as a monk, then in all respects you surpass [the worldly man]."

Li Zhouzhou, courtesy name Gongdu, was a native of Longxi and the son of Cen. He possessed literary talent and lofty ambition. Du Fu composed a twenty-six-verse poem to see him off, the first line of which reads:
"In northern Dai there is a fierce falcon; its offspring are born with entirely red feathers. (Thus it is said.)

Zhou said: "If Śākyamuni were born in the Middle Kingdom, he would have established teachings like those of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; if the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were born in the Western Regions, they would have established teachings like those of Śākyamuni.
As for heaven, let it not exist; if it does exist, only the gentleman shall ascend. As for hell, let it not exist;
if it does exist, only the petty man shall enter. (Li Zhao, *Guoshi Bu*)
When Governor Lu Xun was observing the district of Chizhou, Chan Master Puyuan had resided at Nanquan for thirty years. Xun invited him into the prefectural seat to perform the rites of a disciple.
Xun said, "I, your disciple, also have a modest understanding of the Buddha-dharma. The Master replied, "Your Excellency, throughout the twelve periods of the day..."
"What is it like in the midst? Guo Wenjian said, "Not a single thread of silk hangs upon him. The Master said, "A fellow standing on the steps.
Seeing people playing *shuanglu* (double-six), Wenjian picked up the dice and said, "'Is it so? Is it not so?'—if one simply goes along with the roll, what then?
The Master picked them up and said, "A stinking bone. 'Flowers, eighteen' (*Chuan Deng Lu*)."
Li Jie served as the Circuit Official (xun guan) for Hedong. In the eighth year of the Dazhong era, the śramaṇa Shuyan of Yuelu Monastery in Tanzhou traveled to Taiyuan to seek the Tripitaka.
The Hedong Military Governor, Minister of Works Lu Jun, and the Vice-Governor Wei...
Zhou bestowed this upon him as a gift. He composed a preface for the farewell banquet, saying: "Those who study the Confucian classics take pleasure in disparaging the followers of Śākyamuni.
Their arguments invariably state that during the eras of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, there were no Buddhists at all; the rise of Buddhism originated in the Han dynasty."
It flowed into the Jin dynasty; it spread throughout the Song, Wei, Qi, Liang, Chen, and Sui. This is what was venerated during the degenerate ages.
It ought to be swept away entirely and eradicated like weeds, so that it may not flourish again. The words of those who debate this are superficial;
they may recognize that such is the case, yet they do not know why it is so. I shall explain it with precision. Once, there was a man whose skin was plump and fleshy...
In the former case, the complexion is composed, the vital energy is vigorous, and the spirit is clear; he remains serene and maintains harmony, such that neither medicine nor prayer is required.
Yet, suppose there is another man afflicted by the ailment of wind-moisture (wind-rheumatism), with a hunched back and crippled feet, deaf ears and blinded eyes;
for him, one employs moxibustion and fomentation, and performs rituals of exorcism and propitiation. Why are these two men so different? It is because the sick and the healthy are distinct.
Listen! Alas! Before the Three Dynasties, the world was peaceful and its people were good. The virtues and righteousness of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were disseminated throughout it;
the canons and teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius sustained it. Although the influence of the Way had become slight, its lingering permeation still remained.

Deceit could not overcome sincerity, and the wicked knew how to avoid the good. By the end of the Three Dynasties, the age fell into affliction. Customs and mores were utterly ruined; deceit and force overcame one another, and goodness...
The world treats the weak with contempt and employs the strong with severity; thus, superiors and inferiors provoke one another into resentment, creating a climate of enmity.
The teaching of the Śākya [Buddha] takes pure stillness and emptiness as its meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and gentle humility and yielding as its forbearance (*kṣānti*);

therefore, strife and contention can be brought to rest. It regards frugality and diligent austerity as spiritual practice, and views misfortune or fortune, longevity or early death, as the workings of cause and effect (*hetu-phala*).
Thus, the noble and the humble can find peace; when resentment and strife cease, weapons and bandits do not arise.
When the noble and the humble are at peace, the distinctions between sovereign, minister, and commoner are maintained. This is how the Buddha, the Sage, saves the world from decline.
Were it not for the followers of Śākyamuni, who else could save it? Yet those who debate today do not hold the customs of this degenerate age accountable.

It is difficult to shift their views, yet they especially regard the followers of Śākyamuni as useless. This is like failing to pity a man suffering from illness and instead reviling his physician and the prayers for his recovery;
it shows a failure to consider that the salvation of the world and the propagation of transformation by the followers of Śākyamuni constitute a great benefit.
Moreover, I lament the splendor of their palace walls and the vastness of their assemblies, as well as the expense of their carvings, engravings, and polychrome decorations;

for this reason, I say that they know "that it is so," but do not know "why it is so. During the final years of the Huichang era, Emperor Wuzong carried out a great suppression of the Śākya followers:
he shorn their heads, demolished their dwellings, and cast those images fashioned from wood and clay into the water. As for their doctrines—

The paper scrolls were cast into the fire. Imperial edicts were issued, commanding the Censors to travel throughout the realm on four-horse carriages to conduct inspections; those who dared to conceal anything were to be punished.
Consequently, the famous monasteries and sacred temples throughout the empire were demolished as if swept away, at the very beginning of the Emperor’s reign.
Xuě Shìshì remarked, "It is improper to abolish this [tradition]. You must urgently issue an edict to restore it.

Consequently, from the region south of Lake [Tóngtǐng], those from distant lands, fearing the law and embodying the solemn intent of the court, burned and demolished the scriptures and images until almost nothing remained.

Thus, although the imperial decree has now been promulgated, they are unable to obtain the sacred texts. Dàolín Temple is a magnificent site for excursions on the west side of Xīng; there was once a monk named Shūyán who resided there.

Duchu said: "The capital of Taiyuan was the ancient seat of the state and contains the greatest number of Buddhist temples. Your Excellency, Minister Lu, is a man of universal benevolence throughout the realm;
I shall go there specifically to seek out lost scriptures, for they may still be found. Having presented himself at the military headquarters, the Minister indeed granted his request.
He dispatched messengers in all directions to search for rare texts, and before a month had passed, he obtained five thousand forty-eight fascicles of sutras, vinayas, and śāstras.
It was carried back on a palanquin. Alas! The way of the Śākya to save the world has now been explained.

Had it not been for our enlightened sovereign, who clearly discerned the source of principle, how could this path have been practiced once more? Had it not been for Minister Sīkāng, who was able to venerate the Great Dharma, how could these scriptures have been preserved in their entirety?
And had it not been for the śramaṇa Shū, whose profound understanding of the destiny of the Dharma allowed him to disregard the distance in his quest, how could this have been accomplished?
This is a magnificent occasion. By receiving the Imperial Majesty’s command to promote the school of Śākyamuni, the benefits shall extend to future generations;
its efficacy is such that it cannot be fully described (General Discourse).
Pei Susu, style name Zhongming, was a native of Jiyuan in Mengzhou. He once served as the Inspector of Yuezhou.

He donated his salary to renovate the Great Buddha Hall of Longxing Temple (which is now Baolin Temple). Initially, when the hall had fallen into ruin, the assembly requested Dharma Master Tanyan to repair it.
Huyan said, "This is not due to the power of my own karmic conditions. Three hundred years hence, a patron in crimson robes will come to restore this hall.
The monastic community carved this record into stone. When Hu Yan was appointed to his post, he used his stipend to repair the hall, which indeed fulfilled Huyan’s prediction (Shijian).
Pei Xiu, courtesy name Gongmei, was the son of Pei Su. He maintained a strict and upright character. By day he lectured on the sutras, and by night he composed writings;

throughout the year he never stepped outside his door. When someone presented him with a deer, Xiu would not eat it, saying, "Even my vegetarian diet is insufficient; if I were to consume meat now, later..."
How did he succeed? He was promoted as a jinshi to serve as Censor-in-Chief and concurrently as Chief Minister of the Secretariat and Chancellery.

Xuanzong once remarked, "Xiu is a true Confucian scholar," yet he was fond of the Buddhist dharma and sought out its doctrines. Although his contemporaries mocked him for this, his devotion never waned.
While serving as the Governor of Hongzhou, Xiu entered Longxing Temple and, observing the murals, remarked that their forms and features were...
Huihuo asked, "Where is the eminent monk? No one in the assembly replied. Huihuo asked again, "Is there any Chan monk here?
Someone said, "There is Master Yun who is mingling among us as a sweeper; you may ask him. Huihuo invited him to come forward and questioned him with the same words as before.
Yun called out in a clear voice, "Pei Huo! Huihuo replied, "Yes. Yun asked, "Where are you? At these words, Huihuo attained sudden enlightenment. He then invited Yun to enter the monastery.
The Prefect visited him morning and evening to inquire about the Way, and consequently, [Hui] took Huangbo as his teacher. Later, Hui also traveled with Chan Master Miji of Guifeng;
he entered the latter’s inner domain and received his profound instructions. Those who discuss this consider whether Guifeng was a master of Chan or of the sutras and śāstras.
The Retraction states: Alas! How can those who debate know the direction in which the Great Way tends? Now, the single mind is the synthesis of all dharmas;
it is divided into the precepts, concentration, and wisdom; it is expanded into the six perfections; and it is dispersed into the myriad practices.

Never has non-duality been anything other than the one mind; never has the one mind been at variance with the myriad practices. Zen is but one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); how could it encompass all dharmas?

Furthermore, among the patriarchs, some extensively propagated the Dharma teachings, some devoted themselves exclusively to meditative stillness, some departed like a cicada shedding its shell, and some were extinguished by cremation. Yet the Dharma was necessarily the same, while their practices were not necessarily identical. Thus, Master Mi...
In this Way, insight and vision constitute the wondrous gate; tranquility constitutes the true flavor; loving-kindness and patience constitute the armor and shield;

and wisdom and severance constitute the sword and spear. Thus one breaks down the high ramparts of the internal demons and penetrates the solid ranks of external thieves, so that the two vehicles do not arise.

The Four Quarters were not in a state of prosperity; our Master felt ashamed of this. Loyalty and filial piety cannot be cultivated simultaneously; the burden was too heavy to bear as he departed; our Master felt ashamed of this.
Therefore, he was earnestly intent upon rescuing and uplifting others, and zealously engaged in opening the way for and guiding them. Was he one of the four types of persons who rely [on the Dharma]?
Or was he one of those on the ten stages? How can critics know the direction in which the Great Way tends? (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Left Street).
The Dharma Master Duānfú, titled *Sēnglù*, *Nèigōngfèng*, *Sānjiàotándùn*, and *Cìzǐ*, and known as *Dádá*, passed away. Xuī composed his epitaph, which states in brief:
"One who is a true man, when at home, spreads benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and music, assisting the Son of Heaven to support the world and guide the customs.
When leaving the home-life, he employs compassion, meditative concentration, and wisdom, aiding the Tathāgata to propagate the teachings and benefit sentient beings. [He] renounced...
This man could not be considered a true "great person" (puruṣa). At the age of seventeen, the Master became a bhikṣu;

from then on, he was unrivaled in the world in his mastery of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. When Emperor Dezong heard of his reputation, he summoned him; upon seeing him once, the Emperor was greatly pleased.

Emperor Shunzong admired his character and treated him with the intimacy of brothers. Emperor Xianzong visited his monastery and received him as a guest and friend. Thus, the Son of Heaven came to know him even more deeply.
The Buddha was a Great Sage. At that time, the imperial court was in the process of pacifying the realm, and the Son of Heaven sat upright with hands folded, free from affairs.
He issued an edict to the Upādhyāya, directing him to lead the assembly of monastics to welcome the True Relics from the Spirit Mountain and to establish a Dharma assembly within the Secret Palace.
Soon thereafter, punishments were not cruel and weapons were not used wantonly; infants had no cries of distress, and the rivers and seas had no turbulent waves.

This was truly the brilliant efficacy of employing the True Vehicle (Buddhism) to assist the administration of great governance. During his leisure time, Xiu abstained from wine and meat and composed the "Essay on Encouraging the Arousing of Bodhicitta.

He also authored the "Preface to the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment," the "Preface to the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm," and the "Preface to the Substantiation of the Source of Chan. The world held him in high esteem.
The Essential Points (from the *Old History of the Tang* and the *Lamp Records*).
Li Shangyin:
his courtesy name was Yishan; he was a native of Huai Prefecture. His poetry and prose were magnificent, extraordinary, and archaic, and he was known for the "Xikun Style. His eulogy:
The Buddha’s verse says: "Our Confucian teacher was called Zhongni of Lu. Zhongni took Nantuo as his teacher; I know nothing of Long.
Nantuo took Zhuqian as his teacher, who skillfully entered the state of non-action (*wuwei*). I bow my head to the Great Awakened One. My teacher’s teacher.

Shangyin admired the Way of National Teacher Zhihuan of Wuda, and served him with the etiquette due to a disciple. He once suffered from a severe eye ailment and requested that Zhihuan offer prayers to the Dark Deity.
The three chapters of the "Gatha on Entrusting the Celestial Eye" by Xuanyuan; upon their completion, [his illness] was cured (according to the *Sengtong Shiji*).
Lü Yan, the Real Man Lü Yan, styled Dongbin, was a native of Jingzhao. During the late Tang dynasty, he failed to pass the imperial examinations three times. One day, while at Chang...
While resting at a wine shop, he encountered Zhongli Quan, who bestowed upon him the art of prolonging life. From that time on, no one could fathom his origins.

Once, while traveling to Nianhua Peak at Lu Shan, he inscribed these lines upon the wall of the bell tower of Guizong Temple: "One day, with a body free and easy, The six spirits harmonize, and all is well.
Since there is a treasure within the *dantian*, there is no need to seek the Way; When facing objects without a mind, there is no need to inquire about Chan. Not long after, he passed away.

Passing through Huanglong Mountain, he beheld purple clouds forming a canopy and suspected there was an extraordinary person within. He entered to pay his respects, arriving just as the Master was striking the drum to ascend the hall.
The Master, recognizing him, thought it must be Lü Gong and wished to entice him forward, but cried out in a stern voice, "Beside the seat is one who would pilfer the Dharma!
Lü stepped forth resolutely and asked: "A world is hidden within a single grain of millet; mountains are boiled within half a pint of a cauldron."
"River. [The Master] said, "Tell me, what is the meaning of this? Longzhi pointed and said, "This is a corpse-guarding ghost.

Lü said, "But how can it be, when I have the elixir of longevity and immortality in my bag? Longzhi said, "Even if one passes through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end, one still falls into emptiness and oblivion.

Lü was slightly surprised and flew his sword to threaten him, but the sword could not penetrate. He then bowed twice and requested instruction on the ultimate goal. Longzhi rebuked him, saying, "A half-measure cooking pot."
"I do not ask about boiling mountains and rivers within; how is it that a single grain of millet contains a world?
At these words, Lü attained realization and composed a verse, saying: "Discarding the gourd-bag and smashing the lute, I no longer yearn for gold within the mercury."
Since first meeting Huanglong, I have realized for the first time that my previous efforts were misplaced. Huanglong instructed me to provide him with protection.
Later, I visited Chan Master Jue of Zhidu in Tanzhou, who said: "I traveled through Shaoyang and Chenzhou and descended eastward along the Xiang River until I now met Master Jue.
Observing his Chan studies, they are brilliant and precise; his fundamental nature is pure and refined. He sits quietly with knees drawn close, withdrawing his radiance to illuminate within."
Aside from a single robe, he has no other clothing; aside from a single bowl, he has no other food.

Having distanced himself from the shore of birth and death and shattered the shell of afflictions, it is now the case that the Buddha’s dharma-garment is silent and untransmitted, and the principles of Chan are suspended and nearly extinct.

Will it not be up to our Master to support and revive them? I have composed this one quatrain as a record: The realized one extends his heart to save all beings; Only when the mind is vast can one truly deliver others.
The transmission of the Dharma by the sages and worthies does not depart from the Truth. I pray that you, Master, will explain the meaning of the Coming from the West.
Of the Seven Patriarchs, there is currently no one left [to represent them]. (Wudeng Huiyuan)
*Fófǎjīntángbiān*, Scroll Nine, Revised by the Tiantai Monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎjīntángbiān*, Scroll Ten,
Compiled by the Shamen Xin Tai of Kuaiji.
The Tiantai śramaṇa Zhenqing read [the records of] the two reigns during which the capital was moved from Liangdu to Bian and then to Luoyang, spanning sixteen years.

Emperor Taizu’s surname was Zhu; his given name was Wen. He was a native of Wugou Village in Dangshan County, Songzhou. His father, Cheng, taught the Five Classics to the local community and was known as "Zhu the Five Classics.
When Huang Chao rose in rebellion, Wen served as a vanguard for him, but later he defected from Huang Chao to join the Tang dynasty under Emperor Xizong.

He was granted the name Quanzhong. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Kaiping. On his birthday, he issued an imperial decree ordering the officials to visit the temple to offer incense and pray for his long life.
Qian Liu, the King of Wuyue, sent his youngest son, Lingyin, to become a monk; the Emperor granted him purple robes and bestowed upon him the title of Great Master Wuxiang.
Including the thirty years [of the Later Jin] (according to the *Wudai shi* and the *Bingtong ji*), Emperor Jun’s personal name was Tian;
his courtesy name was Youzhen. He was the third son of Taizu. He ascended the throne in the first year of the Zhenming era of the Later Tang.
The śramaṇa Guixu of the East Pagoda Monastery compiled the *Jinglun huìyào* (Essentials of the Sūtras and Śāstras) and submitted it for inclusion in the Great Canon;
he was subsequently conferred the title of Master Propagator of the Teaching (*Yanjiao Dashi*). (Records from the *Wudai shi* and the *Tongji*)
The Tang dynasty rose from Taiyuan, entered Bianzhou, and moved to Luoyang. It had four rulers and lasted for thirteen years. [The first was] Zhuangzong.
The Emperor’s taboo name was Cúnxù. His surname was Lǐ; his ancestors were people of Shādú who styled themselves Zhūyé. In later generations, they subsequently took Zhūyé as their surname.
During the reign of Emperor Yìzōng of the Táng dynasty, because his grandfather Chìxīn had merit in suppressing Páng Xūn, he was granted the surname and name Lǐ Guóchāng.
Guóchāng fathered Kèyòng, and Kèyòng fathered Cúnxù. When Cúnxù ascended the throne, he changed [the era name].

In the first year of the Tongguang era, on the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, an imperial edict ordered the Chief of Monks (Senglü) Huìjiāng and the Daoist Chéng Zǐxiāo to enter the inner palace for discussion.

A vegetarian feast for a thousand monks was provided. In the second year, an edict ordered Chan Master Xiànguān Jiǎng of Xìnghuà Temple to enter the palace to inquire about the methods of Chan. The Emperor said:
When the Emperor descended upon Daliang, he obtained a priceless jewel. No one had yet come forward to appraise its value. Daowang said, "I beg Your Majesty to examine this treasure.
The Emperor extended his hand and grasped its head and horns. Daowang said, "Who would dare to appraise the treasure of an emperor? The Emperor was pleased.
After Daowang passed away, he was posthumously titled Great Master Guangji (Tongji). [Records from the *Wudai Shi* and the *Chuan Deng Lu*.]
The Jin dynasty originated in Taiyuan and had its capital at Bianliang. It had two rulers and lasted for eleven years. [The first was] Gaozu.
The Emperor’s taboo name was Jingtáng; his surname was Shí. He was the son-in-law of Emperor Mingzong. His father, Xiāoluèjī, originated from the Western Barbarians (Xīyí).

The Khitan ruler established Jingtáng as emperor, and he changed the era name to Tiānfú. Regarding national memorial services, he issued an edict ordering the prime ministers and the hundred officials to go to the monasteries to offer incense and provide meals for the monks, establishing this as a permanent rule.
The śramaṇa Kěhóng of Zhōng Hàn submitted the *Yìnyì* (Phonetics and Meanings) of the *Dàzàngjīng* (Great Canon) in four [volumes].
One hundred and eighty fascicles. By imperial decree, it was entered into the canon (as recorded in the *Wudai Shi* and the *Tongji*).

Emperor Chu’s posthumous name was Chonggui; he was the son of Gaozu’s elder brother, Jingru. In the first year of the Kaiyun era, by imperial decree, he was commissioned to transcribe [the text] for Gaozu.
The Tripitaka was enshrined at Mingsheng Temple to provide merit for the deceased (Tongji). The Han dynasty originated in Taiyuan;
its capital was Bian. There were two rulers for four years. The High Ancestor’s name was Zhìyuǎn; his surname was Liú. His ancestors were from Sha... [text fragment]
The Tuoba people established their capital at Bianzhou;
there were three rulers for a total of nine years.
The Emperor Taizu’s posthumous name was Wei. His surname was Guo, and he was a native of Yao Mountain in Xingzhou. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Guangshun.

On his birthday, he issued an imperial decree for the Prime Minister and the various officials to visit monasteries and temples to establish a *zhusheng daochang* (a ritual arena for praying for the longevity of the sovereign). (*Wudai Shi*)

Emperor Shizong’s taboo name was Ying. His surname was Chai, and he was a native of Xingzhou. In his youth, he followed his paternal aunt to the household of the Grand Ancestor (Taizu), where he was renowned for his prudence and kindness.
Taizu adopted him as a son and invested him as the Prince of Jin. He subsequently ascended the throne. In the first year of the Xiande era, at Kaiyuan Temple in Qizhou...
Dharma Master Yichu presented his compiled work, *The Six Categories of Buddhist Records* (*Shishi liutie*). By imperial decree, it was entrusted to the Historiographic Institute for circulation.
He was granted a purple robe and the honorary title of Great Master Mingjiao (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

During the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, the state of Wu occupied Luzhou. It governed twenty-eight prefectures for four generations over a span of forty-six years. Its founder was King Yang Xingmi, whose courtesy name was... [text truncated]
Huàyuán was a native of Lúzhōu. In the second year of the Tiānfú era of Emperor Zhāozōng, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wú.
When the Southern Táng dynasty occupied Jīnlíng, he governed thirty-five prefectures for three generations over a period of forty-nine years.
Li Bian, whose courtesy name was Zhenglun, claimed to be a descendant of Li Ke, the Prince of Jian’an of the Tang dynasty. He had been adopted as a son by Yang Xingmi of Wu;

when the latter’s own sons could not tolerate him, he requested permission from Xu Wen to adopt the surname Xu and take the name Zhigao. Later, he received the abdication of Wu and established his own state.
The dynasty was named Southern Tang. He reverted to the Li surname and changed his name to Bian; he was the same as the First Lord Li.

At the beginning of the Shengyuan era, he renamed the Xingjiao Temple established by Xu Wen as the Qingliang Great Dharma Field and invited Chan Master Wukong of Chongshou Temple in Fuzhou to reside there.
In the second year of Shengyuan, he renamed Waguan Temple as Shengyuan Temple, and further renamed Baoxian [Temple].

The monastery was the Xingci Temple (originally built by Emperor Wen of the Liu Song dynasty in the second year of the Yuanjia era as the Baoen Temple for his high ancestor; it was abolished at the end of the Huichang era of the Tang dynasty.

In the sixth year of the Taitai era of the Yangwu kingdom, Xu Jingyun, Duke of Piling, rebuilt it for the sake of his deceased kin, naming it the Baoxian Monastery; it was renamed Nengren Temple during the Zhenghe era of the Song dynasty). When Li Bian resided in Jiankang, he held seven assemblies of the *amogha* great vegetarian feast.
A śramaṇa from Central India in the land of Tianzhu presented a palm-leaf manuscript and *śarīra* relics as gifts. Li Bian summoned him.
The monk Zhixuan translated this book along with the illustration of the Elder Li’s image. It was displayed within the borders of his domain (*Wudai Shi* and *Jinling Zhi*).

Li Jing (also written as Jing) was the eldest son of Li Bian; his posthumous title was Emperor Yuanzong. He was the "Middle Lord" of the Li clan. During the Baoda era, he constructed a temple for his late father, naming it—
Fengxian (i.e., Baoning Temple). When Jing moved the capital to Nanchang, he appointed his son Congjia to guard Jiankang. Jing constructed Kaixian Temple on Mount Lu.
After Jing passed away, Congjia succeeded to the throne (*Jinling Zhi* records this as well).
Li Yuyu, courtesy name Chongguang, was the sixth son of Li Jing. Originally named Congjia, he changed his name to Yuyu upon succeeding to the throne; he is the famous Li Houzhu.
He once invited Chan Master Wenyi to reside at Ba’en Chan Monastery and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Jinghui. [He] subsequently moved...
He resided at Qingliang Temple. When Wenyi passed away, Li Yù erected a stupa for him and enshrined his entire body for burial in Danyang, Jiangning County.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Great Fayan" (Dafayan), and his stupa was named "Formless" (Wuxiang) [as recorded in the *Ji載* and the *Chuan deng lu*].

A resident of Shangyuan County died suddenly and then revived, saying that he had gone to the underworld and seen the former ruler, who said: "I was wrongly executed by Song Qiqiu. And... Hè... [text fragment ends]

More than a thousand people from the province submitted as surrenderers, pleading their grievances and recounting their sufferings. "When you return," he said, "you may tell the successor of the throne:
whenever bells are struck in temples and monasteries, my suffering shall temporarily cease. It would be even better if you were to cast a single bell.

During the days I held office, I once enshrined a jade statue of a Heavenly King presented by the Kingdom of Khotan in the left knee of the Buddha at Waguan Temple; no one knew of it. You [should retrieve it]."
To verify this, Li Yù went to the temple to retrieve the jade image, weeping with unceasing emotion. He then commissioned a bell for Qingliang Temple, inscribing upon it:
"In dedication to the late Emperor Xiaogao, may he be delivered from obscurity and emerge from calamity. He subsequently erected a pagoda for the jade image.
He was buried at Mount Jiang (Zeng Zao’s *Leishuo* and *Zhulin*).
Chu occupied Tanzhou and governed thirty-three prefectures. His lineage lasted for six generations over fifty-seven years.
Ma Yin (r.

892–907), whose courtesy name was Batu, was a native of Xu Prefecture. Emperor Zhaozong appointed him as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Tanzhou, and the Taizu of the Liang dynasty enfeoffed him as the King of Chu.
When Chan Master Yun of Shimen moved to reside at Jia Mountain, his route passed through Tanzhou; the King went out of the city to welcome and receive him.
He then asked, "What is the Great Way of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The imperial carriage with its six dragons is a marvel of a thousand ages;
the ceremonial ranks line the jade steps as they emerge from the Golden Gate. The King was greatly pleased and invited him into the Tiance Palace to provide offerings. (From *Shijiàn*).
The Wuyue state occupied Hangzhou. It comprised thirteen prefectures and endured for four generations over eighty-four years under the rule of Qian Liu.
Liu (Liú), courtesy name Jùměi (Jùměi), was a native of Qiántán. During the reign of Emperor Xīzōng of the Táng dynasty, Liu led local militias to defeat and drive away Huang Cháo.

Emperor Zhāozōng appointed him as the Regional Commander (Jiédùshǐ) of the Zhènghǎi and Zhèndōng Armies. In the second year of the Tiānfù era, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yuè. The Taizǔ of the Liáng dynasty conferred upon him the title of King of Wúyuè.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng of the Táng dynasty granted him a jade tablet and a golden seal. He died at the age of eighty-one, posthumously honored with the title Wǔsù (Martial and Austere).
The King (as recorded in the chronicles) once dispatched the śramaṇa Qingwai, together with his younger brother Hua, to the Ayuwang Mountain in Siming to welcome the Śākyamuni Relic Stūpa.
Upon their return by boat to Xiling, the stūpa emitted light at night, making the Zhejiang River as bright as day.

The King personally welcomed it to Luohan Temple and extensively arranged offerings. While the King was stationed in Yue, he suffered from an ailment of the eyes; he then dreamed of an immortal dressed in white robes.
The monk Yan arrived from Yongjia. The following day, a monk from Yongjia indeed presented an image of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), claiming he had obtained it from the sea tide.
The image had appeared in a dream, intending to return [to the temple]. When the Prince of Yue saw the image, his eyes were immediately restored to sight. He then founded a hermitage called Xingfu.

He enshrined it [to cultivate merit; the statue still exists at present-day Yuantong Temple, as recorded in the *Tongji*]. The King invited Chan Master Jingqing Daofu to reside at Tianlong Temple in Hangzhou and further constructed Longce Temple for him to dwell in.
He commanded the śramaṇa Kezhou to preach the sutras in the night at the Tianbao Hall for the sake of the underworld authorities.
Ghosts and spirits manifested their forms to listen to the Dharma. The Emperor bestowed upon Kezhou a golden bowl, purple robes, and an honorary title.
The title *Jingzhi Tongming* (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Qian Hongzuo:
Hongzuo was the son of King Wenmu Yuanguan. He succeeded to the title of King of Wuyue and was posthumously honored with the temple name Zhongxian. He once dispatched...
Senghui traveled to the Double Grove (Śālavatīvana) and opened the stupa of the Great Master Fu Gong of Shanhui.
He obtained sixteen fragments of sacred bone, which were the color of purple gold, along with countless śarīra relics.

He then escorted the sacred bones, as well as a pure water pitcher, an incense burner, a door-knocker, and a mallet, back to Qiantang to be enshrined and venerated in the Guangce Hall. He established Longhua Temple and fashioned a great [image] from the sacred bones.
The statue of the Prince [was enshrined] in the temple (Tongji).
Qian Hongchu—Hongchu was the ninth son of Wenmu; he inherited the title of King of Wuyue and was posthumously honored with the title Zhongyi. He once admired King Aśoka.
The King constructed eighty-four thousand stupas, within which he placed precious caskets; inside these caskets he enshrined the *Yin Xin Zhou* (Heart-Seal Mantra).

After ten years, the work was completed and distributed throughout the provinces (*Tongji*). The King invited Chan Master Daoqian of Quzhou to the palace to receive the Bodhisattva precepts and bestowed upon him the title Cihua.
Chan Master Dinghui established a great monastery on Mount Nan, named Huirui, for the sake of permanence.
Ming invited Qian to live in seclusion. Qian once requested from the King sixteen gilt-bronze Arhat statues for the base of a pagoda.
The King happened to dream that sixteen men were walking with Qian; finding this extraordinary, he granted them to him.
This is why Jingci Temple possesses an Arhat Hall. He once invited Chan Master Xuedou Yan-shou to open the new Lingyin Monastery. The following year...
[Record of the Relocation to Yongming (Jingci Temple Record)]: On Mount Zhiti in Fuzhou, there were one thousand retinues of the Bodhisattva Tianguan.
