The King donated seven precious substances to cast one thousand statues of the Tianguan Bodhisattva and subsequently constructed monastic buildings [Zhiti Temple Record]. Because the King read the *Yongjia ji*, he remarked:

"The 'simultaneous elimination of the four abodes' (*sishu*) mentioned therein is equivalent to this [state of] equanimity; if one suppresses ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tripitaka teachings are indeed inferior."
He asked National Teacher Shao about these words. The Master said, "This is a matter of doctrinal meaning; you should ask Master Jì of Tiantai. He then summoned him and questioned him.
Jì said, "This appears in Zhiyi’s *Miaoxuan*. Since the chaos at the end of the Tang dynasty, many scriptural texts have been lost overseas.
Therefore, ten envoys were dispatched to Japan to retrieve the scriptures and return with them. For this purpose, a temple was built at Luoshan."
Xī said, "This is [the union of] Samādhi and Prajñā" (*Tǒngjì*). Once, when King Wáng was providing a meal for the monastics, he asked Yánshòu, "Is there any true monk who will descend today?
Yánshòu replied, "The Monk Long-ear is an emanation of the Buddha Dingguāng. As soon as this secret was revealed, [Long-ear] sat in the lotus posture and passed away;
his physical body remains preserved (*Fǎxiàngsì Jì*).
Min was based in Fuzhou and governed five prefectures for six generations over fifty-five years;
its ruler was Wang Shenzhi.
Shen-zhi, style name Xintong, was a native of Guangzhou. During the Liang dynasty, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Min.

The Prince once invited the two Chan masters Xuefeng Cun and Xuansha Shi to his palace to seek instruction on the Dharma of the mind. [Xuefeng] then said: "Great King, listen with a sincere heart. This illusory, empty body is Your Majesty’s Dharmakāya;
this knowing, seeing, awakening, and understanding is Your Majesty’s own nature. Contemplate the mind until there is no mind."
"It arises from delusive thoughts. When my own mind is realized as empty, I immediately awaken to the true mark (*dharmatā*). Once the original nature is known, one must let go all at once;
not even a single thread’s worth of further conceptualization should arise. The King paid homage to the two masters, saying, "I, Ji, am fortunate to have encountered this instruction.
He offered twenty ingots of gold, but the two masters would not accept it. The King asked Xuansha, "What of this one true mind?"
"Fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death. From where, then, does this present body arise? The Master said: "This original source of true nature pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Due to deluded thoughts, a single point of conscious nature arises from the false conditions of the parents and undergoes a thousand kinds of suffering;
thus the body undergoes saṃsāra. Since Your Majesty has already awakened to this understanding, you shall not fall into the evil realms. I merely request that Your Majesty..."
The King frequently examined his delusive thoughts, returned to the truth, and harmonized with the Way. He paid homage and joyfully accepted [the teachings] (from the *Xuefeng lu*).

He once established Gushan Monastery and invited National Teacher Yan to be its founding abbot. When Xuansha passed away, he built a stupa for him and was granted the posthumous title Chan Master Zongyi.
Furthermore, he invited Master Ling to reside at the West Cloister of Changle Prefecture and submitted a memorial to bestow upon it the plaque name "Changqing.

When Xuefeng manifested illness, the King ordered a physician to examine him. The Master said, "I am not ill," and ultimately refused to take medicine. After more than a month had passed, he traveled to Lantian and returned;

there, he bathed his body and entered *nirvāṇa* in the middle of the night. Originally, the King had long esteemed the Master’s Way, and thus when he resided at Xuefeng, [the King] acted on his behalf.
He expanded the temple buildings, installed statues, and cast bells to adorn the mountain; he provided offerings to fill the assembly (as recorded by Shi Jian).
Wang Yanjun—Yanjun was the second son of Shen Zhi—had long been devoted to the Buddha-dharma and ordained ten thousand monks; consequently, Buddhism flourished greatly in Min.
Once, when a monk invited Master Luoshan to ascend the hall and preach the Dharma, Luoshan ascended the seat, adjusted his robes, looked around to left and right, and immediately descended.
The King stepped forward, took Luoshan’s hand, and said, “How is this assembly on Vulture Peak any different from today?

The Master replied, “I thought you were just an ordinary layman” (*Chuan Deng Lu*). Later, the King invited Master Mengbi of Jianzhou for a vegetarian feast and asked him: “Master,” he said, “...and harmony. (The text continues with the dialogue.)
"Have you still brought your brush with you? The Master replied, "It is neither a silken-tube pen from Mount Xi, nor rabbit-hair from within the moon.
Wang Yanshi.
Yanshi was the youngest son of Shenzhi. He ordained eleven thousand monks. Once, he constructed a seven-story stone pagoda on a western mound south of the city;
before the work was half-finished, a light like a canopy radiated forth for three nights. When it was completed, the brilliance shone to the very heavens for another three nights.
The Prince was comforted and gratified, and thus he inscribed the name "Jingguang" (Pure Light) upon the pagoda. Furthermore, he established a temple beneath it. (Based on *Jiegu*)
...Briefly:
Nanning occupied Chuangzhou and governed three prefectures for five generations over fifty-seven years. His successor was Wang Gao Jixing.
The Eastern Han dynasty occupied Dayuan and governed eleven provinces for three generations, spanning one hundred and ten years. [During the reign of] Emperor Liu Min, [the state of] Shu...
He occupied Chengdu and governed forty-eight prefectures for two generations over thirty-five years.
Wang Jian’s name was Jian. When Guanhui entered Shu, he presented a poem to Jian, saying: "A single flask and a single bowl, I grow old; ten thousand..."
"Coming all the way from a thousand mountains across the waters. Jian received him with exceptional courtesy and bestowed upon him the title of "Great Master Chan-yueh" (*Shou-gian*).
Later, the Shu kingdom occupied Chengdu, governing forty-six prefectures for two reigns over a period of forty-one years; its ruler was Meng Zhixiang.
Southern Han occupied Guangzhou, governing forty-seven prefectures.
[Its rulers were] Liu Yin and Liu Yan.
Yin was a native of Shangcai. During the Liang dynasty, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nanping. Having established merit in Lingnan, he subsequently came to possess the territory of Nanhai.

Upon his death, his younger brother Yan succeeded him; he changed his name to Gong, and later changed it again to Lian. He then ascended the throne and changed the dynastic title to Han (as recorded in the chronicles).

Initially, when Lian was about to mobilize his troops, he ordered his carriage to go to Master Min at Lingshu Temple to decide whether the course of action was permissible. Min [previously]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
He understood this. He sealed a small casket with his hand and said to his attendant, "When the King comes, bring this out and show it to him. Fayan Min sat in meditation and passed away peacefully.
When the King arrived and heard that Min had already passed away, he was greatly shocked. The attendant then brought forth the casket; when the King opened it, he found a slip of paper which read:
"The Eye and Treasury of Humans and Gods; the Head Seat of the Hall. The King then invited Wenyuan to succeed him on the Dharma seat. Furthermore—
He was welcomed to the prefecture where the Dharma was expounded (*Sengbao zhuan*).

King Zhao Rong—whose personal name was Rong—was the military governor of Zhending and styled himself King Zhao. He once entered Dongyuan to visit Chan Master Congshen, at which time he encountered him.
The Master was sitting in meditation. After Yong had finished his prostrations, those standing nearby asked the Master, "The Lord of the Realm has arrived;
why did you not rise to receive him? The Master said, "You do not understand my meaning. Here, when those of inferior status come, one goes out the mountain gate to receive them."
If a person of middle rank comes, he receives him at the entrance to the meditation hall; if a person of superior rank comes, he receives him upon the meditation seat.
One must not address a Great King as a person of middle or lower rank, for fear of causing the King offense. The King was delighted and invited him inside to provide offerings.

When the Master arrived at the city gate, the entire city’s ceremonial retinue came out to welcome him. Upon entering the palace, as soon as the Master alighted from his precious palanquin, the King then prepared—

He invited the Master to ascend the hall and take his seat in the central position. After a long silence, the Master struck his forehead with his hand and asked, "What official is standing below the steps?
His attendants replied, "These are the venerable elders of the various monasteries and the masters of virtue. The Master said, "Each of them is a spiritual leader in their own region;
had they been standing below the steps, even this old monk would have risen. Thereupon, the King commanded them all to ascend.

"Your Majesty," [the Master said]. On that day, as the vegetarian feast was about to conclude, each person asked questions regarding the Buddha-dharma, and the Master exercised his compassion, awakening them one by one.

One day, the King entered the Eastern Courtyard to visit the Master. The Master did not rise; instead, he struck his knee with his hand and asked, "Do you understand? The King replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Since childhood I have observed the fasts until now I am old; seeing people, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat. The King then asked:
The Master said, "Venerable Monk, at your advanced age, how many teeth do you have left? The Master replied, "I have only one. Wang said, "How can you eat anything with only one?
The Master said, "Even though there is only one, every time I bite down, I hit the mark. Wang praised the Master’s likeness, saying:
"The moon over the emerald stream; the head within the blue mirror. My teacher, my transformation—Zhaozhou of the world" (*Chanlin leiju*).
Song Qiqiu—nothing is known of his origins. While Xu Zhigao served as the Deputy Commander of the Military Affairs for the Huainan Regional Command, he appointed Qiqiu as his chief advisor.
Later, Qiqiu became the Prime Minister of Southern Tang. Initially, the hermit Tan Jingsheng resided on Mount Zhongnan and...

Chen Tuan was his friend. He authored the *Huashu* (Book of Transformation) in one hundred and ten chapters. Once, while traveling to the Three Mao Mountains, he saw that Qiqiu possessed the refined air and spiritual bones of an immortal.
He presented the book to him and requested a preface. Qiqiu, however, clandestinely circulated it under his own name. Among its sixty-six chapters, it says:
"The Lord of Zizhong once told me that, according to the retribution of my past karma, I was a dragon in the Qongchi Lake."
Trapped beneath stagnant waters, it suffered through years of drought and torment until the water turned to mud. Being of immense body, there was no hole large enough to contain it.
As the scorching sun blazed overhead, it was tormented by heat both inside and out. Within its scales and shells, small insects had each taken birth, biting and gnawing at it in bitter agony.
One morning, when the air grew cool and the light of heaven suddenly broke forth, five-colored clouds drifted across the sky; within them—

As for these auspicious signs: his deep blue hair is coiled in spirals, and his golden countenance is as bright as the moon. The mountain spirits and river deities, along with the myriad beings, bow their heads in prostration.

Their voices of praise and joy shake heaven and earth. Celestial incense swirls about, bringing the springtime to every place. I then looked up and wailed in lamentation, entreating him to grant salvation to all living beings.
All the sages said to me: "This is the Great Sage of the West, the Perfectly Awakened One of the World..."
"The Honored One is Śākyamuni. Now that his teachings are circulating in the Eastern Land, he has manifested a transformation body to go to the Middle Kingdom.
Since you have encountered this through the exhaustion of your past karma, I myself shall leap forth into the celestial light and fully explain the principles of your former retributions.
The World-Honored One replied, "Excellent, Son of Heaven! Regarding your filial piety in the past..."

They were loyal to their families and states. Furthermore, out of compassion for the beings of this world, they maintained a mind of protection. Yet, when causes and effects were not yet fully understood, enemies contended with one another;
driven by the perception of self and other, they indulged in cruelty and vented their anger upon other things.
Now that their karmic debts must be repaid, they feel remorse and desire liberation. At such a time as this, if you still harbor thoughts of enmity or kinship, or of hatred, anger, and delusion—
"Do you remember? he asked. "I have heard the ultimate truth, and my mind has become clear and bright; internally and externally, all is utterly empty, abiding like space.

Looking back at my own body, it dissolves away in accordance with this realization. Furthermore, I have become a man and attained the wisdom of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). I take refuge in him [the Lord of Zixiong, whose temple is in Shu]."
When Bian Hao was first born, his parents dreamed that Xie Lingyun entered their room; therefore, he was given the childhood name Kangle.

While serving as a Commandant of the Capital Guard under the Southern Tang, he accompanied Cha Wenhui in the conquest of Jianzhou. All those captured were spared by him. The people of Jian said: [text continues]
When Bian reached Fuzhou, the Buddhist disciples there remained so orderly that the market stalls did not change their positions; thus he was called Bian the Buddha-Son.

Later, when he became the Military Governor (Jiedushi) of Tanzhou, he established vegetarian feasts daily and performed Buddhist rites on a grand scale. The people of Tanzhou called him Bian the Monk (*Wudai Shi*).
Liu Xuxu, courtesy name Yaoyuan, was a native of Guiyi in Zhuozhou. During the Tianyou era of Emperor Zhaozong of the Tang dynasty, he served as a military secretary (military ya-tui).

At the beginning of the Kaiyun era of the Later Jin dynasty of the Five Dynasties, he was appointed as Minister of Works (Sikong) and Chancellor (Pingchangshi), and further served as the Director of the National History Commission (jianxiu guoshi) to compile the *Tangshu*.

The sacred traces of the Buddhas and patriarchs are all recorded therein. He once composed a biography of Shenxiu, which states in brief: "In the late period of the Later Wei dynasty, there was a monk named Bodhidharma.
Originally a prince of the kingdom of India, he left the household life to protect his country. He traveled to the South Sea, where he obtained the sublime Dharma of the Chan school.
Since Śākyamuni, this lineage has been transmitted with the robe and bowl serving as its token, handed down from generation to generation. Initially, he arrived in the Liang dynasty."
He went to Emperor Wu, who questioned him regarding matters of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*); as their views did not accord, he departed for Wei.
He lived in seclusion at Shaoshi Temple on Mount Song and passed away there. That same year, the Wei envoy Song Yun encountered him on Mount Xiang.

Later, when his disciples opened his tomb, they found nothing but his robes and sandals. Bodhidharma transmitted [the Dharma] to Huike; Huike transmitted it to Sengcan; and Sengcan transmitted it to Daoxin.
Xin transmitted it to Hongren; Ren transmitted it to Huineng, and so forth (as recorded in the *Benzhuan* and the *Zhenzongji*).
*Fofa Jintang Bian*, Volume Ten, re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
*Fofa Jintang Bian*, Volume Eleven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai during the Song dynasty.
The capital was Bian. Beginning with Taizu’s gengshen year and ending with Qinzhong’s bingwu year, there were nine sovereigns for a total of one hundred and sixty-seven years.
Taizu...
The Taizu’s personal name was Kuangyin. His surname was Zhao, and his ancestors were from Zhuo. Because the Taizu was born in Luoyang, he was considered a native of Luoyang.

His father, Hongyan, was posthumously honored with the temple name Xuanzu. While serving the Zhou dynasty, the Taizu held the rank of Commander-in-Chief of the Guide Army and Commander-in-Chief of the Imperial Bodyguard.
Having received an imperial decree to campaign against the north, he stayed overnight at Chenqiao Station. The generals and soldiers then offered him their support and enthroned him with yellow...
The robe was conferred upon him. In the first month of the first year of Jiànlóng, he received the abdication of Emperor Gōng of the Zhōu dynasty.

An imperial edict declared that the sixteenth day of the second month of that year, his birthday, would be celebrated as Chángxuán Festival. Eight thousand novice monks were universally ordained (National History of the Dynasty, Section on Essentials).
In the twelfth month, an edict was issued to construct a temple at the site of the battle in Guǎnglíng, named Jiànlóng, and four *qīng* of land were granted. He commanded the śramaṇa Dào...
*Hui-zhu’s Record of the Years*. Initially, Emperor Taizu witnessed Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty melting down the bronze statue of Mahākaruṇika Bodhisattva at Zhenzhou to cast it into coinage.
Taizu secretly sought out the monk Maitreya (Māyī) and asked him, "Has there ever been an emperor in antiquity who destroyed the Buddha?
Maitreya replied, "Why must you ask about ancient matters? You may verify this by observing the current House of Chai yourself."

Taizu said, "The Sovereign (Sejong) is divine and martial, intelligent and wise, and skilled at employing men. He plots for governance day and night, with the unification of all under heaven as his heart's aim.
He possesses the spirit of Tang Taizong; I do not know when the world will be settled. Ma-i replied, "When the Jiazi year arrives, there will be great stability.
Taizu then asked, "Regarding ancient emperors who destroyed the Buddha-dharma, how do they compare to the Great Zhou?"
Māyī said: "Emperor Taowu of the Wei dynasty destroyed monasteries, burned scriptures and images, and executed śramaṇas; consequently, both father and son did not meet their natural deaths.

Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty destroyed Buddhist temples, registered monks, and returned them to the common people; before five years had passed, he was suddenly stricken by a wind-disorder and died in his carriage at the age of thirty-six.
His kingdom also perished shortly thereafter. Emperor Wuzong of the Tang dynasty likewise destroyed the Buddhist temples throughout the empire."
He reigned for six years; at the age of thirty-two, the divine regalia were passed on once more. Yet, Huang Chao and his bandits rose up together. Taizu said, "The world has long been weary of war.
To destroy the Buddha-dharma is not a blessing for the state. What is to be done? Maitreya (Māyī) replied, "A white vapor has already appeared as an omen.
In no more than a few months, by the year of the Monkey or the Dragon, a sage emperor shall arise. When he arises, the Buddha-dharma [shall flourish]."
Relying upon this, [the state] shall also flourish, and its legacy shall endure for generations without end. I request that the Grand Marshal (Taishou) keep this in mind.
Upon his accession to the throne, he repeatedly established Buddhist temples and permitted the ordination of monks every year (as recorded in the *Biographies of Ouyang*).

In the second year, on the anniversary of his birthday, he ordered that virtuous śramaṇas from the capital and all prefectures and counties ascend the dharma-seat to offer prayers for the Emperor, establishing this as a permanent standard. In the third year, he issued an edict to conduct examinations for novice monks (*tongxing*) annually.
Those who attained mastery of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* were granted certificates by the Sacrificial Bureau (*Cibu*) for their tonsure.
In the fourth year of the Qiandé era, an imperial edict dispatched one hundred monks to the Western Regions to seek Buddhist scriptures.

In the ninth month of the first year of the Kaibao era, an edict ordered the Chengdu Prefecture to produce two complete sets of the Tripitaka in gold and silver characters, with Liu Xigu of the Ministry of War appointed as supervisor. In the fifth year, an edict was issued to carve one set of Buddhist scriptures.

The Emperor personally used his troops to pacify the various states. Before and after these campaigns, he commissioned several sets of the Buddhist canon inscribed in gold and silver characters (*Jiegu lue*).
In the eighth year, upon returning from Luoyang to the capital, the Emperor personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and frequently recited it himself.
When Zhao Pu saw this while attending to state affairs, the Emperor said, "I do not wish for those in armor to know of this; you may simply say that I am constantly reading military treatises."
[From the *Beishan lu*].

Emperor Taizong, whose taboo name was Kuangyi, later changed his name to Jing. He was the third son of Emperor Xuanzu and the uterine younger brother of Emperor Taizu. [Reigned during the] Taiping... period.
In the first year of the Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued to universally ordain one hundred and seventy thousand youths throughout the realm (*Guochao Huizhao*).

In the second year, Emperor Shizong of the Later Zhou had abolished Longxing Monastery to convert it into an official granary. At the beginning of our dynasty, the monks of the monastery beat drums to petition for its restoration;

by this time, they had not ceased their efforts. The Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing a sword to interrogate them, saying: "The former dynasty has used this as a granary for a long time. Why do you trouble me with this?"

He was impertinent before the Imperial Court. Furthermore, the secret emissary feared he would be executed immediately. The monk remained composed and said, "The former dynasty was unrighteous; it destroyed images and abolished monasteries.
It is precisely upon this day that we rely on Your Majesty’s sacred court to restore them. Why should this poor monk fear death? The central envoy reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor was deeply moved and sighed in admiration. He issued an edict to restore [the monastery] and bestowed upon it the name Taiping Xingguo (Song Dynasty).

Wen-duan: It would likely be difficult for anyone other than Nanshan to achieve this. With eyes beholding several layers of golden luster, and hands holding a single piece of jade-cold radiance;

[Images] emerged like raindrops. Consequently, he composed this hymn of praise: The Great Sage Śākyamuni is equal to space and yet as minute as a single speck of dust.

may all beings throughout the multitudes be universally saved. In the third year of the Zhenghe era, an imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Yongdao to reside at the Left Street [Monastery].

At Chongxian Xiangji Monastery, in the fourth month, the Governor of Jiazhou reported that a great tree had been broken by the wind and that a monk was in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The Emperor ordered him to be sent to the capital.

*Pipi* (Pǔdēng). In the first year of the Xuānhuá era, the Emperor was deluded by the teachings of Lín Língsù.

"These are all precedents that can be observed. Why does Your Majesty tread upon the calamities of wicked rulers and contravene the laws of the Founding Ancestors?

When that month’s provisions were spent, the monk ordered him to stay in a corridor room, where he could eat the monks' rice and gruel. Thus, he was able to settle his mind and study, eventually gaining a recommendation for office. The monk further provided him with travel expenses.
He was sent away, yet he ultimately emerged as a leader among scholars. Later, while serving in office for ten years, he did not request his stipend for the imperial sacrifices.

When the Emperor asked him the reason, he replied that his private debt of gratitude had not yet been repaid. The Emperor questioned him further, and he answered truthfully. The Emperor said, "Is there such a person among the monks?
He then granted the monk's stipend to the temple where he resided to repay his long-standing virtue. The Master used to rise at dawn to pay homage to the Buddha.

The prayer said: "May those who do not believe in the Triple Gem not be born into my family. May my descendants, generation after generation, enjoy official emoluments and protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Gong’s nephew, Yi-jian, and Jian’s son, Gong-zhu, were both enfeoffed as Dukes of Shen; both were known for their deep reverence for the Buddha-dharma.
While Gong served in the government, he burned incense and submitted a petition requesting that Yan perform a *Lotus Sūtra* vegetarian feast. On the following day, Yan arrived and sat in Gong’s hall.
The Duke was about to depart. He wondered whether he should bow or not. Yan shouted out, "Old man Lü, come out quickly! Whether you bow or do not bow, it matters not.
The Duke was greatly startled and hurriedly went out to bow to him. When the fast was over, the Duke asked about future fortunes and misfortunes.

Yan took up his brush and wrote the two characters for "Bozhou" (Mozhou). Later, when the Duke resigned from the相位 (prime ministerial position), he became the Governor of Bozhou; only then did he realize the significance of the previous prophecy.
(Wuku). Wang Dan, courtesy name Ziming, was a native of Xin in Daming.
He served as Chancellor to Emperor Zhenzong and was posthumously titled Wenzheng. In the second year of the Chunhua era, Hang...

The monk Xingchang of Zhaoqing Temple in the prefecture drew blood to transcribe the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and established a society for the cultivation of pure karma, serving as its leader.

With the participation of one hundred and thirty-two people, including the Councilor Su Yi and Jian, the literati of the time all styled themselves disciples of the Pure Conduct Society (*Jingxing She*).
Over a thousand bhikṣus joined; some have remarked that this was not inferior to the Lotus Society (*Lian She*) of Mount Lu.

Such was the splendor of that day. On the first day of the ninth month in the first year of the Tianxi era, he passed away. One day prior, he entrusted his wishes to Yang Yi of the Hanlin Academy, saying:
"I am deeply weary of this toilsome life. I wish to become a monk in a future existence, finding joy in sitting in meditation within the forest and contemplating the mind.
I pray that after my death, you will request a virtuous master to bestow the precepts upon me, shave my hair and beard, clothe me in the three robes, and cremate my body."
"Do not place gold or jewels within the coffin. Yi made a proposal for the sake of the orphans, saying: "The Duke was one of the Three Dukes.

To enshroud and present him with the ceremonial *gong* robe—how could this be added to the body of a monk? One should simply place the three monastic robes (*tricīvara*) within the hearse; do not conceal precious gems therein. (From the *Xiangshan Yeshu*)

Yang Yi, courtesy name Dayan, was a native of Pucheng in Jianzhou. During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong, he was appointed as a Court Counselor (Zhengyan) and subsequently promoted to Director of the Chancellery (Zhizhi). He was posthumously honored with the title Wen Gong.

At the beginning of the Jingde era, the śramaṇa Daoyuan presented the thirty-fascicle *Chanzong chuan deng lu* (The Transmission of the Lamp of the Chan School), and by imperial decree, Yang Yi was commissioned to edit it.
It was formally promulgated. Yi composed the preface. He once recounted the origins of his spiritual lineage, saying:

"Since the shadow of the Twin Trees faded and the single sandalwood slipper returned to the West, my inner mind has been vast and desolate, knowing not where to turn for guidance. First, I was fortunate enough to receive the constant instruction and guidance of the Great Master Master An;
furthermore, I attained the essential purport of Master Yunmen Liang, whose approach was precisely on the same track as that of Master An. Both [masters] returned from Mount Lu."

Those who have come from Yunju Monastery are all descendants of Fayan. Last year, while serving as the acting governor of this prefecture, I happened to meet Master Guanghui Lián, who was indeed the successor of Nan’uan Nian.
With my monastic duties being simple, I had much leisure after retiring from meals.

Sometimes he would come at my invitation, and sometimes I would send a carriage to follow him; I questioned him in various ways, and all my lingering doubts were resolved. After half a year, [my mind became] expansive...
Yet he did not doubt it. It was as if forgetting and suddenly remembering, as if sleeping and suddenly waking. The matter that had long obstructed his chest fell away with a sudden crash;
the truths unclarified for kalpas of accumulation appeared before him in vast clarity. Thus, his discernment was thoroughly penetrating, and his engagement with others was unhindered.
Now, the karmic conditions for succession truly belong to Guanghui, while the inspiration and stimulation come from Liang.
He emerged from Mount Ao. Yibei’s verse on his deathbed says: "The arising of a bubble and its extinction—these two dharmas are fundamentally equal.

If you wish to know the true destination, look to the east or west of Zhaozhou’s courtyard. (From the *Sengbao zhuan* and its commentary by Jianshi). Yibei composed a preface to the *Qinggui*, which states in brief:
"The Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang [held that] since the Chan school originated at Shaoshi and continued through Caoxi, it had for the most part resided within the Vinaya..."

Although the temple was arranged with separate quarters, it did not conform to the proper regulations for the propagation of the Dharma and the maintenance of the lineage. Consequently, a separate Zen residence was established.
Those who possessed the eye of the Way and were endowed with venerable virtue were titled "Elders" (*chōrō*) and resided in the *bōjō* (abbot’s quarters), which resembled the chamber of Vimalakīrti.
No Buddha Hall was constructed; instead, only a Dharma Hall (*hōdō*) was erected to signify that the Buddhas and Patriarchs had personally transmitted their entrustment there.
The Abbot represents the honored position. The assembled students, regardless of their number or seniority, all enter the Sangha Hall.

Long benches are arranged, and racks and stands are provided for hanging up bedding and requisites. When lying down, one must lean against the edge of the bed with the right side down, sleeping in the auspicious posture.

Because he has sat in meditation for a long time, he merely reclines to rest; this is the fulfillment of the four modes of deportment. The entire assembly of the monastery gathers in the morning and evening for the formal attendance.
When the Elder ascends the hall and takes his seat, the monastic community of the temple stands in a line like geese to listen closely.

As the host and guest exchange questions and answers to stimulate and clarify the essentials of the school, it demonstrates dwelling in accordance with the Dharma. At both times of the midday and evening meals, the distribution is equal and universal, signifying...
This is the simultaneous practice of both Dharma and sustenance (*dharmāhāra*). When performing communal labor (*pǔqǐng*), strength must be shared equally by those above and below.

Should there be those who assume false names or disguise their true forms to mingle with the pure assembly, thereby causing disturbances, they shall be expelled from the monastery; this is to ensure the peace and stability of the pure assembly.

Should anyone commit an offense, they shall immediately be struck with a staff. Their robes, bowls, and ritual implements shall be gathered and burned, and they shall be driven out through a side gate.
As for those who leave [the community], it is to demonstrate their shame: first, they do not defile the pure assembly; second, they do not destroy the outward form of a monk;
third, they do not disturb the public offices; and fourth, they do not leak [secrets] to the outside. When four such people live together, who among the holy and the ordinary can distinguish them?

Furthermore, even when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, there were still groups like the Six Heretics; how much more so in this age of the Semblance Dharma—how could they be entirely absent? It is simply that when one sees a single monk with transgressions...
They immediately used thunderous examples to mock and deride [the rules], failing to realize that slighting the assembly and destroying the Dharma causes far greater harm.

Furthermore, the establishment of laws to prevent misconduct is not intended for the virtuous; rather, it is better to have regulations that remain unviolated than to have violations for which there are no teachings.
How great indeed was the benefit of Great Wisdom Chan Master’s protection of the Dharma!

Lü Yijian—his courtesy name was Tantfu—was originally from Lai Prefecture and later moved to Shou Prefecture. During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he attained the highest office. In... [text continues]
He served as Grand Secretary. In the twentieth year [of the reign], he was enfeoffed as Duke of Xu and posthumously granted the title Wenjing (Wen-ting).

He once received an imperial decree to continue the compilation of the *Fǎbǎolù* (Record of the Precious Dharma) together with Song Sou; from the fourth year of Xiángfú to the third year of Jǐngyòu, they compiled it into one hundred and sixty-one fascicles.
Imperial Preface: Fan Zhongyan, styled Xiwen, was a native of Runan.
During the Qingli era, he participated in the administration of great affairs. His posthumous title was Wenzheng. At the beginning of the Qingli era...

While serving as Pacification Commissioner of Hedong, I stayed overnight at the Baode Post Station and obtained an ancient scroll consisting of one fascicle titled *Verses on the Causality and Realization of the Sixteen Arhats*.
It was not recorded in the Tripitaka. Zhongyan composed a preface for it;

this collection contains seven verses for each of the venerable ones, all of which are words concerning awakening to the source and attaining Buddhahood. As I read them, each verse brought a distinct realization. Just as...
He knew that there were boundless holy teachings within the mundane world, yet the texts of the Great Treasury had been lost.

Consequently, he transmitted them to the śramaṇa Hui-zhe of Jiangling, so that they might circulate in the world (according to the Zheng Family Collection). While the Master was governing Wu, Chan Master Langye Jue came to visit him.

He remained for several days. Under the Master’s words, he realized his true home. He offered this verse to the Master: "Throughout these consecutive mornings we have conversed, dissolving the knot of doubt;

How could this be merely half a day’s leisure in this floating life? I wish to remain with you, Master, until we grow old together, Completely gathering the nature of consciousness to enter the Mysterious Barrier. (Cited from *Zijian*)
I once met with the layman Zeng Hui, who had been my fellow resident with Mingjue since childhood;

though we followed different paths after reaching adulthood, in the Tianxi era, when the official was serving as the governor of Chizhou, we happened to meet one day at Jingde Temple. Thereupon, he cited the *Zhongyong* and the *Daxue*, interweaving them with the *Lengyan Sutra*.
Yanfu tested Zongmen’s words for their substance and clarity. Zongmen said, "This [matter] does not even accord with the teachings of the scriptures, let alone the *Zhongyong* or the *Daxue*.
Scholar, you must understand this matter through a direct and swift path. Thereupon, he snapped his fingers once and said:

"Simply realize it in this way. Under these words, the Official (Gong) attained realization of the ultimate meaning. At the beginning of the Tiānshèng era, while the Official was governing Sìmíng, he sent envoys with gifts to welcome the Master to serve at Xuědòu.
In the preface to the *Yùlù* (Recorded Sayings), he wrote: "Now, in pointing toward the wondrous luminosity of Bodhi, one relies on the expedient means of verbal expression.

Yet, in establishing schools and distinguishing patriarchs, there has often been strife over victory and defeat; by clinging to forms and stagnating in names, few have achieved accord with the truth."
The principle of perfect permanence (*yuan-chang*) (etc., from the *Wudeng Huiyuan*). Li Han was styled Taichu.

At the beginning of the Xianping era, he was appointed as Chancellor and posthumously honored with the title Wenjing. He had a profound mastery of the Buddhist scriptures and particularly detested worldly glory and profit.
He had once spoken of matters concerning earthworks, timber, and military affairs, all of which were later proven true. Wang Dan sighed and said, "Li Wenjing is truly a sage.
His family members advised him to repair their residence, as it was cramped and dilapidated. The Duke replied, "I receive a generous salary and am occasionally granted extraordinary gifts;

by my own calculation, I could certainly afford to have it renovated. However, I reflect upon the Buddhist scriptures, which describe this world as being full of defects and imperfections. How can I..."
Did he attain the fulfillment of his wishes and achieve contentment through his own seeking? At the end of his life, he passed away lying on his right side.
During the height of summer, his corpse was kept for seven days, yet there was no foul odor within the chamber; people said this was proof of his spiritual practice (from the *Mingchen Yanxing Lu*).
Ding Wei, courtesy name Gongyan, passed the imperial examinations during the reign of Emperor Taizong and later served as Chancellor under Emperor Zhenzong; he was enfeoffed as Duke of Jin.

A Hangzhou monk named Shengchang established a "Society for Pure Conduct" with high officials and scholars. Duke Wei composed a poem which said: "Having already attained awakening, what need is there to rely on the water?"
Yun: "While it has not yet ceased, it is ultimately for the sake of profit and fame. I, this humble one, coldly laugh at Tao Pengze, who instead became an outsider to the Lotus Society.
(Zi Jian) There is a memorial for the offering of food to the Sangha, which states briefly: "The Buddha bestowed universal knowledge to nurture all living beings.

Whenever there is a desire to rescue those in peril, one must first manifest auspicious responses. I, a layman seeking official emolument, have received the heavy authority of the Minister of the Interior."
Proclaiming grace upon the vermilion steps, I have been graced by the abundant favor of the late Sovereign. In mending the robes of Zhongshan, I have exhausted my skillful artistry;
yet in blending the soup of Chuan-shuo, it is difficult to satisfy all palates. Only now do I realize that wealth and honor are difficult to preserve from beginning to end.

Even the glory of feasting from tripods cannot compare to the excellence of a simple bowl of soup. Thus, manifesting my submission and reverently giving rise to sincere devotion, I piously offer this white metal.

I have diligently prepared pure offerings to provide meals for monks of high virtue and to repay the profound compassion of Lan Zan. I pray that you may preserve this practice and remain free from ailment.

I humbly beseech that Heaven turn its southern gaze and bestow its grace upon us below, sparing us from being relegated to the barbarian frontiers where our days would be no different from those in the realm of ghosts.
May we be granted a return to the Central Kingdom, so that even in the Yellow Springs we may once again feel the grace of Heaven. With utmost sincerity, I offer this prayer.
Yongyi Fali (from *Yunwo Jitan*). Wang Suishui was a native of Heyang.
He served as a Grand Master of Ceremonies under Emperor Renzong and was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke Zhanghui. Admiring the character of Pei Xiu, he served as Censor-in-Chief.
When the Vice Minister was appointed as regional governor of Qiandang, he went to Xingjiao Temple to pay his respects to Chan Master Xiaoshou.

Their dialogue reached a point of perfect resonance, and they became friends beyond the secular world. Having previously visited Chan Master Shoushan Nian and attained the meaning that lies beyond words, his practice from then on grew ever more profound until he ultimately clarified the Great Dharma.
Together with Yang Dainian, both were renowned as those who had achieved realization through Zen meditation. Previously, this was...

He compiled the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) in thirty fascicles, subsequently deleting its redundancies to produce fifteen fascicles titled the *Yu ying ji* (Collection of Jade Blossoms), for which Hu Zhitang wrote a preface.
At the time of his death, he inscribed a verse: "The lamp in the painted hall has already been extinguished;
To whom can I point my finger and speak? Departing and staying are fundamentally ordinary; The spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow. (*Dong du shi lüe* and *Pu deng lu*)

Lu Gongzhu (呂公著), courtesy name Huishu (晦叔), was the son of Yi Jian (夷簡). During the Xining era, he was appointed as the Governor of Henan. During the Yuanyou era, he served as Chancellor alongside Wen Gong (Sima Guang).
He served four successive emperors, was posthumously titled Duke of Shen, and received the sobriquet Zhengxian (正獻). In his later years, he frequently read Buddhist scriptures.

Dian further investigated the principles of Chan Buddhism. Although Lord Wen did not favor Buddhism, Dian repeatedly exhorted him, saying: "The Buddhist teachings are concise and essential in their core methods.
If one extracts these supreme essentials and understands them, they generally take the rectification of the mind and the absence of discursive thought as their fundamental principle.
Lord Wen agreed with this (from the *Yanshi Jiaxun Yanyong Lu*).

Wang Anshi, styled Jiefu, was a native of Linchuan. During the Xining era, he was appointed as Chancellor and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jing. Later, having resigned from the chancellorship, he returned to Jiankang.
He petitioned to donate his former residence for the establishment of a Chan monastery and requested the śramaṇa Kewen to serve as its abbot. By imperial decree, the temple was granted the name:
Baoning was granted the honorary title of Zhenjing. The Master once attended upon Wenzu, who said to him:
"In your daily life, exert yourself in what is right; if it is not so, firmly cease from it. You should not allow your resolve to waver because of ease or difficulty.
If you now shake your head and turn away because of present hardships, how do you know that tomorrow will not be as difficult as today? (From the *Baotrun*). The Master then questioned Zhang.
Fangping said, "A hundred years after Confucius passed away, Mencius was born; thereafter, there has been no one [of such caliber].

Even if there were some, they would not be pure scholars. Fangping replied, "How could it be that there is no one? There have even been those who surpassed Confucius and Mencius. The Duke asked, "Who were they?"

Fangping said, "Mazu Daoyi, Yangshan Huiji, Guishan Lingyou, Xuefeng Yicun, Yantou Quanhuo, Danxia Tianran, and Yunmen Wenyan. The Duke’s meaning remained unresolved. Fangping said, "The Confucian gate is thin and flavorless; it cannot hold them back, and they all return to the school of Śākyamuni. The Duke sighed with joyful admiration.

Later, he spoke of this to Zhang Shangying, who struck the table in appreciation and said: [The rest of Zhang Shangying's response follows: "Excellent! This is truly the 'Great Matter' (大事). It is not something that can be grasped through mere intellectual understanding. It is like a person who has lost their way in a vast wilderness;

even if they have a map and a guide, they will not find their destination until they actually reach it themselves. Only when one has personally realized it within oneself does one know its true nature. This is why the ancients said, 'If you wish to see the Buddha, look at your own mind. This is indeed the ultimate teaching."

How profound is this discourse! (From the *Wuku*). During the Xining era, when the public was implementing the Green Sprouts Law, his son Pang served as an Expositor at the Chongzheng Hall, secretly assisting his father in ensuring the new laws were strictly enforced.
Upon Pang’s death, the Duke also resigned from the相位 (Prime Ministership). Amidst his leisure and seclusion, it was as if he were in a dream:
he saw an official leading Pang, who bore an iron cangue and wailed before him, saying that he had incurred divine retribution.

Because Liu You practiced the "Green Sprouts" (Qingmiao) method, he petitioned the messenger for liberation from its consequences. The messenger said, "If you build a monastery and provide a vegetarian feast for the monks, you may be exempted.
Consequently, he donated his residence to establish a monastery to dedicate merit for the deceased (from the *Yanshi Jianguo Yulu*).

In the eighth year of the Xining era, when the Duke was once again Prime Minister, one day after the audience concluded, the Emperor asked, "Is Buddhism beneficial to the Middle Kingdom? The Duke replied, "Between the noble man and the petty man..."
All knew to fear [evil] and follow what was good; how could this be anything less than a small but vital remedy?
(From the *Biannian*).

Sima Guang, whose courtesy name was Junshi, was a native of Xia County in Shan Prefecture. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he was appointed as Chancellor. He was posthumously granted the title of Taishi and enfeoffed as the Duke of Wen.

He was posthumously honored with the title Wenzheng (Literary Rectitude) and styled Shu-shui Xiansheng (Master of the Su Water). He once composed a verse on the interpretation of Chan, the preface of which states:
"Wen Zhongzi regarded the Buddha as a sage of the West. If Wen Zhongzi’s words are indeed true, then the mind of the Buddha may be known."

Those who speak of Chan today delight in using obscure language to bewilder one another and employ grandiose claims to outshine others, leaving students wandering aimlessly and further sinking into delusion.
Therefore, I have expanded upon the words of Wénzhōngzi to explain them, composing six verses on Chan.
If this is indeed the case, then it may even be practiced within the Middle Kingdom. The first says: "Wrathful anger is like..."
Fierce flames; sharp desires are like keen blades. Constantly filled with grief throughout the day—this is called the Avīci Hell. The second says: Yán Huí found peace in the humble alley;
Mèng Kē nurtured the *hàorán* (vast and courageous spirit). Wealth and honor were like floating clouds—this is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The third says: Filial piety reaches the spiritual intelligences; loyalty and trustworthiness extend even to the barbarian borders. When one accumulates goodness, a hundred auspicious signs arrive;

this is called the law of cause and effect. The fourth says: One’s words serve as a teacher for a hundred generations; one’s conduct serves as a model for the world. Over time, these cannot be obscured;
this is called the indestructible body. The fifth says: Benevolence is the secure dwelling of the humane person; righteousness is the straight path of the righteous person. To practice...

His sincerity has been thus for a long time; this is called the Treasury of Radiance (*Prabhāsa-garbha*). The sixth [verse] says: "Cultivating the mind of the Way within a single body, its merit covers all things;
becoming a worthy one or a Great Sage—this is called a Buddha or a Bodhisattva. You once transcribed the *Heart Sūtra* to present as a gift to a monk.

I further inscribed the following at the end, stating briefly: "Tuan-chi (Han Yu) rejected Buddhism, yet he praised Da-dian for transcending the physical body and overcoming himself through principle.
This must have been because his own mind was free from obstructions. Viewed from this perspective, Da-dian did not fail to attain anything regarding the Buddha;
what Tuan-chi rejected were merely the outward traces."
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Ten, Revised by the Tiantai Monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Eleven,
Compiled by the Shamen Xintai of Kuaiji.
Tiantai śramaṇa Zhenqing read this biography of Ouyang Xiu. His courtesy name was Yongshu.
A native of Yongfeng in Jizhou, he participated in the administration of high state affairs at the beginning of the Jiayou era, serving as Grand Master of the Crown Prince (Taizi Shaoshi).
He retired from office and was posthumously granted the title Wenzhong (Loyal and Virtuous). In his later years, he chose to reside in Ying and styled himself the "Six-One Recluse" (Liuyi Jushi).

Having been appointed as the Commissioner for the Transport of Hebei from the Censorate, he was demoted to the post of Governor of Chuzhou. The following year, he returned to Luling; while his boat was moored at Jiujiang, he passed away.
While traveling to Mount Lu, Zongxiao entered Donglin Yuan Tong Temple to pay his respects to Chan Master Juren Nengzhuo.

When Zongxiao first arrived, Nengzhuo gestured for him to take a seat, and they engaged in philosophical discussion. Zongxiao admired Han Yu’s polemical writings that sought to exclude Buddhism and Laoism;
Nengzhuo therefore said to him, "Han Yu took the refutation of Buddhism as his merit, comparing himself to Mencius in his opposition to Yang Zhu and Mo Di. This was merely his desire for victory."
The extreme nature of these names is such that when Tuōzhī (Han Yu) denounced the Buddha as a "barbarian ghost" (*yígǔi*), I beg to briefly examine this.

The Buddha is a sage who descended from Tuṣita Heaven and took birth in the family of a holy wheel-turning monarch in the Central Kingdom. How can he be called a "barbarian"? The Buddha is neither born nor extinguished;
he has existed eternally through vast kalpas, revered by humans and devas. How can he be called a "ghost"? These are not the words of one free from great arrogance.
Indeed. Tuizhi’s seventh-generation ancestor was named Qidang. During the Yongxing era of the Later Wei, he came from the Xiongnu Helian Chuqie to surrender to the Tabgach (Tuoba) clan;
thus, he went from the Western Rong tribes to the Northern Di tribes. Yet Tuizhi alone does not observe the taboo of his ancestor’s name, and how dare he slander the Buddha, the Sage?
Tuizhi fears the calamity of praise or censure in historical compilation, yet he fails to realize that slandering the Buddha [is a greater offense].
To go further is even more fearsome. You have taken up the challenge of refuting Buddhism and Daoism that Master Tu (Han Yu) initiated, and you now join him in harmony with it.
This will cause future scholars who prize their reputation to take the houses of Han and Ouyang as their model;

will this not be a blemish upon your great virtue? There is a proverb that says: "He who excels at reviling others will himself be reviled in turn. You have composed the *Benlun* (Treatise on the Origin), laboring with tireless diligence to...
"Defaming the Buddha has become their primary occupation. How could they fail to defame you with a chorus of voices before the Heavenly Hearing?

Your words—claiming that the rites of hunting, mourning, ancestral sacrifices, and village altars constitute the very foundation that surpasses Buddhism—are like Han Yu’s *Yuan Dao* (On the Origin of the Way), which in truth does not yet understand the Way.
Xu Xiu replied with alarm and shame, saying: "The doubts within my breast have now been resolved."
"What instruction will the Master provide? Nan said, "The Way of the Buddha takes the awakening of the mind as its foundation. You have realized the Way throughout many lifetimes;
you were specifically born in Donghua as a renowned Confucian scholar because you failed to maintain mindfulness. Because you were biased toward worldly teachings, you forgot your original nature.

Truly, if you apply a mind that regards the holy and the ordinary as equal, silently embodying this realization, you will suddenly cast off your pride and repent for all your past errors. He then observed:

When the root of honor and disgrace is seen as empty and birth and death are realized as being of one essence, then pure mindfulness will be ever-luminous and the true nature will be uniquely revealed;

only then can one inquire into this Way. From that time on, Xiu experienced awakening, and when he participated in high government affairs, he frequently praised [Fayan] Ne before the ministers and officials.

His letters and inquiries were never interrupted throughout the year (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks Outside the Canon*). Han Qi honored him with the title "Mingjiao" (Enlightened Teaching).

Chan Master Song presented his *Fujiao bian* (Compilation for Assisting the Teaching) to Lord Gao. Upon reading the text, Lord Gao said to Lord Han, "I did not expect to find such a person among the monks;
I shall go to meet him at dawn. Lord Han accompanied the Master to see him. Lord Gao conversed with him all day long and was greatly delighted (*Preface to the Hujiao bian*).
Previously, when Lord Gao was serving as an official in Luoyang, he visited Mount Song. He dismissed his attendants and officials and went forth, letting his mind roam freely.
He arrived at a temple where tall bamboos filled the courtyard and the scenery was fresh and bright. The official rested beside the steps of the hall;
there was an old monk reading a sutra with composure, who did not look up or respond much when spoken to. The official found this strange and asked, "Have you lived on this mountain for long?

The monk replied, "For a very long time. He further asked, "What sutra are you reciting? The monk said, "The Lotus Sutra. The official remarked, "In ancient times, when eminent monks faced the threshold of life and death..."
"In every case, they depart with laughter and ease. What path leads them to this? He replied, "It is simply the power of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).

He asked again, "Why is it that nowadays there is such silence and emptiness [of such occurrences]? The old monk laughed and said, "The ancients were in concentration and wisdom at every thought-moment;

how could they have been distracted at the moment of death? People today are in distraction at every thought-moment; how could they attain concentration at the moment of death? The official sighed in great admiration. (From the *Ziji*).
In the intercalary eighth month of the sixth year of the Jiayou era, the Master served as a State Councilor and concurrently as the Commissioner for Translating and Polishing Buddhist Scriptures.

Having ascended to the two central ministries, he suffered from frequent illness. He once dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where ten men, wearing ceremonial caps and robes, were seated in a circle.

One man said, "State Councilor, how have you come to this? You ought to return to your residence at once. The Master took several steps toward the gate and went back to question them, saying, "Are you not..."

"Is this what the Śākyas call the 'Ten Kings'? He replied, "Yes. He then asked, "When people of the world provide meals for the monastic community and recite scriptures to cultivate merit for the deceased, is there truly any benefit?
He replied, "How could there not be benefit? Once he awoke from his dream, his illness had already vanished.
From that time on, he came to have deep faith in the Buddha-dharma. Ge Shengzhong of Danyang obtained this account from Jianzai Chen Yuyi; Yuyi obtained it from [Dongpo].

The Duke’s grandson, Shu, clearly understood this (as recorded in Ou Gong’s biography and the *Yunyu Yangqiu*). While residing in Yingzhou, the Duke renounced wine and meat, set aside sounds and sights, and sat in silent meditation with his mind extinguished.
He ordered an old soldier to go to a nearby temple to borrow the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

having recited it to the eighth fascicle, he passed away (this account comes from Wang Xingzhi’s words—his name was Zhi, a native of Ruyin; because his father had studied under the Duke, he obtained the facts).

Zhao Bian, courtesy name Yuedao, was a native of Xian’an, Quzhou. He styled himself Zhifei Zi (The One Who Knows His Faults). Serving as a Censor-in-Chief, he prosecuted and impeached officials without avoiding those of noble rank or power;
thus, the capital dubbed him the "Iron-Faced Censor. He rose to the rank of State Councilor and was posthumously honored with the title Qingxian (Pure Contribution). At first...
He studied under Chan Master Faquan of Mount Jiangshan and attained a realization. He then went to Chan Master Chongyuan of Tianbo Monastery in Daming to inquire about the essentials of the mind.

The Master said, "You stand at court to deliberate on state affairs, honoring the transformative teachings and clarifying the relations between ruler and subject; how do you have leisure to devote yourself so intently to this?
The Master replied, "I have heard that the principle of the separate transmission is something inherently possessed by every person; how could others possess it while I, Wenbian, do not?"
"Can you? I wish for you to investigate and clarify this. The Master then instructed him to contemplate the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
Later, while at Qingzhou, as he sat leaning on his armrest in the public hall, he heard the sound of thunder and attained a sudden, great realization. He composed a verse, which says:

Sitting in silence in the public hall, leaning idly upon my armrest, The source of the mind is unmoving, as still as water. A single clap of thunder opens the aperture at the crown of my head, Awakening me to what was there from the beginning.

Regarding his family background: when the Duke led his forces into Yue, a severe drought and a great epidemic occurred; despite long prayers, no response was received. At that time, Dharma Master Shen Zhisheng resided at Xingfu Temple.
The Duke invited the Master to escort a statue of Avalokiteśvara into the provincial administration seat. After he prayed earnestly for one night, rain fell like pouring water.
The epidemic also subsided. The Duke memorialized the court, and the Emperor granted the temple where the Master resided, Xingfu, the name Yuantong and bestowed upon him the title Shenzhi.
At the beginning of the Yuanfeng era, he retired from public life to reside in Quzhou. He frequently associated with mountain monks and rural elders.
In the eighth month of the seventh year, a great star fell in his courtyard; the Duke conversed with his son Ji as if all were normal, then suddenly sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
(Stele for the Divine Way and the Universal Lamp).

Xia Song, courtesy name Ziqiao, was appointed Vice Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs during the Huangyou era. He was enfeoffed as Duke of Zheng and posthumously honored with the title Ying Gong. This Duke...
During his tenure at the Hanlin Academy, he, together with Tripiṭaka Master Weijing, presented the *Xinying jing yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of Newly Translated Scriptures) in seventy fascicles.
Having attained awakening through a karmic trigger during a conversation with Chan Master Cong of Guyin, he once asked Chan Master Shanglan Pu:
"When the hundred limbs fall apart and scatter, which among them is the Elder’s own self? Pu replied, "I left Qiyang on the twentieth day of last month. Pu then...
The questioner asked, "Which one is the Master's own? The Master replied with a verse: "Do not mistake the foremost function before the wind;
where in the great void can thought be placed? If this mountain monk wishes to convey the message, it is when the moon rises over ten thousand miles of cloudless sky. (Pudeng)

Zhang Fangping, styled Andao, was a native of Songcheng. At the beginning of the Xīníng era, he participated in high-level governance and was posthumously honored with the title Wéndìng. Once, while serving in Zhōuzhōu, he happened upon a copy of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* at a monastery;
as soon as it fell into his hands, he felt a sudden sense of recognition, as if recovering a long-lost possession. Upon opening the scroll...

Before he had finished [the copy], his karmic obstructions were cleared away like ice melting. Upon examining the calligraphy closely, the traces of his own hand appeared vividly. From this, he attained realization.
He once used the four opening verses of the sutra to elucidate the essential point of the mind. Su Shi wrote a preface for the end of the scripture (*Lengqie jing xu*).

Zeng Gongliang, courtesy name Mingzhong, was a native of Jinjiang County in Quanzhou. During the Jiayou era, he was appointed as Chancellor. He retired from office with the rank of Taifu and was posthumously honored with the title Xianjing and the fief of Lord of Lu.
Once, while on leave to observe the mourning period for his mother, he returned home; a local monk named Yuanda boarded his boat and arrived [with him].

In Qiandao, he entered Tianzhu Temple to pay homage to the Great Being (Mahāsattva). Upon entering the gate, he saw a woman dressed in plain white who said to him, "The former Minister Zeng will enter the Zhongshu Secretariat at the age of fifty-seven;
you, Elder, shall likewise receive the title of Master in that same year. After she had spoken, she vanished. When Gongliang reached the age of fifty-seven, he indeed was appointed as Chancellor.
Yuan Da was subsequently granted the rank of Grand Master in recognition of his debt of gratitude to the late Minister Zeng. Initially, there was a monk named Qing...
Cao Tang was over ninety years old when Lady Zeng entered the temple to offer a vegetarian feast and bestowed clothing and other items as alms upon him.

Qing was moved by her intention; when the lady gave birth to a son, Qing sat in meditation and passed away. Thus we know that Gongliang’s previous incarnation was the monk Cao Tang (from the *Tongji*).

Wen Yanbo, courtesy name Kuānfú, was a native of Jiexiu in Fenzhou. He served throughout four successive reigns. Emperor Zhezong appointed him as Grand Preceptor (Taishi) and granted him leave from office;
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lù and posthumously honored with the title Zhōngliè. While serving as the Governor of Luoyang, he once observed a fast and proceeded to Long’an Temple.
While paying homage to a sacred image, he suddenly saw it break and fall to the ground. Without showing even the slightest sign of reverence, he merely looked at it and departed.
A monk nearby asked, "Why did you not prostrate? The official replied, "Since the image is already broken, with what shall I prostrate?

The monk said, "It is like a mound of earth by a public road that people dig up to fashion into an image. The wise know it is but earth; ordinary people say the image has come to life. The image—[is but earth].
"Fundamentally, there is neither birth nor extinction; the path likewise has neither newness nor antiquity. Upon hearing this, the Duke attained a realization.

From then on, he pursued the Way with great vigor, single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha and vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land. He burned incense at dawn and sat in meditation at night, never slackening for even a moment.
He made this aspiration daily: "May I always be diligent and assiduously cultivate all virtues; may I realize the essence of the mind and extensively deliver all sentient beings."
Whenever he encountered anyone, he would exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name, vowing to establish a karmic connection with one hundred thousand people to be reborn together in the Pure Land.
The layman Chen Ruru praised him, saying: "I know your spirit and bearing are as vast as heaven; you vow to establish a connection with one hundred thousand for the West.
You do not seek a livelihood for yourself alone; everyone shall board the ferry at the riverhead together. The Duke served as a Minister of State.
At that time, Master Yuan was residing at Tianbo Temple in the prefectures of Zhen and Wei. One day, he took his leave. The Duke said, "The Master is advanced in years; where will you go now?
The Master replied, "I am going to enter parinirvāṇa. The Duke said to his son, Jiafu: "Master Yuan’s Way and tone are profound and subtle;
his speech and laughter possess true flavor. He is no ordinary monk. Go to visit him. When [Jiafu] went, the Master had indeed already passed away while seated in meditation (from the *Baoguan*).
Su Xun, courtesy name Mingyun, styled Laquan, was a native of Meishan. Initially, he failed in the jinshi examinations.

Upon reaching Xunyang, he ascended Mount Lu to pay his respects to Chan Master Ne and inquire about the Dharma; there he attained its essential meaning. During the Jiayou era, Ouyang Xiu submitted his writings to the throne.

He presented twenty-two essays, including the *Zhiquan* and the *Shulunheng*, at court. He was summoned for an examination at the Sheyuan (Academy of Secretaries) and appointed as a School-Book Official (*Jiaoshu lang*).
He once composed the "Record of the Yuanjue Monastery in Pengzhou," which states in part: "When a person dwells in a place, they must find joy therein.
To dwell there without finding joy, yet not leave because one finds no joy—this is a mind that cannot even govern itself."
How much less could one possibly govern others? Since the Tang dynasty, scholars and officials have vied with one another to speak in opposition to Buddhism and Daoism.
Consequently, those among their followers who sought knowledge within our ranks of scholars often betrayed their own masters in order to seek admission among us;
and we, for our part, welcomed their arrival and received them with courtesy.
Lingche, Wenchang, and their like have cut themselves off from their own teachings. Alas! Return to your parents and restore your household;

only then will I permit you to rebel against your master. That a son does not return to his father, that a wife does not return to her home, and yet rebels against one’s master—all such things cannot stand for even a single day in the world. While I was in the capital...
Master Pengzhou Sengbao Cong sought my acquaintance with great diligence. Upon arriving in Shu, I heard that he had returned from the capital;
for many years he had lived as a simple layman, subsisting on vegetarian food to set an example for his disciples. Consequently, the Yuanjue Monastery where he resided flourished greatly.
One day, he recounted to me the deeds of his former master and the reason why the monastery was given its name.
I request that you compose a record for this. I admire Yongcong for not having betrayed his teacher; therefore, I write this record, saying:

The monk Pingrun of Longxing Temple in Pengzhou lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-śāstra* (The Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra), and thus the temple was named after him. Originally, the temple was dilapidated and had not been repaired.
When Zhun arrived, he first obtained a small plot of vacant land to construct halls and buildings.

After two successive monks had passed away, it reached the time of Cóng, who consolidated several neighboring monastic dwellings into this monastery to complete the project. This is the record (from his collected works).

Zhou Dunyi, courtesy name Maoshu, style name Lianxi, was a native of Chongling. During the Xining era, he was appointed as a Circuit Intendant for Judicial Review (Ticheng). He was posthumously honored with the title Duke Yuan.
There was a stream in Chongling called Lianxi; therefore, he took Lianxi as his style name. Later, he resided at Mount Lu, where he delighted in its secluded beauty and built a dwelling there.
He also named his study after the creek, "Lian," so as not to forget its origin. At that time, Foyin was residing at Luanchi. The Duke went to visit him, and they discussed the Way together.
The Duke asked: "The *Zhongyong* says, 'What Heaven mandates is called nature; following nature is called the Way. Yet in the Chan school, it is said that 'no-mind is the Way.
What does this mean? The Master replied: "If you have doubts, seek another teacher. The Duke said: "Seeking another is certainly not impossible, but ultimately, what constitutes [the Way]?"
The Master said, "The green mountains fill the eyes; look as you please. Thereupon, the monk attained realization.

One day, suddenly seeing weeds growing before the window, he remarked, "This is exactly the same as my own state of mind. He presented this to the Master in verse: "Originally there was no delusion, now there is no awakening;
Through the fusion of object and subject, the hidden depths are revealed. Weeds grow deep outside the window, pines stand by the path; All day long they cause people to ponder."
"One never tires of looking upon it. The Master replied, "The substance of the Great Way is vast and all-pervading; why restrict it to the moving and the planted, the flying and the hidden?
Walking, observing, sitting, and contemplating, there is no obstruction; yet when one seeks it through form and sound, the mind itself becomes weary.

Thereupon, he appointed the Master as the head of the Qing Song (Green Pine) Society, following the precedent of the White Lotus Society (*Zi Jian*). The Master transmitted the *Taiji Tu* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate) to Mu Xiu, who in turn transmitted it...
From Zhong Fang; Fang transmitted it to Chen Tuan. This is one of its teachers. Indeed, Chen Tuan was the teacher of Māyī (Máī).
The "Zhèngyì Xīnfǎ" (The Correct Method of the Heart of Change) is a commentary by Chen Tuan based on the transmission of Māyī Yá. Master Tóng of Dōnglín expanded upon this.
Among Master Tóng’s disciples, Hóngyì wrote a work titled *Jìwén* (Records of What Was Heard), which states that the study of nature and principle (*xìnglǐ*) truly originated from [this tradition].
Regarding the two masters Donglin and Yizong: Yizong transmitted [the teachings] to Zhouzi (Zhou Dunyi). Thus, Liu Houchun’s poem states:

"The learning of Li Ao (Lianxi) was obtained from a high monk. Later, Yu Bosheng also said: "Among the Song Confucians, only the two masters Lianxi and Kangjie attained significant insights into Buddhist scriptures early on" (as noted in his *Biography* and *Essentials of the Study of Nature*).
The Master inscribed the *Liu Yi Ting* (Pavilion for Leaving Clothes), saying: "Tuoji [Mencius] himself claimed..."
"Master, you have fundamentally explored the Way and profoundly refuted the teachings of Śākyamuni. I do not know what kind of person this Dadian was;
please send me several letters and kindly return my robe. (Xingli Qunshu)

Cheng Hao (also known as Cheng Yi). His courtesy name was Bochun. A native of Henan, his posthumous title was Mingdao. During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, he served as a Censor. While serving in the "inner ranks," he once remarked:
"Regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the manifestation of radiance, at first I could not fathom its meaning; recently, however, upon examining the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*, it precisely explains it."

This should be clearly understood. All of these are metaphorical designations for responding to capacities and shattering delusions, which are called "light" (*āloka*). The liberation from the defilements of the mind is called "clarity" (*prabhāsvara*).
These are merely metaphors for the radiance of one's own mind; by means of this, one is able to teach and transform others, and the illumination is inexhaustible.

The world exists solely within the luminosity of the Sage’s single mind. This is why the various sutras all begin by describing the emission of light (as seen in the stone inscription at Yungai Temple).
Whenever the Duke saw Buddhist monks reading Buddhist scriptures with such dignified composure and solemnity, he would say to his students:
"When reading any scripture, you must always act in this manner. Those who read books today have their very countenances already fallen into indolence."
I have become indolent. How can one preserve the Master? (From *Xingxue zhiyao*). One day, Master Mingdao visited Dinglin Temple.

He happened to see the assembly entering the hall; they moved with dignified decorum and majestic bearing, while the drums were struck and the bells tolled, and both inside and outside were solemn and quiet.
Whether sitting or rising, he strictly adhered to the *Qinggui* (Pure Rules). Duke Gong sighed and said, "The rites and music of the Three Dynasties are all contained herein" (*Hongyi Jiwen*).

His younger brother was Yi, whose courtesy name was Zhengshu and style name Yichuan. At the end of the Yuanfeng era, he was appointed as a Lecturer at the Chongzheng Hall by imperial decree as a Tongzhilang.
He entered the service of the Imperial Library to provide instruction to the Emperor. He once sent a letter to Chan Master Lingyuan Qing to inquire about the essentials of Chan. The Master...
The reply, in brief, stated: "I have presumptuously relied upon your excessive kindness by being expected as one who knows the Way.
Although I have not yet had the joy of meeting you face-to-face, I have heard that you have long devoted yourself to this Way and have visited almost every great master in the land.
Yet, you still consider me insufficient because you have not seen me. Recently, there was a certain Master Zhe who spoke of your realization."
"Examine the essentials of the Dharma; later, contemplate them deeply. One will believe and enter into the truth that is not false" (from the *Record of Master Lingyuan*).

Su Shi, whose courtesy name was Zizhan and sobriquet Dongpo Jushi, was appointed to the Hanlin Academy at the beginning of the Yuanyou era and subsequently promoted to Inner Hanlin Academician. His posthumous title was Wen.
Zhong initially attended Chan Master Zong of Donglin. While discussing the "discourse on the insentient," he attained realization and subsequently offered this verse of karmic resonance:
"The sound of the brook is itself the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains is surely the pure and serene body.
Last night, eighty-four thousand verses were produced; How shall I present them to others in days to come? When the official was exiled to Huangzhou, Foyin resided at Mount Lu’s Guizong.
He maintained external friendships with scholars. When Foyin moved to reside at Mount Jin, the Duke was released from his post and appointed as the Governor of Hangzhou.
Passing by Mount Jin, he encountered Foyin entering the meditation hall; the Duke went straight to see him. The Master said, "There is no place here to sit.

The Duke replied, "I shall temporarily borrow the Four Elements of the Preceptor to serve as a meditation seat. The Master said, "I have a turning phrase. If you can answer it, I shall grant your request. If you hesitate—"
[The official] deliberated. He then left behind the jade belt he was wearing. The Master immediately placed the belt upon a small table.

The Master said, "For this mountain monk, the four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist. Where, then, does the Honored Secretary intend to sit? As the official hesitated, the Master called to his attendant, saying, "Take away this jade belt;
it shall serve as a permanent talisman for our mountain gate. He then presented his own patched skirt as a gift in return. The official composed a verse, which begins: "Illness..."

Bones too frail to bear the girdle of jade; my dull faculties still fall within the range of the arrow’s point. Wishing to have him beg for alms in the courtesans’ quarters, I thus gave him this old monastic robe from the clouds and mountains.
This girdle has seen many people like passing travelers; its transmission to me is likewise leisurely. Its brocade patterns fall in perfect harmony with its true form;
I shall give it to the old man Wan-hui, who feigns madness. Your son, Dai, was four... (Note: The final character "四" [four] appears to be a fragment or an incomplete notation.)
He had been unable to walk for a year. Upon arriving in Hangzhou, he requested Dharma Master Biancai to shave his head and bestow the "touching of the crown" (mó-dǐng) upon him;
within a few days, he was able to walk again. The official composed a poem in thanks, which says: "The Master came to touch my crown; I rose and walked, chasing the fleeing deer."

During the Shaosheng era, [Suzhou] was exiled to Huizhou. At Nanhua Temple in Shaoyang, the monk Chongbian requested that the Master transcribe the stele for the Sixth Patriarch composed by Liu Zongyuan.
He further inscribed the following upon it: "Śākyamuni established his teachings through literature;

when these were translated into the Middle Kingdom, they necessarily relied on those among the Confucians who were skilled in speech before they could be transmitted far and wide. Thus, regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras, up to the *Laṅkāvatāra*..."
The text is rigorous, its details exhaustive and refined, and its excellence stands alone; this is because Fang Rong served as the scribe for the dictation.
When Liu Zhitou was exiled to the south, he began his study of the Buddha-dharma and composed the various steles for Caoxi and Nanyue, which are peerless throughout antiquity and the present.

Although there is currently no stone carving of the *Nanhua* (Southern Flower), Master Chongbian remarked: "Since the Tang dynasty, many have praised and recounted the Patriarchs, yet none [have equaled it]."
As for Tongliang, who was like Zihou, it is because his words, when traced back to their source, accord with those of Mencius.

How could we not cause students to see them daily and recite them constantly? When the Master was in Huizhou and received the order to relocate to Danyang, he carried a scroll of Amitābha Buddha with him on the day of his southward journey.
When people asked the reason for this, the Master said: "This is my official warrant for rebirth in the Western Paradise."
In the seventh month of the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, the Master passed away in Piling.
At that time, Qian Jiming was by his side and asked, "The Master has studied Buddhism throughout your life; how will you fare on this day? The Master replied, "Even these words are not accepted.

Furthermore, when the Elder Weilin of Mount Jing asked after his illness, he said, "It is indeed true that the Master’s practice has reached this point, yet you must still exert further effort. The Master—
