He replied at once, "If you apply effort, you will immediately be cured. His words ended and he passed away (from the *Benji* and *Tongji*).

When Master Gong’s mother, Lady Cheng, died, she instructed that her remaining belongings, such as hairpins and earrings, be used to commission an artisan to paint an image of Amitābha Buddha to dedicate for her posthumous merit. He praised it with this verse:
"The Buddha, by means of Great Perfect Enlightenment, Pervades the worlds of the ten directions. I, through inverted perceptions, Arise and perish within birth and death. Thus it was said.
Why is it that by means of a single thought one attains rebirth in the Pure Land? I have created karma since beginningless time, yet in a single thought there is already more than enough.
Since I am born from a single thought, I shall likewise be extinguished by a single thought. At the place where birth and extinction are utterly exhausted, I and the Buddha are identical.
It is like throwing water into the ocean, or like the bellows being blown by the wind; even with the great wisdom of a Sage, one could not distinguish between them. May I...
"My former parents and all sentient beings—wherever they may be, let it be the West; wherever they encounter, let it be the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
May every person attain the Infinite Life, neither departing nor arriving. In the preface to his transcription of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, he wrote:
"The *Laṅkāvatāra-abhisaṃbodhi-sūtra-ratna* is that which was spoken by previous Buddhas; it is the most subtle, wondrous, foremost, true, and definitive meaning. Therefore, it is called the Buddha."
The Chapter on Mind and Speech. Dharmatrāta entrusted the Dharma to the Second Patriarch, saying: "I have observed all the sūtras and teachings existing in China;
only the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* can serve as the seal for the mind. From patriarch to patriarch it has been transmitted as the mind-dharma, like the *Nan jing* of the physicians."
Every sentence contains principle, and every character contains the Dharma. Those who attain realization in future generations will spiritualize and clarify them;

like a bowl spinning a pearl, or a pearl spinning within a bowl, there will be nothing that is not possible. If one were to invent new ideas while discarding prior learning as useless, [one would err].
To be neither ignorant nor deluded is simply to be enlightened. Master Yuequan (Mr. Zhang Gongdao), having attained a mind of vastness, realized pure awakening.

During the Qingli era, while serving as the Governor of Chuzhou, he happened upon this scripture in a monk’s quarters. It appeared to him like an old possession; the traces of the original calligraphy were still vivid.
Overwhelmed by a mixture of sorrow and joy, he sighed deeply and entered into realization through it. I, Shi, have studied under this master...

I have been at this gate for thirty years. You, sir, considering me one who may be taught, have bestowed upon me this sutra and provided three hundred thousand coins to print and distribute it throughout the regions of Jiang and Huai.
As for this, the Elder of Jinshan, the Great Master Foyin Liaoyuan, said:

Printing and distributing [this text] is subject to exhaustion; however, if it is transcribed and carved [into woodblocks], it will be inexhaustible. Su Shi therefore transcribed and carved it (at the end of the scripture).
Su Zhe, styled Ziyou, was titled Mr. Luancheng and also known as the Elder Dongxuan. In the early Yuanyou period, he was appointed to office.
The Secretariat Drafter, Hanlin Academician, and Vice Director of the Chancellery once visited Chan Master Shun of Shanglan to inquire about the Dharma of the mind.
Shun showed him the section on the causes and conditions of the "nose" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and he attained realization.

He presented a verse, saying: "In middle age I heard the Way and realized my former errors; By chance we met, the aged Master Shun. Having finally investigated the 'nose,' I have encountered the true countenance. [He then] shook [his head].
My head does not require another’s hammer or tongs; what business has this master with withered vines and tattered rags? Who am I, with my white wine and green salt?
With shame before the waning moon over the eastern eaves, I drink a cup of nectar as smooth as molasses.

Foyin resided at Mount Jinshan. When Ziyou went to pay his respects, he first presented him with a verse, saying: "Coarse sand offered to the Buddha, the Buddha joyfully accepts; A strange rock offered to the monks, the monks..."
"I do not disdain it. You have come from afar empty-handed; do you still wish for more? I have nothing further with which to augment it. The Master replied:
"Brought by empty hands, it is difficult to let go; the Three Worthies and Ten Sages gather their heads to gaze upon it. Only such an offering can be truly enjoyed."
Even the wooden horse and the clay ox find joy. Ziyou composed the "Record of the Monks' Hall at Xixian on Mount Lu," which states in brief:
"Xixian occupies the upper reaches of the mountain; to its right it leans against a stone cliff, and to its left it overlooks flowing springs. At the foot of the stone cliff stands the monks' hall.
The Elder Zhiquan [observed] that after sixty years the tiles were ruined and the wood was decayed, so his disciple Huiqian exerted himself..."
He renovated it. Those who come seeking the Way obtain the joy of food, drink, and peaceful dwelling, free from external disturbances;

all this is due to the power of these two relocations and his tireless effort. Now, when a scholar dwells amidst the dust and filth of the world, with chaotic changes encountering him daily before his eyes, he never for a moment forgets the Way in his heart—how much more so when on the cliffs of deep mountains and the banks of wild waters, where there is a hall?

They have a place to dwell and food to satisfy their hunger; yet this is not because honor and disgrace fail to reach their minds, but rather because they are so preoccupied that they do not reflect upon them.
Why is this? Confucius said, "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening.

Now, those who rush about amidst worldly affairs without hearing the Great Way may toil until their teeth fall out, yet I know they will have nothing with which to face death. If only for a single day they were to hear it...
The Way—though one may die for its sake, there remains no other concern. Furthermore, in his *Treatise on the Three Teachings*, he wrote:
"The *I Ching* says: 'That which transcends form is called the Way; that which is below form is called the vessel.

Since the Five Emperors and the Three Kings, the world has been governed through vessels of form, leading the people by means of ritual and music and regulating them through punishments and administration. While the Way operated within these measures, the people remained unaware of it."
Thus it is. Laozi embodied the Dao and remained unentangled with worldly things; Confucius even compared him to a dragon.
Since the Eastern Han, the Buddha-dharma first entered China; its teachings corresponded with those of Laozi, both being what the *I Ching* calls "that which transcends form.
Yet the scholar-officials of the Han were unable to clarify this, though from the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, they understood it roughly.
Those whose fondness for them is profound wish to propagate them throughout the world; those whose aversion to them is deep wish to eradicate them from the world.

Both of these positions are erroneous. To wish to eradicate Buddhism and Daoism because their Way is the same as our own Way, yet to wish to practice it because its Teaching is different from our own Teaching—both have missed the mark. Yao Qin established [the dynasty] over a mere small territory...

In the corners [of the empire], he invited both monastics and laypeople to translate scriptures and discuss the sublime mysteries; those who came numbered several thousand. Yet before long, the House of Yao perished.

As for the Buddhist affairs in Jiangnan under Emperor Wu of Liang, they were the likes of which had never been seen in previous generations—reaching the point where he offered his own body as a slave.
When father and son alike fell into the hands of Hou Jing, commentators observed the failures of the Qin and Liang dynasties and concluded that it was because of the Buddha-dharma.
This is sufficient reliance. Later, Emperor Taiwu of the Northern Wei deeply trusted Cui Hao. Hao did not believe in Buddhism;

he urged the Emperor to expel the monastics, destroy the scriptures, and demolish the temples. Once the Buddha-dharma had been extinguished, Hao himself was also executed along with his entire clan for no other crime.

During the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang, who sought longevity and yielded to the private interests of the Daoists, he leveled Buddhist sites and suppressed the monks; yet before even a year had passed, he suddenly died from the toxicity of his elixirs.
[Emperor Wu] passed away. Those who debated the matter observed the calamities of the Wei and Tang dynasties and concluded that the Buddha-dharma must not be provoked.

Both of these views, however, represent but a single-sided perspective. The Way of the Buddha and Laozi is not the private teaching of any one individual; it has existed since the beginning of heaven and earth.
The gentlemen of antiquity employed it to regulate their vital energy and nourish their minds. Its loftiness cannot be compromised, and its...
Purity must not be defiled; Heaven, Earth, the spirits, and humans will all regard it with reverence.
This is the way by which the Sage achieves speed without haste and arrives without traveling. The Way is omnipresent within all things—how could it be subject to criticism?

Indeed, if one governs the world through physical forms and implements, guiding it with ritual and music and regulating it with punishments and administration, [it is the Way that makes this possible].
The Way operates within this interval, yet the people do not perceive it. All things grow together without harming one another;
the Way proceeds in parallel without contradiction. They merge so completely that their boundaries are no longer seen, and the world is transformed.
Is this not indeed the enduring intention of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius? (From the *Benji Chuandeng*).
Yang Jiejie, courtesy name Cigong, was a native of Wuweishan. He styled himself the "Wuweizi" (The Man of Non-action).

His official career reached the rank of Shangshu Zhukelangzhong (Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial) and he served as the Superintendent of Criminal Justice for the Two Zhejiang Provinces. Having studied under various renowned masters, he later followed Chan Master Tianyi Huai.
Youhuai often cited the pithy sayings and kōans of Layman Pang, urging him to investigate them deeply and reach profound realization.

Later, while serving as a ritual official at Mount Tai, one day upon hearing a cock crow and seeing the sun rise like a great platter surging upward, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. Jie took the path of Pure Land as his personal conviction;
he painted a sixteen-foot Amitābha Buddha to carry with him for constant contemplation. At the time of his death, he was moved by the vision of the Buddha coming to welcome him.
He passed away while sitting upright in meditation. He once composed the "Record of the Rotating Tripitaka Library" for Huikong Chan Monastery at Baoshan, which states in brief:
"The Dharma-realm is fundamentally without sentient beings; sentient beings arise from deluded vision. The Tathāgata is fundamentally without verbal teachings;
verbal teachings exist for the sake of sentient beings. Deluded vision is the illness of sentient beings; verbal teachings are the medicine of the Tathāgata. One uses medicine to treat the illness."
Thus, there is no illness that cannot be cured. By using words to awaken one from delusion, there is no delusion that cannot be awakened. This was spoken by the Tathāgata out of necessity;

it was recorded by the worthy and wise out of necessity. Therefore, Ānanda compiled them into the Sūtras, Upāli codified them into the Vinaya, and the various Bodhisattvas expanded them into the Śāstras.
Although the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are divided into the Three Piṭakas, [they are in essence one].

Precepts, concentration, and wisdom are rooted in the one mind. The "Treasury" (Zang) is used to demonstrate its capacity for containment; yet the mind cannot be allowed to stagnate or become obstructed.

For this reason, the Great Being at the Twin Trees (Śākyamuni) received sentient beings according to their capacities, using provisional means to manifest the ultimate reality. Thus, the various teachings were gathered together to form the Treasury.

Taking the precious treasury as the wheel, when the teaching relies upon the wheel, the teaching flows forth without obstruction; when the wheel manifests the teaching, the wheel turns on without end.
Thus, those who peruse the teaching awaken to the principles of transformation and adaptability; those who behold the wheel shall surely never regress.
Only then do they wander at ease within the ocean of nature, attaining liberation and forgetting the trap. There is not a single thing that does not turn the wheel of Dharma.
There is not a single speck of dust that does not return to the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*). Who, unless they possess profound wisdom, could be capable of such a realization?
The *Ten Doubts Treatise* of Tiantai states briefly: "If attachment is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī.
Saha is a defiled land; Sukhāvatī is a pure land. The lifespan in Saha is finite; the lifespan in that land, however, is—

It is immeasurable. This Sahā world is replete with all manner of suffering, whereas that land is peaceful and blissful, free from suffering. In this Sahā world, beings revolve through birth and death according to their karma;
in that land, upon a single visit, one eternally realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Such are the differences between the pure and the defiled, the lifespan, the suffering and joy, and birth and death. Yet sentient beings remain in profound ignorance of this—how lamentable! It is further said:
The radiance of Amitābha pervades the entire Dharma-realm; he embraces and never abandons those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Holy and ordinary beings are of one essence, as their capacities and the Buddha’s response correspond. Within the minds of all Buddhas, every speck of dust is a realm of Ultimate Bliss;
within the hearts of sentient beings, every thought is the Pure Land and every moment is Amitābha (from the *Benji*).

Wen Tong, courtesy name Yuke, was a native of Zizhong in Dongchuan. From his youth, he was renowned for his literary talent. He excelled in painting bamboo with ink, achieving a level of exquisite refinement.

He once served as the governor of both Yangzhou and Huzhou. On the eighth month of the third year of the Yuanfeng era, he bathed, donned his ceremonial cap and robes, sat upright, and passed away. This is Wen Tong.
When Duke Cui Gongdu heard of this, he was astonished and said to others: "Yesterday, when I took my leave of Yuke at the south of the prefecture, Yuke asked, 'Will you come again tomorrow?
When I went back a second time, Yuke slowly said, 'The scriptures state that those who do not speak falsely have tongues that cover their faces.
Yuke then immediately protruded his tongue and drew it up to his eyebrows, folding it over three times. Gongdu was greatly amazed. Now...
Upon hearing of his death, it was further confirmed that he was a man who had attained the Way (from the *Dongdu Shilüe*).

Zhū Shòuchāng, whose courtesy name was Kāngshū, lost his mother when he was seven years old. Upon reaching adulthood, he resigned from office and drew blood to write [the name of] the Golden... (in gold ink).
He traveled through the four quarters in search of the *Diamond Sūtra*. After fifty years, he entered the state of Qin and found his mother in Tongzhou; she was already seventy years old.
Many officials and gentlemen composed songs and poems to praise this event, and Su Shi wrote a preface for them.
Zhang Bo’end (Bo’end):

His given name was Yongcheng and his style name was Pingshu. A native of Tiantai, he studied the Way of the Primordial Unity (*hunyuan*) in his youth. When Lu Xian, Director of the Dragon Diagrams Office, was serving as the Governor of Chengdu, Bo’end went there to rely upon him.
There he met a transcendent person who bestowed upon him the secret instructions for the elixir of gold (*jindan*) and the regulation of the firing process (*huohou*).

He attained the Way and authored the *Wuzhen pian* (Treatise on Realizing Truth), which was transmitted to the world. He had previously traveled extensively to consult various Chan masters, gaining significant insights and awakenings.
Later, upon reading the collected works of the Patriarch Xuedou, he suddenly and fully realized the nature of his own mind. He composed songs and verses to express this principle, stating:

"Those who cultivate the Golden Elixir alone without awakening to the principles of the Buddha are like the ten immortals in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, subject to the retributions of the various realms of existence. Unfinished.
He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. His remains were cremated, and from them were obtained hundreds and thousands of śarīras of a deep azure-blue color.
Subsequently, even after his death, there were those who again beheld him (according to the *Tongji*).

Hu Su, courtesy name Wuping, was a native of Jinling in that prefecture. During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he served in the Hanlin Academy for ten years and rose to the rank of Vice Director of the Chancellery.

He was posthumously honored with the title Wen Gong. In the third year of the Zhi Ping era, he departed from the Chancellery to serve as the regional governor of Hangzhou, where he frequently visited Jingjue Yue.
The Dharma Master consulted on the sublime Way and observed the etiquette of a disciple. He once composed the "Record of Tianzhu Monastery on Mount Wulin," which states in brief:
"When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, the Perfect Teaching was propagated; the karmic conditions for Avalokiteśvara were secretly harmonized within the Middle Kingdom."
The journey of Sudhana’s pilgrimage extended throughout the south; Caoqi transmitted the teaching of the One Mind, and the Tiantai school established its Three Contemplations.

Gateways for salvation opened one after another, and monastic groves stood in mutual view. Fragrant sandalwood abounded here on this shore, and the grand atmosphere of the Mahāyāna flourished even more in other lands.
Is this not the brilliance of Li and the sagacity of Xun? That nature is Prajñā is especially evident here.
Is it not concentrated in the southeast? Tianzhu Temple is the preeminent monastery of Yuhang, and Feilai Peak is the wondrous crag of Wulin.
During the Jin dynasty, there was a Buddhist monk named Huirui who pointed out that this mountain was but a small ridge of Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
It is unknown in what year it flew here; he hung his staff and established a monastery, which was initially called Fanning (Translating Scriptures). In the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty...
The Imperial Preceptor Zhiguan expanded it and renamed it Tianzhu Monastery. At the end of the Tang dynasty, bandits arose and the monastery was burned down.
King Qian Liu of Wuyue established the Hall of Five Hundred Arhats. During the Song dynasty, the name was changed to Lingshan Xiangfu.

A person from the Central Plains invited the Great Master Zunshe to lead the assembly and expound the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school. At the beginning of the Tianxi era, Prince Wenmu...
When Duke Ji arrived in the prefecture, he submitted a memorial to restore the original quota [of monks] (and so forth).

The Buddha, with a mind of non-arising and boundless vows of practice, manifests throughout the three realms to deliver sentient beings. The splendor of wood and earth, however exhaustive, cannot adequately praise his virtue;
the engraving of metal and stone, however magnificent, is insufficient to exhaustively investigate his merit. Those who dwell here should keep this in mind.
Receiving the protective shade of the Dharma, he succeeds to the life of wisdom;

taking *samādhi* as the pure essence and the six *pāramitās* as the wondrous function, he ferries across the sands of sentient beings to repay the Buddha’s kindness, proclaims the tide-like sound of the Dharma to extol the Emperor’s power.
The remaining subtle benefits extended to those sentient beings (from the Temple Stele).
Shao Yong, courtesy name Yaofu, resided in Luoyang for forty years. He lived in poverty while delighting in the Way; he used no stove in winter and no fan in summer. At night...
He did not attend formal banquets for several years; he made his place of rest and sleep his "Cottage of Peace and Joy" (Ān-lè-wo) and styled himself the "Master of Peace and Joy" (Ān-lè-xiān-shēng).
His *Huangji jingshi shu* in twelve fascicles and his *Jigar geci* were circulated in the world.
Cheng Mingdao said: "As for the transmission of the Way of the Sages, Master Shao succeeded in transmitting it to Li Tingzhi; Tingzhi transmitted it to Mu Xiu."
Xiu transmitted it to Zhong Fang; Fang transmitted it to Chen Tuan; and Tuan transmitted it to the Wayfarer Māyī. By tracing its source and flow, one finds that its origins have a clear beginning.
The Master had a poem on studying Buddhism which says: "Eating to satiety and wearing fine clothes are not easy to sustain;
As the days grow long, what can one do with the seasons of sorrow? In my youth, seeking fame, I turned to Confucius; In my old age, fearing death, I draw near to Śākyamuni."

The more one vainly seeks to sever conditions, the heavier those conditions become; the more one strives to eliminate illness, the more the ailments multiply. The vast expanse of the Yangtze River is ever like a single roll of silk; fortunately it was windless, yet waves arise once more.
At the beginning of the Xining era, he was summoned as a Secretary of the Court for the Compilation of Writings (*Zhuzuo Zuolang*), but did not go.
After his death, he was posthumously titled Master Kangjie. Zhu Xi praised him, saying: "A man of genius born by the decree of Heaven, his brilliance and vigor transcending the age. He rode forth...

Whipped by the wind and struck by lightning, he surveys the boundless expanse; with his hand he probes the Moon Cave, and with his feet he treads upon the Celestial Root. Within his leisure lie the past and present;
within his stillness dwell heaven and earth (*Guangji*).

Fu Bi, courtesy name Yanguo, was a native of Henan. During the Qingli era, he was appointed as Academician of the Zizheng Hall. He served as Chancellor to Emperor Shenzong, was enfeoffed as Duke of Zheng, and later as Duke of Han.
He was a member of the "Gathered Elders of Luoyang" (Luoyang Qiyin Hui). He died at the age of eighty, posthumously receiving the title Wén.
Lord Zhong initially had not yet found his direction within the School of the Lineage (Zongmen). Lord Zhao Qingxian exhorted him with a letter, saying:
"I humbly observe that Your Excellency’s wealth and honor have reached such an extreme; your virtue and character are so flourishing; your fortune, longevity, health, and peace are so fully prepared;
and your retirement and leisure are so sublime. Yet, that which you have not yet paid much attention to is the One [Vehicle] of the Tathāgata..."

"It is simply a matter of a great causal condition (*mahā-pratyaya*). If you can seek with single-minded sincerity that which is to be realized and awakened to, then on another day I shall congratulate you from my quarters.
Gong Qingxian thus exhorted and encouraged him. Thereafter, he did not cease his efforts toward this Way day or night (as recorded in the *Tongji*).

When Bi heard that Chan Master Yong was presiding at Touzi and that his Dharma assembly was preeminent throughout the Huaidian region, he went there to resolve his doubts. It happened that Yong was ascending the high seat for the assembly.

As he sat, he observed that [Zhao] was looking around like an elephant king turning in a circle. Gong felt a slight realization and, adopting the etiquette of a disciple, hurried to the master’s quarters.
He ordered an attendant monk to request an entry interview. Upon seeing him, [Zhao] immediately said, "The Minister has already entered; Fu Bi is still outside.
Hearing this, Bi broke into a sweat that soaked his back, and he attained great enlightenment. He subsequently sent a verse to Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben.
The Master said: "Upon first meeting Master Yong, I attained profound realization. Through successive conditions, I have inherited the mind of my late teacher.

Though people in the southeast may speak of the vast distance between mountains and rivers, I face the *lingguang* (numinous light) and the *miaoyin* (wondrous sound) [Pudeng] every day. He once wrote in a letter to Yuanzhao: "I, Bi, have devoted myself to the ancestral Way for many years.
I have always regretted not encountering a person of clear vision to enlighten my ignorance and coarseness. Although I have long heard..."

Your profound virtue is such that I have had no cause to seek an audience with you. Yesterday, by fortunate chance, as I was appointed to govern Bozhou, whose borders adjoin those of Yingchuan, the local official Zhang Bishu requested that you, Master Yong, visit me. We remained together for nearly a month;

through the power of your compassion and skillful means, you enabled me to attain realization. Unexpectedly, in my old age, I have been able to hear the ultimate teaching. What a blessing! What a blessing! Although I, Bi, have attained this...
I take refuge in Master Yǒng; however, the ultimate source derives from the Old Monk (Lǎohéshàng).

I further pray that you will bestow your compassion and receive me, granting me your guidance from afar so that I may reach what I have not yet reached—thereby becoming like Páng Yùn under Nányuè Huáì and Běi Xiū under Bǎizhàng Huaihāi.
What is the difference? (From the *Yánxíng lù*).
*Fófǎ jīntāng biān*, Scroll 12, re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎ jīntāng biān*, Scroll 13.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai; Du Yan.
Yan, whose courtesy name was Shichang, was a native of Shanyin in Yuezhou. During the Qingli era, he was appointed as Prime Minister;

at that time, he was popularly known as the "Pure and Incorruptible Chancellor. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Qi. Because Zhang Fangping was fond of Buddhism, Yan often ridiculed and found him strange.

There was a physician named Zhu who moved between the two gentlemen. One day, the Duke summoned Zhu to examine his pulse. As Zhu was leaving, he said to the messenger, "Go and tell the Duke: 'Please look...'"

He had not yet finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. When [Zhang] Zai arrived, he invited him to sit and said, "I had expected you to be a man of broad understanding, but it seems you have recently become dull-witted.
The subtle words of the sages do not go beyond Confucius and Mencius; what kind of talk is this so-called *Śūraṅgama*? Jizang said, "You have not read this sutra yourself;
how can you know that it does not surpass Confucius and Mencius? Thereupon, he took out the scroll from his sleeve. Zhang Zai examined it.
Before he realized it, the axle had come to an end. Startled, he said, "Fangping knew this but did not tell me. He immediately ordered his carriage to go and see him.
Fangping said, "It is like losing an object and suddenly finding it; one should simply rejoice at having found it, rather than regretting its late discovery" (Tongji).
Wang Gu was styled Minzhong and was a native of the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). He was the great-grandson of Wang Hu, the Minister of the Three Primes.

Gu had formerly traveled to Huanglong and Cuiyan, where he became a fellow practitioner of Chan alongside Huitang, Yangqi, and others; furthermore, he attained realization in the Dharma-gate of Amitābha’s Pure Land. Thereupon—
He composed the *Zhǐzhǐ jìngtǔ juéyí jí* (Collection for Resolving Doubts Concerning the Direct Pointing to the Pure Land) in three fascicles.

He also compiled the *Fǎbǎo lù* (Record of the Dharma Treasures) in ten fascicles, which serves as a catalog for the various cases of the Tripitaka arranged according to their sequence, while explaining their underlying causes and conditions.
All matters concerning the chronological order of the Buddha’s assemblies and the variations in the Chinese translations are recorded therein (*Tōngkǎo*).

Li Zunxū (also written as Li Zūnxū). His courtesy name was Yòuhé. He had spent many years investigating the essential points of the school. Upon hearing the causal conditions cited by Cízào, he suddenly attained clear realization of the Great Dharma.
He composed a verse, saying: "To practice Chan one must be an iron man; when the hand touches the heart, judgment is immediate. One proceeds directly toward the..."
Ascending to Bodhi: do not concern yourself with any right or wrong; illuminate all entanglements and seal them.
During the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng, Zūnxù widely propagated the *Guǎngdēnglù* in thirty fascicles. The Emperor bestowed upon it the title *Tiānshèng Guǎngdēnglù* and composed a preface.
Zūnxù’s hymn in praise of the Buddha states: "Confucius was hailed as the Great Sage; Lǎozǐ was titled the Ancient Sovereign. From above heaven to below heaven..."
There should be no further comparison (from the *Chuan deng lu*).

Lü Huìqīng—whose courtesy name was Jífú—was a native of Fújiàn. He styled himself the Iron Boat Layman (*Tiěchuán Jūshì*) and rose to the rank of State Councilor (*Cānzhèng*). Regarding the Dharma-realm...
I had long been contemplating and savoring [the teachings]. Later, upon reading Master Li’s *Huayan He lun* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Avatamsaka), my mind was suddenly enlightened.

I spoke a verse, saying: "I have long desired to see Mañjuśrī, And directed my thoughts toward Mount Wutai. Who would have known that from within the yellow scrolls, He would point out the arrival of the Sublime Light?

(From the *Pudeng lu*) Huiqing, while on leave from his military service at the border, traveled to Mount Wutai. Upon reaching the Central Terrace (*Zhongtai*), clouds and mist suddenly gathered from all four directions.
A violent wind and thunderous rain shook the forests and ravines. In an instant, there appeared a creature resembling a dark-blue dragon, half-emerged from amidst the clouds and mist.

Huìqīng was greatly startled. When the weather cleared slightly, he saw a youth with a black body and disheveled hair, wrapped from his feet to his shoulders in reed mats, baring his right shoulder, and holding a Buddhist scripture (*bàn*). He asked Huìqīng, "What did you see that caused you such alarm?"
[The Master] said, "I have encountered these adverse conditions due to obstacles from my youth. The boy asked, "What do you seek that has brought you here?
He replied, "I wish to see the Great Being (Mahāsattva). The boy asked, "For what purpose do you wish to see him?

He replied, "I have often studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and hope that the Great Being will inspire in me a mind of understanding, so that its commentaries and exegeses may circulate. The boy said, "The wondrous intent of the Buddhas is simple and clear."

[The Master] said, "The intent of the commentaries by the former masters can be understood; for instance, the commentary on the 'Ten Stages Chapter' (Daśabhūmika-parivarta) did not exceed a few sheets of paper, whereas today's commentaries number nearly a hundred scrolls.
These have shattered the Great Way. Huìqīng said, "How dare a mere youth rebuke his predecessors? The youth smiled and said, "You are mistaken, sir.
Here, every blade of grass and every tree is none other than Mañjuśrī. Huìqīng immediately bowed his head and prostrated himself.
In the interval before he rose, the youth manifested the form of a Great Being (Mahāsattva), straddling a lion; he then vanished into the clouds and could no longer be seen.
Huìqīng repented his transgressions and vowed to see the youth again. Suddenly, the youth appeared upon the incense table and rebuked him, saying:
"Why do you remain attached to such extreme signs of permanence? Huìqīng replied: "I truly wish for all people of the world to behold the Great Being’s manifestation of transformation."
This was indeed his true likeness. He then commanded a court painter to depict it; in an instant, [the original] was no longer seen (*Huayan Ganying Zhuan*).
Chen Shidao, whose courtesy name was Wuji and sobriquet Houshan Jushi, was a native of Pengcheng. From his youth, he applied himself with diligence and was fond of learning. During the Yuanyou era...

During the Zhongxing era, Su Shi and Sun Jue recommended Cheng to the court. He was appointed as a Professor at Xuzhou. In the third year of the Yuanyufu era, an imperial edict was issued to oversee the construction of the Tai-ling Mausoleum.
Lou Yi, the Magistrate of Dengfeng, requested that the remaining labor be used to repair the Shaolin Monastery, which he named "Facing the Wall" (Mianbi) and "Orchid Society" (Lanshe).
Cheng Dao composed a record for it, which stated in brief: "In the school of Confucius, Yan Hui, Min Ziqian, and Ran Geng all left no successors."
After Zhonggong came Xunqing; after Zengcan came Mengke; and after Duanmuci came Zhuang Zhou.
Yet, after Xun, Meng, and Zhuang, there was no further record. As for the lineage of the Li clan, it passed to Guanyin;
after Yin, there was again no further record. From Śākyamuni, twenty-eight generations later came Bodhidharma; and after another six generations...
As for Caoxi, fifteen generations have passed until the present day; yet that those followers of Confucius and Laozi wish to examine its source and course is a mistake (from the *Houshan ji*).
Li Gou, courtesy name Taibo, was a native of Xunjiang. In the second year of the Huangyou era, Fan Wenzheng memorialized his recommendation to the throne;

consequently, he was appointed to an official post at the Imperial Academy and subsequently served as a lecturer (*shuoshu*) at the National University. He died shortly thereafter. He once composed the *Qianshu* (The Hidden Book), in which he exerted himself in refuting [certain doctrines].
The Buddha. Master Mingjiao Sōng brought the *Fujiao bian* (Compilation for the Propagation of the Teaching) to visit him. At that time, Chǒu was intent on reading Buddhist scriptures;
he then said with regret, "Our own school's discussions have not yet reached the level of a single fascicle of the *Heart Sūtra*. How could the Way of the Buddha be easily understood?
A disciple of his named Huáng Hànjié challenged him with a letter, to which Chǒu replied, stating in brief: "The people’s desire for goodness..."
This is simply their innate nature. When the Confucian scholars of antiquity were employed by the world, they necessarily had means to instruct and guide them;
the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, mind, intellect, and all the limbs of the people all had something to govern them, so how could they have had leisure to attend to heterodox paths?

When the Confucian scholars of later ages were employed by the world, they lacked such means to instruct and guide them; thus, the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, mind, and intellect of the people—[were left unguided].
"The remains have no master; having abandoned the Buddha, where shall one go? (From the *Zhongwen ji* of Chen Ying).
Chen Guan, courtesy name Yingzhong, styled Liaoweng, and also known as the Layman Huayan, was a native of Shaxian County in Nanjian Prefecture. He once...
He served as the Censor-in-Chief and was posthumously titled Duke Zhongsu. His integrity in court was as rigid as bone and sinew, possessing the spirit and vigor of the ancients.

He once visited Chan Master Lingyuan Qing, holding fast to his own learning and experience in his quest for intellectual understanding. The Master asked, "To which school do you cling for understanding? When did you happen upon this harmony?"
"One must practice by setting aside mind, intellect, and consciousness; one must study by cutting off the paths of the holy and the ordinary. Only then will it be possible.

Thereupon, the Master attained enlightenment and sent a verse to his teacher, saying: "Sitting upright in the study hall, ten thousand activities cease; The sun is warm and the breeze gentle, the plants and trees are serene."
Who can recognize events from two thousand years ago? They now reside right before one's eyes. The memorial submitted at the beginning of the Xuanhua era stated:
"The traces of Confucianism and Buddhism differ, yet their Way is the same. Those who do not know how to employ them utilize their outward traces;

this is like the Liang dynasty’s observance of fasting and the Han dynasty’s quest for immortals. Those who know how to employ them utilize their inner spirit; this is like the ancestors of our Song dynasty."
If one employs their outward traces, one becomes mired in them; being mired, one can be attacked. If one employs their underlying mind, one attains penetration;
being penetrated, one cannot be criticized. By employing the "non-action" (*wuwei*) of Laozi, the people find rest;
by employing the "beneficial aid" (*raoyi*) of the Śākya [Buddha], none in the world can contend with him. Laozi said, "The wise do not speak. The Śākya said, "Cease, cease! Do not speak."
The Master Kong said, "I silently apprehend it. Is this not that which the ancestors practiced in person, rather than something that can be discussed by those who merely speak?
(Zi Jian). The Venerable [Zhanran] composed the "Eulogy on the Three Thousand Gates," which says: "Inconceivable provisional existence is not a partial provisional existence;
this provisional existence fundamentally possesses all phenomena. True emptiness is not empty of anything; perfect centrality is perfectly complete."

It is simply the Middle Way. Therefore, the first of the four gates is the inconceivable provisional (parikalpita). The ordinary person’s mind possesses [the Buddha-nature] just as the Buddha possesses it;
yet, through attachment and grasping, it is not perfected and thus not fully possessed. Only the single character "possession" (ju) reveals the essence of our school.
Those who enter this school are extremely rare. Master Gao once said: "The essentials of the Buddha-dharma do not reside in words and letters, nor do they lie outside them."
It is apart from words; it does not depend on much reading—just one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is sufficient.

The essential point of this sutra consists of only nine characters: *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. These nine characters in the Sanskrit language correspond to a single character, "Awakening" (*jué*), in the Chinese language.
This very character is the "Sincerity" (*chéng*) of the *Zhōngyōng*. Regarding all that has names and... [text continues]
All characteristics, as well as cognition and vision, are swept away as being empty and false. That which is established is solely these nine characters.
These characters are one; the object they signify is one. This is the "One" that penetrates all, not the "one" of two, three, four, or five.
This is the "thing" that is insincere and devoid of substance; it is not a thing among the myriad things that are distinct and diverse.
Having passed the age of fifty, you ought to pay close attention; do not continue to be negligent. This does not conflict with your daily affairs in a hundred ways;

it depends solely on not forgetting it in your mind. Simply read it once a day. If you read it a thousand times, its meaning will become clear of itself. Had you known this early, you would have attained it early.
[This is from] the *Wenxian Tongkao*. Liu Anshi (Anshi), courtesy name Qizhi, was a native of Daming.
His style was Yuancheng. During the Yuanyou era, he served as a Secretariat Drafter (*Zhongshu Sheren*). He once...
It is said: The words of Confucius and the Buddha are like the beginning and end of one another. Confucius spoke of "no arbitrary intention, no compulsion, no stubbornness, and no self.
The Buddha spoke of "no self, no person, no sentient beings, and no life-span. Their words are as if uttered by a single person.
However, while Confucius took the Three Bonds and Five Constants as his Way, [the Buddha’s] doctrine of "form is emptiness, emptiness is form" [is different].
I have merely opened up the beginning of this matter so that others may realize it for themselves. The mind of Confucius is the Buddha-mind.

If there were no Three Bonds and Five Constants in the world, chaos and disorder would arise once more, and humanity would be left with no survivors. How could such a state be the intention of the Buddha?
Therefore, the minds of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism are all one; it is only their institutional arrangements that differ.

Furthermore, it is said that when great scholars of antiquity and the present day have written treatises to disparage the Buddha-dharma, there is indeed a reason for this. Moreover, if that tail is heavy, then this head becomes light.
Today, those who are disciples of Confucianism and Buddhism each uphold their own teachings, like the three legs of a tripod. Would it be permissible to lose even one leg?
In that case, the tripod would surely overturn. The petty scholars of this world do not understand this principle;
seeing predecessors who perhaps disparaged Buddhism, they likewise follow suit in reviling it, claiming that there is nothing worthy of being taken from the Buddha-dharma. This is incorrect.
Many officials treat Chan as a mere amusement, yet this matter is the ultimate teaching of the Buddha—how could it be treated as a joke for a moment’s laughter?
This too should be cautioned against. As for that which is called the single character "Chan" (Dhyāna), this principle also exists within the Six Classics;
the Buddha merely changed its name. Since Bodhidharma came from the West, this talk has spread widely, and as a result, the Buddha-dharma has fallen into decline by now.

People merely recognize external forms and appearances. Had he not come, the extinction of the Buddha-dharma would have occurred long ago. Furthermore, those of superior capacity and keen intelligence mostly delight in [this teaching].

Because his teachings were thus disseminated, they became widely circulated. Although I have gained strength from the Confucian tradition and the venerable masters during my journey southward, it cannot be said that I have failed to gain strength in this matter as well. Is there any worldly affair greater than birth and death?
If one focuses solely on investigating birth and death until a point of insight is reached, then regardless of nobility or meanness, fortune or calamity—[the truth will be realized].
"Your merit is slight. The Senior Gentleman understands this perfectly well; he simply does not speak of it. He continued, "Lord Wen composed a treatise to disparage the Buddhists, saying:
'Their subtlety cannot surpass that of our own books; as for their absurdities, I do not believe them. I asked him, 'What is this subtlety? He replied, 'It is non-self (anātman).
Throughout the thousands of scriptures and myriad treatises, they resolve upon nothing but this single word, 'self. I asked further, "And what is [the absurdity]?"
Tàn said: "As for their claims that heaven and hell are not to be believed, they say that the Buddha established these merely to lead people from evil toward goodness.
Furthermore, Zou Yan stated that beyond heaven and earth there are eight or nine realms such as the Divine Continent (Shenzhou) and the Red County (Chixian).

Zhuangzi said that regarding what lies outside the six directions, the sage preserves it but does not discuss it. Since these are beyond the reach of the ears and eyes of ordinary people, how [can one know them]?"
Knowing that they were non-existent, the Duke said, "I merely wish to support the teachings" (*Ming Dao Ji*).
Cha Dao, whose courtesy name was Zhanran, moved his residence to Hailin. He was exceptionally filial; he even cut through ice to seek carp to nourish his mother. By means of his writings...

His conduct was in harmony with the times; he promoted the worthy and virtuous and served as a Court Attendant (D aizhi). While serving as the Governor of Xiangzhou, Chan Master Cong of Shimen requested him to compose a record for the Sangha Hall.
It states briefly: "Since the Buddha-dharma spread widely and Bodhidharma came from the West, those possessing the root of faith have sought to realize the original source.
They wore robes that could not ward off the cold and ate food that did not suffice to fill their bellies. Yet, as the True Dharma gradually became diluted..."

As human affairs grew lax, Master Baizhang constructed buildings to provide shelter for the elderly and the infirm. Recently, Zen monasteries have vied with one another to build grand and magnificent structures.
Young beginners now lie at ease within them, unaware that those who solicit donations labor their bodies to the bone, while those who provide the wealth seek blessings and repent for their sins.
To those who understand cause and effect, staying there is like lying upon an iron bed; it would truly be a grievance.
This is the enemy. Unless one personally and diligently cultivates the embryo of the holy (āryagarbha) day and night, there is no other way.

Next, as for those who associate with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and are resolved to seek liberation, their physical forms may be temporarily accommodated, for they are protected by dragons and spirits.

Yet, if their minds are turbid and entangled by the afflictions (kleśa), and while their bodies enjoy warmth and comfort, they fail to examine their ignorance (avidyā) and do not realize that their life is shrinking away; if they merely memorize words and claim this to be the ultimate goal, their records will eventually come to an end.
They passed away and fell into those evil realms. What a man of such fierce resolve, possessing an unshakable mind!

Huang Tingjian—whose courtesy name was Luzhi and whose style name was the Recluse of the Valley (Shan谷)—was exiled as the Vice Governor of Fuzhou; consequently, he was called the Elder of Fuzhou (Fuweng). Later...
He was banished to Qianzhou and stayed at Kaiyuan Temple. The temple possessed the Mowei Spring, and he was thus called the "Elder of Mowei.
During the Yuanyou era, he served as a Grand Astrologer (*taishi*). He once visited Chan Master Huanglong Xin to seek a shortcut to entering the Way. The Master said:
"As for what Confucius said—'My disciples, do you think I am hiding anything from you? I hide nothing from you'—Grand Astrologer, in your daily life..."
"How do you theorize this? the Master asked. The official attempted to respond, but the Master said, "Not so, not so. The official was left in a state of persistent confusion.
One day, while attending the Master on a mountain walk, the osmanthus flowers were in full bloom. The Master asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the osmanthus?

The official replied, "I do. The Master said, "Is there anything I have hidden from you? Thereupon, the official attained realization. He subsequently visited Chan Master Xinxin of Huanglong, who asked him:
Xuefeng said, "Death is certain; one must die. When a scholar dies, both [body and mind] are burned into a pile of ashes.
Where will you meet him? The Master (Dongshan) was speechless. Xuefeng said, "What you have attained through studying under Huitang has not yet been put to use.
Later, while exiled to Qian-nan, he suddenly had an awakening and said, "I have constantly been deceived by the old monks of the world for so long. Only Daxin..."

The people were unwilling to comply; this may be called acting with true sincerity. While you were in Qian, you abstained from alcohol and severed all carnal desires, reading the Tripitaka for three years.
You often said: "Gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and insult, suffering and pleasure—these eight winds never depart from one another within the four modes of deportment.
Even the ancient sages of supreme wisdom could not stand outside the reach of these eight winds."
Indeed, it is because one does not know unless one studies the Way. You have a text of your vows which states briefly:

"From the distant past until now, due to delusion and craving, I have drunk wine and eaten meat, thereby increasing my thirst for desire and entering the forest of false views, failing to attain liberation.
Now, before the Buddha, I make this great vow: from this day forth, throughout the future eons, I shall no longer indulge in lustful desires. May it be so. From this...
From this day forth, throughout the entirety of future worlds, I shall no longer drink alcohol. From this day forth, throughout the entirety of future worlds, I vow never again to eat meat.
By means of these vows of endurance made for the sake of all future time, may my faculties and sense objects be purified, and may I be fully endowed with the ten kinds of patience (*daśakṣānti*).
Without depending on the instruction of others, may I enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), follow in the footsteps of the Tathāgata, and [act] within the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings.
In the midst, he manifests the performance of Buddha-works; the ten directions are transparently penetrated, and he is adorned with myriad virtues.
Throughout every land and within every atom, he seeks to bear witness for me and dispel the clouds of my delusion. I bow my head to him who is equal to space, with a single, piercing intensity.

In a letter to Hu Shaoji, you wrote: "You have gained considerable strength in the Way of the Sages. As for the method of curing illness, you should seek deeply into the joy of Chan (Zen) to illuminate and break through the cycle of birth and death."
When the root of these things is severed, worry, affliction, lust, and anger have no place to set foot. Once the disease has no root, its branches and leaves cannot cause harm.
Master Cong of Touzi and Master Yan of Haihui were of lofty and venerable conduct; they did not fall short of the ancients and are both worthy of being approached.
If one follows scholars of mere literary composition and learns false speech and flowery rhetoric, it only increases the seeds of ignorance. Written by [Author].
The Record of the Chengtian Monastery in Jingnan states briefly: "Confucians argue that the expense of a single Buddhist temple is equivalent to the assets of a hundred middle-class families;
it is truly a parasite upon the grain and silk of the common people. Even I would say this is so.
However, the good people in the world are few while the evil are many. While the King’s system of punishment and reward governs them from without, the Buddha..."
If blessings and calamities are used to govern the internal [self], then what contribution would this not be to the worldly teachings? Yet Confucian scholars have often sought to suppress them;
what is the reasoning behind this? The *Brief Record of the Renshou Pagoda at Ci’en Temple in Jizhou* states:
"When Emperor Wen of the Sui was still in obscurity, a strange person presented him with a handful of śarīras and said: 'With these, bring forth blessings...'"

The common people, because of this, suddenly could no longer see him. Later, when the Zhou dynasty lost its mandate and Emperor Wen of Sui received the Mandate of Heaven, he changed the era name to Renshou.

By imperial decree, thirty portions of the śarīra were distributed and stūpas were erected in high and prominent locations throughout the empire; all of them emitted light and manifested auspicious omens.
In the second year, fifty-three remaining portions of the śarīra were again distributed among fifty-three provinces, all of which were selected for their excellence.
The monk of virtuous conduct (De-heng) oversaw the protection of the project. Upon arriving at that prefecture, he divined an auspicious site to build a stupa;
Jishi Monastery in Jiji Prefecture was one of them (*Chuanteng lu* and *Benji*).
Chao Shuo zhi, whose courtesy name was Yidao, was a native of Jibei. He styled himself Jingqian and served as an Attendant Censor (*Dai-zhi*).

He once composed the preface to the *Renwang Banruo Jing* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) and the inscription for the Stele of Dharma Master Mingzhi. While serving as the Superintendent of the Salt Fields in Mingzhou, he frequently visited Nanhu Lake.
He visited Mingzhi and, upon hearing the teachings on the "Three Thousand Worlds and Contemplation" (*sānqiānjìngguàn*), joyfully vowed to study them. He mastered their essential principles;

in his later years, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* daily and styled himself a "Tiantai Teaching Monk" (*tóngjì*). He also engaged in the study of Chan Buddhism; thus, Huang Shan谷 (Huang Tingjian) wrote of him:
"Master Nian sits emaciated in meditation, guarding his mind like a tiger in its cage. Shuo once provided a brief reply in a letter to Zhao Heshun.

It is said: "Our Śākyamuni Buddha and Amitābha Buddha, out of compassion for these sentient beings, have established this Dharma-gate outside of the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates through their shared power of aspiration; Śākyamuni has brought it forth."
Amitābha is its master; Śākyamuni brings one forth into it. Amitābha is its home; Śākyamuni provides the medicine for its ailments.
Amitābha causes one to remain alive throughout one’s life; Śākyamuni’s land is like a transient inn, while Amitābha’s land is like one’s native village.
Looking from Western India toward the Land of Peace and Bliss is like looking from China [toward the same].
Anle Guo (One of Peace and Bliss).

Hu An Guo, courtesy name Kang Hou, posthumous title Wending. During the Shaosheng era, he presented an essay for the imperial examination consisting of nearly ten thousand words; Emperor Zhezong personally [reviewed it].
He was promoted to the third rank and appointed as a Registrar of the National University (*Taixue lu*). During the Jianyan era, he was appointed as an Attendant Scholar of the Huigyou Pavilion.

Later, he retired from office with the title of Academician of the Baowen Pavilion. In his later years, he styled himself "Cao'an" (The Hermitage). Having long relied upon Chan Master Cai of Shangfeng, he attained the meaning beyond words.
When a Chan practitioner raised the story of "Killing the Cat" to question him, the Master replied with a verse: "Holding heaven and earth in my hand,"
The mechanism of killing and enlivening is deployed freely and transversely according to the occasion. Though the whole hall is filled with hares and horses, there are no dragons or elephants;
this majestic great function remains entirely unknown. Furthermore, he wrote in a letter to Shangfeng: "Mount Zhurong resembles the sky over Ducheng;
ten thousand ages of rivers and mountains are before one's eyes. One must believe that Sīxin has never died; last night the autumn moon was once again full" (Pudeng).

Zhang Shangying, whose courtesy name was Tianjue and sobriquet was Wujin Jushi (the Infinite Layman), could memorize ten thousand words daily as a child. Zhao Bian recommended him, and he was summoned to the capital.
He presented to Emperor Huizong, in June of the fourth year of the Daguan era, a "Petition for the State from a Grass Hut" tucked within his sleeve. [End of fragment]

When the Duke entered the government as a high minister, there had been a long drought. That evening, it rained heavily, and the Emperor bestowed upon him the two characters "Shānglín" (The Rain of Shāng), written by his own hand. Initially, having entered a Buddhist monastery and seeing that the Tripitaka was so solemn and orderly, he was displeased and said, "Is the teaching of our Sage Confucius not equal to the books of these barbarians? Sitting up late at night in deep reflection, he leaned over his desk with his brush poised. His wife, Lady Xiáng, asked, "Why do you not go to sleep? The Duke replied: "I am thinking of how the Buddha, in his compassion, took on the form of a human being to teach the Way. He manifested as a prince, renounced his throne, and became a monk. He traveled from country to country, converting those who were deluded. He taught the people to cultivate their minds and abandon worldly desires. He forbade killing and encouraged the practice of charity. He established the precepts to restrain the mind and the monastic rules to regulate conduct. He caused the people to be filial to their parents and respectful to their elders. He taught them to be benevolent and righteous, to be modest and cautious, and to be pure and sincere. Thus, when one dies, they do not fall into the three evil realms; instead, they ascend to the heavens and enjoy happiness. This is truly a great benefit for the world. As for our Confucian teachings, they merely emphasize ritual and music, and focus on governing the state and regulating the family. They do not speak of transcending the world or seeking liberation from suffering. Therefore, I have been reflecting on this matter. Lady Xiáng said, "If you wish to study the Buddha's teachings, why not simply read the scriptures? Why must you harbor resentment toward them? The Duke sighed and said, "I am indeed lacking in wisdom.

He then set aside his brush and went to sleep. The next day, he summoned a monk and requested the scriptures. He read them through from beginning to end and found them to be profound and vast. He then prostrated himself before the Buddha and said, "I have been ignorant and narrow-minded. I have slandered the Buddha’s Dharma. I pray that you will accept my repentance. From that time forward, he devoted himself to the study of the scriptures and became a lay devotee. He built a hall within his residence to enshrine the Buddha’s image and established a vegetarian feast every month on the eighth day. He also provided for the monks' needs and supported the monastic community. His reputation for piety spread throughout the realm. It is said that because of his devotion, the rains fell in due season, bringing peace and prosperity to the land. This is the story of how the Duke of Zhōngyì converted to Buddhism.
He said, "I am currently composing this 'Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha. Xiang said, "If you have already stated that there is no Buddha, what treatise could there be?
You ought rather to compose a 'Treatise on the Existence of the Buddha. Gong fell silent and desisted. Later, he visited his colleagues and saw the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* before a Buddhist shrine.
He opened it at random and saw the passage: "This illness is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element. At that moment, he suddenly attained realization.
He borrowed the *Heart Sūtra* and read it carefully. Xiang said, "Only after reading this sūtra can one begin to compose a 'Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha.
From this, the Master gained deep faith in the Buddhist Way. He first visited Chan Master Zong of Donglin and subsequently received his seal of approval (*inka*).

While serving as the transport commissioner for Jiangxi, he met Chan Master Yue of Doushuai; they conversed together at night regarding matters of the Zen school. The Master said, "Recently, I have been studying the *Transmission of the Lamp*..."

Regarding the karmic encounters of venerable masters, I have only harbored doubt concerning the story of Deshan placing down his alms bowl. Yue said, "If you harbor doubt regarding this story, then everything else is merely mental calculation and intellectual interpretation;
how could it ever reach the realm of great peace and bliss? Gong was incensed; he rose repeatedly from his mat.
Toward the fifth watch of the night, he unconsciously kicked over his urinal. Suddenly, a great realization dawned upon him.

He immediately knocked on Yue’s door and said to him, "I have already caught the thief. Yue asked, "Where is the stolen property? As the Official hesitated, Yue said, "Commissioner, please rest for now.
The following morning, the Official composed a verse, saying: "The drum is silent and the bell has sunk; returning with the alms bowl, at Yantou..."
His words were like thunder: "Indeed, you shall live for only three years. Could it be that he had received a prophecy from him? You have composed the *Dharmapāla-śāstra*, which begins:
"Confucius said, 'If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening. Does he take benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness to be the Way?
If so, Confucius certainly possessed benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness. Does he take longevity and eternal life to be the Way?"
He then said, "To die this evening would be acceptable. Was this not truly seeking to hear the Way?
Is it not the path of unsurpassed Bodhi—the realization of the nature and awareness of the mind—taught by the Great Awakened Compassionate Honored One? Otherwise, why would Liezi say to Confucius:
"I have heard that in the West there is a Great Sage who does not govern yet is not in disorder, and who does not speak yet is trusted"?
It acts spontaneously without being transformed; vast and boundless, the people are unable to name it.
That Liezi studied under Confucius and yet so abruptly recounted this teaching proves that he was indeed not a deceiver. Confucius was a sage, and even he revered this Way.
Yet those who study Confucius today, before having read even a hundred or a thousand scrolls of his books, first make the refutation of Buddhism their urgent task.

Why is this? Xu Fu, whose courtesy name was Shichuan, possessed extraordinary talent and a strong spirit; by the age of seven he was already capable of composing poetry, and was thus recognized by his maternal uncle, Huang Shan谷 (Shangu).
Once, he inquired about the Way of Chan with the Chan Master Lingyuan Qing. The Master replied in a letter, stating briefly:

"The reason the sages of old perceived the world as being like shadows and echoes, and understood the Holy Way as being like a temporary lodging, was for no other reason than that they had personally penetrated the source of the mind...
(and so forth). Toward the beginning of the Jingkang era, he served as a Vice Minister in the Department of State Affairs and shared the same aspirations as his fellow court officials.
He hung his alms bowl at Tianning Monastery’s Zemo Hall and applied himself diligently to the study under Yuanwu. Yuanwu, too, rejoiced in his transcendent realization.
One day, [Zhaozhou] went to the Secretary’s Office and, pointing to Yuanwu’s head, said, “This old fellow’s feet have not yet touched the ground.
Yuanwu turned his face away and said, “How could a turtle ever escape from inside a jar? Zhaozhou bowed and said, “Fortunately, this old fellow...”
When Jiageng pointed his foot at the ground, Wuzhuo said, "Do not slander others" (Pudeng). The *Fuhufa lun* (Treatise on Protecting the Dharma) states:
"The heart of the Layman Wujin in protecting the Dharma may be called ultimate. Within the Three Teachings, there are admonitions and warnings in all of them.
Yet, that which is bitter to the mouth is a potent medicine; that which is contrary to the ear is loyal counsel. In truth, those who point out and rebuke the faults of Yang Xiu are I [myself]."
To know this is to realize there is nothing else; it is what is meant by "punishing one to warn the hundred. Those who read this should understand it fully.

Jiang Zhiqi—his courtesy name was Yingshu—was selected for the Xianliang Fangzheng (Worthy and Upright) examination during the reign of Emperor Renzong. He was tested on six treatises and rose to the rank of Hanlin [Academician].
Lin Xueshi served as Vice President of the Bureau of Military Affairs. He once composed a preface to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which states in brief:
"Zhiqi formerly suffered from the difficulty of reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the rarity of obtaining a good edition.

When Lord Zhang, the Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince and retired official, bestowed this scripture, Su Zizhan of Meishan transcribed it and carved it into printing blocks for the permanent endowment of Jinshan Temple."
The Elder of Mount Jinshan, the Great Master Liyuan Foyin, has sent this to me for my inspection. Zhiqi speaks of it, saying:
"The sutras spoken by the Buddha comprise twelve divisions in total, yet they amount to as many as five thousand scrolls.

During the period when the True Dharma was circulating, there were those who attained awakening and entry [into the truth] upon hearing but half a verse or a single phrase; indeed, such instances were beyond counting."

This serves as a measure of the number [of teachings]. Reaching the period after the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma, when the Sage had long departed, people began to drown in words and letters;
they encountered the hardship of "entering the sea to count its sands," becoming arrogant and failing to comprehend the single true essence.

Thereupon, the Patriarchs appeared, directly pointing to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha, establishing this as the "Separate Transmission outside the Teachings. Regarding movement...
In the mere instant it takes to utter these words, those of superior faculties and sharp instruments have already perceived and attained them through direct observation.
Zhiqi visited Zhang Gong at the Southern Capital and personally heard him recount how, after serving as Director of the Three Departments and Hanlin Academician, he was appointed to govern Chuzhou.
One day, he entered a monastery in Langya and saw a scripture case; upon opening and looking inside, it was the *Lengyan* [Sutra].
It was a sutra. Suddenly, he realized it was something he had written in a previous life; the calligraphy was perfectly distinct.

He considered this to be the result of karmic conditions from past habituation. When people, possessing this one true and indestructible nature, undergo birth, death, and transmigration within the realm of heaven and earth, the number of such worldly cycles is so vast that even if one were to break all the grasses and trees under heaven to use them as counting sticks, they would not suffice to calculate them.

One can indeed calculate it; however, because one has sunk into the cycle of birth and death, the conscious spirit becomes exhausted and can no longer remember it. Only those whose minds are perfectly bright and unclouded know this.

It is like the case of Lord Zhang, who, having passed the imperial examinations with two successive high-scholarship degrees for his elegant compositions and grand treatises, [was later unable to recall them].

He served as an attendant and held the highest offices of state; for over forty years he moved between the imperial court and its halls, his heroic character and meritorious deeds spreading through the ears and eyes of the people.
Thus, there is no room for doubt that his former incarnation must have been a great spiritual teacher (*mahāsattva*).
That he was able to recall the events of his previous life—how could this not be considered truly credible?
Guo Xiangzheng, whose courtesy name was Gongfu, held the official rank of Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Dianzhongcheng). He had a residence known as the "Hermitage of Drunken Recitation.
Gongfu traveled from Dangtu across the river to pay his respects to Chan Master Baiyun Yuan of Shuzhou. The Master asked, "Is the ox pure? Gongfu replied:
"Chun! The Master rebuked him. Gongfu immediately stood with his hands folded in reverence. The Master said, "Chun! Chun! Nanquan and Dayue were no different from this.
He then presented a verse, saying: "When the ox comes into the mountains, there is plenty of water and plenty of grass;
when the ox leaves the mountains, it bumps into things to the east and to the west. One day, he went to Huangmei Dongsan to invite Chan Master Yan to preach the Dharma. Thereupon...

Before the Dharma seat, he held up the incense and said: "This single portion of incense is burned within the burner to form clouds of light that pervade the entire Dharma realm, as an offering to my elder brother, the Zen Master, the Hall Head.

I humbly pray that from within these clouds, upon this vast and square Dharma throne, you will split open your face and manifest the physical likeness of our late Master for all people to behold. Why is this so?"
We met long ago by the side of White Cloud Rock; yesterday and today, matters are not the same. The night is still and the water cold, so the fish do not feed;
a single burner of incense wafts with the breeze of white lotuses. (Compiled by Ziji and the General Record)

Qin Guan, whose courtesy name was Shaoyou and sobriquet Taixu Gong, was a native of Gaoyou. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, Dongpo recommended him to the court as a man of "Worthy and Rectified Integrity" (Xianliang Fangzheng).
He was appointed as a Doctor of the Imperial Academy (Taixue Boshi) and served as a Compiler at the National University (Guozibianxiu). Dongpo had also previously recommended him.
Regarding the Duke Wang Anshi, Anshi said: "You, Lord Qi, have spoken of Master Qin incessantly; I have obtained his writings and have not laid them aside from my hands.
Observing that your family has served the Buddha for generations, I heard of the reputation of Master Duan Shizi.
One day, when Duan arrived at Gaoyou, Guan invited him to ascend the seat at Guanghui Temple. Duan pointed to himself with his hand and said: 'There is no one above heaven...'"
Two moons. In the human world there is but a single monk. A hall of wind and cold; the meaning of a thousand ages is clear. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* regarding Guanken.
There is a record of the Five Hundred Arhats (*Pañcāśat-arhat-citra*). See also the records of Baolin and Longjing (details are found in the *Huaihai ji*).
Lin Bu, courtesy name Junfu. Mei Shengyu composed a preface for Lin’s poetry, which states in brief:

"During the Tiānshèng era, I heard that on the western shore of Níng-hǎi there was a gentleman named Lin, whose outstanding reputation was like that of a lofty peak or a cascading spring—lovely to behold from afar."
The closer one approaches him, the purer he becomes; drawing from him, one finds his sweetness and purity never wearying.

During the Xianping and Jingde eras, the Emperor was preparing for the rites of Feng and Shan, yet before an imperial summons could be issued, the Master passed away, never reaching old age in a time where he might have exerted his influence. Thus it was when he died.
He was posthumously titled Master Hejing. He once composed a poem to see off the Chan Master Ciyun, saying: "High banners and bear-drawn carriages hide the silent bell-chamber;
The shade of the *táng* trees grows thick with long green moss. The Chancellor’s prestige is so great that visitors are few;
Pure discourse must surely await the arrival of this man of the Way. At Tiantzhu, amidst the rugged peaks, he briefly closed his door; The fragrance of incense drifted upon the incense-needles.

The upper robe for traveling; amidst the cries of white monkeys, the Stone of Master Sheng. Do not send a formal letter of protest because I return late. In response to the poem by the Great Master Ciyun of Tiantong:

The color of the mountain beyond the forest flies toward me; I still feel ashamed that I have long been a neighbor here. Following the winding path of a single stream, my dreams wander to the people of the Five Indias.

I decline visitors so the weeds in the empty garden may flourish; I sink into such deep meditation that dust fills the surface of my desk. If the evening clouds have any... [Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.]
[Response: Yes. Please accept my frequent greetings (from the *Benji*). Yin Zhu, courtesy name Shilu, was a profound scholar of the *Chunqiu*.
At the beginning of the Qingli era, he was appointed as Record Keeper (*Qiji Sheren*), but was subsequently demoted to serve as Supervisor of Junzhou.
Shui passed away. His grandson was Yin Hejing. Initially, when Shi Lu’s illness became critical, Fan Zizheng ordered Zhu Yan to go by night to visit him.
Shi Lu asked Yan, "How is my life and death? Yan replied, "The pulse is not favorable.
Shi Lu said, "I know it myself. He then spoke of how he had long studied Buddhism under Chan Master Fazhao, saying, "Now..."
He relied upon this. At evening, when the third drum was struck, he withdrew his attendants, leaned against his desk, and passed away; his spirit remained undisturbed (*Fujiao bian*).

Bao Zheng, whose courtesy name was Xiren, served as the Vice Minister of the Censorate during the Qingli era. Later, he was appointed to the Bureau of Military Affairs and posthumously received the title Xiaosu. Heaven...
He was by nature stern and never showed a smile. People said that Lord Bao’s smile was as rare as the waters of the Yellow River becoming clear.
When he served as the Governor of Jingzhao, a citizen came forward and testified, "I once entrusted one hundred taels of white gold to you; it has been lost. I have now returned it to my family."
The son would not accept it. The Duke hoped to summon the son back to return it, but sighed in wonder at this. He immediately summoned the son and spoke with him.
The son declined, saying, "During my late father's lifetime, there were no silver coins privately deposited in another house. The two men yielded to one another for a long time.
The Duke then entrusted the gold to a temple within the city to cultivate merit for the afterlife and offer it as a memorial for his departed spirit (from the *Benzhuan*).

Jiang Gongwang, courtesy name Minbiao, was a native of Diaotai. During the reign of Emperor Huizong, he was appointed as the Left Assistant Censor-in-Chief. He maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced pure cultivation;
he composed the *Bodhi Text* and the *Text on the Expedient Means of Buddha-Recitation* to exhort both the clergy and the laity. His son died young, and he appeared in a dream to his maternal uncle.
He said, "I have received instructions from my father to go to Tianning Temple to read the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, so that he may be reborn in a favorable realm.

My father’s practice and cultivation are already complete; there is a golden tablet in the Netherworld which says: 'Gong Wang of Yanzhou, though holding a position of official censure, aspired to the truth of suffering and emptiness.
He personally engaged in incense-offering and cultivation, his mind free from attachment, never forgetting [the Dharma] whether in motion or stillness.'"

In his Buddhist discourse, he never deviated from the essential spirit of the tradition; his name was already inscribed upon the dark portal of liberation, and his body would surely return to the Pure Land.
At the end of the Xuande era, while serving as the Prefect of Guangde Commandery, he suddenly passed away facing west without illness. Gongwang once said:
For those of sharp faculties, every thought-moment does not arise, and every mind has no objective referent. The six sense-faculties are profoundly still, and all consciousnesses subside.
Every dharma is entirely true, and every gate is free from dependence. In a mere flash, one attains the true and actual contemplation.

For beginners and later students, the only times they may temporarily suspend their mindfulness are when exchanging greetings with guests or during the times of urination and defecation; even these should be avoided if possible. If one cannot yet avoid them, [one must remain mindful].

Regarding the consumption of pungent vegetables: even while sleeping before the onset of deep darkness, or even while attending to household affairs and various types of labor, one need not abandon them, nor do they pose any mutual hindrance.
From moment to moment and sound to sound, one should recite the sacred name with mind and mouth;
how could any further perverse thoughts or evil considerations dare to sprout in the heart? Thus, it naturally becomes pure and unmixed. If one can fully restrain the six [sense-faculties]...
With the faculties pure and mindfulness continuous, one will achieve samādhi within ten days or a month. This is what is meant by "this mind creates the Buddha;
this mind is the Buddha. Those of superior faculties and great capacity transcend directly in a single thought-moment; those of ordinary disposition should skillfully contemplate the expedient means.

Yang Shi, whose courtesy name was Zhongli and sobriquet was Master Guishan, was a disciple of Mingdao. His learning possessed a profound foundation, and he became a preeminent Confucian master of his generation.
During the reign of Emperor Huizong, he served as the Director of the National University. He once remarked: "Wei Sheng Gao begged for vinegar in order to give it away to others."
Confucius did not consider this to be straightforwardness. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "A straightforward mind is the Great Dharma Hall.

When it comes to this point, the principles of Confucianism and Buddhism are truly no different. Furthermore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Activity, cessation, indulgence, and extinction—these are the four illnesses.

"Activity" refers to forced cultivation; "cessation" refers to non-weeding; "indulgence" and "extinction" refer to doing nothing (from the *Ming Dao Ji*). At that time, he was a friend to Chan Master Zong of Donglin.
Shan said to Master [Zhaozhou]: "Although your Zen studies are profound, you have not yet attained anything in the Confucian learning.

The Master replied: "As for the most essential points of Confucian learning, I remember a little. But tell me, when it says 'the gentleman finds self-satisfaction in whatever he enters,' what is it that he attains?
At that time, Shi remained silent. The Master then spoke to Shi about the ten consciousnesses. Regarding the eighth, the *āmalavijñāna* (amala-consciousness), this is called...
