This occurred at a time when neither good nor evil had yet sprouted. At that moment, he asked again, "Is it true, as Mencius says, that human nature is good?
The Master replied, "It is. He then asked, "In what sense can one say that nature is good? The Master said, "The primordial nature does not stand in opposition to evil."
Later, Zhu Xi remarked that this statement by Elder Zong was indeed [profound] (*Xishan Dushuji*).
You Ze, whose courtesy name was Dingfu, studied together with Yang Shi at the gate of Yi Chuan. During the reign of Emperor Huizong, he was appointed as a Censor.
The Censor once visited Chan Master Kaifu Ning to request instruction on the essential point of the mind. The Master said, "The Way does not reside in speaking or demonstrating.
Speaking and demonstrating are merely skillful means. You must rely upon yourself to know where you return. Seeking an external Buddha with form is not compatible with you.
The Censor remained silent. Later, he sent a letter to the Master, saying: "Confucianists cling to the roles of father and son, ruler and..."
"Your subjects—wives, husbands, brothers, and friends—each fulfill their respective duties; there is none among them who does not accord with the Way.

The teachings of Śākyamuni claim that the world is illusory and seek to lead people to transcend the ordinary and oppose the Way. Since their fundamental principles differ and their applications are distinct, how can their sounds enter the ears and their meanings penetrate the mind?
The Master replied: "People are submerged in the dust of passions and the net of craving. Day and night they contemplate and scheme, without a single moment’s rest."
One must exert effort to resolve this; I pray you will gather back the wandering of the mind. Only then can one transcend birth and death.

If one merely categorizes similarities and differences, exhausting oneself within the confines of the relationship between father and son, my habits will continue to perfume from within and my attachments will stain me from without.

How could I then be able to achieve union with the Way? If one can reverse these habitual tendencies, the mind will naturally attain penetration and the Way will naturally be realized. Otherwise, it is difficult.
"Speech and tongue are contention" (Zi Jian).
Han Ju, courtesy name Zicang, was appointed as *Zhengzi* at the beginning of the Zhenghe era and eventually served as *Dai-zhi* of the *Huiyou Ge*. He belonged to the Jiangxi School of Poetry.
This is the first [point]. He once sought the Way from Chan Master Qing of Caotang, sending him a letter that said: "Recently, I have been reading the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp).

My understanding surpasses mere intellectual speculation, and it resonates quite well with my mind. However, worldly entanglements are as manifold as a thousand threads, and emotional habits are as diverse as ten thousand strands; it is not easy to dissolve them."
"There must be a vital point for clarifying the mind; do not be stingy with your instruction.

Qing replied, "If you wish to investigate this matter, let neither good nor evil arise in your mind, as both can obstruct the eye of wisdom. You need not read many texts either, for they block the door to self-awakening.
Having received this guidance, Zicang expressed his realization, saying: "The bells and tripods of the court and the mountain forests are no different."

To reach the state where the interests of leisure dwell within the tranquility of stillness, one brings all that is heard and seen back to empty illumination; thus nourishing one’s nature and preserving the mind, one asks no more of others.
By Lü Zhengji.
Zhengji was a Scholar of the Hall of Manifesting Propaganda (Xianmu Ge). He attended Chan Master Qian’an Ren of Changlu, who once asked him, “Who is it that hides a pearl within his robes?
The Master rose, shook himself, and said, “There is not a single thing. Zhengji responded with respectful assent.
The Master presented him with a verse, saying: "You have now arrived intimately at Changlu; Shaking out your robes, you possess nothing.
Should you encounter anyone on your way who asks of you, Simply say: 'The wind is fierce and the waves are rough. Zhengji then offered a verse of his own:

"A needle meeting a magnet—our affinity was established long ago. For a thousand years I stood alone in the cold of the snowy courtyard. If a Zen practitioner asks about the path ahead, Ten thousand..."
It is not difficult to reach Chang’an from here. The Master approved [of this] (at Ziji).

The Southern Song dynasty began in the *dingwei* year of Emperor Gaozong’s reign and ended with the last ruler in the *bingzi* year. It comprised seven emperors over a period of one hundred and fifty years.
Emperor Gaozong, whose personal name was Gou, was the ninth son of Emperor Huizong. His mother was Lady Wei. Emperor Huizong had dreamed that the King of Wusuku, Qian, entered his chamber.

The Emperor was born thereafter; he was initially enfeoffed as Prince Kang and ascended the throne at Songzhou. On the day Dingwei, the first year of Jianyan was established. The Emperor traveled to Weiyang.
In the first month of the second year, he issued an edict for Keqin, the abbot of Jinshan, to enter the imperial presence.

Eight persons dispatched by the Emperor escorted the Master up to the hall and granted him a seat. "I have long known that your Way, Master, is lofty and wondrous; may I hear of it? the Emperor asked.
The Master said, "Your Majesty governs the world with benevolence and filial piety; all living beings within the realm are bathed in its radiance.
Even the grasses, trees, insects, and other creatures each find their proper place—this is the mind transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Outside of this mind, there is no other mind.
If there were another mind, it would not be the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the name Yuanwu.

[The Emperor] conferred [upon him] the title. The Master, by imperial decree, went to the Yongxi Chan Temple in Yangzhou to preach the Dharma. The Emperor asked the Master how he was finding it at Mount Jinshan.

He replied, "Mount Jinshan is situated in the midst of the Great River. Your servant is old and ill; I wish to return to the mountain forests to spend out my natural years. Thereupon, an edict was issued for him to reside at Yunju in Jiangxi.
Three years later, the Jurchen were about to reach Yangzhou, and the Emperor crossed the river to—
He traveled from Zhenjiang to Hangzhou. Hangzhou was elevated to the status of Lin’an Prefecture. On the twelfth month, he arrived at Mingzhou.
In the fourth year, he reached Zhang’an Town in Tāizhōu. On the third day of the first month, he entered Jīn’áo Mountain Temple, where a monk was offering prayers before the Buddha.

These were all words concerning the preservation of the state during times of distress. The Emperor asked which scripture they were from; the monk replied, "The *Golden Light Repentance for Protecting the State* (*Jinguangming huoguo chanwen*).
In the second month, while the Emperor was stationed at Jiangxin Temple in Wenzhou, he heard that the monks’ prayers and offerings were most devout, and he was pleased.

He bestowed upon the temple the plaque name "Longxiang" (Dragon Soaring). In the *Xinhai* year, the reign title was changed to Shaoxing. In the second year, while the imperial camp was stationed in Lin’an, he had the Dharma Master Fadao accompany him on his travels.

During the Southern Tour, the Emperor issued an edict for Dao to enter the palace and have an audience. The Emperor spoke to him with composure, saying, "The Retired Emperor was deluded by a sorcerer and destroyed your monastic form and robes.
I have removed this branding for you, Master. Dao replied, "I could not bear to destroy or remove the ink applied by the Retired Emperor.
The Emperor laughed and said, "This monk remains stubborn to the end. By imperial decree, Dao was appointed to reside at Taiping Chan Temple in Donglin. Five years later, the Emperor...
He visited Shang Tianzhu, where he offered the Wan-sui Xiangshan incense burner to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. He summoned the abbot Yingru for an audience, whose responses pleased the Emperor;
consequently, gold and silk were bestowed to encourage the restoration of the temple. In the seventh year, an imperial edict appointed Zonggao as the abbot of Nengren Chan Monastery at Mount Jing.
In the eighth year, an edict was issued granting silk and ordination certificates (*du-ji*) to all monks and nuns throughout the realm. In the ninth year, a general amnesty was proclaimed.
An imperial edict was issued to establish Baoen Guangxiao Chan Monastery in various military prefectures and circuits as a place for the posthumous offerings for Emperor Huizong.
In the twenty-sixth year, when Zonggao returned from Meiyang, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Guangli Chan Monastery in Yuyang, Mingzhou.
In the twenty-eighth year [of the reign], an imperial edict summoned Miaogao to reside once again at Mount Jing.
In the thirtieth year, an edict conferred the posthumous title of Venerable Ciyun upon Tianzhu, styling him the Dharma Master Chanhui and the Patriarch of Repentance; his stupa was named Rui Guang.

Toward the end of the Shaoxing era, the Emperor, having been moved by a dream, invited the image of the State-Protecting Mārīcī-devī and enshrined it at Zhong Tianzhu Temple to pray for favorable rain and sunshine.
The temple’s plaque was subsequently changed to read Tianning Wanshou Yongzuo Chan Temple.

Initially, in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era, Vinaya Master Yuanzhao passed away and his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Lingzhi on West Lake. Upon this occasion, light emanated from the site of the stupa;
the Emperor personally came to inspect it and bestowed the posthumous title of Vinaya Master Yuanjian Jieguang Dazhi. The Emperor had once inscribed [the name] in gold within the imperial palace.

The *Gang*, *Yuánjué*, *Pǔmén pǐn*, *Xīnjīng*, and the *Verses of the Seven Buddhas*. During my leisure time, I have personally perused these [based on the *Jīgǔ lüè*, *Tǒngjì*, and inscriptions from Zhōngzhú].
Emperor Xiaozong’s taboo name was Shèn. His original name was Bòcóng; he was the son of Prince Cēng of Xiuzhou and a seventh-generation descendant of Emperor Taizu.
Bòcóng was born in Xiuzhou, where there was an auspicious omen of a "fine grain" (jiáhé). Following the death of the Crown Prince, Gāozōng selected Bòcóng and raised him as his heir.

In the palace, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Puan and established as a Crown Prince, being granted the name Wei. At the end of the Shaoxing era, his name was changed to Shen, and he was established as the Heir Apparent.
At the age of thirty-six, he received the internal abdication [of the throne] and changed the reign title to Longxing (as recorded in the *History*).
While the Emperor was still in the princely residence, he dispatched the Inner Supervisor Huang Yanjie to Jingshan to command Chan Master Gaofeng to propagate the Dharma within the mountains.
Regarding Banruo (Prajñā), the Master spoke a verse, saying: "Great root, great vessel, great power; shouldering the great task is extraordinary.
A message is transmitted upon the tip of a single hair; throughout the entire world it is manifest and unrevealed. The Emperor praised this highly.
Upon the enfeoffment of the Prince, he again dispatched the Inner Official-in-Chief to Jingshan to provide offerings for five hundred arhats and bestowed three [buildings] upon Miaoxi Hermitage.
[He composed] verses and true eulogies. Furthermore, he praised the Monk with the Cloth Bag (Pūgakaśyapa), rhyming with the style of Emperor Gaozong:
"The bag contains heaven and earth; the staff carries sun and moon. Rough and rugged, he is the peerless among sages. Dull and simple, he is the preeminent among monks.
When his command is issued, one blow leaves a scar upon every person. To provoke the potential of others, one must see blood when killing. Distinct, distinct—it is clearly one [truth]."
"Melting the Snow from the Brazier. In the seventh month of the first year of the Longxing era, the Emperor ascended to Xuande Hall and composed a eulogy for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, saying:
"Ah, the Great Being! Originally self-perfected and all-pervading, yet manifesting speech to serve as the world’s sovereign. His illumination is non-dual; he regards all with equal compassion.
Responding immediately to every stimulus, his wondrousness is inconceivable. In the ninth month, he issued an edict summoning Chan Master Gaofeng.
He inquired about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, but the Master remained lying ill and did not rise; nevertheless, he was specially granted the title "Dahui" (Great Wisdom).
In the second month of the third year of the Qiandao era, the Emperor visited Shang Tianzhu Temple to pay his respects to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
He asked the abbot, Ruone, why the temple performed the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* repentance ritual annually. Ruone replied, "The Great Brahmā Heaven King is the lord of this Sahā world. Śakra..."
Śakra, Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens, governs from above while overseeing the lands below. The Four Great Kings of the Quarters have sworn together to protect the state and its people.
Therefore, the Buddha preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-samādhi* for the sake of the devas; this is the scripture for the flourishing era of an imperial sovereign.
"Therefore, it is appropriate that this be repaired every year. The Emperor was pleased. He promoted Nŏk to the rank of Right Street Monk-Registrar (Yujang Sŏngnok).

On the eighth day of the fourth month of the fourth year, he issued an edict for Nŏk to lead fifty monks into the Inner Contemplation Hall (Naegwanchang) to perform the *Ratnaketudhāraṇī* (Kumgang Sammae) ritual for the protection of the state.

After the meal, he commanded Nŏk to preach the Dharma. The Emperor was pleased and promoted him to Left Street Monk-Registrar (Jajang Sŏngnok), granting him the title Hwigwang (according to the *Gigeomnok*). In the tenth month of the sixth year...
By imperial decree, Xiatang Huiyuan, the abbot of Chongxian Monastery on Gaotingshan in Hangzhou, was appointed to serve as the abbot of Lingyin Chan Temple.
One day, while the Emperor was visiting Xiadu, he saw a water-strainer and a walking-observance Avalokiteśvara image in the kitchen of Foguo Mountain.
He summoned Huiyuan and asked, "Since this mountain once flew here, why does it not fly away? Huiyuan replied, "Movement is not as good as stillness. Furthermore—
A questioner asked, "If one uses a net to scoop up sentient beings from within the water, what does one use to scoop up sentient beings within the fire?
Yuan said, "They have their own path that reaches through the heavens. He was asked again, "What does Guanyin recite while holding his rosary in his hand?

Yuan said, "Seeking others is not as good as seeking oneself. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-Sea" (Zi Jian). In the second month of the seventh year, he summoned Yuan.
He entered to have an audience in Xuande Hall and was granted a seat. The Emperor asked, "How can one escape birth and death?

Yuan said, "If one does not awaken to the Mahayana, one will ultimately never be able to escape. The Emperor asked, "How does one attain awakening? Yuan said, "As for the nature that is inherently present, there is no one who does not awaken upon investigating it.
The Emperor asked, "What is it like after awakening? Yuan said, "Only then does one know that liberation is manifest before one; there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything remaining."

[The Emperor] saw his hair and nodded in approval (*Jigulüe*). In the third month of the second year of the Chunxi era, the Emperor visited Shangzhu Temple and bestowed one seal for the Baiyun Hall and one seal for the Lingyin Zhizhi Hall, each being a single piece.
[He was appointed] to oversee the affairs of the Buddhist teachings (*Shangzhu Stele*).
In the spring of the third year, an imperial edict summoned Deguang, the abbot of Ba’en Guangxiao Temple in Taizhou, to have an audience with the Emperor.
In the second month, Guang crossed the river. The Emperor asked, "In antiquity, there was one who crossed by floating a straw hat; can this be called supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)?

Guang replied, "Within our school, we do not value supernatural powers; we only value the clarity of the eye. The Emperor was pleased and issued an edict for Guang to reside at Lingyin Temple, succeeding Yuan in the abbacy.
In the eleventh month, he summoned Guang to the Inner Contemplation Hall. The Emperor asked, "Is my mind the same as the Buddha-mind?"
This was a different [question]. Guang said, "Directly beneath, there is no second person. The Emperor said, "If that is so, then the Buddha is the mind, and the mind is the Buddha.
Guang said, "To manifest all phenomena is the mind; to be free from all phenomena is the Buddha.
He asked again, "What did the Old Śākyamuni accomplish during his six years in the Snow Mountains? Guang said, "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten. The Emperor—

The Emperor was greatly pleased and conferred upon him the title *Fozhao* (Monk-Inspector). In the autumn of the seventh year, he summoned Bao Yin, the abbot of Xuedou Temple, for an audience at Xuande Hall.
The Emperor said, "The sages of the Three Teachings are fundamentally one in this principle. Bao Yin replied, "It is like empty space;
east, west, south, and north are originally no different from one another. The Emperor remarked, "Nowadays, the scholar-officials study Confucius..."
"Most people are merely skilled in words and language; they do not see the Way of the Master, nor do they know the mind of the Master.
Only the followers of the Śākya school do not teach by means of written characters, but point directly to the source of the mind, enabling sudden awakening and entry.
Thus, they are not disturbed at the moment of death and rebirth—this is what makes them superior. Yan said, "It is not only that scholars of later generations do not see the Master..."
Regarding this mind, at that time Yanzi of the Confucian school was hailed as the one who embodied it in its entirety;

yet he could only say, "Looking for it, it seems to be before me; suddenly, it is behind me," or "It stands there, as if towering and distinct. The Emperor asked, "What kind of person were Zhuangzi and Laozi?
Yunmen replied, "They were simply the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna within the Buddha-dharma. This is because the Hīnayāna regards the body with loathing, as if it were a pair of shackles."

Abandoning wisdom is like discarding a mixture of poisons; it is as if a transformative fire were to incinerate one’s body. This is precisely what Zhuangzi meant when he said: "The form may indeed be made like withered wood;
the mind may indeed be made like extinguished ashes. As for those of the Mahāyāna, they realize Bodhi only after they have fully delivered all sentient beings.
This is exactly as Yi Yin said: "I am one among the people of Heaven who has awakened first; I shall use this Way to awaken them."
"Among these people, if there were even a single individual who did not receive its benefits, it would be as if I had pushed him into a ditch myself.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict appointing Yin to reside at Mount Jing. In the spring of the tenth year, the Emperor annotated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuanjue jing) and commanded Yin to carve printing blocks for its publication.
He requested an imperial seal for his retirement at Taiguan-ām. The Emperor bestowed upon the hermitage the name Byeopung (Record of Memorial Responses).
In the sixteenth year, the Emperor abdicated the throne and retired to Namhwa-gung. He composed the "Treatise on the Origin of the Way" (*Wonyo-non*), which states in brief:

"I observe that Han Yu’s *On the Origin of the Way* speaks of the confusion between Buddhism and Daoism and the mutual subordination of the Three Teachings; however, it is merely prolix in its phrasing and remote in its reasoning. When one evaluates the Sage..."

Their application of the mind is not yet clearly evident. Why is this? The followers of Śākya exclusively investigate nature and destiny, cast aside external forms and physical bodies, and do not cling to names or appearances;

how then can they be compared with ritual, music, benevolence, and righteousness? Nevertheless, they establish the five precepts, saying: "Not killing is benevolence; not committing sexual misconduct is propriety;
not stealing is righteousness; not drinking intoxicants is wisdom; and not speaking falsely is faith. In this regard, they are indeed similar.
How distant is Zhongni (Confucius) from this? The Book of Laozi identifies three things as its treasures: benevolence, frugality, and not daring to take precedence over the world.
The gate of Confucius speaks of being mild, kind, respectful, frugal, and yielding. Is it truly contradictory to the Sage Confucius?

It is merely that the ignorant followers of the later traditions of the Three Teachings cling to these distinctions and treat them as different. I, the Emperor, maintain that one cultivates the mind through Buddhism.

"To nourish life through the Way of the Elder (Laozi) and to govern the world through the Way of the Confucian (Ru) is indeed appropriate" (*Shengzheng lu*). Emperor Guangzong’s posthumous name was Dūn;
he was the fifth son of Emperor Xiaozong. At the age of forty-four, he received the abdication from the position of Crown Prince and honored Emperor Xiaozong [as his father].

He served as the Retired Emperor (Taishanghuang). At the beginning of the Shaoxi era, when the Emperor resided at the Zhonghua Palace, he issued an edict permitting Dharma Master Ruone to enter and exit by palanquin.

He presented his commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, for which the Emperor composed a eulogy. In the first month of the fourth year, an edict was issued appointing Chan Master Fozhao Deguang to reside at Mount Jing.

Emperor Ningzong’s posthumous name was Kuò. He was the son of Emperor Guangzong and was initially enfeoffed as Prince Jia. In the first year of the Qingyuan era, an imperial edict permitted Fozhao to return to Yuyang Monastery to retire at Dong’an.
In the third year, an edict appointed Chan Master Chongyue to reside at Lingyin Monastery.
Emperor Lizong’s original name was Yujü. He was the son of Prince Xilun and a tenth-generation descendant of Taizu, as well as the nephew of Ningzong. His name was later changed to Mingdi.

At the age of twenty, he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Baoping, the first year of which fell in that year. In the fourth year, there was a drought, and an edict was issued to provide protection.
Chan Master Huikai of Ning Temple ascended the seat in Wende Hall to pray for rain; his prayers were answered, and he was granted the title "Buddha-Eye.

In the first year of the Jiaxi era, Empress Dowager Wang passed away. An imperial decree summoned Chan Master Shifan of Mount Jing to an audience at Xiuzheng Hall, where he was presented with a golden-embroidered monastic robe.
He was then ordered to ascend the seat in Ciming Hall to preach the Dharma, while the Emperor listened from behind a lowered curtain.
He was bestowed the title Fojian (Buddha-Mirror). Following the passing of Emperor Gongsheng Renshile, the Emperor again issued an edict for Master Shanfan to ascend the seat.

Subsequently, the Master requested to retire to the mountain forests, whereupon he was further granted the title Yuanzhao (Perfect Illumination). In the first year of the Chunyou era, the Emperor dreamed of Avalokiteśvara sitting amidst bamboo and rocks;
upon waking, he had a portrait drawn and carved in stone, inscribing the imperial eulogy: "The spiritual powers are most subtle—hidden and manifest."
It is unfathomable. His merit is boundless; how swift is his response! May the seasons be harmonious and the harvests bountiful, blessing our people.

May weapons be laid aside and punishments cease, bringing peace to this kingdom. He further inscribed the four great characters "Great and Vast Responsive Manifestation" above the sacred name of Guanyin.
He also transcribed one scroll of the *Heart Sūtra* and bestowed it upon Upper Zhi for carving into stone. Furthermore, he composed a thousand-verse hymn.

A Buddhist verse says: "One Buddha is not two; how could a thousand Buddhas differ? They are like water everywhere, or the moon reflected in the present moment—neither coming nor going, neither arising nor ceasing.
After the plum blossoms have bloomed, there is deep snow in the village ahead.

He also inscribed the four great characters "Yingmeng Mingshan" (Famous Mountain Answering a Dream) and bestowed them upon Xuedou Chan Temple in Siming (along with the temple's administrative records and its stele).

Zhang Jun, whose courtesy name was De-yuan and sobriquet Ziyan, was appointed as Chancellor during the Shaoxing era. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of He, and during the reign of Emperor Xiaozong, he was further enfeoffed as the Duke of Wei.
His posthumous title was Zhongxian. He was the father of Nanxuan. When Master Qinquan of Yuanwu returned to Sichuan, he resided at Zhaojue Temple.
At the temple, the Duke asked the Master about the Way. The Master said, "Yantou said: 'To reject external things is superior; to pursue external things is inferior.
If you can swiftly turn back from within objects, all things will stand in the shadow of your realization. The Master further showed him this verse: "Retract the radiance and gather the splendor;
trust in the true nature. In every matter, all is perfected; in every object, all is new. If there is a mind within, there are still objects."
"How can one move forward to reach the thoroughfare? The Duke bowed in acceptance and offered this verse: "The teaching transmitted outside the scriptures is the pivot of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
Originally there is neither awakening nor delusion. When drifting clouds have dispersed, the blue sky remains; The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night.
The Master approved, saying, "In your days as a high minister, do not forget to protect the Teaching. This occurred when Chan Master Dahui was in Quanzhou.
In the province of Zhuzhou, Master Yunguan was residing in Shu; Yuanwu personally entrusted him as his successor, declaring that he had truly attained the marrow of the Dharma.

When the Master returned to the capital, Yuanwu immediately invited him to Mount Jing in Lin’an Prefecture, fearing that the Master might wish to remain in seclusion and thus determined to bring him there by all means.
He then sent a letter to Liu Gongyan, the Magistrate of Quan, urging him to set out. The Master rose from his seat with a start. Gong was residing in Changsha;
his mother, Lady Qin, had been seeking the Way from Dahui. When the Lady’s illness became critical, she said, "I shall never see Teacher Miaoxi again in this life.
I have a private debt of gratitude that remains unpaid. Gong then dispatched three messengers to Yichun.
He set out for the Master’s dwelling and traveled with double the usual speed. Upon his arrival, the Lady had already passed away. The Master addressed the Teacher, saying:
"My late mother wished to provide for the Venerable Master for one year as a reward for her virtue. Now that she is no longer here, I respectfully follow her final instructions.
I pray that you will deign to remain for the duration of the *navarātra* (the nine-month summer retreat), so that I may fulfill my reverent service and console my late mother’s wish."
Second, he extended the heart of a filial son and subsequently lodged him in the Eastern Hall of Guangxiao Temple to fulfill his utmost sincerity and reverence (*Za jian* and *Da hui nian pu*).
Toward the end of the Shaoxing era, when the Master was serving as the Governor of Jiankang Commandery, he once composed a biographical sketch of Master Baoshi, which states in brief:
"The Master’s name was Baoshi. He was a native of Jinling. During the Yuanjia period of the Song dynasty, he manifested his presence at an ancient tree in the Dongyang Market."
In the midst of an eagle’s nest, the wife of the Zhu family heard the crying of an infant; she subsequently took him in and raised him. Consequently, he took Zhu as his surname.

Later, she donated her residence to become a monastery, which is the present-day Baolin Monastery. The Master’s facial features were like a mirror and his hands were like eagle claws, unlike those of ordinary children.
At the age of seven, he entered Zongshan Daolin Monastery in the capital, where he served Master Sengjian and practiced the discipline of Chan meditation.
At the beginning of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he suddenly left this monastery. He had no fixed dwelling and carried a single *khakkhara* staff.

He hung items such as a knife, a ruler, a whisk, a mirror, and silk cloths from it. He walked barefoot through the marketplace with his hair several inches long, eating and drinking without discrimination.
At times he would go several days without eating yet show no signs of hunger; at other times he would eat several times a day yet show no appearance of satiety.
During the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty, his extraordinary deeds were widely renowned, and those among the gentry and commoners who venerated him were beyond counting.

When Emperor Wu of the Liang ascended the throne, he treated the Master with even greater honor and courtesy. Once, the Master requested minced fish from the Emperor; although the Emperor granted his request, he felt a certain distaste for it. The Master then...
He spat water into a basin, and the fish were alive as before. A piece of wood was floating in the river, moving upstream against the current.
The Emperor, the Master, and the commoners watched it; the Master raised his staff and gave a single beckoning gesture, and the wood followed him to the bank—it was sandalwood.

The Emperor commanded the court artisan Yu Sengshao to carve an image of the Master. Once it was completed, it was a perfect likeness, save for the lack of beard and hair. The Master then plucked out his own hair.

He tucked [the image] into his two sideburns, and his hair grew along with it. The Emperor ordered Zhang Sengyou to paint a portrait of the Master’s true likeness, but he was ultimately unable to complete it.
The Master then used his fingernail to part the opening of his face, revealing the form of the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara, and said:
"Vipaśyin Buddha first set his mind [on this] long ago; yet until this very day, the wondrous [form] has not been attained. When Xu Ling was three years old, his father took him to see [the Master].
The Master stroked his head and said, "This is a stone qilin from the heavens.
In the winter of the Bingyin year of the Zhongda Tong era, the Master moved the golden statue from Hualin Garden to his own quarters. The Emperor asked, "Are you going to leave me?
Less than ten days later, in the twelfth month of that same year, he manifested illness. The Emperor ordered music to be played day and night without ceasing. This continued until the sixth day.
He passed away at Xinghuang Temple, and his entire body was interred on Mount Zhong. The Imperial Princess Yong’an erected a five-story stupa for him.
In front of the stupa, the Kaishan Vihāra was constructed, which the Liang dynasty bestowed as the "Stupa of the Wondrous Enlightenment Master Appearing in the World."

In the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era, the temple was granted the name Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple. During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong, by imperial decree, the entire realm was required to avoid the Emperor’s given name;
thus, he was referred to simply as Master Bao (Bao Gong). Consequently, the title Daolin Zhenjue (Dao-lin True Enlightenment) was bestowed upon him.

Emperor Gaozong further conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Ciying Huigan (Compassionate Response and Wisdom Inspiration), and his stupa was named Gan-shun (Response and Accordance).
Hu Yin, whose courtesy name was Mingzhong and sobriquet Zhid Tang, served as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonial during the Jianyan era.

When his sons were once attending him while he sat in audience, after several cups of wine, he sang the "Memorial on Sending Out the Army" by Zhuge Liang and recited the memorial drafts of Chen Li’ung, remarking: "He may truly be called a hero."
He was a man of such caliber. King Sui (Wang Shun) abridged the *Chuan Deng Lu* and renamed it the *Yu Ying Ji* (Jade Blossom Collection).
Yin composed the preface.
Zhang Jiu Cheng—whose courtesy name was Zishao and whose style was Wugou Jushi—studied under the school of Yang Shi. During the Shaoxing era, he [presented himself] at court...
The Emperor remarked, "His loyalty and integrity are commendable," and he was promoted to first place. He was subsequently exiled to Nanan, where he styled himself the Layman of Hengpu.

He served as a Compiler of the Secretariat. Once, he visited Chan Master Qing of Shanquan and asked, "Is it true that everyone possesses this matter and that each person achieves its full realization? Qing replied, "Yes. The official asked, "If so, why is it that no one has it?"
Zhaoqing entered the hall. From within his sleeve, he produced a rosary and asked, "Whose is this? The official looked up and down, unable to respond.
Zhaoqing then tucked the rosary back into his sleeve and said, "If it is yours, then take it. As soon as there was even a moment of deliberation, it was no longer so.

The official was struck with awe and attained realization. He then contemplated the "Pine Tree" koan. Suddenly, hearing the sound of frogs, he attained liberation and entered into realization, composing a verse.
It is said: "In the springtime moonlight, a single croak of a frog / Shatters heaven and earth into one family.
At such a time, who can understand it? At the head of the ridge, with aching feet, there was Xuansha. You and Wang Yingchen ascended Mount Jing and sought the Way from Dahui.
You discussed with the Master the principle of "investigating things" (*gewu*). The Master said: "You only know of 'investigating things,' but you do not..."
Zhaozhou knew that when the object is investigated (*wu ge*), the profound meaning is suddenly realized. He offered this verse: "Zishao investigates the object; Tanhui, the object is investigated.
If you wish to know the 'One Thread' (*yiguan*), two five-hundreds make one thousand. (from *Chuan Deng Lu*). Zishao once said:

"Whenever Jiucheng hears the kōans cited by the Elder of Mount Jing, he attains a sudden, all-penetrating realization, as if a thousand gates and ten thousand doors were opened without even a single step being taken. Nine.
I have finally accomplished this great matter of my life’s end at the feet of the Elder of Jingshan. I dare not let this single offering of incense prove ungrateful to him (from the *Nianpu*).

Lü Benzhong, courtesy name Jurén, attained the jinshi degree at the beginning of the Shaoxing era. He was appointed as a Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren). Throughout his life, he suffered poverty because of his poetry;

he was devoted to Chan Buddhism and suffered from illness. He was so thin and emaciated that he seemed unable to bear even the weight of his clothes. He established the "Poetry School of the Transmission of Robes" in the Jiangxi region.
[Diagram]. [He] promoted Huang Shan谷 (Shan谷) as the patriarch of poetry and listed Chen Wuyi and others, totaling twenty-five individuals, as his dharma heirs.
Benchong once sent a letter inquiring about the essentials of Dahui’s Chan; Dahui replied in a letter, stating briefly: "A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt.
If the doubt regarding the *huatou* is shattered, then a thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are shattered all at once. If one..."
He asked people: "How is the Buddha’s teaching? How is the Patriarch’s teaching? And how are the teachings of the venerable masters of all quarters? [The others replied:
"There will never be a time of awakening throughout eternal kalpas. [The Master said: "Awakening is already present within one's own fundamental nature."

You Mao (surname You), courtesy name Yanzhi, styled himself Suichu. During the Shaoxing era, he was appointed as Secretariat Vice-Director. When Zhang Nanxun received the notification of his appointment, he remarked, "This is truly a 'Secretariat Vice-Director'.
He eventually served as Minister of the Ministry of Rites and was posthumously honored with the title Wenjian. Upon hearing of Buddhism, [he said:]...
There exists a supramundane Dharma toward which his heart yearns. Seeing Chan Master Guizong of Mount Lu, he intended to plan a life of seclusion.
Zhu Wen Gong sent him a poem with the lines: "Do not hasten to escape into Chan; first complete your karmic ties within the mundane realm.

Later, when he was appointed as the Governor of Taizhou, Emperor Xiaozong personally dispatched an edict from the palace, asking: "What magnificent sights are there on South Terrace? Yan Zhenqing replied: "Taiping [Valley]."
"Great fortune! May the State Qing endure for ten thousand years. The Emperor said, "I have heard that the Stone Bridge *Āryasatya* suddenly appears as five hundred powerful men.
With what method do you deal with them? Yan-zhi raised his fist and said, "Your servant possesses the Vajra-King Precious Sword.
The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the four characters "The Elder Suichu. When Yan-zhi arrived at Tiantai, he first...
Cizai Linmin (Zijian). Zhang Shi, courtesy name Jingfu, style name Nanxuan, served as a Secretariat Editor. He visited Chan Master Wanan Yan and said:

"The locus of the Way can be dwelled upon by the mind, but it cannot be sought through effort. The Master asked, "What do you say to this? The Master said, "One who understands medicine has little illness.
The Official said, "When there is seeing, there is immediately seeing; when there is conceptualization, there is immediately deviation.
What then? The Master said, "To know it is the same as not knowing it. The Official said, "At the very moment of knowing, how is it? The Master said, "Hearing the sound and seeing..."
His physical appearance remained as usual. The Master suddenly attained a profound realization and composed this verse: "Hearing sounds and seeing forms remain just as they always have been;

If one examines them with maturity, the subtle and coarse principles will naturally manifest. It is like the void containing the azure sky— Not even the slightest hair’s breadth of excess exists. (Zi Jian)

Li Haohao, style name De-yuan, served as Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices at the end of the Shaoxing era. He frequently studied the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* and visited Chan Master Ying’an Hua to inquire about the Way of Chan.
Within less than ten days, he had ascended to the inner sanctum of its realization. He then sent a verse to his colleague, Kang Jiao.
The Master said: "At the gate is the shop of Sunbin; at home dwells the wife of Ganzi. Sleeping by night and rising early in the morning—who awakens and who is lost? (Zijian)
Wang Shipeng (王十朋), courtesy name Guilin (龜齡), was a native of Yongjia (永嘉). During the Shaoxing era, he ranked first in the imperial examination.
He styled himself Master Meixi (梅溪先生), and his *Meixi Ji* (梅溪集) remains in circulation today. He served as high as the Censor-in-Chief (侍御史). The Master once visited Xue... at Nanning in Chuzhou.

Chan Master Tangxing asked: "The Buddhas of the past taught the Dharma by observing the faculties of beings and speaking accordingly; based on those words, they established meanings that could be recited and studied.
Yet the Chan school rejects written texts, claiming that the ultimate Way cannot be sought through principles and that true reality cannot be understood through consciousness or intellect.
They insist that one must see one's nature to become a Buddha. Having rejected written texts, why then do you still carve the Tripitaka?"
[The student asked: "Why is it that the circulation of the sutras [is necessary]? The Master said: "The sutras are the words of the Buddha, and they take the mind as their fundamental principle.
If the mind is not clarified, one merely clings to the words of the Buddha. To seek understanding through intellectual reasoning alone is like describing food—it can never satisfy one's hunger.

The essential point lies in establishing a firm resolve and practicing with diligence. If one does not do so, yet wishes to accomplish the work of a sage or a worthy, one will never reach the state of ultimate holiness."
"How can the stage of the Worthy (ārya) be attained? (Zi Jian). He once dreamed of traveling to the Stone Bridge at Tiantai, where several hundred divine monks came out to welcome him.
Pointing to him and the assembly, they said, "That is the former-life Venerable Head Seat Yan; he once transcribed this stele.
Later, when he personally arrived at the Stone Bridge, the scene was no different from what he had seen in his dream. He then composed a poem, saying: "Before reaching the Stone Bridge..."
He was a man of prior knowledge. When he entered the eye [of the world], it was as if entering a dream. The monks called me "Yan the Head Seat.

In a previous life, he had once written the inscription for the Stone Bridge. In the *Meixi ji* (Anthology of Meixi), there is a passage concerning Wang Jinggong and Chan Master Fohui Quan which asks:

"From which scripture does the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower originate? Quan replied: "It is not recorded in the Tripitaka. Jinggong said: "Recently, while serving in the Han Garden..."

The *Jian Dàfàn Wáng Wèn Fó Juéyí Jīng* (Sūtra on the Great Brahmā King Questioning the Buddha to Resolve Doubts), in three fascicles, records that during the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there was a Brahmā King who offered a golden *pāra* flower to the Buddha and requested him to preach the Dharma. The World-Honored One ascended the seat and held up a flower to show the assembly;
among the millions of humans and devas, none could comprehend it, yet only Kāśyapa broke his countenance with a slight smile. The World-Honored One said: "I have the True... [The text continues].
The Dharma-eye Treasury and the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* were entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
The assembly was opened;
his name was Kāi, with the style name Tiānyóu. He served as a Minister of the Interior. In the *xīnwèi* year of the Shàoxīng era, Chán Master Fóhǎi Yuǎn resided at Sānqú.
Guangxiao asked, "What is a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? Yuan said, "The lanterns and the pillars; the cats and the dogs.
Guangxiao then attained realization and presented a verse, saying: "Ha! This blind donkey, a pestilence in the monastic groves! With one roar that shakes the earth, the celestial mechanism is leaked.
If someone asks further what it is like, I will lift my whisk and strike them across the mouth. Yuan said, "That is acceptable."
A single wedge. Furthermore, he sent a letter to Daohui, saying: "Now, fortunately, the worldly entanglements of my private life have all come to an end.

Dwelling in leisure and doing nothing, I am currently urging myself on with great intensity to fulfill my original vow. My only regret is that I have not yet been able to receive your personal instruction and guidance.
I have presented each and every one of my life's failures; you will surely be able to penetrate and illuminate this mind. I hope you will provide me with detailed exhortations and warnings. Daily.
"How should one apply oneself to practice so as not to stray into other paths and instead accord with the original ground? Such statements contain no small amount of error;
yet, as you have just now submitted this sincere inquiry, it is difficult to conceal or evade [the truth], which is truly pitiable.
I prostrate myself deeply. Dahui replied in his letter: "At all times, within states of stillness and excellence, you must by no means forget [this]. You must..."
"Mount Mi, let it go! These two phrases—simply practice them with earnestness from your own feet forward.
Do not fear what has already passed, nor is it necessary to deliberate upon it; for deliberation and fear obstruct the Way.
Simply make a great vow before all the Buddhas, vowing that this mind shall be firm and never again fall back. Rely upon the empowerment of the Buddhas.

Upon meeting a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), one may, under a single word, suddenly forget birth and death and realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Thus continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom, one repays the immeasurably great kindness of all Buddhas.
If this is so, then after a long time, there is no reason why one would not attain awakening. (From *Dahui Shu Wen*)
Li Guangguang, courtesy name Taifa, was a native of Shangyu. During the Shaoxing era, he participated in high-level government affairs and was posthumously honored with the title Zhuangjian.

While serving as the magistrate of Xuancheng, it happened that the abbot’s seat at Zhangjiao Temple was vacant; he drafted a formal petition requesting Chan Master Long (i.e., Long of Huqiu) to serve as the presiding abbot. He once sent him a letter...
Dahui asked about the essentials of Chan meditation. Dahui replied in a letter: "The Great Minister, Chancellor, has long since manifested what you have studied in your conduct.
When faced with the juncture of calamity or fortune, you are like refined gold entering the fire—its brilliance becomes even more manifest.

Furthermore, you possess the certain knowledge that the Huayan doctrine of the multi-layered Dharma-realm is not at all empty talk; thus, you will certainly no longer harbor thoughts of it as being anything other than the truth. As for the rest..."
The seven perversions and eight inversions—whether contrary or compliant, correct or deviant—are likewise not other things. I pray that you constantly maintain this contemplation;

Miaoxi is also therein. On another day, let us follow one another to the shores of profound stillness and form the karmic conditions for the incense and lamps of future lives, thereby accomplishing the manifold layers of the Dharma-realm to substantiate this matter. How could this be anything less than a great benefit?

(From a Letter). Li Bingbing, whose courtesy name was Hanlao, served as a State Councilor. He was deeply devoted to the ancestral Way. Upon meeting Dahui, he [discussed] Zhaozhou’s "The Dog Has No Buddha-Nature" case.
Baihua attained a realization. Later, he sent a letter to seek clarification, saying: "Recently, I visited the Chamber of Deliberation and was humbly moved by your inspiration.

My obscurations suddenly gave way to a profound realization. Reflecting upon myself, I find my faculties and consciousness to be dark and dull; all the learning and understanding of my life have fallen into the realm of emotional views (*dṛṣṭi*).
My every taking up and rejecting was like walking through thorny brambles in tattered rags—only to become further entangled. Now, with a single laugh, it is all suddenly released."
My doubts have been resolved; my joy and gratitude are beyond measure. Were it not for the Great Master’s compassionate and detailed guidance, how could this have come to pass?
Since arriving in the city, I have donned my robes and partaken of meals, embracing my children and grandchildren, with every aspect of life remaining as it was.

Having no sense of attachment or clinging, nor any notion of something extraordinary, even my residual habits and old karmic obstructions have somewhat diminished. As I prepare to depart, I offer these earnest words.
I dare not forget these words. I reflect deeply that although I have recently entered the gate, the Great Dharma is not yet clear;

when responding to circumstances and engaging with others, I am still unable to be unimpeded in every encounter. I further hope for your guidance and instruction so that I may ultimately reach my destination and, it is hoped, remain without blemish at this Dharma assembly.
(Letter) Dahui resided at Mount Jing, where he completed the construction of the Qianseng Pavilion (Thousand Monks Hall). Changbing composed a record for it, which states in brief:
The Master was the twelfth-generation descendant of Linji. Because his Way was great, those who were gathered under him were numerous; because his gate was steep, those who ascended it were rare;
because his essential meaning was precise, those who attained awakening were intimate with it; and because his discourse was lofty, those who heard it were struck with wonder.

Furthermore, scholars from the four quarters came in such numbers that their shoulders brushed and sleeves met; yet when the Master encountered them, he never condescended to employ artful words or gestures in his reception.

Though he was treated with persistent refusal and kept at a distance, the Master would not leave; though he was shunned, his intimacy only increased. It reached the point that even when water was splashed on him and he was driven away, the space outside his door was always filled with visitors' shoes.
The monastery was a hundred *li* from the city; it was from the time of National Teacher Dayuan of Tangguo that the brambles and weeds were first cleared away.

He drove away the dragons and snakes and took up residence there. The monastery possessed no permanent endowment; rather, the divine dragon of the mountain truly assisted in the conditions for its propagation.
At the beginning of the Master’s arrival, the assembly numbered only three hundred; by the second year, the Dharma seat flourished greatly and the assembly reached nearly two thousand.
Since the monastery had only two monks’ halls, which were insufficient to accommodate them, he further constructed a ten-bay multi-storied pavilion to the east of the temple for Vairocana.
Facing south, it rises prominently in the center. To its left and right, seating arrangements for a thousand monks are aligned, with beds set in rows;

beneath them, meals and gruel are provided. I once inquired about the Way from the Master, and upon hearing his words, I sighed, saying: "It is not difficult to complete this pavilion; the difficulty lies in gathering such a multitude.
It is not difficult to gather such a multitude; the difficulty lies in practicing the Way so that one's followers do not fail to arrive."
As for the difficulty of completing a single pavilion, what is there in the Master’s achievement that is worth speaking of?
Yet those who merely follow conventional and mediocre practices consider it something extraordinary—is this not truly pitiable? (From the *Dahui Nianshu*)
Feng Jie (also read Jie), courtesy name Jichuan, was a native of Suining in Shu. He styled himself the Layman Budong. From his youth, he sought instruction from various renowned masters;
finally, he resided at Longmen under Chan Master Foyan Yuan. One day, while walking together with Yuan in the Dharma Hall, a servant boy...

As his son hurried through the courtyard, he recited: "Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. He patted the back of Jie from afar and said, "How wonderful! Thereupon, Jie attained realization.
In the Ding-si year of the Xiang-er period, he was appointed as a Palace Attendant (Jishi Zhong). It happened that Dahui was about to ascend the hall at Mingqing Temple.
Huì descended from his seat. Zhìjué pulled him back, saying, "Every time you speak to the scholar-officials, Master, you say, 'In this life, I shall not become such a creature.
Why then do you suffer defeat today? Huì said, "The entire earth is this Venerable Gǎo. Where do you see him?
As Zhìjué was about to reply, Huì struck him with his palm. Zhìjué said, "I brought this upon myself. Because of this...
During the summer retreat at Mount Jing, he named his quarters the "Immovable Pavilion" (Budong Xuan). Later, he served as the Prefect of Luzhou;
wherever he went, he never grew weary of the Way. He once composed this verse for himself: "Beyond my public duties, I delight in seated meditation; Rarely have I let my side touch the bed.
Though I manifest the form of a lay official, The name 'Elder' is proclaimed throughout the four seas. This was in the autumn of the twenty-third year of the Shaoxing era.
He requested retirement. He informed his relatives and acquaintances that he intended to pass away on the third day of the tenth month.

On that day, he had a high seat prepared in the rear hall and received visitors as usual. Between the hours of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. and the Snake (9–11 a.m.), he descended from the steps, faced the imperial palace, and performed a solemn prostration.

He wrote a verse: "Third of the first month, eleventh; Ninth of the middle month, seventh of the last. The old man’s words are exhausted; Gūjié’s eyes turn red. Having finished writing, he took up his staff.

He passed away while sitting upright with his knees pressed together. After the Jianyan era, he took up the oars [of his efforts] to recover lost portions of the Tripitaka from famous mountains and great monasteries.

Using his own stipend, he printed and distributed copies to supplement them; there were forty-eight sets totaling more than five thousand scrolls, intended to prolong the life of the sovereign and bring peace to the myriad people.
His disciple Pu Daping once recorded these deeds in a memorial. There also exists a collection of his recorded sayings and verses on ancient cases (*gū*).
In the world [he was known as] Chuandeng (Lamp of the Dharma).
Mi Youren, style name Yuanhui, was the son of Mi Fu. He styled himself the Elder Languid and Unskilled. In literature, calligraphy, and painting, he deeply inherited his family’s tradition.
Dharma (Fǎ). During the Xiǎngshòu era, he served as Vice Minister of Works and acted as Acting Minister of War. He once visited Hǔqiū Mountain and inscribed by hand: "The Buddha said:
'Even across hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created is never forgotten; when causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself.
I observe that among all sentient beings in the sea of suffering, many frequently create grave and heavy karmic offenses."
Alas! Few are able to know that there are retributions for good and evil, which follow form like a shadow and respond to sound like an echo.

That they do not know to fear is simply because their clothing and food are insufficient; driven by the delusions of craving, they forget righteousness for the sake of profit, and thus arrive at this state.
How could they further concern themselves with falling into the hells to undergo suffering within the cycle of rebirth? I exhort all sentient beings: do not...
They perform various karmic deeds and practice manifold virtues. A poem by a predecessor says: "I only fear that the mind of one who has become a monk is not yet resolved;

once the mind of a monk is resolved, he surpasses all others. These words are truly apt. Those who have left the household life abandon their objects of attachment, yet if they have not entirely transcended to realize the Supreme Vehicle, when compared to those in the secular world who create deep karma, the difference is like that between clouds and the earth.
Zhou Bida (courtesy name Zichong), a native of Luling in Jixian, passed the Examination for Broad Learning and Grand Prose in the Shaoxing era.

During the Chunxi era, he was appointed as the Right Prime Minister and enfeoffed as the Duke of Yi. He once composed the Epitaph for Master Foguo Guang, which states: "The Dharma does not exist in isolation."
Arise! The Way does not travel in vain; there must be those who continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Who are these people? They are Chan Master Fozhao.
The Master’s name was Deguang; his surname was Peng. He was a native of Xinyu County in Linjiang Commandery (and so forth).

I have heard that the seasonal conditions and causal links—like the meeting of a needle and a magnet, or the simultaneous pecking and piercing—are things that the sages of antiquity could not force. To use a metaphor: it is like carving a raft.
Those who travel by boat increase their pride; how much more so when the Dharma words spoken before the Imperial presence have already been circulated throughout the world?

As for the source of his realization of the Way and the essential means by which he engaged sentient beings, the disciples of the monastic communities each preserve his recorded sayings (*yulu*). For now, I have briefly recounted the general outline of his life in this world. The inscription says:

"I have heard that among the myriad forms of life, each possesses Buddha-nature. Yet there are those among humanity who have not yet seen it, or who see it but not exhaustively. How magnificent is this Light!"

Master Gong had cultivated the precepts and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*) through his past habits; he entered the gate of awakening all at once and subsequently transmitted the mind-seal (*citta-mudrā*).

His merit and wisdom were both perfected, and his practice and understanding progressed together. When the majestic Emperor Xiaozong met with the Master, seeing a sage through a sage, he spoke with him and experienced profound realization.

In his later years, the Master returned to Dong’an, never tiring of guiding and introducing others. At eighty-three years of age, his karmic conditions were exhausted. Do not say that the mirror is clear only in the past or present; it is so now.
Hidden! Since not a single thing fundamentally exists, what use is there for illumination and reflection? Do not say that the valley is empty; when there is a knock, there is a response accordingly.

Since the ten directions are all void, why discuss decay and extinction? Plucking leaves and picking flowers, binding the wind and catching shadows—when you brought these questions to the one within the stupa, he simply smiled with a slight laugh.

Qian Duānlǐ (錢端禮), courtesy name Chùhé (處和), style name Sōngchuāng (松窓). He served in office as high as Minister of State (Cānzhèng). He once studied under Chan Master Yuán (元) of Huguo Temple and attained realization.
During the Chūnxī era, he manifested a slight illness; he invited Chan Master Xíngjī (行機) of Píngtián to his inner chambers, where he sat in the full lotus posture.

While conversing and laughing, he suddenly said to Ji: "This floating world is illusory; fundamentally, there is no coming or going. The four elements and five aggregates must ultimately reach their end.
Even Buddhas and Patriarchs, though possessed of great majestic virtue, cannot escape this one matter.
It is because earth, water, fire, and wind temporarily congregate that the deluded take them to be themselves. As for the various sages of antiquity, their coming and going were of their own accord."
"In this present life, I am thus; how joyful it is! Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away (*Chuan deng lu*).
Shi Haohao, style name Zhigong, was a native of Siming. During the reign of Emperor Xiaozong, he was appointed as Chancellor and enfeoffed as Duke of Wei, later as Prince of Yue.
In the year of Yisi during the Chunxi era, he retired from official life to return to Siming, where he styled himself the Layman Zhenyin.

He frequently sought the essentials of the Dharma from Master Zhilian of Nanhu. Thereupon, he established the Yuebo Pavilion at Donghu, emulating Mount Putuo by constructing a grotto chamber to enshrine the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara).
When Hao visited Jingshan, he observed the grand ceremonial protocols of Emperor Wu of Liang and remarked upon the [merit of] Baoen [Temple]. The text continues with "du" (crossing/attaining).
"The Way of the world lies herein. Thereupon, he established a temple on Mount Yuebo and fashioned images of the ten realms. Together with renowned monks, he researched and codified ritual protocols;
these were compiled into four fascicles and circulated throughout the world. His son, Miyuan, served as Chancellor to Emperor Ningzong and was enfeoffed as Prince of Wei.
Yu, the son of King Wei; and Songzhi, the son of Mizhong, Grand Scholar of Guandwendian—these two served as ministers to Emperor Lizong.
King Wei established Qishan Temple in Mingzhou and provided hospitality for travelers along the way. Hao once composed a eulogy for the portrait of Master Fazhi of Nanhu, which says:
"The single seat at Vulture Peak remains solemnly present on Mount Tiantai; thirteen generations later, he was born again."

A man of extraordinary talent, he proclaimed the Way at Siming. His lecture halls were grandly opened, and his fame spread across the vast ocean; his teachings resounded like thunder and rolling clouds.
When Emperor Zhenzong ascended the throne, imperial envoys arrived in succession. Having grasped the great essentials of the Dharma, the Emperor’s decree was majestic and expansive.

He was bestowed the title "Fazhi," and the imperial calligraphy shone brilliantly upon him. From that time forth, later scholars have all looked up to his towering eminence. Like the fragrance of orchids and chrysanthemums, they share a single root. Alas!
This is the pillar and foundation of the Dharma-palace; the salt and plum for the cauldron of the Teaching.
Thus, this illusory reflection shall remain free from dust through the ages (from the *Song Shi* and the *Tong Ji*).

Qian Xiangzu, whose style name was Xiangzu, served as Chancellor during the reign of Emperor Ningzong. While serving as Governor of Jinling, he once sought instruction from Chan Master Wuyong Quan of Baoning, and later sought instruction from Chan Master Yuan of Ciyuan at Huguo Temple.
The Master said: "If you wish to investigate this matter, you must first attain the mind."
"When both [subject and object] are forgotten, only then is it possible. If attachment to the Dharma has not been forgotten, even to accord with the principle is not yet awakening.
The Duke said, "As soon as one involves the lips and tongue, one falls into conceptual thought; how can this be? The Master said, "Since there is originally no wound, do not injure it.
The Duke was suddenly enlightened (as recorded in the *Zi Jian*). The Duke once established ten guest-houses in his native region, all of which he named after the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
He established Shang’an Gao-seng-liao as a place for discussing the Way. After the Minister of the Left resigned and returned home, he devoted himself even more to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
When he was suddenly stricken with a slight illness, a monk who came to inquire after his health replied: "I do not crave life, nor do I fear death;
I shall not be reborn as a god nor as a human, but shall surely be reborn in the Pure Land. Having said this, he sat in the lotus position and passed away. At that time, the heavens...

The drums resounded and a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air. Before the ceremony had concluded, all the people of the commandery heard a voice from the sky saying, "Prime Minister Qian shall be reborn in the Western Pure Land as the Bodhisattva Ciji. (From the *Jingtu zhuan*)

Wang Rihui, whose courtesy name was Xuzhong, was a native of Longshu. He served as a Master at the National Academy and composed commentaries and exegeses on the Six Classics totaling several hundred thousand words.
One day, he discarded them all, saying, "These are merely products of habitual practice and are not the ultimate Dharma. I shall now turn toward the Western [Pure Land]."
He returned [to his former practice]. From then on, he resolved his will upon the recitation of the Buddha’s name, performing a daily liturgy of one thousand prostrations.

One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name with a forceful voice, he suddenly said, "The Buddha has come to receive me. He stood upright and passed away. A *Pure Land Text* (Jingtu wen) by him circulates in the world. He once said:
"While it is truly supreme to attain great enlightenment through Zen meditation and thereby transcend the cycle of birth and death, those who reach such a state are likely few. If..."
Cultivating the Western Pure Land cuts directly through the cycle of birth and death without a single flaw remaining.
Therefore, I now exhort those who practice Chan meditation to set aside a brief moment each day to cultivate the Way of the West.

If you achieve great awakening and thereby transcend saṃsāra, yet find that the Buddha-ground is still far off, what could be more appropriate than proceeding to visit Amitābha Buddha to pay homage and show respect? (From the *Jingtu wen*)
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Fourteen, Re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing;
*Fófǎ Jīntáng Biān*, Scroll Fifteen,
Compiled by the Shamen of Kuaiji, Xintaī.
Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhenqing reads Zhu Xi.
Zhu Xi, courtesy name Yuanhui, styled Haian, was a native of Xin’an. During the Shaoxi era, he was appointed as a Court Attendant of the Huanchang Pavilion. Li... [text fragment]

During the Song Dynasty, he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor (Taishi), enfeoffed as Duke of Huiguo, and bestowed the posthumous name Wengong. In his youth, the Duke took no pleasure in reading the conventional examination essays (*shiwen*).
Instead, upon hearing a venerable master preach on Chan, which directly points to the fundamental mind, he suddenly awakened to that single point of radiant, numinous awareness.

At the age of eighteen, he requested to take the imperial examinations; at that time, he followed Liu Pingshan, who presumed that the Duke’s interest lay solely in the pursuit of the examination curriculum. Subsequently, [Pingshan] searched through his...

The box contained nothing but a single volume of Chan Master Dahui’s Recorded Sayings. During a period of prolonged rain, while dwelling in seclusion for a vegetarian fast and reciting the sutras, he composed a poem that said:

"Seated upright and alone with nothing to do, I casually peruse the Buddhist scriptures. For a time, I rest from the entanglements of worldly dust; Transcending all, I am one with the Way... (and so forth).
The Master once sent a letter to Chan Master Daoyuan of Kaishan, in which he wrote: "Previously, I received the instructions of Miaoxi..."
"This must be because you have been retaining written words from the past and calculating with your consciousness; you must not allow even a single thread’s worth of this to remain in your breast.
Instead, simply keep the 'dog' koan in mind and remind yourself of it from time to time. I vow to receive a single word to alert me to what I have failed to grasp.
The Master replied, "For twenty years I was unable to reach the ground of non-doubt. Later, I suddenly realized my error and pressed forward with courage."
He then severed it himself with a single stroke, taking up this "one thought" *kōan* of the "dog" phrase. He did not engage in deliberation, nor did he engage in forced interpretation;

he did not pursue intellectual knowledge, nor did he insist on a presumptuous realization. Thereupon, Master Gō attained awakening. When the Master passed away, Gō offered a memorial service with a written text, which stated in brief:
"In the past, when I followed my studies and read the *Yì*, *Yǔán*, and *Mèng*, I investigated and observed how the ancients..."
The Sage, not measuring his own capacity, desired to emulate his style; yet the Way was cut off and the path blocked, so in the end he could find no way through.

He went down to consult with the Elder regarding what ought to be practiced, and they all told him that it was essential to achieve awakening—that the discourse on awakening does not emerge outside of Chan.
At that time, I then wished to study under him. The Master departed for Xianzhou, while I resided by the shore of Lake Tan; we were separated by but a single ridge.
I could only gaze up at him in reverence. In the autumn of the Bingyin year, the Master came to Gongchen, and I was finally able to enjoy his company;
our conversation became intimate day by day. One day, I burned incense and asked him about this matter. The Master replied, "It is certainly not so.

Only then did I realize that throughout my life I had been needlessly enduring hardship, drifting further and further from the Way with no way to find its source. Before a year had passed, the Master [was accused of] slander.

I am leaving. Because of my official duties, I have been unable to remain settled. During my travels back and forth, I encountered you three times; each time I saw you, I stayed for several days to consult with you on the morning and evening.
You were pleased by me and spoke to me about the ailments of Chan practice, while I was moved by your kindness yet regretted not having realized the truth sooner.
We parted three months ago, and the letter I received last mid-autumn was no longer in your own hand. I know your illness is a matter of concern. [The] monk from the other day...
I came wishing to go and see him. With joy, I wrote a letter saying, "This is well," and having finished writing it, I sent it off.

My servant returned quickly with news that a fellow passenger on the same boat had reported his death. I was startled and sent someone to call for an inquiry as to the cause. Alas, how painful! Why was he snatched away so suddenly?
I reverently reflect upon my teacher, who possessed perfect and universal knowledge; yet I alone have not awakened, being unable to achieve even a single [virtue].

Kui (or Kuí) offered gold to provide for the offerings and wept before the spirit’s altar. He prostrated himself as if toward the void, transcending all things. (From the *Ziji*). Someone asked Zhu Xi, saying:
"Why is it that nowadays many scholar-officials in their later years are led away by the Chan school? He replied: "It is because they are superior to you.
Throughout your life, you have read many books and memorized numerous writings; these are merely the means by which you sought [official position]."
Those who harbor schemes for fame, profit, and official emolument cannot rely on anything at this point; therefore, they are subdued by him. For him, it is effortless.
Who among men would not joyfully hasten toward such a state? Wang Anshi studied many principles throughout his life, yet in the end he donated his residence to become a temple.
He further remarked, "It is simply because he has cleared away the clutter within his mind."
Jie said, "As for those in our own dynasty—Duke Li Wenjing, Duke Wang Wenzheng, Lord Yang Wengong, Yuan Cheng of Liu, and Duke You of Lü—who were they?

They all went to study him [Confucius]. Furthermore, it is said that the Buddhist scriptures' explanations of the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, the four great elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and so forth, are all extremely subtle and exquisite; therefore, the predecessors remarked that this [Buddhism] is Confucianism."
This is something Mencius did not reach. Furthermore, it is said that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are themselves the *hun* and *po* souls.

The *Huayan he lun* (Treatise on the Combined [Commentaries] of the Avataṃsaka) explains the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination. The Buddha’s original teaching was to exhaustively abandon all worldly affairs;

yet later, he spoke of the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), where not a single speck of dust is received, while at the gateway of myriad phenomena, not a single dharma is abandoned. Xi also said that the general purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is simply this:
Regarding the two questions posed by Subhūti, "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?", it is therefore said:
"One should not give rise to the mind dwelling on dharmas; one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on form; one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere.
This answers the question of how to dwell. Furthermore, it says: "Whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation, I shall cause them all to enter [nirvāṇa]."
He brings them to extinction through *nirvāṇa* without remainder. This is the answer to the question, "How does one subdue the mind?
What is meant by "subduing the mind" is not merely seeking to suppress this [individual] mind;

it means thoroughly subduing the minds of all sentient beings in the world, entering *nirvāṇa* without remainder—which is simply the single character "one" (一無). From this point onward, it is nothing but this.
"Ananda, if one sees that all marks are no-marks, one sees the Tathagata; this means that being free from marks is itself called the Buddha. Furthermore, he said:
"The study of the Śākya clan has points of great similarity with our Confucianism. For instance: 'There is a thing prior to heaven and earth;
formless and fundamentally silent, it is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither with the four seasons. And again: 'When it falls, it is not something else.'"
"Things, whether horizontal or vertical, are not dust; mountains, rivers, and the great earth fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
He also said, "If a person recognizes the Mind, there is not an inch of soil upon the great earth. Look at what kind of insight this is!
How could these petty Confucian scholars ever escape his grasp? You should strike them down for him (from *Zhu Zi Yu Lu* and *Yi Jie*).

Lu You (陸游), courtesy name Wuguān (務觀) and sobriquet Fàngwēng (放翁), was the grandson of Lù Diàn (陸佃) and a native of Shānyīn (山陰), Yuè (越). He served in office as far as the Director of the Imperial Library (Bìjiàn [祕監]).
He once asked Chan Master Sōngyuán Yuè (松源岳): "May I hear of the learning transmitted through the mind? The Master replied: "Since it is already the mind..."
[The Master] said, "How could this be obtained through hearing? The Duke attained realization and offered this verse: "How many times have I driven my carriage into the imperial city?
Whenever I met a monk, my eyes were equally clear and bright. Only today do I realize the distinctiveness of the Chan school: To speak of existence or discuss emptiness, one must listen with the eye.
While the Duke resided at Mirror Lake (Jinghu), his relationship with Chan Master Tuduce was increasingly deep. When Cedi (Cai) resided at Mount Shuangjing, he received [the transmission of] life.

The funeral rites were held for seven days. He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. The Duke wept and composed a poem, saying: "The towering Dragon Gate of ten thousand fathoms collapses; A solitary figure flits away once more toward the west.
Dust settles upon the white whisk, the corded meditation seat grows cold; Dewdrops fall on the green pines as the egg-shaped stupa is completed."
Gazing afar at your return, you will no longer be bound by the four great elements; yet we shall surely meet again to speak of three lifetimes. I, Fangong, have deeply lacked spiritual cultivation;
thus I cannot avoid the sorrowful sentiment of parting from you in this mortal world. (Zi Jian)
Ye Shi (Shi), styled Water-Mind (Shuixin) Master, has his *Water-Mind Collection* (*Shuixin ji*) circulating in the world. In a letter to the Chan Master Shiyuan Lian, Shi wrote:
"I have often maintained that since the Buddha entered China, he began as a heterodox teaching, yet came to become entangled with the Way of the Sage."
I have recently investigated his writings and reconciled his doctrines; they truly accord with the teachings on the nature of life and destiny (*xingming*).

However, while the categories he sets forth are numerous, there are many points of internal contradiction. Since he says that it cannot be sought with the mind, yet also says that it cannot be attained without the mind, what is correct and what is false?
What is contradictory and what is to be followed? I hope you will not be sparing in your instruction to awaken me. The Master replied: "I am honored by your inquiry."

The admonitions in Buddhist scriptures are numerous, and there are many points where they appear to contradict one another. I venture to set forth my humble observations: the Buddha takes precept, concentration, and wisdom as his fundamental tenets.
When the objective realm encompasses the six sense faculties, the mirror of the mind remains unmoved; thus, amidst all conditions, one is not deluded.

The bright illumination of the sun and moon, the moistening of rain and dew, the flowing of water, the blooming of flowers, the soaring of kites, and the leaping of fish—all these are fully possessed within our own nature. The essential point lies in unifying all manifold differences into one.
Illumination! When principle and phenomena are blended and fused, as days pass and months deepen, the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness will naturally seal one’s own original mind.

If you can withdraw your gaze and turn back your hearing, there is fundamentally no Buddha apart from the mind; there is no need to inquire into numerous categories, for many words are mutually contradictory.
From this, it is clear that [Zhang] Shid returned to his studies. In a letter to Zhu Wen-gong, he wrote: "While in Jingzhou, I had leisure time to read Buddhist scriptures.
Thereupon, I realized that the accounts of the world beyond, though marvelous and extraordinary, are fundamentally not in conflict with the Way;

this is truly because readers do not examine them deeply. (Cited from the *Zijian*). He once composed a preface for the Tripitaka at Faming Temple, which states: "In the past, there was a lecturer at Faming Temple on West Lake..."

Jizhong resided there; he possessed virtuous conduct and a powerful force of aspiration. Consequently, even though the area was reduced to a wilderness of weeds and brush, scholars in official carriages and hats constantly traveled to that commandery for a hundred years.
When his son Zhen established the two administrative orders (*xiang*) and Master Chang renovated the halls and pavilions, the monastery was finally completed.

Master Chang was exceptionally austere; his robes and shoes were worn through, and his food never exceeded a single meal. Nevertheless, students flocked to him like clouds, and he responded to them all.
The teachings gushed forth like a spring. People remarked that the flourishing of Tiantai at East Yekshang Tianzhu could not surpass this.

Since Zhiyi established the two principles of *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation), those who inherited and expounded them had caused them to proliferate further; both Zhong and Chang also produced their own commentaries.
Consequently, his disciples Miaozhen and Pujie wished to compile the learning of these various masters into a "Teachings Canon" (*jiaozang*) and place it within the monastery.
He led the men and women of the prefecture to cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, thereby commemorating the deeds of Liang Wudi and continuing the legacy of Emperor Xiaowen.

His resolve is truly boundless and his ambition far-reaching. Now, as for those who regard the body as a mere lodging and yet do not cease in their grand adornment of monasteries, and who consider speech to be a superfluous growth and yet transmit it through written texts for ever longer—this is indeed something I cannot understand.
