I have often reflected on this...
He questioned Chǎng, but Chǎng was likewise unable to speak (from his collected works).

Zhēn Dèxiù, whose courtesy name was Hīyuán, was originally surnamed Shèn; he changed his surname to Zhēn to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Xiàozōng. During the Duānpíng era, he served as a Grand Councilor.
His posthumous title was Wenzhong, and his style name was Master Xishan. When he governed Hunan, the people of Tan established a living shrine for him.
One night, an inscription appeared on the wall, which read: "The world knows you do not cherish fame, Yet the people of Xiang yearn to place your likeness upon the wall.

In the West, another living Buddha has emerged; In the South, two stars of longevity are now added to the pole. For nearly a century, you have been a spirit of rare excellence amidst ten thousand vessels."

May you be blessed with a long life for eight thousand springs; there is no need for further records of a memorial shrine, for the mouths of the common people throughout the four seas shall serve as your epitaph.
I once inscribed a preface to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* (Yíjiào jīng) transcribed by Yang Wén-gōng, stating: "This is indeed the final instruction of the Sage Gautama to his disciples.
Yet among those who study Buddhism today, few regularly recite or practice it. This is because since the separation of Chan and the Teachings..."
Students often believe that Buddhahood can be attained without relying on language or written texts; they thus disregard the scriptural teachings in their quest for what is called "Chan.

While this approach may be lofty, when it comes to the point where their bodies and minds become inverted and fail to withstand scrutiny, they are actually no better than those who recite sutras and uphold the Vinaya, who at least remain within the steady bounds of formal discipline.

This will not lead to great error. Now, observing this sutra, it takes upright mind and right mindfulness as its primary focus, and speaks profoundly of upholding the precepts as the foundation of meditative concentration and wisdom.
It goes so far as to say that the way to restrain the mind is like herding an ox or driving a horse.
Do not allow yourself to be dissolute; eliminate anger and cease delusion; stifle desire and diminish seeking.

Only then may one proceed from seclusion to diligence, and from meditative concentration to the cultivation of wisdom. This possesses a gradual sequence of steps, unlike the talkers of today who believe that one can leap directly to the stage of a Tathāgata.
Those who study the Buddha’s teachings should not consider this approach circuitous and [therefore reject it].
If one asks whether Zen is swift, from the perspective of our Confucian tradition, the teaching of the Sages takes "learning from below" as the foundation;

only then can one "attain the ultimate. This is the same principle. For those who study Buddhism to seek meditative concentration and wisdom without first observing the precepts is like a Confucian who abandons the classics and the cultivation of will, neglecting the rites of sweeping and responding to others, while rushing toward great achievement.
How could one possibly grasp the subtlety of the nature of speech and the Way of Heaven? I maintain that the existence of this scripture for Buddhists is like the *Analects* for Confucians;
while the *Vajracchedikā*, *Śūraṃgama*, and *Awakening of Faith* scriptures are comparable to the *Book of Changes* and the *Doctrine of the Mean*.
There is no one who can suddenly reach the *Changes* and the *Mean* without first studying the *Analects*. Such is the relationship between the teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism.
While their ultimate goals are certainly different, there is a sequence for studying that cannot be altered. In the postscript to the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he writes:
"Since my youth, I have read the 'Universal Gate' chapter. Although I have not yet been able to deeply understand its meaning, I have often attempted to gauge it with my own reasoning, saying:
'This is a parable of the Buddha. Long ago, Lord Li Wen asked Master Yaoshan..."
Chan Master Yan asked, "What is it like when a malignant wind blows a boat and drifts it into the realm of ghosts? The Master replied, "Why does this young man Li Ao ask such a thing?

When Wen Gong (Li Ao) became startled and anger appeared on his face, the Master laughed and said, "To give rise to this heart of resentment and anger is itself for the black wind to blow the boat and drift it into the realm of ghosts. Alas! Yaoshan may truly be called one who is skilled at awakening others.
It is thus with human beings. By inferring from this, one knows that the blazing intensity of profit and desire is a pit of fire, while the drowning in greed and attachment is a sea of suffering.
A single thought of purity turns the fierce flames into a pond; a single moment of alertness brings the boat to the other shore.
Though bound by calamities and afflictions, one dwells wherever one may be; like shackles falling away of their own accord, I have no fear.

When wicked people invade or treat me with violence, I harbor no anger or resentment; like a wild beast fleeing for itself, I am free from malice. One who reads this sutra should contemplate in this manner.
Thus one knows that the Great Being of Potalaka truly acts for the sake of others; his words are not idle speech. Reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it says: "I have read the *Śūraṅgama*;
I know that the six roots originate from a single external condition. The six sense objects flow forth and become the six [consciousnesses] that follow after objects."

Sinking away and unable to return of one's own accord, the Tathāgata takes pity on sentient beings and teaches them skillful means so that they may know that the very door through which they exit is the path back home.
Therefore, in this sutra, he points directly to the gate of Nirvana without the slightest concealment.

If sentient beings can cleanse their minds and practice the Dharma, such that sensory objects do not condition one another and the sense faculties find no external counterparts, the flow will reverse and become entirely unified, and the six functions will cease.
As one practices, the flow of the Dharma enters and permeates day and night; when it merges with the flowing stream of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, one may attain Buddhahood within one's own body.
Fearing that sentient beings might not yet know from which of the six sense faculties to proceed, the Tathāgata had twenty-five disciples each speak of what they had realized.
Among them, Avalokiteśvara was foremost in the perfect penetration of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

His words were as follows: "At first, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the flow and loses the object of hearing. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.

Thus gradually increasing, the hearing and that which is heard both come to an end. When the hearing has ended, one does not dwell therein; when the awareness of what is aware becomes empty, that emptiness and awareness reach ultimate perfection.
When the emptiness and that which is emptied are extinguished, and birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one. If one can thus [attain] this perfection..."
If one pulls out a single root, all roots are liberated. In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, one traverses the three voids and becomes no different from the Buddhas.
Furthermore, while reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon reaching the section on the four fruits of arhatship, he set aside the scripture and sighed, saying:
"Is what the *Srotāpanna* realizes not precisely what Avalokiteśvara meant by 'first, within hearing, entering the stream and losing the object'? He then entered [meditation].
The "stream" (srotas) is not a substantial dharma. It is simply the state of not entering the six sense-objects, abiding peacefully and eternally; this is what it means to "enter the stream.
As for the Sakṛdāgāmin, they are called "once-returners," yet in reality there is no coming and going. The Anāgāmin is called "non-returner," yet in reality there is no non-returning.
For to go is to enter the sense-objects, and to come is to return to the source. Although the Sakṛdāgāmin is able to return, [they have not yet fully realized this].
Yet one has not yet reached the state of non-going. The Anāgāmin is not only one who does not go, but is also one who does not come.
Upon reaching the Arhat, the intention of going and coming is exhausted; there is no dharma that can be attained. Thus, what are called the four fruits are in reality a single dharma;
they differ only in the depth and shallowness experienced through the three stages of emptiness. When I examine the words of these two sutras, they are fundamentally like two halves of a tally.

[The Master] agreed. Yet, as some in the world do not understand this, he spoke clearly [in the *Wenxian Tongkao*]: "When Chan Master Sanjiao Song resided at Jingci Monastery, the Duke entered his quarters and asked:
'Is there a scriptural basis for people requesting monks to recite sutras? The Master replied: 'Buddhist scriptures can forge the mind and refine its nature;
through them, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arise. [These include] the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The former masters..."*]
Reciting this, one realizes the Way; those who hear or see it all obtain benefit. The Duke then read through various sutras (at Ziji Monastery).
Liu Kezhuang, courtesy name Qianfu, style name Houchun, was preeminent in his poetry and prose, which were vast, magnificent, and transcendent. During the Chunyou era, he was appointed...

He served as Secretary of the Bureau of Secretaries concurrently with the position of Lecturer at Chongzheng Hall. He was subsequently promoted to Editor of the Secretariat Library. His collected works, comprising fifty scrolls, were circulated in the world.

Among them were his "Ten Poems on the Explanations [of Buddhist Terms]," the first of which, the "Eulogy on Gautama," states: "The world transmits that Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty first dreamed of the Golden Body;
why not observe that in the *Liezi* it is said there is a sage in the West? The "Eulogy on Vimalakīrti" states: "His facial complexion was emaciated..."
The melon is yellow; the eyebrows are long, covered in snow-white hair. Who would have known that the four worlds beneath heaven reside within a single meditation seat?
Śāriputra (the Good Wealth) sang: "Emperor Yao visited my uncle; Confucius questioned the Great Lǎn. Thus it is that this youth has also traveled everywhere to seek instruction. Bodhidharma sang:
"To take the mind directly as the Buddha is the highest teaching of the West. Only then do I know that beyond the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius,"
There are heroes of their own kind. The Sixth Patriarch’s verse says: The bright mirror steals from Shenxiu; Bodhidharma offends Wolun.
Taking back the old robe and bowl, He monopolizes them so they are not passed to others. Tancheng’s verse says: Meeting chaos, where can one go?
Following conditions, even staying is peaceful. One can take the likes of Shi Hu And view them merely as seagulls. Zhidun’s verse says: If by form...
Upon seeing me, one might almost mistake my appearance for that of a commoner: Master Lin lacks a beard and hair; Master Chengguan lacks a cap and kerchief.
Master Zhigong sang: "The temple is the foremost in Jiangzuo; he personally welcomed me into the imperial palace. Yet in the Jingju Hall, how could they starve the old Lord Xiao to death? Mazu sang:
"If it were not for his great spirit, he would merely be a man of petty wit. When the Old Man let out a single shout—"
The student was deaf for three days. Deshan’s verse says: "This old man’s staff—just a light touch leaves a scar.
Even if a Buddha comes, give him thirty blows; this fellow here need not eat. (From the *Benji*).
Chen Guiqian, Guiqian.
He served as high as the Grand Councilor for Military Affairs (Shumishi). When Zhen Xishan inquired about matters concerning the Chan school, Guiqian replied in a letter, stating briefly:

"I have received your inquiry regarding the affairs of the Chan school; this immediately reveals your open-mindedness and delight in the good. Looking at my own shallow and leaking knowledge, how could I be worthy of such an honor?"

This is so. Nevertheless, I venture to set forth my humble observations regarding whether or not one should contemplate the *huatou*. As I see it, there is originally no fixed doctrine on this matter.
If one can realize that in a single thought-moment there is no arising, then the whole body is the Buddha; where else would there be a separate *huatou*?

It is only because of the habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes that we turn our backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses, such that in a single instant, thought after thought arises and ceases like...

It is like a monkey picking up chestnuts. The Buddhas and Patriarchs, having no choice, provisionally established skillful means, causing one to chew upon a "head-word" (hwa-tou) that has no flavor, such that the conscious intellect has no way to function.
This is like exchanging honeyed fruit for a bitter gourd; it serves only to wash away your karmic consciousness and possesses no real meaning.
Yet those who study nowadays forcibly create artificial interpretations upon the head-word, or—
To explain each point individually would take us far afield from our immediate task.

However, in the Zen school, one must thoroughly perceive the natural radiance of one’s own original ground to reach the ultimate realization. This ground is inherently present in every person, yet it is obscured by adventitious delusions.
Unless one undergoes intense refinement through practice, it will never become clear and pure.
Zhang Yi, whose style name was Yuezhai, held the official rank of Zhimige Xueshi. After meeting Chan Master Miamie Jie, he informed him of his realization through a letter, stating:
"In the past, when I visited Choushi, I was graced by your instruction. Since returning, while attending to external affairs..."
Using this as a whip, he sat in meditation for one day. Upon raising the "dog" koan, his chest and mind suddenly opened up like the vast void, entirely free of obstruction.
The words and phrases of the Patriarchs are the gateway to entering the Way; to cling to them without letting go is a great illness.
From that time on, worldly conditions and mundane thoughts no longer required deliberate expulsion; they were purified from within. This is the public record of the ancients.
Reflecting on what I previously found bewildering, I now have no further doubts (Zi Jian). Zhi once awakened to the Way upon hearing the sound of a bell, composing a verse that said:
"A single strike of the bell / Blocks the faculty of hearing / A thief is driven away from the lump of flesh. When someone asked which school he followed, he replied:
"The god Śūnyatā has a black face. Later, he donated his residence to establish Huiyun Temple and invited Po’an Xian to serve as its abbot.
The Chan Master’s inscription for the founding of the monastery states: "To relinquish a forest dwelling and establish an *āraṇya*—how could this be a minor matter?

We request that the Patriarch ascend the curved bamboo chair solely for the sake of the Great Matter. Moreover, as the founder acting as the first patriarch, you must expound the Gate of Non-duality for the sake of the assembly.

Such a favorable opportunity is rarely encountered; one who possesses the virtue of benevolence need not yield. Chan Master Po’an’s fame has spread across rivers and seas, and his Way is held in high esteem."
At Min and Emei, he traveled extensively through the various schools until he was struck by Miam, who knocked his nostrils out of place.

One day, he brought it forth and peeled back his own skin at Lengquan. Who would have thought that such fragrance need be so heavily emphasized? An old layman happened to meet him; indeed, an old enemy is difficult to escape.
There is no need for many words—why trouble yourself with such a long journey? Take leave of the green pines by the northern stream.
Passing through several layers of clouds emerging from the mountain peaks, he gazes upon the green waters of the Southern Lake. May he enjoy a ten-thousand-year lifespan as stable as a mountain.

Lin Xi-yi, whose style name is Yan-zhai, served as a Zhong-da-fu (Minister of the Second Grade) and Director of the Bao-mu Pavilion, and was later appointed as the Commissioner for Chengdu Prefecture. Yù... [text fragment]
Regarding the *Juguan* (Local Observations), there are commentaries on the works of Zhuangzi, Laozi, and Liezi by the three masters that circulate in the world.
He once composed the "Epitaph for Chan Master Duanqiao Lun," which states in brief: "I consider Fu Zhenggong [to be comparable] to Huayan Ying, and Fan Wenzheng to Gu Jianfu."
Zhang Ziyuan and Yuan Gao Dahui both revered him as men of eminent merit and great age;

thus, the monastic community has regarded him as a pillar of the Dharma until the present day. How could the Master’s attainment of the Duke Wei be any less than theirs? Without the Duke, one could not have known the Master;
without the Master, the Duke could not have been attained. Their great capacities and great functions are fully contained within their recorded sayings.
Thereupon he inscribed this eulogy: "The teaching of Duanqiao was not transmitted through words and phrases; that which can be transmitted has already been序 (prefaced) by Zhuxi.

The Master served as a stabilizing pillar amidst the degenerate dharma of the monastic forests. When I observe his beginning, there is indeed a unique interest; how could there be any doubt regarding the hemp and the arrow?"
What did you awaken to at Laṅkā? Why was there no accord within Wuzu’s room? What sound did you hear that finally caused the sweat to flow?
Why now, Master, does the board not stop sounding? What is this sound like? It must have a place of descent. I have composed this inscription for those who come to transmit it further.

Zheng Qingzhi, styled Qingzhi, served as Chancellor to Emperor Lizong and was enfeoffed as Duke of Wei. He once composed the epitaph for the Venerable Miaofeng Shan, which states: "The Dharma of the Western Mind is inconceivable;
Truly pure and wondrously luminous, without a single thread of defilement. The speech of the broad and long tongue encompasses Mount Sumeru—who [could fathom it]?"
To recognize the pointing finger as the moon is an error; the ancient adept who sat facing the wall for nine years transmitted the Dharma not through bowl or robe.
It is neither Buddha, nor Dharma, nor any worldly affair. Penetrating earth and penetrating heaven, it radiates brilliance. When all remaining dust is cleared away, both are forgotten.

For one who has awakened, there is no delusion—who then could be deluded? I recognized Miaofeng when I saw him again; his speech was true and his appearance was ancient. There is nothing [superfluous].
He was as extraordinary as a wild crane that flies off with the clouds. Though the zither is played, what gain or loss can there be?
With snow thickening and plum blossoms thinning, he closed the gate by the spring. Boundless springtime essence resides in a single withered branch;
viewing life and death as true play, only the lofty stele standing beside him knows his state. He also built Dongshan Temple at Hengxi in Yinzhou, modeled after Xie An’s Mount Dong.

Wu Qian, whose courtesy name was Lizhai, served as Chancellor to Emperor Lizong. While en route to his place of exile, he stayed overnight at Jiedai Temple in Fengting and said to the monks of the temple:
"In the past, Mañjuśrī told the World-Honored One: 'When I first entered the inconceivable samādhi, I bound my mind to a single object.'"
If one practices for a long time until mastery is achieved, no other thoughts will arise, and the mind will always be conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This binding of the mind to a single object is the very ladder for becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch. What is called "binding the mind to a single object" includes such practices as the visualization of the sun, the moon, the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the tuft of hair between the eyebrows), or the white spot on the bridge of the nose;
although these matters are superficial and mundane, their underlying principle is profoundly subtle. As Zhaozhou said:
"An old monk’s twelve periods of the day consist of only two moments of 'miscellaneous' mental engagement: those for eating porridge and rice.
When Guishan asked Lan’an, 'What do you do during your twelve periods of the day? An replied, 'I herd oxen. Guishan asked, 'How do you herd them?
An said, 'Whenever it enters the grass, I pull it back by the nose. These are all instances of binding the mind to a single object. After this, the Venerable..."
Furthermore, he generates skillful and subtle expedient means, causing the student to contemplate a "critical phrase" (huatou),
such as "The dog has Buddha-nature," "Three pounds of flax," "A dried-up shit-stick," "The monk's robe from Qingzhou," "The radish of Zhenzhou," or "The cypress tree in the courtyard," and so forth.
These are all points where the path of reasoning is blocked, intended for people to examine one case at a time.

As they look again and again, and doubt arises after doubt, they must never let go throughout the twelve periods of the day. Suddenly, when their nostrils flare open with a single burst, that is precisely where the person establishes their dwelling and sustains their life.
These are all evidences of binding the mind to a single object. This is the monk of this temple [who says].
Some practitioners may indeed maintain rigorous purity, reciting sutras and prostrating to the Buddha without their ribs touching their mats;
this is truly rare even within the Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya schools and may be called "diligence. Yet, with such a foundation, one can further advance a step further:

by binding the mind to a single object and practicing meditative concentration to give rise to wisdom, every person is a Buddha—a ready-made koan within oneself that requires no borrowing from others.
One sets up a grand shop for precious jewels, yet it is a pity that one spends an entire lifetime merely within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Even if, by virtue of observing the precepts and cultivating merit in this life, one does not lose the human form in the next, one will once again labor at worldly affairs.
From one shell to another, when will there ever be an end? Should one happen to stumble even slightly, one will remain prostrate for eternal kalpas, unable to rise. As it is said:
"If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life shall it be delivered? These words are most piteous and urgent.
Old Man Lüzhai was unable to deliver himself first, yet he first vowed to deliver others. I have written this to emulate his giving of the Dharma (Zijian).
Liu Mimi, styled Jingzhai, authored the *Sanjiao Pingxin Lun* (A Balanced Discourse on the Three Teachings). Its opening states:
"I have observed that China has possessed the Three Teachings since Fuxi drew the eight trigrams, from which Confucianism began; and since Laozi composed the *Daodejing*..."
The Classics established the Way, and thus Daoism began here; from Emperor Ming of the Han’s dream of the golden man, Buddhism began here.

This is the sequence of the Three Teachings in China. Generally speaking, Confucianism establishes its teaching through rectitude, Daoism establishes its teaching through honor, and Buddhism establishes its teaching through greatness.
When observing their love for life and abhorrence of killing, they share the same benevolence; when viewing others, they regard them as...
To act with impartiality oneself is the same [principle]. To punish anger, suppress desire, prohibit transgressions, and prevent wrongdoing is the same practice of cultivation.
To be like thunder to the deaf and the sun and moon to the blind is the same influence on social transformation.
Judging from coarse appearances, the principles of the world do not exceed the two paths of good and evil; thus, the intent of the Three Teachings is none other than to desire that people—

It simply returns to what is good. In China, Confucianism rectifies the fundamental principles and human relations; it clarifies ritual, music, law, and government so that they extend everywhere without contradiction.
Thus, heaven and earth and all things find their proper places and receive their nourishment. Its contribution to the world is truly great.
Therefore, although the First Emperor of Qin sought to eliminate Confucianism, Confucianism ultimately could not be removed. As for Daoism in China...
It causes people to maintain themselves through purity and emptiness, and to sustain themselves through humility and weakness.

It thoroughly washes away the habits of worldly confusion and entanglement, leading one back to the realm of stillness, silence, and non-action (*wuwei*). Its contribution to the teachings of the world is thus supreme.

When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty sought to eliminate the Way [of Buddhism], he found that the Way could ultimately not be eliminated. In China, Buddhism leads people to abandon the ostentatious...
In terms of reality, one turns away from the false to return to the true; through the practice of vigor, one attains peaceful conduct;
and through self-benefit, one reaches the benefit of others. As a refuge for the people, there is nothing that surpasses this.

Even when the emperors of the Three Wu periods sought to extinguish Buddhism, the Buddha could ultimately not be extinguished. When Li Shiqian of the Sui dynasty discussed the three teachings, he said of the Buddha: [text continues]
The Daoist is the sun; the Buddhist is the moon; the Confucian is the five planets. Is it not the case that these three luminaries in the heavens are indispensable, one missing another?

Likewise, these three teachings in the world are likewise indispensable, one missing another. Although their relative merits differ, they must not be allowed to be neglected in favor of one another (this is a balanced assessment).
The capital of Liao was Shangjing (Upper Capital). Its national name was Qidan. The imperial clan of Taizu was Yelü, and his personal name was Abaoji. Taizong moved the capital to Liao.
Beginning from the Bingzi year of Taizu and ending with the Jiachen year of Tianzuo, there were nine sovereigns over a period of two hundred and nine years.
The capital was moved to Shangjing; the state name was changed to Jin. The太祖 (Taizu) belonged to the Wanyan clan; his personal name was Aguda. He was the eldest son of Yangge Taishi.

In the sixteenth year [of his reign], he proclaimed himself Emperor and changed the state name to Jin. Upon reaching the reign of Shizong, the capital was moved to Yan, and the Tai... was established.
From Emperor Zu Wuxu to Emperor Jin Aiwu, there were nine sovereigns for a total of one hundred and seventeen years.
Emperor Taizong (r.
923–926), whose personal name was Sheng, was the second son of Yang Ge. He changed the era name to Tianhui and invited the Jintan Ruixiang (Auspicious Sandalwood Image) to Yan.
In the capital, a water and land assembly (*śrāddha*) was held for seven days and nights, enshrined at Minjungsa Temple for offerings.

Emperor Hixong (whose personal name was Dàn), the legitimate grandson of Taizu, changed the era name to Tianquan. He once issued an imperial decree for the Great Master Haehye to [ascend] the throne...
In the capital, he established Dajuching Monastery beside the palace and universally ordained one million monks and nuns, followed by a general amnesty for the empire.

He further issued an edict appointing the two Chan masters Haihui and Qinghui to reside at Chujing Monastery. A sandalwood image was invited from its original temple to the Jiqing Pavilion of the monastery for veneration.
When Haihui passed away, the Emperor personally enshrined his relics in five locations where stupas were erected; he was specially posthumously titled "Buddha."

King Sejong further conferred upon the State Preceptor for Awakening and Protection (Gak-woo Gukdaeseonsa) the honorary title of Grand Master of Pure Wisdom and Buddha-Wisdom Protecting the Nation (Cheonghye Bulji Huguk Daesa),
along with a golden-bordered robe.
The temple name of Emperor Shizong was Yong. He was the grandson of Taizu. He changed the era name to Dading and moved the capital to Yan.
By imperial decree, Daqingshou Monastery was constructed, and he issued an edict appointing Chan Master Mingxuan Yi as the first patriarch of the founding generation.

An imperial decree ordered the Crown Prince to descend with incense and grant twenty thousand coins and twenty *qǐng* of irrigated fields. Furthermore, by imperial decree, Chan Master Yi was commissioned to establish Qing’an Monastery in Dongjing. [He] ordained...
There were five hundred monks who held the Pañcavārṣika assembly. For twenty years, by imperial decree, the Xiyin Chan Temple was established on the western mountains of Yanjing;
furthermore, Chan Master Zhiyi was summoned by edict to open the mountain, granted fields, and provided for the assembly and the ordination of monks.

Emperor Zhangzong, whose personal name was Jing, was the son of Emperor Xianzong Yuncong. Before Yuncong had been formally enthroned, he passed away, and Zhangzong ascended the throne as the Imperial Grandson (Huangtaisun).
He changed the era name to Mingchang. In the fourth year of his reign, he issued an edict for Chan Master Wansong to ascend the seat within the imperial court.

The Emperor personally performed the rite of welcoming [the Master]. Hearing the Dharma he had never heard before, he was awakened and moved with deep emotion. He personally presented a *saṃghāṭī* robe made of fine silk and brocade, approaching the seat to offer it as a gift.
The ladies of the inner palace and the high-ranking relatives prostrated themselves and knelt in reverence, each offering their most cherished treasures as acts of worship and support.
The Buddhist service for the Universal Deliverance Assembly was established. For consecutive days, auspicious clouds stretched continuously across the horizon.

From then on, harvests were bountiful and songs of joy filled the roads. Every year, when the vegetarian feast was held, auspicious omens were constantly perceived. When the Emperor’s carriage visited Mount Yan, there were verses stating:
"The realm of Tuṣita within the Golden World; the palace of Brahmā amidst blue lotuses. In the fourth year of the Cheng’an era, the Emperor...
By imperial decree issued following the late Empress Dowager’s final testament, the Helong Prefecture was ordered to construct Daming Monastery and build a nine-story pagoda.
Thirty thousand monks were ordained and granted ordination certificates (duce) as an offering for her posthumous merit.
Donghae Hou, whose name was Yunji, was the seventh son of Emperor Sejong. When Emperor Zhangzong passed away without an heir, the ministers followed his last will and enthroned him.

He changed the era name to Dà'ān (Great Peace) and reigned for four years. It was in the thirteenth year of this era that the auspicious sandalwood image arrived in the Jin state. This is the year in question.
They were welcomed and installed in the imperial palace of the capital for veneration (the above from the *Jin zhì*).

The *Jin guo zhì* states: Although many members of the nobility and prominent clans within the Buddhist faith renounce their sons and daughters to become monks and nuns, Chan is predominant while Vinaya is scarce.

In the capital, they are titled National Preceptor (*guoshi*); in the provincial headquarters, they are titled Registrar of Monks (*senglù*) and Rectifier of Monks (*sengzhèng*); and in the subordinate prefectures...
The head of the provincial administration is called the Dugang; the head of the county is called the Weina. Their tonsure and ceremonial deportment are equal to those of the Southern Song dynasty.
The titles conferred upon them are Daishi (Great Master) or Dade (Virtuous One), and they are all granted the purple robe and the title of Guoshi (State Preceptor). They wear robes of true vermilion.
The positions of Senglu (Registrar of Monks) and Sengzheng (Corrector of Monks) are limited to a three-year term, and both wear purple robes. The Dugang also serves for a term of three years.

Those masters who possess a title are granted the purple robe; those without one follow the usual custom. Regarding disputes among the *śramaṇa-vinaya* (monastic administrators) of both monks and nuns:

matters involving punishments of the cane or below are settled and dispatched locally; those involving punishments of the cane or above must all be submitted to the Office of the Monastic Registrar (*senglu*) and the Chief Administrator (*dugang*).

Li Zhichun, whose courtesy name was Chunfu and self-designation was Pingshan Jushi, was a native of Hongzhou. He was a jinshi degree holder during the Cheng’an era of Emperor Zhangzong’s reign and served as an official up to the rank of Shushang Yousi Dushi.
By nature he was brilliant and far-reaching; there were no books in the world that he had not read.
He was particularly proficient in the works of Zhuang Zhou, Lie Yukou, the *Zuozhuan*, and the *Zhan Guo Ce*, and his own prose was also roughly capable of emulating them.
After the age of thirty, he read Buddhist scriptures extensively; subsequently, he took up and studied the texts of the various schools of Daoxue (Learning of the Way).
Once he attained realization within his own mind, he unified the three schools into one.

He took the explanations of the former scholars and provided annotations for those points that were inconsistent, composing a definitive work titled *Mingdao jishuo* (Collected Explanations for Proclaiming the Way) (contained in the *Huang Wenxian ji*).
The preface to the *Mingdao jishuo* states: "Before Heaven and Earth were produced, the Sage existed in the Dao; after Heaven and Earth had been produced..."
Furthermore, the Way resides in the sages. Therefore, since the birth of the human race, there has never been one who became a sage without attaining the Way.
The minds of Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi are revealed in the *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*); the minds of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu are revealed in the *Odes* and the *Documents*.
All of these were great sages who attained the Way. If the sages did not rule as kings, the arts of the Way would have...

[The text] is fragmented. There was Laozi, who roamed beyond the mundane world; fearing that people of future generations would become obstructed and find no way of entry, he spoke loftily of the time before Heaven and Earth were born, purifying [the mind] through the Way and its Virtue (*moral*). There was Confucius, who roamed within the mundane world;
fearing that people of future generations would be dazzled and have nowhere to turn, he discussed earnestly the period after Heaven and Earth had already come into being, and...
They sealed [their teachings] with benevolence and righteousness; thus, there are no words among them that do not have slight points of mutual conflict.
Nevertheless, whether blowing or exhaling, pulling or pushing, beginning or ending, east or west, the will of the Dark Sage and the Plain King likewise all has its ultimate destination.
Their disciples feared that these elements would not harmonize and would consequently lead to fragmentation.
Master Zhuang Zhou followed the current downstream, proceeding from the Heavenly Man to the Sage; Master Meng Ke followed the current upstream, proceeding from the Good Man to the Divine Man.
Like two halves of a tally, the doctrine of "sagehood within and kingly rule without" is fully contained therein.
Alas! Since the passing of the Four Sages, Lie Yukou’s writings have diverged from the truth; Xun Qing’s work is eclectic rather than pure;
Yang Xiong and Wang Tong presumed to be sages themselves through usurpation; and Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu allowed their minds to run wild in the pursuit of literary style.
Thus, the Way of the Sage has been like a single thread, untransmitted for fifteen hundred years. Yet, as for the books of the Buddhists...
It comes from the West, at a distance of many tens of millions of *li* from China.

When verified through its texts—winding and composed in parallel prose—and translated through successive layers of interpretation, its ultimate words and subtle principles accord perfectly with the spirit and essence of our own ancient sages.
It is simply that his disciples were unable to elucidate his underlying intent. How could it be that the traces of the Sage would ultimately perish beneath ten thousand ages and beyond the four seas?
Various Confucian scholars have secretly adopted his teachings to corroborate our own scriptures.
Beginning with Li Ao, and continuing down to recent times, Wang Anshi and his son initiated this movement in the past, while Su Shi and his brother harmonized it in the present.
They provided commentaries on the *Great Changes*, the *Book of Poetry*, the *Book of Documents*, the *Analects*, the *Mencius*, as well as the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi.

Subsequently, the teachings of the School of the Western Creek (Lǎn-xī), the Water of Sòu (Sù-shuǐ), Héng-qú, and Yì-chuán arose in succession. Furthermore, there were those from Shàng-cài, Guī-shān, Yuán-chéng, and Héng-pǔ.
Their followers further assisted them, and the writings of Donglai, Nanxuan, and Huian spread far and wide. Consequently, their words became both grand and commonplace.
How fortunate I am to have encountered the discourses of these various masters; in my heart, I know that the ancient sages have not died and that the Great Way is about to be unified.
Yet, fearing that after unification it may again diverge, I have annotated those points where they do not accord with antiquity.
The *Shengren yue ming dao ji shuo* (The Sage’s Utterances on the Way: A Collection of Explanations) states [the collection comprises two hundred and seventeen chapters].
Yila Zhenqing—Zhenqing’s courtesy name was Chucái; his original surname was Ye-lü. When the Jin dynasty extinguished the Liao, Zhenqing returned to the Jin and changed his surname to Yila.
Là (1147–1230) styled himself the Layman Zhànrán. He once composed the "Postscript to the *Míngdào jíshuō*," which states in brief:
"When Lǐ Píngshān was on his deathbed, he presented the *Míngdào jíshuō* to Jìng Dìngchén, saying: 'This is my final work of severing ties with the world. You must keep it secret;
there will surely be one who appreciates its true sound. When Dìngchén heard that I was seeking to purchase Píngshān’s writings, he [offered this to me]."
This manuscript was forwarded to me by Master Wansong Xiu. Upon reading it, I wept with emotion for several days.
In the past, I had seen the *Mingdao ji* (Collection on Proclaiming the Way) and felt indignant toward it; I wished to write a critique to rectify its errors and obscurities, but lacked the leisure.
Who would have thought that Pingshan had anticipated me and taken the lead, providing a preface to act as a needle for the chronic, incurable ailments of the scholars of Jiangzuo?
This illness—may it serve as medicine for the scholar-officials of the Central Plains who suffer from this same malady.
*Fófǎjīntāngbiān*, Volume Fifteen, re-edited by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
*Fófǎjīntāngbiān*, Volume Sixteen.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xintai of Kuaiji;
reviewed by the Śramaṇa Zhenqing of Tiantai. The Yuan edition.
The capital was Yan. Beginning with Shizu and ending with Shundi, there were eight sovereigns in total, for a period of one hundred years.
Regarding Shizu:
his personal name was Kublai, his clan was the Qiwowen, and he was a member of the Mongol tribe; he was the fourth son of Ruzong.
In the Gengshen year, he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Zhongtong, Year One. A general amnesty was proclaimed, and monks and nuns were universally ordained.
In the twelfth month, the Indian monk Ba-nian-si-ba was appointed Imperial Preceptor (Dishi); he was granted a jade seal and charged with presiding over the affairs of the Buddhist teachings.

In the fifth month of Year Two, fifty *qing* of land each in Huai’ang and Xingzhou were bestowed upon the monk Zicong (the former Grand Protector Liu), and the Qingshou Temple was likewise granted land.
The Great Being Haiyun [performed] a great Buddhist service at Hetao Temple for seven days and nights on land spanning five hundred *qing* during the third year of the reign (November).
One thousand five hundred taels of silver were bestowed [upon him] (*Yuan Shi*). In the first year of Zhizheng, the *jiǎzǐ* year, he resided in Yan;
an assembly was convened to ordain monks, and by imperial decree, the National Preceptor Panmidalesiaba ascended the throne to confer the secret precepts.
In the eighth month, Liu Bingzhong was appointed as Grand Preceptor (Taibao) and Director of the Secretariat (Cangling Zhongshu Shengshi) (*Tongzai*).

In the second year, an imperial edict was issued to the General Directorate of Monks (Zongtong Suo), stating that those among the monks who had mastered the five great scriptural divisions were to be selected for office. Those possessing virtuous conduct were appointed as State and Prefectural Monastic Registrars (Senglü).

They were also authorized to appoint the officials of the Chief and Deputy Directories (Zhengfu Dugang). Furthermore, the three schools of study were established in each administrative region to lecture upon the three types of Chan.
In the first month of the third year, an imperial edict was issued for monks and Daoists to pray for blessings at the monasteries and observatories in the capital.

By imperial decree, the monk Ji was appointed as the presiding leader (zongtong) and took up residence at Qingshou Monastery. In the eleventh month of the sixth year, Buddhist rites were performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple for seven days and nights.
In the seventh year, by imperial decree, the Vajra Master Dam-pa was invited to preside over Renwang Temple.
In the twelfth month, the Great State-Protecting Renwang Temple was established at Gaoliang River. An imperial edict was issued to revise the colors of monastic robes.

In the fifth month of the eighth year, Buddhist rites were performed on Qionghua Island. In the eleventh year, the national name was established as Yuan. In the ninth year, the monks of the capital were assembled.
The Tripitaka was recited for nine assemblies. In the fourteenth year, the Great Sage Wan’an Temple was established.
In the second month, an imperial decree appointed the monks Kang Jixiang and Lianzhen Jiagawa as General Superintendents (*zongshe*) of the Buddhist teachings in Jiangnan;

monastic land taxes were abolished, and those who disturbed temple precincts were forbidden (from the *Yuanshi*). On the first day of the first month of the fifteenth year, a ritual assembly was held to provide vegetarian meals for the monks. In the eighteenth year...
By imperial decree, with the exception of the *Daode jing*, all other scriptures such as the *Huahu jing* were to be completely incinerated.

An edict was issued for the scholars of the Hanlin Academy—Tang Fang, Wang Gou, Li Qian, Yan Fu, Li Zhu, Wang Pan, and others—to compose a commemorative stele (the full text is contained in the *Tongzai*).
On the nineteenth day of the first month of the twenty-fifth year, Yang Nianzhenga, the General Superintendent of Buddhist Teachings for Jianghuai, assembled [the clergy] at the Jiang...

The Southern Chan teachings reached Yanjing (Beijing), where he inquired about the Dharma. Yunfeng Miaogao, the abbot of Mount Jing, expounded them in such a way that they accorded with the Emperor’s wishes (the details of this matter are fully recorded in the *Tongzai*).
The Emperor once asked the Imperial Preceptor, "What merit is there in repairing temples and building pagodas? The Preceptor replied, "Its blessings will shade the great thousand-fold world system.
Consequently, the Renwang Temple was constructed. After the Preceptor had finished the imperial vegetarian feast, golden flowers rained down from the sky. The Emperor asked, "Why?"
Therefore, these auspicious omens appeared. The Master said, "The Emperor’s inner mind-flower has blossomed; thus Heaven rains down golden flowers in praise.
The Emperor asked the Shu monk Yuan-yi, "Why is it that the followers of Confucius and Laozi are so few, while the followers of the Tathāgata are so numerous?
Yuan-yi replied, "The wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few; the poor regret that even one body is too many. The Emperor then established a great *jiezhi* (precept-holding) ceremony.

Light emanated from various places. The Emperor asked the Imperial Preceptor, "From where does this light come? The Preceptor replied, "Through the mutual resonance of cause and response, the Buddha’s light has manifested.
The Emperor summoned ten eminent monks to offer sustenance in the inner palace; the Emperor sat upright and motionless.
The various virtuous ones likewise remained silent. The Emperor then said, "This is true merit.

In his leisure from the myriad affairs of state, the Emperor personally offered food and recited prayers while holding a rosary. The Emperor summoned his ministers and said, "I govern the world with the true mind of primordial enlightenment, which is non-dual.
It is like watching a海东青 (Haidongqing) hawk seize a wild goose; because the mind is non-dual. The Emperor looked upon them.
He restored all the taxes on the temple lands and estates throughout the realm and universally enabled the monastic community to settle their minds and cultivate the Way.
His *Shilu* (Veritable Record) comprises over a hundred chapters; word for word and phrase for phrase, he took the propagation of the Teaching as his own responsibility (*Hongjiao ji*).
He reigned for thirty-five years and reached the age of eighty. In the national language, he is called Emperor Shiche'en.
Emperor Chengzong.
His posthumous name was Tiemu'er. He was the grandson of Emperor Shizu and the third son of Emperor Yuzong Zhenjin. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Yuanzheng.
In that year, he issued an edict summoning Master Yin of Yuetai to the imperial court; upon his audience, he pleased the Emperor's mind and was granted the title Tonghui.
The Chan Master, along with his golden-embroidered Dharma robe, was honored; in the first year of the Dade era, a thousand ingots were issued to establish Lintao Temple.

Previously, the Great Emperor (Shizu) had wished to establish a Buddhist temple at the sublime site of Mount Wutai but had not succeeded. The Emperor now fulfilled that intention by constructing the temple.
He was granted the name Mansu Yuguk-sa (Myōshū Yūkoku-ji). King Myeongjong commanded State Preceptor Jingak Munjae to serve as its abbot.

In the third year [of his reign], he appointed Great Zen Master Hongji as the General Superintendent of Buddhist Teachings for Jiangzhe. In the ninth year, the monk Ning Ilsan of Putuo was dispatched to Japan bearing an imperial edict.
When Jianzang of Lianzhen passed away, the king provided funeral expenses of five hundred taels of gold, one thousand taels of silver, and ceremonial silks.

Ten thousand bolts of silk and three thousand ingots of paper currency were granted; furthermore, he was commissioned to construct a stupa and a temple. In the national language, he is called Emperor Wan-erh-du (Wan-erh-du Huangdi).
(From the *Yuan Shi* and *Tongzai*).
Emperor Wuzong.
His personal name was Haishan. He was the eldest son of Emperor Shunzong Dalama Bal. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Zhida.
In the first year, he dispatched fifteen hundred soldiers to repair the Buddhist temples of Mount Wutai. The Emperor traveled to the Upper Capital and constructed a Buddhist temple there.

Furthermore, in the capital, he bestowed seven hundred and fifty taels of silver, two thousand two hundred strings of paper currency, and three hundred bolts of silk upon Haotian Temple to sponsor a great *shuilu* assembly.

During the Zhida era, by special imperial decree, Master Yuansou Duan was granted the posthumous title "Huiben Zhengbian" (Wisdom and Correct Eloquence) along with a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* (as recorded in the *Yuan Shi* and his funerary inscription). In the national language, this is called *Qū*.
Emperor Lü (Lühuangdi). Rénzōng.
His posthumous name was Àiyù Lībá Dāobādá. He was the second son of Shùnzhōng and the younger brother of Wǔzōng. Year of the Water Rat (Rénzǐ).
Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Huangqing. In the first year, he appointed the Western monk Zangbu Banba as National Preceptor and bestowed upon him a jade seal.

He also granted Dapuqing Temple one thousand taels of gold, five thousand taels of silver, and ten thousand ingots of paper currency. He further ordered the restoration of Puan Temple on Mount Xiangshan (according to the *Yuanshi*).
In the first year of Yanyou, he issued an imperial decree to construct the Candana Auspicious Image Hall and conferred an additional title upon Chan Master Puan.
[Bestow] a title. The Imperial Edict stated: "I have heard that the Buddha-dharma takes emptiness and stillness as its primary principle.
As for those who follow this learning, how could they wish to establish names and titles or extraordinary appellations to display them to the world and future generations?

Yet, it is through these that our state may manifest the intent of honoring virtue and delighting in the Way. Since my accession to the throne, I have heard of Nanquan Mountain on the road to Yuanzhou..."

The Great Virtue Chan Master Huìqìng of Cíhuà Chán Monastery, whose posthumous names were Pǔān, Jìgǎn, Miàojì, Zhēnjué, and Zhāoxuáng, succeeded the lineage of Línjì and transcended the realm of Huáyán. His virtue illuminated his own era, and his beneficence reached those yet to come;
his Way was most venerable and manifest, and I have long cherished a deep admiration for it. You may add the title "Stupa of Miraculous Auspiciousness" to the Stupa of Dìngguāng.
(Tongzai). In the third year, he established the Great Water and Land Assembly at Mount Jinshan and commanded Master Yuansou Duan to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.
Upon the completion of the ceremony, he entered the palace for an audience in the private hall; his composed discourse deeply accorded with the Emperor’s inner thoughts.

Consequently, the Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-Sun Shining Everywhere" (Furi Puzhao) along with a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* (Taming). In the sixth year, he was granted monastic rations for the monks of Daixingjiao Temple. 1000 *shao* of rice.
Twenty thousand ingots [of silver] and ten thousand ingots of paper currency from Qianyuan Temple were provided to generate interest for the expenses of restoration (Yuan Shi).
When the Emperor heard of the Way of Mingben of Tianmu Zhongfeng, he invited him but he did not come;

the Emperor then fashioned a *kāṣāya* robe with golden patterns and bestowed it upon him, granting him the title Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui and bestowing the plaque "Zhengzong" (Orthodox Lineage) upon Lion Monastery.
Chan Temple. An imperial edict commanded the Hanlin Academician and Chief Counselor, Lord Zhao of Wuxing, to compose an inscription for the temple stele as a gift (as recorded in the *Guanglu*).
In the national language, he was called Emperor Buyantu.
Emperor Yingzong. His posthumous name was Shuode’erla; he was the legitimate son of Emperor Renzong. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Zhizhi.

In the first year [of his reign], he issued an edict for each administrative circuit to establish a Hall for the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi). He commanded the construction of the Stele for the Hall of the Imperial Preceptor (*Tongzai*). Furthermore, he performed great Buddhist rites at the Baoci Hall.
The Western monk Yabala was appointed as the Yuan Yongyan Jiao Tripiṭaka Dharma Master and invested with a golden seal.

Furthermore, he was ordered by Bayizhu to construct Shouanshan Temple. He also performed Buddhist rites in the Guangtian Hall, where he cast bronze statues of the Buddha and enshrined them in the Yudede Hall.
He further performed Buddhist rites in the Wende Hall and appointed the monk Hong as the Patriarch of the Shiyuan School.

The Emperor conferred upon him the rank of Rongludagu. When the Emperor traveled to the Upper Capital, he dispatched an envoy to bestow upon the monk Chesa Jia-di two hundred and fifty *liang* of gold, two thousand five hundred *liang* of silver, twenty thousand *kāṣāyas*, and various amounts of silk, banners, and tea.
He also dispatched the mantra-master Duerzhi to the two kingdoms of Yaji and Banbu to retrieve Buddhist scriptures and construct a golden stupa.
In the capital, the Buddha’s *śarīra* were enshrined. An imperial edict was issued to all offices throughout the realm, ordering monks to recite one hundred thousand sections of scripture.

Furthermore, an edict was issued for the four temples of Wanan, Qingshou, Sheng’an, and Puqing in the capital, as well as Jinshan Temple on the Yangtze River and Wanshengyuguo Temple on Mount Wutai, to perform the *Shuilu* (Water-Land) Assembly for seven days and nights. In the third year, the Emperor commanded the monk Ruyi to transcribe [the scriptures] in gold.
The *Zizang jing* (Sūtra on the Treasury of Characters). In this year, he summoned Master Zhantang Cheng to the capital for an audience at Mingren Hall.
By imperial decree, he was tasked with collating the Tripitaka—Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras—at Qingta Temple and was specially granted a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya*.

The Emperor, who held the Way of Tianmu Zhongfeng in high esteem, sent incense and robes, dispatching an envoy to his residence to pay his respects. The Emperor [acted] for the sake of Gekian Huang...
The Emperor (from the *Yuan Shi*, "Guang Lu," "Epitaph"):
The Prince of Jin (referred to in history as the Taiding Emperor), whose name was Yesün Temür, was the eldest son of Xianzong Gamara and the legitimate grandson of Yuzong. That is to say—

The reign title was changed to the first year of Taiding. The Emperor traveled to Zhongdu and performed Buddhist rites in the Kunang Hall. He ordered monks to perform Buddhist services within the inner palace.
To suppress thunder, he had an image of Mahākāla fashioned and enshrined in the Huicheng Pavilion of the Yanchun Gate.
He also performed Tibetan Buddhist rites at Anshan Temple. On the day of Guihai in the sixth month, he established a prayer hall (禮拜寺).
In the capital, the rites for the Buddha Kṛṣṇadanta (Black Tooth) were performed at the Crystal Hall. The Emperor received the Buddhist precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (Ti-shi).
A portrait of the Imperial Preceptor Phags-pa was painted and distributed to all provinces, ordering that it be enshrined in statues for worship.
In the second year, he commanded the Western monks to perform incense-offering rites at the Yanhua Pavilion. In the third year, Shuxiang Temple was constructed at Wuyue.
Tai Shan was granted three hundred *qǐng* of land. The Western monk Gongge was appointed as Imperial Preceptor (*dìshī*) and bestowed with a jade seal.
He was ordered to perform Buddhist rites at Tianyuan Yanshou Temple. In the first year of the Zhihe era, he was commanded to perform Buddhist rites within the imperial palace.
The Emperor presided over the Xingsheng Hall and received the precepts of Amitābha Buddha from the Imperial Preceptor. He then ordered one thousand monks...

The people held a grand assembly at Zhenguosi Temple. By imperial decree, the Imperial Preceptor ordered monks to perform Buddhist rites in Yanguanzhou and constructed two hundred and sixteen stupas to suppress the flooding of the sea (from the *History of Yuan*).
Emperor Wenzong, whose personal name was Tugh Temür, was the second son of Emperor Wuzong. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Tianli (Heavenly Calendar) in the first year.

He abolished the Xuanzheng Yuan and established sixteen Regional Directorates for the Propagation of Buddhism (*Guangjiao Zongguanfu*). He then commanded the people of Gaochang to perform Buddhist rites.
Yanchun Ge. In the second year [of his reign], he ordered the former residence at Qianjing to be renamed Longxiang Jiqing Monastery.

He also established Chengtian Husheng Monastery (according to the *Yuanshi*). Having heard of Zhongfeng’s lofty conduct, the Emperor subsequently conferred upon him a posthumous title and a commemorative stele; the title was Zhijue.

The pagoda was named Fayun (Cloud of Dharma). Emperor Renzong summoned Yu Ji, a scholar of the Quizhang Pavilion, to the private audience hall and commanded him to compose the inscription for the Zhongfeng Pagoda (*Guanglu*).
When Longxiang Jiqing Temple was completed, a master of eminent virtue was selected to serve as its founding abbot; Chan Master Xiaoyin Yun was the first chosen for this role.
He was specially promoted to the third rank of the civil bureaucracy. The following year, he was summoned by imperial post to the capital, where he had an audience at the Quizhang Pavilion.
He was granted a seat and consulted him on the essentials of the Dharma; his responses were in accord with the Imperial will (as recorded in the Stele Inscription).
An edict was issued granting one hundred and fifty *qǐng* of official fields in Pingjiang to Longxiang Temple and Chongxi Temple.

By imperial decree, all temple lands belonging to various monasteries—whether held since the Jin or Song dynasties or bestowed by successive reigns—were entirely exempted from rent. Furthermore, those who were required to pay rent were likewise exempted from corvée labor.

Those monks who had returned to lay life were permitted to re-enter the Sangha. On the anniversary of Emperor Wuzong’s death, three hundred and forty Korean and Chinese monks were ordered to recite the two Tripitakas at Chong’en Fuyuan Temple.

In the first year of the Zhishun era, the Emperor, the Empress, and Prince Yan received Buddhist precepts; the Western monk Xuni Dieba Dalaban was appointed as the National Preceptor of the Tripitaka.
The Master was granted a gold seal. When the Emperor visited the Upper Capital, he ordered Western monks to perform Buddhist rites within the imperial carriage.
He further commanded Western monks to perform Buddhist rites for one month each at Mount Wutai and Mount Wuling to pray for the longevity and prosperity of the Crown Prince.
An envoy was dispatched to summon Zhao Shiyen to Jiqing. One thousand copies of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* were to be transcribed in gold leaf using Uyghur script.
An imperial decree was issued for one entire collection (*bka' 'gyur*) of Buddhist scriptures to be transcribed in gold leaf.
It was further commanded that Western monks perform Buddhist rites at Mingzhong Pavilion on Mount Wansui (History of Yuan).
Shundi Shundi.
His personal name was Tuohan Temür. He was the eldest son of Mingzong. Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Yuntong.

In the first month of the second year, he abolished the Guangjiao General Administration (Guangjiao Zongguanfu) and re-established the Acting Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (Xing Xuanzhengyuan). In this same year, [the temple] Da Puqing...
The abbot of the temple, Shanda Mili, submitted a memorial requesting that the *Collected Works of the Late Master Mingben* be included in the Imperial Canon.

The Emperor approved the petition and conferred upon it the title of *Guanglu* (Extended Record). In the third year of the Zhizhi era, the monk Kalama from the Western Regions was summoned to the capital;
he was titled *Guanding Guoshi* (State Preceptor of Consecration) and granted a jade seal. In the eleventh month of the first year of the Zhiheng era, an edict was issued appointing Yongming.
A copy of the Tripitaka in golden lettering was transcribed at the temple, and the tax and grain levies for the entire country were remitted.

In the twelfth month of the third year, an edict was issued to transcribe the Tripitaka in golden lettering. In the twelfth month of the sixth year, an edict was issued to re-establish Hwaguk Inwangsa Temple.

In the second month of the seventh year, Buddhist rites were performed at Heungseonggung Palace, and two thousand ingots of paper currency were bestowed. In the twenty-eighth year, the kingdom was abolished.
The Emperor Da Ming, recognizing that he had obeyed the mandate of Heaven, withdrew and departed; he was posthumously titled Emperor Shun (Yuan Shi).
Prince Shen’s surname was Wang, his personal name was Zhang, and his style name was Haiyin Jushe; he was a prince of Goryeo who served during the reign of Renzong.
The Prince Consort (Fu-ma) Taiwei, having heard of the Way of Tianmu Zhongfeng, once sent a messenger to follow the Master to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma;

yet, finding this insufficient, he requested Emperor Renzong’s permission to go and see him in person. Thereupon, he traveled ten thousand *li* carrying incense, ascending the mountain to pay his respects.
Upon rising, he said to those around him: "I have observed many people, but none possess such supreme merit and virtue as this Master."

Having received the Master’s instruction, he was moved to tears. The King then constructed a pavilion before the cliff called "True Limit" (*Zhēnjiè*) to commemorate his attainment of the Dharma (from the *Epitaph for Zhongfeng*).
In a letter concerning the Dharma, the King wrote: "Your disciple, the Grand Marshal, Prince of Shen, Zhang, prostrates himself a hundred times and offers salutations.
To the presence of the Great Zen Master, the Monk Zhongfeng of Tianmu: Zhang is one of meager virtue who has, by fortune, been included among the imperial kin. As for my rank..."
Although my official emolument is honorable, I have always adhered to the Buddha’s transformation; I look up to the entrustment at Mount Ling and cherish the hidden radiance beneath the Bodhi tree.

Whenever I face the true image [of the Buddha], I gaze upon it with sincere longing. As for the cultivation of sublime matters and the listening to the unfolding of the teachings of the Vehicle, I have indeed engaged in these to some extent;
yet, regarding the "one upward step" of the Chan school, I know not where to turn. I humbly understand that our Master has transmitted the Way from Tianmu.
I name this letter to simplify the Emperor’s mind. It is truly because the rivers and mountains are so remote that we are still hindered from serving you in person.

We thirst for the *amṛta* of your teachings and long to be moistened by the rain of flowers; our longing is extreme. I reflect with reverence that the harmony between Heaven and Man has brought your Dharma-practice to a state of constant excellence.

Now, I have specially dispatched Hongyao to respectfully carry incense of faith as a substitute for my own prostrations. For a long time I have admired how you, O Venerable One, have cultivated your loftiness among the springs and rocks, while many [others] in other lands...
I have respectfully requested the Abbot, yet you have not yet granted your consent. Alas, the formless Dharmakāya, which seeks to remain hidden, is ever more manifest.

Why not emerge in the world to deliver sentient beings and extensively open the way for their benefit? Furthermore, I have long desired to travel and behold the sacred sites and holy realms of Jiangnan.

If I might receive your permission to come south during the autumn and winter months, I shall first seek an audience with you upon my arrival. I pray that you will rouse your compassion to save us. I venture to set forth these humble sentiments in advance; I hope you will grant me your favor.
Prayer for Fazhao (from the Extensive Record).

Liu Bingzhong, whose courtesy name was Zhonghui, later took the religious name Zicong upon following the teachings of the Śākya clan; he only changed to his current name after being appointed to office.

His ancestors were originally from Ruizhou and served the Liao dynasty for generations. His great-great-grandfather served the Jin dynasty as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Xingzhou and settled there, thereby becoming a native of Xingzhou.
His father, Ren, served as the Recorder (Lushi) of Xingzhou. When Yelü Bingzhong was born, his physical bearing was exceptionally refined and extraordinary;
his will and spirit were brilliant, vigorous, and unrestrained. At the age of eight, he entered school and recited several hundred words every day. At the age of ten...

At thirteen, he served as a hostage at the headquarters of the military commander. At seventeen, he served as a clerk in the administration of the Xingtai Prefectural Commandant’s office to support his parents.
He was often despondent and unhappy. One day, casting down his brush, he sighed and said: "My family has been of the scholar-official class for generations."
"Is this not to be submerged in the life of a mere scribe? When a man of integrity does not find his place in the world, he should retire from public life to pursue his own aspirations.

He then abandoned his official career and lived in seclusion among the mountains of Wuan for a long time. Later, Chan Master Xuzhao of Tianning Temple invited him to become a monk and appointed him as a secretary.
He subsequently traveled to Yunzhong and resided at Nantang Temple while Shizu was still in the period of concealment.
At the residence, Master Hǎiyún was summoned to Yúnzhōng. Hearing that [Yáng] Bǐngzhōng was widely learned and possessed many arts, he invited him to travel with him.

Upon entering the presence [of the Emperor], his responses met with imperial approval, and he frequently received the Emperor’s inquiries. Bǐngzhōng had perused no book without mastery; he was particularly proficient in the *I Ching* and Shào Yán’s *Jīngshì Shū*.
As for astronomy, geography, calendrical science, the three *Shì*, and the *Liùrén* divination—all were within his reach.

He was thoroughly proficient in all branches of *duñjiu* (the *duījiǎ* system), and when discussing matters of state, he did so as easily as pointing at objects in the palm of his hand. The Emperor (Shizu) held him in great esteem.

When he went to attend to his father’s funeral, the Emperor bestowed upon him one hundred taels of gold for the funerary equipment. Upon the completion of his mourning period, he was summoned again and, by imperial decree, returned to Helin.

He submitted a memorial of several thousand words. Although Bingzhong remained in the presence of the Emperor, he did not change his monastic robes; thus, people of the time [regarded him with respect].
He was styled the Secretary Cóng. In the first year of the Zhìyuán era of Shìzǔ, Wáng È, the Director of the Hanlín Academy, submitted a memorial stating:
"Bǐngzhōng’s rustic attire and informal titles are deeply unsettling; it is appropriate to rectify his dress and cap and honor him with a high-ranking office.

Upon reviewing the memorial, the Emperor appointed him to the rank of Guānglù Dàfū and the position of Tàibǎo, with the duty of participating in the affairs of the Zhōngshū Shěng, and [entrusted him] with the Hanlín Academy.

He was posthumously honored with the title of Grand Preceptor (Taishi) and the posthumous name Wenzheng. Emperor Renzong further enfeoffed him as the Prince of Changshan.

Initially, when Emperor Shizu campaigned against Yunnan and attacked the Song, Li Bingzhong assisted him. He held that taking life to cherish all beings is the virtue of Heaven and Earth, and that the Buddhists take compassion and the salvation of sentient beings as their core purpose.
Through skillful means (*upāya*) to rescue and protect, those whose lives were saved were beyond counting. Since childhood, Bingzhong had been fond of...

He studied until old age without ever flagging. Although his rank reached the pinnacle of ministerial office, he lived in a simple chamber and subsisted on vegetarian fare, remaining serene all day long without differing from his former habits.
He styled himself the "Recluse Who Stores Spring" (*Zangchun Sanren*) and found contentment in verse. His poetry was detached, leisurely, and tranquil.

Judging by his character, he was a man of refinement. He authored a collection of writings in ten volumes. Having no sons, he adopted Lan-zhang, the son of his younger brother Bing-shu, as his heir (from the *Yuanshi*).—Wang Pan.

Pan, courtesy name Wenbing, was a native of Yongnian in Guangping. His family had followed the profession of farming for generations. He was promoted to the rank of Grand Master for Merit (Zide Dafu) and retired from office.
Living in leisure, he did not engage in idle speech or laughter. He passed away at the age of ninety and was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Ming with the posthumous title Wenzhong.

On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the eighteenth year of the Zhiyuan era of Emperor Shizu, the false scriptures of the Daoist Canon were burned; the Emperor then commanded Pan and others to compose [the catalog].

The inscription states briefly: Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Xianzong, a follower of the Daoist school produced a work titled *The Scripture on Laojun Transforming into a Buddha* along with diagrams of his eighty-one transformations.
These were carved onto printing blocks and widely disseminated; their contents are vulgar, base, and preposterous.

His intention was to disparage the Buddhist community while exalting his own teachings. The Great Master Lanma of Kapiśa, who presided over the assembly, and the Elder Fǔ of Shaolin reported this to the throne.

At that time, the Shizu resided in the imperial quarters. By imperial decree from the Xuānzōng, the two groups—the monks and the Daoists—were ordered to go before His Majesty to debate their respective doctrines.
The two groups made a mutual agreement: if the Daoists prevailed, the monks would bow their heads in submission.

The Daoist said, "If the monk is superior, then the Daoist shall shave his head and become a monk. The monk asked the Daoist, "You have written that the Buddha converted the barbarians to become a Buddha.

Now, what is the meaning of 'Buddha'? The Daoist replied, "'Buddha' means awakening. It refers to awakening to heaven and awakening to earth, awakening to the yin and awakening to the yang, and awakening to benevolence and awakening to righteousness.
The monk said, "This is likely not so. That which is called awakening is self-awakening and [awakening others]."
His awakening and practice were perfected; because his three types of awakening were perfectly clear and bright, he was titled "Buddha" (Awakened One).

How could it be that he merely awakened to heaven and earth, yin and yang, benevolence (*ren*), and righteousness (*yi*)? The Emperor said to his attendants: "I previously knew that 'benevolence and righteousness' are the words of Confucius.
To claim that the Buddha awakened to benevolence and righteousness is an erroneous statement. The Daoist official then brought the *Shiji* and other historical texts...

Seeking to gain the upper hand, the Imperial Preceptor Paṇḍita Dharmapāla asked eight questions. He asked, "Does the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) contain the account of Laozi converting the barbarians?
The Master replied, "No. He asked again, "What scripture did Laozi transmit? The Master replied, "The *Daode jing*.
He asked, "Is there an account of converting the barbarians within the *Daode jing*? The Master replied, "No. He continued, "Since it is not in the *Shiji*, nor is it in the *Daode jing*..."
Furthermore, it is absent within [the scriptures]. It is thus evident that it is a fabrication and a falsehood. Yao Shu, the Minister of State, said: "The Way has been betrayed.

His Majesty’s command was to inflict punishment according to the agreement. We, your subjects Pan and others, have heard that the Laozi’s practice of the Way takes purity and stillness as its primary principle and non-action as its foundation.
He dwells in humility and modesty, and practices self-effacement to remain below others; he possesses no greed, desire, or love for victory.

Subsequently, its branches and sub-sects proliferated, and its followers grew increasingly numerous. As errors were inherited and falsehoods established, a hundred forms of boastful exaggeration emerged.
What was once pure underwent a transformation into filth; what was once non-action underwent a transformation into doing everything.

Indeed, the teaching of Śākyamuni is vast, expansive, and supreme, beyond comparison with other doctrines. Throughout a thousand or ten thousand generations, it has been honored by sage emperors and enlightened kings.
There are none who do not revere and honor him. To the east, he extends beyond the Fusang tree; to the west, he reaches the limits of the Meigu valley.

From the icy heavens and the cinnamon seas, across mountains, rivers, and the great earth—including insects, plants, and trees, and all beings of the hundred thousand myriad kinds born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, whether sentient or insentient—all rely upon the Buddha’s protective shade.
All that lives, moves, and rests between heaven and earth finds that, throughout all above and below, only the Buddha is most honored.
He transcends the realm of conditioned existence and returns to the ultimate truth of non-obstruction. His wisdom pervades the three realms; his spiritual power is wondrous throughout all directions.

Its benefits extend throughout the great trichiliocosm, yet its efficacy remains without a presiding agent; such is the magnitude of its greatness. Wherever the compassionate vessel reaches, no one who is drowning is left unassisted;

wherever the rain of Dharma falls, all living beings are moistened. We, the subjects Pan and others, respectfully record this so that those who study the teachings of Laozi may be alerted thereby. (From the *Tongzai*)
Cheng Wenhai (Wenhai). His courtesy name was Jufu. He avoided the taboo name of Emperor Wu, hence he was known by his courtesy name. He styled himself Xuelou (Snow Tower).

During the reign of Emperor Renzong, the Zhan... was established.
The Hall of the Sandalwood Image. Ju-fu composed its record, which states in brief: "The Way has no form, yet the author of the *I Ching* necessarily modeled it upon physical appearances.

Lin entrusted the śarīra to be distributed among both ordinary beings and sages; the thousand-spoked wheel of his walking traces remains constant through antiquity and the present.
This was not a display of supernatural powers within illusory realms, but rather the actual opening of expedient means at the ferry-crossing of delusion.

How could it be that it chooses its location for acceptance? It is simply because it responds according to conditions. When one gazes at plum trees to quench thirst, there is no one who does not look upon them with the same intent;

when one floats bamboo leaves to speak of returning home, who is there capable of sharing the journey? Only our Sagely Son of Heaven has reached a level of realization that surpasses the former sages.

To the Compassionate, Perfectly Enlightened Sovereign: May you live long through the years and seasons, eternally dwelling in the Buddha-land; may you aspire to the time of the Tathāgata, sitting and observing the realms of humans and devas.
Thus, he commanded Li Kan, Grand Master of the College of the Worthies, and the venerable elders of the Chan school to record its origins and details.

in the eighth year, the *xīnmǎo* year, he thought to repay his mother’s kindness and ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for her. King of Udyāna, from himself...

The image leaped into the air and bowed its head toward the Buddha. The Buddha stroked its head and bestowed a prophecy upon it, saying: "A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, you shall..."
It has brought vast benefit to humans and devas in China. Thus, this auspicious image remained in the Western Regions for one thousand two hundred and eighty-five years;

He resided in Bianliang for one hundred and seventy-six years; he lived in the present-day Sheng'an Temple in Yanjing (Beijing) for twelve years;

In the third month of the Dingshu year of the Great Yuan, the palace in Yan was struck by fire. The Minister Shima Gong welcomed [the image] back to Sheng’an Temple, where it has resided for fifty-nine years now.

In the twelfth year of the Zhiyuan era of Emperor Shizu, four high officials including Boluo were dispatched to prepare a ceremonial procession with guards and musical performances to welcome [the image] to Renzhi Hall on Mount Wanshou, where the Great Sage was enshrined.
In the twenty-sixth year [of the reign], the image was enshrined from Renzhi Hall in the rear hall of Wannansi Temple.

Emperor Shizu personally attended and performed great Buddhist rites. Calculating from the year the image was commissioned by King Wuyuan until the third year of the Yanyou era, a total of two thousand three hundred and seven years have passed (etc.).
The sages of antiquity taught the people to honor their ancestors and remember the distant past.

Regarding the Way of Repaying the Fundamental Source, within the rites of sacrifice, the tablet of wood serves as the representative in the ancestral temple, while a descendant serves as the *shī* (corpse-substitute) during the ritual.
