Is this not perhaps derived from the customs of the Western Regions? Now, the Buddha is the Honored One of both the mundane and supramundane realms;

what need is there to praise or describe him? Nevertheless, to truly know the Buddha as the Buddha, it certainly does not reside in his physical form, much less in that which merely resembles his physical form.
Yet, if one does not seek him through such resemblances, there will likewise be no place to turn.
Because of this heart of devotion, the formless Dharma-body must rely on forms to manifest its truth;

the ultimate Way transcends words, yet one ascends to its subtlety by means of words. If one remains earnest and mindful even toward that which is coarse, then one’s progress will likely approach the ideal.
For even with the hardness of metal and stone, one cannot guarantee that they will endure forever; now, with...

A single piece of wood has endured for such a long duration. Yet, while the Buddha’s own protection was indeed most thorough, how could human preservation have been achieved by the efforts of a single hand or foot alone?
Alas! Tracing back more than two thousand years, it was only upon reaching Your Majesty that the virtuous edict was issued to record these great achievements;
this was not due to any delay, but rather because of the flourishing and enlightened governance.
It was only upon reaching this point that [the practice] truly flourished; even beyond the formal sacrificial rites, it was invariably embellished with these literary expressions.
Thus, the gradual permeation of this transformation was vast—was this not magnificent? (Tongzai)
Zhao Mengfu, style name Ziyang, was a native of Wuxing. He was a descendant of Prince Qin De-fang, the son of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty.

In the twenty-third year of the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, Cheng Jucheng, the Censor-in-Chief of the Provincial Administration Commission, received an imperial decree to search for and recruit men of hidden talent. At that time—
The Southland obtained Mengfu; he was brought in for an audience. Mengfu’s talent and spirit were brilliant and transcendent, his divine countenance radiant as if he were a man among the immortals.
Emperor Shizu looked upon him with delight and seated him above Ye Li, the Right Vice-President of the Secretariat.

Some remarked that Mengfu was a scion of the Song imperial clan and should not be permitted to stay near the emperor's person, but the Emperor would not listen. He served in successive offices until he reached the rank of Hanlin Academician.
Shi received his imperial edicts. He passed away in the sixth month of the first year of Zhizhi (1321) at the age of sixty-nine.

He was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Wei and granted the posthumous title Wenmin (Yuan Shi). When Mengfu was four or five years old, he heard Lady Qiu describe her dream of a monk entering their bedchamber during her pregnancy;
upon waking, Mengfu was born. Consequently, from the age of eleven or twelve, he already delighted in copying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Later...
Whenever he spoke with the monks, they immediately treated him as if he were a member of their own family. This has continued until now, for sixty-five years.

Amidst the daily bustle of worldly affairs, he has been unable to achieve any profound realization or penetration, and he constantly sighs over this himself (referring to his preface to the *Huayan jing hebu*). Qiu Mingfu deeply revered the Way of Zhongfeng of Tianmu;
whenever he received a letter from the Master, he would invariably burn incense and bow toward it, and in his replies to the Master, he always referred to himself as a "younger brother."

The Master’s disciple, Duke [Zhang], was appointed as the Intendant of Confucian Studies for Jiangzhe. He sought the essential points of the Master’s mind, and the Master explained for him the principle of guarding the emotions and restoring one's nature.

Later, when the Duke entered the Hanlin Academy, he again sent a messenger to inquire about the general meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master replied with a single scroll titled *A Brief Exposition of its Meaning*.
Whenever the Duke saw a composition by the Master, he would invariably transcribe it by hand; he also painted a portrait of the Master to present to his fellow practitioners.

[Extensive Record]. Zhongfeng has one hundred and eight verses of exhortation for the cultivation of Pure Land practice. Mengfu composed a eulogy stating: "The Verses on the Pure Land were composed by Master Zhongfeng.
There are one hundred and eight verses, corresponding to one full cycle of a prayer bead rosary.
Out of pity for sentient beings wandering on mistaken paths, he describes the Buddha-realm of Ultimate Bliss; sometimes he drives them toward it, and sometimes he..."
They are enticed and led forward; yet when they arrive, they are one and the same. The disciple Zhao Mengfu, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Within the trichiliocosm, among sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each and every being is a Buddha, and each and every mind is the Pure Land. Yet, from beginningless time, all these sentient beings—due to...

Delusion, craving, and desire increase the turbidity of affection; the senses, objects, and fetters stain them so that one does not realize it for oneself. Thus, one wanders through birth and death and falls into the evil realms.

My teacher, the Great Monk Zhongfeng, out of compassion and pity for all sentient beings, earnestly composed these one hundred and eight verses to universally inform all sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Such is the piercing pain of suffering from illness and the like; if a person relies upon what the teacher has [taught]...
Instructing and exhorting: In every single thought-moment, be mindful of that Amitābha; having finished each thought-moment of mindfulness, remain in non-thought.
One will naturally be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Amitābha Buddha will come to receive and guide them, so that they sit directly upon a golden lotus pedestal.
The lotuses in the pond are like chariot wheels; a gentle breeze blows their fragrance throughout the Dharma-realm. Kalaviṅkas, śārikas, and parrots, along with white cranes—
Peacocks broadcast wondrous sounds; upon the golden realm’s pathways stand trees of the seven jewels. Seated in tranquil repose, he enjoys this supreme and exquisite bliss.
All evil and miserable realms have ceased to exist; all have been delivered by my Teacher. Yet, in truth, there is no sentient being who has been delivered by my Teacher.
"Since it is through the purity of the minds of sentient beings that the Buddha-land is pure, I now prostrate in homage.
I again praise the great vows of my Teacher" (as recorded in the *Guǎnglù* and the *Běnjí*).
Yuan Yue (style name:
Bochang), a native of Siming, was recommended for the position of Archivist at the Court of Imperial History by Yan Fu, Cheng Wenhai, and Wang Gou at the beginning of the Dade era.
He rose through the ranks to serve as Academician and Lecturer at the Hanlin Academy. His posthumous title was Wenqing. He authored the Qingrong ji.

While traveling through the world, he composed the *Preface to the Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules for the Chan Forest), which states in brief: "The teachings of Śākyamuni are divided into three schools.
Those who do not dare to transgress even a single precept in their movements and daily activities constitute the Vinaya school. The study of Bodhidharma is not so;

it seeks to discipline oneself beyond the constraints of rules, casting off the physical frame and discarding formal boundaries, such that those who merely observe conventional propriety are unable to participate."

Yet, his actions followed his heart without overstepping the boundaries of propriety, ultimately harmonizing with the natural order. This, then, is the efficacy of cultivating one's nature (*shanxing*):
by briefly setting aside external matters to regulate the internal, it is here that this principle is made manifest.

Even when lust and anger are both termed "the Way," the Great Hero (the Buddha) employed these as expedient metaphors intended for those of superior intelligence; the foolish, failing to discern this, take them all to be [literal truth] for themselves.

[This state of] license causes those who teach [the Dharma] to worry. Consequently, they established monastic regulations (*qinggui*) and devised various preventative measures (as detailed in the text).

The Stele Inscription of Huayan Monastery states: "The Great Hero said: 'Nature is fundamentally and supremely good; it is transformed by following desires. Desires arise from delusion.'"* *Note: The original Chinese text contains a lacuna indicated by "云云" (yún yún), which signifies that the full passage has been omitted. The provided excerpt ends with the citation from the Huayan Monastery Stele.*
One's nature becomes increasingly obscured; thus, one becomes entangled with things and subject to transformations.

When this reaches the point of turbulent agitation and pervasive entanglement such that life and death can no longer be distinguished, there arise the doctrines of repentance and resolution, and the doctrines of posthumous veneration.

If one can thereby sever attachment to life and detach from death, then the fundamental nature will be profoundly empty and free from defilement or burden. How could the Way then be afflicted? Thus says the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: [The text continues with the citation: "With words..."
Wealth and nobility serve as metaphors; it concludes with the return to truth and the restoration to the primordial state.

This enables those whom the world admires to enter through sensory objects and awaken by means of sensory objects, thereby entering the signless (*animitta*). Thus, these metaphors possess profound significance.
In the *Biographical Account of Master Cizhao* composed by the monk E, it is briefly stated: "The words of the Buddha are vast and expansive; there are those who have translated and refined them..."

It is like the dark sacrificial wine (*xuánjiǔ*) manifesting its sincerity; it is as if hidden behind a plain inner garment (*chóngyī*), concealing its adornments. Its marvelous features are displayed and its mysteries revealed;

whether great or small, direct or winding, each fulfills its proper function. This accords with the words of the Confucian scholars and transmits a message of eternal truth beyond doubt. (From *Qīngróng jí*)

Yu Ji, styled Bosheng, was the fifth-generation descendant of Yu Yunwen, the Chancellor of the Song dynasty. His ancestors were originally from Sichuan. His father, Yu Ji, served as the Magistrate of Huanggang during the Song;
after the fall of the Song, he resided temporarily in Chongren, Linchuan. It was at the beginning of the Dade era that he first arrived in the capital. Because... [text continues]
His subjects recommended him for the appointment of Professor of Confucian Studies at the Capital Academy. He was subsequently appointed Assistant Instructor at the National University.

From the rank of Jiangshilang, he advanced through twelve promotions to the title of Tongfeng Dafu. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Renshou County and posthumously granted the honorific title Wenzheng.

He once cleared out a side chamber and inscribed upon it the poem of Shao Yaofu, titling it "Shao'an"; thus, the world came to know him as Master Shao'an. Whenever he received practitioners from outside the secular world, he would invariably inquire [of their spiritual attainments].
He refuted their arguments, asserting that because the teachings of the sages were not clearly understood, scholars had no fixed standard to rely upon.

If one cannot gain deep insight into the distinctions and similarities between our Way and heterodox doctrines, yet seeks to surreptitiously investigate the origin of nature and destiny (*xing-ming*) and the causes of life and death, it is certain they will fail to achieve a decisive realization and return [to the truth] (from the *Yuanshi*). He once said: "The Buddha [takes] causality..."
The two laws of fruition subdue and win the hearts of the people of the world; whether one is wise or foolish, noble or base, none can escape these two characters.
In composing the epitaph for Master Jianjian, it is said: "Since ancient times, extraordinary and eminent men have perhaps appeared only once in many generations.
Why is it that such figures do not constantly appear in the world? I have heard it said: how could there not be [such men]?"

Such a person indeed! Amidst the profound obscurity of worldly affairs and the entanglements of conventional learning, there were those for whom these things were insufficient to captivate or detain them.

Thus, they cast themselves off, emerging from the realm of floating and sinking, arising and ceasing, to seek that which is the ultimate state of primordial beginning—such were all of these individuals.
As the epitaph for Master Huixi states: "Hearing of the Buddha..."
As for the lineage of this Master: those who practice *dhyāna* take awakening as their standard in guiding others. They ensure that one reaches a state beyond the reach of discursive thought;

when the time is ripe and the conditions respond, they decisively open the way for realization. Thus, words are uttered and meaning is understood; once understanding is realized, words vanish and are forgotten.

This is what is meant by "not establishing written words. How could this be a deception? As it is briefly stated in the *Zan lüeyu shuilù yuánqǐ*: [The text continues with the verses on the water and land origins.]
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, just as a mani jewel manifests the five colors according to conditions.

How is it that through successive kalpas, consciousness and karma act as causes for one another, and ignorance revolves through the cycle of birth and death via the faculties and their objects? Out of compassion, our Buddha bestows the power of skillful means.

Just as a great king of physicians cures chronic ailments, gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, light to those in darkness, and coolness to those tormented by heat—how much more so for you who wander through the six realms of existence, suffering according to your karma; without relying on the Buddha’s grace, by what means could you purify yourselves?
The Inscription on the Bell of Bao Guo Temple in Hangzhou states: "By the power of my great vow of compassion, I employ this great sound to perform the work of a Buddha.
It fills all of space, its essence unimpeded; wherever there is an interval, it awakens beings to liberation.
For humans, devas, dragons, and the ocean—without end or limit—for those of the past, future, and present, all who are encompassed by this single sound are made equal and identical to my own reward."
Guo Ruobao was a Buddha-like being who dwelt forever in steadfastness to proclaim the wondrous Dharma (*Sha’uan ji*).

Jiesi Jiesi, whose courtesy name was Manxiang, was a native of Fuzhou in Longxing. At the beginning of the Dade era, he was promoted to the rank of Shoujinglang (Court Official for the Transmission of Scriptures). He held office successively...

He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yuzhang County and posthumously granted the title Wen’an (Wen’an). He once composed a preface to the *Zhongfeng Guanglu* (Extensive Record of Mount Zhongfeng), which states in brief:

"The cultivation and growth of the monastic community must be carried out according to the Way. If one does not follow the Way, yet instead seeks profit, comfort, and sustenance, succumbing to greed, desire, anger, and hatred..."
Anger—these are all merely axes for felling the forest and frost or sleet that brings down the harvest.

As for elucidating the Dharma, one must necessarily cause speech to cease and reliance on intellectual understanding to be severed; only when one practices true practice and attains actual realization can it be called the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-lineage.
Its refinement is stable and profound, its examination and discernment are precise and clear, leaving nothing to the imagination.
Borrowing [from others], there is no turning back or compromise; it is truly formidable, as awe-inspiring as scorching sun and biting frost.

As for its awakening and exalting [the spirit], it is like the four great rivers and their myriad tributaries—winding through thousands of turns and ten thousand bends, surging over mountains and crashing against rocks, never ceasing until they reach the sea.
Such is the manifestation of its great capacity and great function within the written word (from the *Guanglu* and the *Yuan Shi*).
Feng Zizhen was a native of Youzhou. He styled himself the Layman Haixu. His brilliance and talent were roughly equal to those of Chen Gangzhong, whom Gangzhong held in deep awe.

When his wine had reached its peak and his ears were warm with excitement, he commanded two or three attendants to prepare his brushes for ink, waiting for Zizhen to write rapidly so that it would be finished in an instant according to the number of sheets of paper (from the *Yuanshi*).
He once composed one hundred poems on the plum blossom (*meihua*) to present to Master Zhongfeng.
Furthermore, he composed for Zhongfeng a hymn and eulogy for the Pure Land, along with a preface, titled: "The One Hundred and Eight Hymns on the Pure Land by the Chan Practitioner Huanzhu."

Regarding the counting of beads for the rosary: if a person recites the name of Amitābha in every thought-moment—just as the various worthies of the Jin and Tang dynasties, such as Liu Yimin and Bai Xiangshan, jointly participated in the Pure Land Society—this person will obtain immeasurable merit and shall immediately attain the manifestation of the Pure Land before them.
On the day they sit in silent meditation while holding the beads, there are one hundred and eight verses consisting of three thousand and twenty-four words.
"Originally, not a single word was ever spoken. At that time, the student of vows, Feng Zizhen, prostrated himself in homage and offered this eulogy:
"I observe Master Huanzhu: within illusion, he dwells nowhere. Though he does not dwell in illusion, he is able to awaken those who are like illusory people.
O illusory person, you should know: defilement and purity are relative. Though it is defiled, it is the very nature of purity—the Pure Land."

It should be manifested before one. Therefore, the Master of the Illusory Abode (Māyā-vihārin) expounds these verses on the Pure Land. Originally, there was no need to speak these verses; yet once spoken, they are many.
In his hand he holds the mechanism of the ancient Buddhas, its count equaling that of a rosary. When the Good Spiritual Friend observes them, he sees that these verses are not of this world.
Even if the ancient Buddhas were to appear, what they would say would be just like this. To awaken is to realize it through a single verse—hundred and eight.

The same applies to the gāthās. An ordinary person is deluded by a single gāthā; how much more so by one hundred and eight? Each gāthā consists of four lines, and in every line the meaning is fully revealed.
Though the number of characters exceeds three thousand, in reality there is not a single character. When one is deluded by the gāthās, they rotate the prayer beads;

when one awakens through the gāthās, they rotate the beads of mindfulness. If a person, within this context, is entirely without thought regarding each [character], then in the state of non-thought they recite the Buddha’s name—this is non-thought.
Nor is there any [other place]—with crimson nails, deep-blue hair coiled like a conch, and various marks such as the *ūrṇā-kośa* on the forehead.

Those with eyes who gaze upon him see his moon-like face shining like the sun’s orb and his four-colored lotus blossoms emitting subtle, wondrous, and pure fragrances; all those born there dwell in a pure land.
Why then seek the Western Quarter? Such people behold Amitābha and all attain peaceful dwelling.

Liu Guan, courtesy name Daochuan, was a native of Dongyang. He once served as a Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichang Boshi*). He composed a preface to the *Recorded Sayings of Master Zhuyuan Dao*, which states in brief:
"Chan has its mechanisms and military has its tactics; therefore, discussing Chan is like employing troops. One must reach the point of the guest [attacking]..."

The Master simultaneously confronted both the traces and their functions, causing them to vanish together; thereafter, he forgot the Dharma to realize the Dharma and forgot the mechanism to accord with the mechanism.

His supreme, wondrous, perfect, and luminous realization is beyond words. When the First Patriarch of Shaolin traveled eastward carrying the Way, he held that while the Buddhas of the three periods truly possess no dharma, they have never failed to embody the Dharma. The Way is not burdened by words, for words burden the Way. As it is said:

The teaching that one need not rely on words and letters to see one's nature and become a Buddha is intended to sweep away the emotional dust of manifold consciousnesses and to reveal the essential point for clarifying the mind;
it is not merely a means to correct the faults of those who compose treatises and act as masters with their flowery rhetoric and prolix discourse.
Huang Min (style name Jinjing) was a native of Yiwu, Wuzhou. He passed the jinshi examination in the second year of the Yanyou era and was appointed as the Vice Magistrate of Ninghai, Taizhou.
He rose through seven promotions from the rank of Jiangshilang to Zhongfeng Da Fu, and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiangxia, posthumously honored with the title Wen.

Xian. He had thirty-three volumes of the *Ri-sun-zhai-gao* (Drafts from the Daily Diminution Studio). Pu-ming, along with Ye-guan, Yu-jí, and Jie-xi-si, were known as the "Four Talents of the Scholarly Forest" (*Yuanshi*).

He once composed the "Record of Huqiu Temple," which states in brief: "Since the Buddhist teachings have spread throughout the Middle Kingdom, wherever the Dharma-banner has been erected, it has invariably been at a famous mountain of the world;
none of these have failed to be magnificently constructed with precious structures and splendid adornments."

It is situated to house the excellence of its geomantic form, intended to manifest that the sacred mountain has not yet dispersed, and to serve as a refuge for the great assembly, so that those who come may behold its appearance and give rise to faith.
Although the work of painting, dyeing, wood, and earth seems to involve conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*), such matters do not obstruct the underlying principle.
By following the principle, one accords with the practical task; this is the ground of pure awakening.

This is precisely the great monastery. When phenomena are integrated with reality, they return to the ultimate principle; even piling up earth and gathering sand all result in the attainment of Buddhahood.
Indeed, the characteristics of the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of all worlds have never existed outside the realm of mind and consciousness.

Were it not for riding upon the power of skillful means and sporting within that which is like an illusion, how could one possess such great adornment as the supreme cause for unsurpassed enlightenment?

Ah! This is the Epilogue to the Record of the Pagoda Cloister of Master Zhigong of Mount Jiang: "As for the Sage Master, acting as an emissary of the Tathāgata, he secretly assisted the machinery of transformation;
riding upon skillful means, he manifested birth, and employing supernatural powers, he gathered and guided the multitudes."

Inconceivable matters are indeed beyond the capacity of ordinary sentiment to measure (from the *Benji*). Here, the Venerable One inscribed his hermitage as "Rest" (*xi*), and Lord Gong composed an inscription for it, saying:
"If one says the hermitage is not the person, who would be burdened by its name? If one says the person is not the hermitage, with what would the name entangle him?
That which rests is the environment; that which is able to rest is wisdom. Is it the hermitage or the person? The dependent and the primary are non-dual. [End of] *Chā*.
At that moment, subject and object are both forgotten; how short are ten lands, and how long is a single breath?
Do not grow weary and stop halfway. To leave this grass hut is not your dwelling place.

Hu Changru (Changru), courtesy name Jizhong, style name Shidang, was a native of Yongkang. He served as the Assistant Magistrate of Ninghai and later resided in Wulin, where he passed away while seated in meditation.
He once constructed a study named Yanle (The Joy of Yan Hui) and associated with Zhao Mengfu, Han Mingshan, Duan Jifu, and Guo Sidao.
The gentlemen discussed the Way within the Hall of Rectification. Ji Zhong had once composed the "Treatise on Great Unity," which stated:

"One thousand four hundred years after the passing of Mencius, the Way became submerged and its transmission was severed. Only with the emergence of Master Zhou did that which was submerged shine forth again and that which was severed be restored.
The two sons of the Cheng family of Henan received the transmission of Master Zhou; the transmission of Master Zhou originated from Zhuanggu."
Chan Master Shouya of Zhulin Monastery was four generations removed from Chengzi before reaching Zhu Xi, the Duke of Wen.
After the Duke, Zhang Qinfu investigated this Way and only then realized its point of liberation, saying:
"What I heard at Zhulin the other day, which I had not yet reconciled with, has not deceived me after all. It turns out that this matter is ten parts identical to Chan learning."
They are similar in that those who study do not know Chan, and those who practice Chan do not know study; they strike at one another without ever piercing the core of the ailment.
This is truly laughable (as discussed in the *Dàtóng lùn*).
Han Xingxing, courtesy name Mingshan, was a native of Shanyin. He was the eighth-generation descendant of Han Qi, Duke Zhongxian of Wei. He lived in seclusion and did not serve in office;

he was posthumously titled Duke Zhuangjie. He was thoroughly versed in the classics and histories and possessed a profound mastery of the Buddhist scriptures (*nèidiǎn*). He once remarked: "The Buddha resides in the Western lands; his customs and teachings..."

There is indeed a difference. Yet, they are exceptionally capable of exhorting and transforming others. I observe that among people today, there is no one who performs Buddhist rites without first rectifying their mind and maintaining right mindfulness.

Even the most ignorant men and women, when wishing to hear the sutras or worship images, invariably prepare themselves through fasting and purification (*upavāsa*), maintaining reverence and casting off worldly desires before engaging in the practice.
Even if our Sage were to be reborn today, his exhortations for people to do good would not exceed this.
This, I fear, is likely beyond our current capacity. I once said to Zhu Zhonghong, a disciple of Yanlezhai: "The Buddha passed away long ago;
yet later generations treat him with such reverence and recite his words. Do you think the Buddha intended for people to act this way? Did he teach them to do so?
If one were to force others to follow oneself, who would be willing to comply? People nowadays..."
Even a single phrase or essential teaching uttered by him could not be contained within a single village; how much more so, then, are the words of the Buddha, which extend for many millions of *li*.
Everywhere the light of the sun and moon reaches, all are converted and brought to faith. Hearing this, Zhonghong remained silent.

He then composed the "Preface to the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* Commentary on Aiding Manifestation," stating: "The Hero of the World appeared to benefit the world, universally rescuing the deluded masses according to their capacities."

It establishes the teaching, shatters the two attachments to self and dharmas, dispels the two doubts regarding seeds and manifestations, opens the essential gate of the Mahāyāna, and reveals the general purport of the sūtras—is this not the Diamond Sūtra? Its words are profound and its intent subtle;
no discourse can exhaust it. It was truly through the Great Being entering the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* that he received the secret words of Tuṣita and transmitted them.
Devaputra assisted in the transmission of the holy teachings, translating the verses of the *Eighty-Verse Prajñāpāramitā* and severing twenty-seven kinds of doubt.

His internal discernment was crystal clear; it was as if all were unified under a single principle. As for his polishing of the phrasing and his commentaries on the sub-commentaries, their intent became manifest; through his exegesis of the sutras, the underlying principles were revealed.

His meanings were invariably rooted in the two treatises (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*), and his explanations consistently integrated the words of the various masters. Truly, he was a helper to the *Vajracchedikā*.
This work, titled *Xianhu* (Manifesting the Hidden), was composed by the Dharma Master Ding of Shanyin as an aid for manifesting [the truth]. Two hundred years have passed since then.

Now, Master Tong of Bieping has propagated the teachings and contemplations (*jiaogan*) and, having attained realization through this book, carved it at his chamber in Baolin Temple, requesting me to record its colophon.
Alas! One points to the finger to see the moon; once the moon is seen, one forgets the finger. One relies on the sutras to see the nature; once the nature is seen, [one transcends the words].

One may forget the sutras; yet even the sutras can be forgotten, how much more so their commentaries. Nevertheless, the written words do not depart from the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the exposition of the treatise is certainly not external to suchness (*tathatā*).
By comparing them according to the excellence of their merit, this work demonstrates the proper method for receiving and upholding [the teachings].

When the two emptinesses are perfected, one forever transcends the fault of abiding in signs (*nimitta*). May the fourfold assembly practice accordingly and together receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood.

Ouyang Xuan, courtesy name Yuangong, was a native of Jijun. He was successively promoted to Grand Master for Academic Petitions (Hanlin Xuexi Chenzhi), Minister of the Rank of Glorious Emolument (Ronglu Dafu), Director of the Office of Imperial Edicts (Zhizhigao), and concurrently Editor-in-Chief of the National History (Xiuguo Shi).
He was posthumously honored with the title Wen Gong. He once remarked: "Master Cheng loved to read Buddhist scriptures throughout his life; however..."
It does not equal the breadth of Zhu Xi’s learning nor his exhaustive investigation of similarities and differences. He composed the Stele Inscription for Master Tánfāng Zhōng, which states in brief:
"In the *Xìzhī* year (1321), the Master resided at Jiāngshān. On the twenty-fourth day of the first month of the *Yǐchǒu* year of Tàiding (1325), the Prince of Liáng arrived in Jiānkāng.
That evening, the temple was destroyed by fire. The following day, the Prince visited the temple and asked the Master, 'How shall we restore it?'"

"How is this? the King asked. The Master replied, "Fortunately, there is a great donor present. The following year, they cast a bell from bronze. The King offered a precious jewel for it to be melted in the furnace;

once completed, the jewel was brilliantly visible as an inscription upon the bell. When Emperor Wansui questioned the Master again, saying, "Since the temple has been destroyed, upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell?
the Master replied, "The Buddhas of antiquity have passed away, but the Buddhas of the present have returned. The King [was moved].
The King was greatly pleased. He once personally lifted a hoe to break ground and establish a foundation, providing the funds and entrusting the Master to build a Buddhist temple named Chongxi.
One day, he asked the Master, "What is meant by the 'coarse porridge of Jiang' mentioned by the monks?
The Master replied, "I thought Your Highness had forgotten. He asked again, "And what is meant by the 'three pairs of socks' mentioned by the monks? The Master replied:
Having traversed every mountain and river within the realm, today I have personally arrived at the palace of the Brahma King.

In the first year of the Zhihe era, the King ascended the Great Jewel Throne and changed the reign title to Tianli. He dispatched an envoy bearing incense to Mount Jiangshan to express gratitude to Master Baogong and to thank him for his efforts.

In the spring of the second year [of the reign], an envoy was dispatched to specifically confer upon the Master the title of *Dazhong Dafu* (Grand Officer of Central Magnitude), *Guangci Yuanwu Dacianshi* (Great Zen Master of Universal Compassion and Perfect Enlightenment), and the position of Abbot of Da Chongxi Wanshou Monastery, concurrently overseeing Jiangshan Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple.

In the second year of the Zhizheng era, the High Official Na Lin, the Director of the Xuanzheng Yuan, invited the Master to reside at Mount Jing. In the fifth year, by special imperial decree, the Master was appointed [to this office].

He resided at Dàlóngxiáng Jíqìng Temple. In the third month of the sixth year, he retired to Guǎngcí Hermitage. In the seventh month, the temple was destroyed by fire. The Master was struck with alarm;
mindful of the profound kindness of the late Emperor, he rose once more to take charge of the temple affairs. In the seventh year, the temple was completed. In the eighth year, he passed away.
His body was cremated, and the resulting *śarīra* relics were beyond counting (the inscription is not recorded here).

Deng Wenxuan, courtesy name Shanzhi, was a native of Basi. He served as a Hanlin Waitzhi (Attendant-Redactor) concurrently with the post of Bianxiu (Compiler) at the Guoshiyuan (Bureau of National History).
His posthumous title was Kangzhuang. He composed the "Epitaph for Master Gong of Shilin," which states: "The Way of the Buddha is neither existent nor empty; it is neither defiled..."
It is not pure; it is the school of the True Dharma. The laity are ignorant of its fundamental source, and their clamor and delusion overflow like turbulent waters.

Without a ferry or raft, how can those drowning be rescued? Words are the trap for the principle; once the principle is attained, the words are forgotten. If one clings to verbal explanations, the Great Way will become overgrown with brambles. Only Master Shilin was a preeminent figure of the Jetavana Grove.
With a single thought, his countenance shone brightly, and he thoroughly penetrated the myriad dharmas. There is fundamentally no dharma to be found; this is awakening.
For the sake of the deluded masses, he emerged through the wisdom of skillful means to act as a guiding teacher. With Mount Nan as its encircling screen, the Sun of Wisdom rests upon its summit.

Since the Master’s passing, the mountains have been empty and the clouds cold; yet the Master has not perished, for emptiness is devoid of arising and ceasing. This inscription is engraved upon the mountain slopes to clearly manifest [his legacy] to future sages.
Zhang Zhu (also written as Zhù), courtesy name Zhongju, style name Tui’an, was enfeoffed as Duke of Lù. He composed poems on twenty-three sites at Mount Heng;
here, only several stanzas are recorded. Regarding Banyue Temple, he wrote: "Banyue is a temple of the Southern Qi; it is the first station of Master Sī."

He cleared the space of the abbot’s quarters and sat firmly to sever the cycle of rebirth. In palm-leaf volumes, he gathered the sutras; like the *tandava* flower, he scattered them across the dharma assembly.

The mountain spirits must surely come night after night to pay homage before the Buddha-lamp. One day, while seated upon the cliff, he said: "Beneath this sacred peak of the First Stage, I have returned once more to preach the sutras.
The deities responded by joining their palms in reception; even the rocks nodded their heads to listen. Clouds and cranes followed his flying alms-bowl as he crossed the lake.

The dragon entered the pure vase; to this day, where the flowers fell, a single lamp shines eternally in its green light. The inscription on the second stupa reads: "The temple was ancient from a former dynasty;
the karmic traces of the mountain forest are now empty. The Dharma-body is without illusion or decay; the enshrined bones possess their own spiritual powers.
The precious offerings are coral and azure; the pearl-light of the śarīra is crimson. With no other cause, may this single incense offering be dedicated within the Buddha hall. The third life.

The Master said: "At the place where the divine monk entered nirvana, how could there be past, present, or future? I still remember the Stone of Three Lives; its heart, though ten thousand ages old, is difficult to grind away.

The earth buries the ancient Chan temple; the mountains shroud the deep mountain shrine. On long days, the bells and chants are idle; the maples and cassias rustle in the wind. Regarding the Stone of Settled Mind:
"When sitting in meditation, a hundred thoughts cease; within the square inch of the heart, all is profound stillness. As for appearances, there is no distinction between self and other."
Having already judged the true and the stubborn through the realization of emptiness, the *chimei* (goblins) come to test me; the *cūḍapanthaka* has departed and does not return.

Following others’ laughter at this deluded monk, I gaze upon the mountains throughout the long days. At the Zhuanjing Pavilion, it is said: "Since the time of the First Patriarch of Caoxi, many sages have appeared on Mount Heng."
The lamp of the lineage has been transmitted; the secret seal is passed on. The sound of the Dharma resonates through the myriad pipes of the wind;

the nature of Chan shines like the moon in the sky. Cherish the parable of polishing the brick; the subtle faculty must explain itself. Dahui’s Pagoda: This is the place where Dahui expounded the sutras. The grove was originally that of Anāthapiṇḍada.
He carved into the clouds to enshrine the śarīra; he spurred the stones to raise the stupa. The wind-bells occasionally ring amidst the silence. The heavens...
The lamp suddenly flickered on and off. Whenever the śramaṇa came here, he would circumambulate it three times and recite "Namo.
Yang Weizhen—whose courtesy name was Lianfu—was a native of Zhuji in Yue. During the Taiding era, he attained eminence through his mastery of the *Hongci* (Grand Prose) style and profound learning.

He was appointed to the Office of Examinations and sent to Tiantai. Through successive promotions, he reached the post of School Superintendent for Jiangxi, where he was proficient in all five classics.
In his later years, he resided in Wusong, where he constructed the Penglai Xuan Ge (Peach Blossom Terrace Mysterious Pavilion) outside the eastern gate of Hecheng.

There, he gave himself over to literary pursuits, living with carefree indifference amidst the Nine Peaks and Three Lakes. He once composed the "Record of the Image of Mahākaruṇā Bodhisattva," stating: "The Abbot of Chexi Guangfu Temple..."
The monk Zhuyin Daoshi obtained a sacred wooden plank measuring three feet and six inches from beneath the ancient shrine of Zhang Qian.
Its substance was as hard as stone, its color a deep violet-blue, and its grain formed patterns like golden threads. When burned, it emitted a fragrance like that of cypress.

The Master commissioned a carver to fashion it into an image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. He entrusted this task to his friend Xun, who then sought my assistance for the inscription. Formerly, at Chengdu Fa... [text continues]
Master Minxing fashioned an image of the Thousand Hands and Eyes from great sandalwood and sought a preface from the Daoist Master Dongpo. The Daoist Master said:
"The reason for doing so is to speak in terms of a single hair and a single pore. It is said that by lifting a single hair, the head moves with it;
by plucking a single pore, the body changes with it. A hair is simply a pore. The Daoist Master’s metaphor was excessive.
Furthermore, while ordinary people cannot simultaneously employ both hands, both feet, both eyes, or both ears, the Bodhisattva responds to them all without confusion;
thus, the wise person likewise employs five faculties at once. There are even performers who can smile and weep on different sides of their face at the same time.

If one causes a Bodhisattva to divide his hands into separate entities for the purpose of grasping, and within that grasping further divides the instruments into movement and stillness, there are certain capacities that are simply impossible to achieve.
If such a performer considers himself superior to the Buddha-dharma, then how could the Buddha-dharma possibly be considered supernatural?
Now, if a single hair is plucked, the head feels pain; yet if a single hair is burned, the hair itself never feels pain. If a fingernail is shaken, the finger [feels it].
As for this pain: if one cuts a fingernail, the nail itself never feels pain. Why is this? I have put this to the Bodhisattvas, yet even the Bodhisattvas could not provide an analogy for me;
thus, the capacity of practitioners to respond through their teachings has reached its limit. Your Master is as wise in letters as the ancient Qisong;
if you are likewise wise in the Way, I venture to pose this question to you. The verse says: "If Yu had not caused the waters to flow westward, Ji..."

Millet does not grow in winter; there are things that can and things that cannot. All things have their fixed places: the *gonglue* (a type of wasp) incants and becomes a *ming* (grain moth), while the dung beetle embraces and becomes a cicada.
When the transformation of things occurs in this way, why should the Buddha not be so? The rhinoceros gazes at the moon, and its horn contains the lunar brilliance;

the elephant hears the thunder, and its tusks produce the "thunder-flower. When the resonance of things occurs in this way, why should I not be so? One who is moved by things and transforms things is a great disciple of the Buddha.

Su Dainian (Sū Dànián), courtesy name Chānglíng (Chānglíng), style name Xījìan Jūshì (Xījìan Layman), was a native of Yangzhou. He once composed a preface to the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Zhòngfāng Lún, which states in brief:
"In the past, at Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa smiled when the flower was held up; at Shaolin, the Second Patriarch attained peace while facing the wall."
The Mind: Is it not the one stroke revealed upon the crown of the head? This is what is called the "special transmission outside the teachings.
Since the time of Caoxi, the lineage has branched and divided; some used the staff, some the shout, some held up a pitchfork, and some raised a finger.
Although these functional expressions differ from one another, in pointing students toward a secret resonance with the direct source, they are one and the same. —Fengtai.

Master Zhongfang Lun had, in his early years, traveled extensively to study under various spiritual teachers (*kṣāntika*). His practice was steady and profound, and his realization was precise and authentic.

Upon attaining the status of a seated master and donning the formal robes, he became an object of veneration for monastics from all quarters. Observing his expositions of the Dharma, one sees that his insight was clear and penetrating;
he caused students to utterly abandon their "thieving minds" (*tōushin*), ensuring that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity would not fall into decline. His...
In the realm of religion, how could this be considered a minor contribution?
This is the postscript to the re-edited and re-carved *Fófǎ Jīntāng Biān* (The Golden Wall and Moat of the Buddha-Dharma),
Volume Sixteen, compiled by the Tiantai monk Ruxing.
After my teacher, the Venerable Xiangxian Qing, had entered into the stillness of parinirvāṇa, he once reviewed this compilation with great care.
One day, he showed it to me, saying: "The Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Mahākāśyapa, and the Buddha-dharma to kings and ministers.
This was because, were it not for the disciples' internal succession, where could the life-force of wisdom be entrusted? And were it not for kings and ministers as external guardians..."

If [the teachings] are not protected, then the Dharma will decline. Therefore, since the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, sagacious rulers and worthy ministers have not failed the entrustment.
This is why Master Tai (Dao’an) compiled this collection. I wished to put it into practice but did not succeed; you, sir, ought to undertake it.
In the winter of the Wuxu year of the Wanli era, while traveling in Yunjian, I met with Lord Lu (Zhongbo), Official Yuan (Bibu), Censor-in-Chief Yu (Qianxian), and fellow provincial jinshi.

The dukes Qian and Jiang deliberated upon the restoration of the "Golden Fortifications" (the essential defenses) of our illustrious dynasty for inclusion in the *Tongkao* (Comprehensive Examination). Recalling the aspirations of their predecessors, they subsequently planned to publish the original compilation as a pioneering guide for those seeking out lost fragments from all quarters.
Some, however, raised doubts, saying: "The world is well-acquainted with the tireless efforts of Han Yu and Zhu Xi to exclude [certain works]."
I have now included it fully within this compilation. Why? I replied: "Not so. I have heard that the five flavors complement one another to form harmony;
thus, the Way of the Xia, Yu, and Tang dynasties was not abandoned. Alas! If one earnestly seeks what is correct, then even rejection and slander may serve as a profound means of elucidation.
The Buddha-dharma is majestic, filling heaven and earth and spanning past and present; the more time passes, the more its light shines. Thus we know that [it must be protected]."
As for the power of those who uphold the Dharma, how can one know that this is not simply the mutual reinforcement of those who revile the Dharma?

The Preface to the Holy Teachings serves as a golden wall; the Memorandum on the Buddha’s Relics is likewise a golden wall. The Treatise on Protecting the Dharma serves as a boiling moat; the Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha is likewise a boiling moat.
This is why Han Yu and Zhu Xi initially condemned it, yet ultimately were compelled to affirm it; they feigned opposition in the light while secretly supporting it in the dark. I know this.
It cannot escape outside the Buddha-nature. Alas! Were it not for the three Wu emperors, who would have known that the Sangha could not be extinguished?
Were it not for Han Yu and Zhu Xi, who would have known that the Teaching could not be abolished?
Reaching our Ming Taizu, the August Emperor Gao, divinely gifted with sagehood and spirit, he propagated the Mahāyāna vehicle; for two hundred years, how magnificent has this been!
Yet, there are occasionally one or two who, having gathered up the remnants of the spittle left by Han Yu and Zhu Xi, engage in idle mutual vituperation.

How is this different from the sun and moon having already risen, while people remain in darkness and confusion, unable to distinguish them? Will they not be held in perpetual derision by those of great capacity? Alas!
Master Tai’s heart is truly diligent; advancing, it may broaden the profound breast of the wise, and retreating, it may dissolve the verbal karma of those bound by narrow-mindedness.
The spirit is immersed in the palm-leaf manuscripts; the dragon roars from the withered tree. Only then does one come to know that the ancient sovereign and the Sage possess but one tongue:
neither censure can diminish them, nor praise can augment them. Formerly, on Vulture Peak, eighty thousand bodhisattvas vowed to protect and uphold [the Dharma]. The World-Honored One declared:
"I have sixty thousand bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who shall protect and uphold my Dharma after my parinirvāṇa. If these were to be compiled...
Are these not the manifestations of sagely sovereigns, worthy ministers, renowned scholars, and eminent sages? Are they not those who, by the power of their vows, act as envoys of the Tathāgata?
In the summer month of the Gengzi year, on the anniversary of the Buddha’s descent into the world, the carving was completed.
Originally ten fascicles, it is now divided into sixteen fascicles. I have presumptuously inscribed this at the end of the tablets to record it.
This is all that can be said of the years.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Ruxing of Ciyun Chan Monastery on Mount Tiantai.
